en: May the speech of Śrīmad-Vidyācakravartin— composed as the commentary named *Saṃjīvanī*, which illuminates the universe through its own expansions consisting of genus, quality, and so forth, enriched with the excellence of refinement, and characterized by simple composition— protect me.
This commentary, titled *Saṃjīvinī*, is being composed by Śrī Vidyācakravartin upon the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, which was first conceived by Ācārya Rucaka.
The author of this work has provided only a portion of the examples here regarding *dhvani*; I shall complete it with my own verses, which are consistent with his principles.
May poets who are devoted to the doctrine of *dhvani*, having examined my commentary with subtle scrutiny,
even if they are already conscious [of its merit], further expand the empire of literature (*sāhitya*).
What is the use of such extensive detail? If some dull-witted person should find fault with this *Saṃjīvinī* commentary, he is merely finding fault with his own lack of learning.

In this regard, prefacing it with a salutation to his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) who is the presiding authority, he declares the subject matter to be expounded in this treatise by saying, "Having paid homage to the Supreme...
Indeed, all speech is measured by four stages: Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī;
as the Śruti says: "Speech is measured in four quarters," and so forth.
In this context, that which is called *parā* is form without substrate (*nirupadhika*).
The three beginning with *paśyantī*, however, are with substrate (*aupādhika*) because of their grossness; they stand in the place of a physical body (*vigraha*).
As the scripture says:
The supreme, non-departing Speech is the light of one's own true nature within;
when that [nature] is perceived, the authority of the three [states] ceases.
Indivisible from the phonemes, with its sequential order entirely withdrawn,
Paśyantī rests upon the vital breath and is like the fluid within a peacock’s egg.
The middle [speech], which is grasped by the intellect and assumes a fixed form of phonemes, consists of internal discourse; it does not reach the ear.
Manifested through the activity of the palate and lips, revealing the understanding of others,
and easily accessible to all human beings, this is considered the external *vaikharī* speech.
Thus [it is said].
In this context, with respect to the triad of supreme speech beginning with Paśyantī, the first is called Parā because it is the eldest;
the second is Paśyantī because it is oriented toward the universe;
and the third is Madhyamā because it is neither internal nor external, being situated in the middle.
The fourth [speech] is *vaikharī*, so called because it proceeds for the purpose of awakening the dull-witted (*tupara*).

Alternatively, it should be understood that *vikhara* refers to the aggregate of the body and senses— wherein *kha* means pleasure and *akha* means pain— and *vaikharī* is that which exists therein (*tatra bhavā*), because it specifically bestows (*rāti*) those experiences.
Intending exactly this, it was said: "Speech, whose body is threefold," and also "fourfold. Of what nature is that Goddess?

The meaning is that she is playing with the four steps beginning with *para*; because every form is preceded by name, she seeks to conquer this entire world; she consists of all worldly transactions; she is composed of splendor (*dyuti*) due to her capacity to reveal her own nature; she is capable of both praise and being praised; she is composed of beauty (*kānti*) because she destroys the blinding darkness of non-reflection (*avimarśa*); and she is composed of movement (*gati*) because her expansion is unimpeded.
Having paid homage to this [Śakti]:

for "homage" (namaskāra) indeed means the disclosure of the majesty of the one to whom homage is paid through the abandonment of the separate sense of ego (ahaṅkāra)—that is to say, a state of aesthetic resonance (sāmarasya).
For that which is supreme is Śaktitva.
That which is *paśyantī* is application;
that which is *madhyamā* is engagement;
and that which is *vaikharī*, moreover, is the completion.
The powers such as Parā and the others are the very nature of the speaker who possesses those powers.
Having thus paid homage to this Speech, the intended meaning of the *alaṅkāra-sūtras* composed by him for his own [disciples] is now stated;
the heart [of the matter] is being opened.
In what manner?
By way of its function (*vṛtti*), that is, by way of its essential nature as a literary composition (*sandarbha*).

Now, desiring to compose this work according to the perspective of the *dhvani* theorists, he sets forth the positions of Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, and others as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words beginning "In this matter, first, Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa... and so on.
This is the general position regarding the view [of poetry]:
for that which is called "poetry" consists essentially of distinguished word and meaning;
therein, the meaning is the expressed (*vācya*).
And that which is implied, as for example: "O pious man, stay confident; that dog has been killed today by him who dwells in the thicket on the bank of the Godāvarī river—a maned lion."
In this case, when the wanton woman speaks, the injunction to wander about as a righteous person— intended to remove the fear of dogs— is established as the expressed meaning (*vācya*),
because it is directly signified and thus cognized without mediation;
whereas the prohibition against wandering on the banks of the Godāvarī due to the presence of lions is the implied meaning (*pratīyamāna*).

Because it is perceived immediately after the syntactical connection of the sentence-meaning as being unconditioned by linguistic convention (*asaṅketita*), the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna-artha*), which is distinct from the expressed meaning (*vācya*), consists of three branches according to its application— namely, the nature of rasa, matter (*vastu*), and poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*). Being endowed with aesthetic charm (*sacamatkāra*), being the domain of the poet’s creative effort (*kavisaṃrambhagocaratva*), and being the object of repose for the perception of connoisseurs (*sahṛdayapratītiviśrāntiviṣayatva*), it constitutes the soul of poetry (*kāvyātmā*).

The masters of Dhvani maintain that its qualities, such as sweetness (*mādhurya*), assist it through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-vṛtti*), just like bravery and the like [assist a person]; whereas figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) such as simile (*upamā*) assist it through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-vṛtti*), like bracelets and the like [adorn a person].

Others, however, hold that all three types of the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna*) belong strictly to the category of figures of speech, because they serve to embellish the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
Now we shall explain the text part by part.
Here, in this path of poetry (*kāvyamārga*), they consider [the following] to be included within the category of ornaments (*alaṅkārapakṣa*).
The point is that the reality is otherwise;
in order to demonstrate that which they consider [to be so] as something qualified, he says "For instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth.

In cases such as *paryāyokta*, *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, *samāsokti*, *ākṣepa*, *vyājastuti*, *upameyopamā*, and *ananvaya*, only the literal matter (*vastumātra*) is perceived, but not rasa or an ornament (*alaṃkāra*).

Because here the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is rooted in indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and since it is impossible for rasa or figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) to be suggested when they are rooted in indication,
*paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is the expression of a meaning that is actually being apprehended through a different mode of expression.

As he will state: "Paryāyokta (periphrasis) is the expression of what is to be understood by means of a different manner [of speech]. For example: "Whose soldiers, having touched the clusters of blossoms of the Pārijāta tree—which were cherished by Śacī through the enjoyment of her hair in the Nandana grove—felt as if they had committed a sin."
Here, Hayagrīva’s victory over heaven is made known through the effect characterized by the touch of the *pārijāta* blossom from the tree of death (Sāvadhajña) belonging to his soldiers.

When the understanding of the relevant subject arises from an irrelevant one through a relationship such as that between the general and the particular, this is Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description).

As he will state: "Aprastutapraśaṃsā occurs when there is the cognition of the relevant subject from an irrelevant one, whether through the relation of general and particular, cause and effect, or similarity."
Just as there is nothing whatsoever that the mistress of the house has not prepared for her husband,
so too must she provide hospitality for the traveler who arrives unexpectedly at the appointed time.
There is nothing devised by the Lord that is not the provisions for the traveler Time, who is ever intent on his journey, and whose wife is Destiny.
Thus [ends the commentary on the verse].

Here, just as there is nothing that has not been prepared as provisions for the journey by the wife for her husband who is habituated to constant wandering, so too there is nothing that has not been prepared as provisions for the traveler that is Time; in this context, from the unstated general form—that "Time devours everything"—the stated specific instance, namely the slaying of Prahasta, is implied.
*Samāsokti* (synecdoche) is that figure in which an irrelevant subject is understood through the similarity of its qualifiers.
As he will state: “When the irrelevant is implied through the similarity of qualifiers, it is *samāsokti*.
For example: “The face of night was seized by the moon with [its] passion aroused and with trembling pupils;”
Just as she did not perceive the entire garment of darkness before her, even though it had slipped away due to her passion.
Here, by means of the similarity of qualifiers such as "having the passion [of love] removed" and so forth, the unmentioned narrative of the hero is understood.
*Ākṣepa* (paralipsis) is the apparent negation of a contextual matter—whether already stated or yet to be stated—for the sake of suggesting its specific excellence.
As he will say: "Paralipsis is the semblance of a negation for the sake of suggesting the specific excellence of two contextual matters, whether already stated or yet to be stated."
For example: "O fool!
The claim that 'he is my beloved' is far from the truth; she would die [if you left her], and this would be a disgrace for you. This is what we call a word of Dharma."
"O messenger, it is not our business whether you are dear to her or not;
she is dying, and this is your infamy—we speak these words of truth."
Thus, in the example "O messenger, I am not a messenger," the negation of being a messenger conveys the fact that she is indeed a distinguished messenger.
When praise and blame lead respectively to the understanding of blame and praise, it is *vyājastuti* (feigned praise).
As he will state: "When blame and praise are understood through praise and blame, it is *vyājastuti*."
For example: "O Ocean, you who have effortlessly surpassed the Bodhisattvas—what is the use of further words?

There is no one else like you who has undertaken the vow to bestow benefit upon others. Out of compassion, you provide assistance to the desert even as it bears the burden of infamy for its refusal to perform acts of kindness for thirsty travelers."
In this context, the statement "you perform a service for me" conveys censure through praise.

If the status [of being the standard of comparison] belongs to both the standard and the object of comparison alternately, it is *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison), as he will state: "When that occurs between two things by way of alternation, it is *upameyopamā*."
As in: "The water is like the sky, and the sky is like the water; the swan is like the moon, and the moon is like the swan.
Here, the exchange of the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) excludes the third type of *sahacārins*.
When one and the same thing functions as both the standard and the object of comparison, it is *ananvaya* (self-comparison).
As he will state: "When one and the same thing serves as both the standard of comparison and the object compared, it is *ananvaya* (non-correspondence).
For example: "In battle, Arjuna was like Arjuna in his celebrated prowess.
Here, there is an exclusion of a second peer.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) and so forth is intended.

Among these, such as *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), that which is perceived as a mere fact—such as the conquest of heaven and the like—apart from rasa and alaṅkāra, appears as the very self through all means of valid cognition; yet, by closing one's eyes like an elephant (*gajanimīlikā*), it is regarded merely as an embellishment of the expressed meaning (*vācya*).

The meaning is as follows: how can that [suggested sense]—whose expressed meaning has been subordinated and which transcends the level of the expressed—be an embellisher of the expressed? By what manner was this established by Udbhaṭa and others?
“Projecting the other for one’s own establishment; surrendering oneself for the sake of the other”—this is by way of two modes (*bhaṅgī*).
*Bhaṅgī* means a manner or type.
Herein, this is the intended meaning (*āśaya*).
In figures such as *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) and others, this implied meaning is based on indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And indication is of two kinds: one is "non-abandoning of its own primary sense," as in "The spears enter" (*kuntāḥ praviśanti*), and so forth;
the other is "abandoning of its own primary sense," as in "A hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), and so forth.

In that context, regarding the expression "the entrance of the *aja-hats* (goat-slayers)," since it is impossible for spears (*kuntās*) to enter by themselves, they imply (*ākṣipya*) the *kauntikas* (spearmen), through which entry becomes possible.
Therefore, because it implies others for its own establishment, there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) therein;
that is, for the sake of establishing its own entry and so forth, there is the implication of another, namely the *kauntika*.
In the case of *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning), however, the primary meaning of words such as "Ganges" is absolutely untenable.
Therefore, the definition is "the surrendering of oneself for the sake of another.
For the sake of another—namely, for the purpose of providing a location for the hamlet and so forth—the surrendering of oneself is the relinquishing of one's own essential form.

And thus, in the example of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), "O Nandana, they were touched by Satī," the soldiers' disrespectful touching of the *pārijāta* blossom cannot occur without implying the conquest of heaven; therefore, this is an "implication for the sake of its own establishment" (*svasiddhaye parākṣepaḥ*), according to the principle of the spears (*kuntādinaya*).
This should be understood similarly in the example of *samāsokti* (synecdoche), "With passion aroused... as well.

When there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of leadership, since the connection with the night and so forth as possessing a garment of darkness is possible, it is *ajahatsvārtha* (not abandoning its own primary meaning).
Now, in the example of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), "He does not exist," the primary meaning is irrelevant to the context;
in the example of *ākṣepa*, "I am a young girl," the negation of the role of a messenger is merely apparent; and in the example of *vyājastuti* (feigned praise), "O you who have conquered pride!"...

Since neither of the two—figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) nor metaphorical identification (*gauṇī*)—can achieve both unity and multiplicity simultaneously, the primary meaning is absolutely untenable.
Therefore, the definition is "the surrendering of oneself for the sake of another.
With this distinction of objects in mind, it was stated: "in two ways, as appropriate."
"Yoga" means fitness; the sense is "without transgressing that.
Thus has the disagreement among Bhāmaha and others regarding *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) been shown.

Now, he introduces the disagreement between Rudraṭa and others concerning *rasadhvani* (suggestion of rasa) and *alaṅkāradhvani* (suggestion of a figure of speech) with the words beginning "By Rudraṭa also... and so forth.

The *bhāva* ornament and the *preya* ornament are stated to be of two kinds. For it is said: "That is *bhāva* by which, through a cause that manifests without obstruction, a transformation [in another] reveals that person's intention as well as its underlying motive."
Thus it is said.
Rudraṭa has stated that the figure of speech *bhāva* (emotional state) is of two kinds, namely *bhāvasthiti* (the persistence of emotion) and *bhāvaśānti* (the subsidence of emotion).
The meaning is that this is like the function of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy);
for even though varieties such as *sandhi* (fusion) and *śabalatā* (intermixture) are possible within the figure of *bhāva*, they are included here.
For he will say: "The emergence of entities, junctures, and variegation (*śabalatā*) are distinct figures of speech.
He reveals the superficiality even in [figures] such as metaphor (*rūpaka*), stating:
"Metaphor (*rūpaka*), Illuminator (*dīpaka*), Apoha (*apahnuti*), Equal Pairing (*tulyayogitā*)," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), illustrations (*nidarśana*) and other such figures will also be characterized.
In that regard, the figure of simile (*upamā-alaṅkāra*), though implied, is not mentioned as a subordinate element because it serves only to beautify the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
The sense is that even this [position] is without substance.

Because the figure of speech *upamā* (simile) serves as a cause for the beauty of the expressed meaning (*vācyasobhā*), it is subordinated; yet, having been brought forth [by that subordination], it abides among those [other figures] with predominance. Now, he reveals the nature of *rasa* (sentiment) and *bhāva* (emotion) as they are not commonly perceived: "The figures *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and so forth. In this context, *rasa* when it has become subordinate is the figure *rasavat*.
The sentiment (bhāva) is the "Beloved" (preyān);
the semblance of a sentiment (rasābhāsa) is the "Powerful" (ūrjasvī);
and the semblance of an emotion (bhāvābhāsa) is the "Composed" (samāhita).
Thus, rasa, bhāva, and so forth have been described as causes for the beauty of the expressed meaning; however, the sense is that even this is weak,
because the status of rasa and the others as figures of speech (alaṅkāra) is not constant.
Because it is the object of embellishment (*alaṅkārya*) when it occupies a state of predominance.

Regarding the phrase "as a poetic fancy" (*utprekṣātva*): the meaning is that even though it is suggested (*pratīyamāna*), it is itself stated as being the object of embellishment, even while remaining suggested.
That too is profound;
for it has been established as a settled doctrine that in the state of being perceived, every poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) possesses the nature of being the object of adornment (*alaṅkārya*).
Indeed, the threefold subject matter—consisting of the thing itself (*vastu*), the poetic figure, and aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—is precisely designated as that which is to be adorned.
The meaning is that [the author] has not considered the very thing that ought to be adorned— the life of poetry— as such.
Having thus presented the view of those superficial observers who, being averse to an investigation into the vital essence of poetry, find delight in mere ornaments,
[he now addresses] those who are intent upon the vital essence of poetry.
He presents the various views correctly with the words "But by Vāmana," and so forth.

By stating that [the secondary function] is "based on similarity," he casts a glance at those who claim that the secondary function (*gauṇī*) is a verbal operation based on a relation [of identity], thereby indicating them as objects of refutation.
For the Master of Dhvani does not accept the inclusion of the secondary function within indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

By asserting that "metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) based on similarity is the ornament of indirect speech (vakrokti)," [the author] has stated that a certain variety of suggestion (dhvani) rooted in indication—namely, that called *atyantatiraskṛtavācya*—is indeed the soul of poetry; yet, being [regarded as] an ornament, it was not recognized as the object to be adorned (*alaṅkārya*).
He says, "merely qualified by qualities," to show that even that part which is not the object to be adorned was nonetheless described as such.

By the use of the word "only" (*kevala*), independence from *rasas* and *alaṅkāras* is indicated. That very *rīti*—which consists of qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and the like that are independent of *rasas* and *alaṅkāras*, which is of the nature of a structural property (*saṃghaṭanā-dharma*), and which takes the form of the Vaidarbhī and other styles—is said to be the soul of poetry.
And thus it was aphorized by him: "The *rīti* is the soul of poetry."
And it has been proclaimed: "Even if its virtues are unknown, the speech of a true poet pours forth a stream of honey into the ears;
for even before its fragrance is perceived, a garland of *mālatī* flowers captivates the eye."
The sense is that this too is incorrect.
For instance, word and meaning constitute the body of poetry,
while alliteration, simile, and so forth are like bracelets, crowns, and other ornaments.
Since it is established that the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha) is the very soul [of poetry],
these *rītis* stand on the same footing as *anuprāsa*, which is an external phonetic ornament (*varṇālaṅkāra*) distinct from verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*).
This is because both possess the nature of being attributes of phonemes (*varṇadharma*).

With this intention in mind, the *vaidarbha* and other *rītis* (styles) were analyzed by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and others in the context of discussing *vṛtti*, alliteration, and phonetic ornaments (*varṇālaṅkāra*).
The author of this work will also analyze them therein.

For those of superficial intellect, there arises the delusion that these [styles], which are actually *vyañjaka* (suggestive), are the self [of poetry] due to their close proximity to the *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) that is suggested.
Since this applies equally to alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the like, such partiality for mere stylistic form (*rīti*) is trivial.
In reality, however, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) alone is the soul of poetry.
Now, [the author] states "by Udbhaṭa and others" to show that even they did not discern the distinction between poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāra*).
“Sameness” means having the same genus (*sajātīyatva*).
The reason for this is stated: “because difference is established merely by way of the object.
By the inclusion of the word “merely,” the absence of difference in their own nature (*svarūpa*) is indicated.

Their intention is that the essential nature, defined as the cause of the beauty of poetry, is indeed of only one kind. To demonstrate the difference in their respective domains, he says: "The arrangement," and so forth.
“The qualities of composition are the properties of form, whereas the ornaments are the properties of word and meaning”—
the sense is that this [view] as well is not profound.
Furthermore, because *guṇa* (excellence) and *alaṅkāra* (ornament) are inherently and fundamentally distinct in their nature:
for *guṇas* are attributes of the *rasa*, which is the principal element (*aṅgin*), whereas *alaṅkāras* belong to the word and meaning, which are the subordinate elements (*aṅga*).
Moreover, *guṇas* are invariably causes of excellence, while *alaṅkāras* are not necessarily so.
Qualities (guṇas) exist by way of inherence (samavāya), whereas ornaments (alaṅkāras) exist by way of conjunction (saṃyoga).
As it has been said: "Those attributes of the aesthetic flavor (rasa), which is the possessor of qualities, are like bravery and other traits of the self."
Those qualities, being of unshakable stability, would be the causes of excellence.

"Those figures such as alliteration (anuprāsa), simile (upamā), and so forth, which at times assist that excellent [poetry] by way of its constituent parts, are ornaments, like necklaces and the like."
Thus it is said.

This being the case, with respect to the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), the excellence of poetic embellishment resides precisely in the qualities (*guṇa*); for just as one accepts the status of poetry even when the ornaments are not manifest, it is not so when the qualities are unmanifest.
As it has been said: "But [poetry] may sometimes be without ornaments."
Regarding this preeminence of both the *guṇas* and the *alaṅkāras*, he states—on the grounds that even there the view of the ancients is incorrect—that "in this way, they are merely *alaṅkāras*.

Then, with the intention of showing that the view of the *dhvani*-theory is closer to those of the author of the *Vakroktijīvita* and Bhaṭṭanāyaka, he says: "The author of the *Vakroktijīvita*, however," and so forth.
The meaning is that its nature consists of speech characterized by the artful expression of wit; that is to say, its essence is speech endowed with various modes of cleverness.
By stating that he "declared it to be life," the absence of any stubborn attachment to mere poetic ornamentation is illuminated.
With the intention of showing that another subtle, essential element has also been discerned by him, he says: "and the predominance of the function."
The function consists in the communication of rasa; it is this that attains primacy,
and not the subordinate element which is merely an ornament— this is the sense.
Furthermore, he states "abhidhāprakāra... and so forth, asserting that for this [poetic figure], the level of the expressed meaning alone is accepted as the ornament (*alaṅkāra*).

And regarding the threefold suggested meaning—consisting of fact (*vastu*), ornament (*alaṅkāra*), and rasa—which exists therein, he asserts that its view is that the primary importance belongs solely to the function characterized by the communication of that [suggested sense]; thus he says "satyapi ca... and so forth.

"Metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) consists in resorting to indication (*lakṣaṇā*); its 'crookedness' (*vakratā*) refers to the entire realm of *dhvani*, such as that where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*), and so forth.

This being the case, he states—namely, "merely a variety of expression"—to show that this view differs only slightly from the perspective of *dhvani*. Now follows the opinion of Bhaṭṭanāyaka, beginning with "But by Bhaṭṭanāyaka," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is accepted through bold assertion" (*prauḍhoktyābhyupagatasya*): *bhoga* (enjoyment) is a conventional usage imagined by one's own mind; "bold assertion" (*prauḍhokti*) refers to that by which something is accepted—this is the meaning.

By stating that such a function of suggestion (*vyañjanavyāpāra*) constitutes the very soul of poetry, he declares that this function, in which the natures of word and meaning are subordinated, possesses primacy.
And he states that this operation is not worldly: "In that case as well, because it is the producer of denotation," and so forth.

Among those operations, "in the state of being the producer of denotation" (*abhidhābhāvakatve*) refers to the capacity whose object is the referent of the convention directly. Denotation (*abhidhā*) is the power [of a word] directed toward the object of the linguistic convention.
*Bhāvikatva* (poetic vividness) is the power of making common those objects perceived as uncommon.

Having transcended these two functions [of *vibhāva* and *anubhāva*], the function consisting of the relish (*carvaṇā*) of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—which is otherwise known by the name "enjoyment" (*bhoga*)—is accepted as primary because it is the locus of repose within the *vibhāvas* and so forth once they have been made common.

In this view, the aspect regarding the predominance of the function of "enjoyment" and other such transactions is distinct from the view of the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*, who posits a function imagined solely by his own intellect.
Now, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "The author of the *Dhvani*, however," and so forth.
The author of the *Dhvani*, moreover, has established as his final doctrine that the very essence of poetry belongs to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) whose nature is the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
The reason for this is: "because the function of suggestion (*vyañjanavyāpāra*) must necessarily be admitted."
Of what kind [of word]? Of that which has transcended the three operations known as denotation (*abhidhā*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and intentionality (*tātparya*).
Intentionality (*tātparya*) is the power of syntactic integration (*samanvaya-śakti*) that arises immediately after the comprehension of the individual word-meanings.
By saying "having transcended these three," the state of the fourth level is also indicated.

Regarding the phrase "resounding, illuminating," etc.: since this triad of well-known synonyms—namely *dhvanana* (resounding), *dyotana* (illuminating), *pratyāyana* (making known), and *vyañjana* (manifesting)—must necessarily be accepted, there is no other way to account for the cognition of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) if these were not accepted;
therefore, the meaning is that the suggested meaning itself is the soul (*ātman*).
Now, one might ask: why should the operation of *vyañjanā* (suggestion) not be the primary [meaning]?
To this, he says: "Because the operation lacks the status of being the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
It lacks the status of being the sentence-meaning because, due to its imperceptibility (*apratyakṣatva*), it is unfit for verbal definition (*nirukti*).
Indeed, all the powers of objects are inferred solely through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the cognition of their effects and so forth;
therefore, the operation (vyāpāra) is not primary.
Furthermore, whatever reason is given for its primacy is itself shown to be applicable only to that which is suggested (vyaṅgya).
But the function belongs to the word alone; thus he says, "of the sentence-meaning itself.
The fact that [the sentence-meaning] is to be embellished by qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras), and its status as the locus of final repose, are the reasons for its primacy.
Therefore, he has established the conclusion that the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha) alone is the soul of poetry (kāvyātman).
Then he further adduces more arguments, beginning with "by way of the object of the function" (*vyāpārasya viṣayamukhena*).
The very establishment of the nature of the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) and the like occurs solely by way of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).
Therefore, it is impossible for [suggestion] to be the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthatva*).

Just as the apprehension of its own nature occurs by way of the object, so too its predominance and its capacity for investigation occur by way of that very object; thus he says: "because of its predominance through that [object]," and "because it lacks the quality of being investigated in its own nature.
Furthermore, he says: "of the object alone," meaning that only the object is capable of possessing the full status of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
The full weight [of the argument] rests on such points as the direct attainment of its own nature, its primacy by virtue of itself, and its being the object of investigation in its own form.
For it is only the specific [object], characterized as the implied meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), that can endure these [attributes].
Therefore, he says, "Therefore, the object alone [is the self]," because it is logical for the object alone to possess the nature of the self (*ātmatva*).
Because it is capable of bearing the entire burden [of poetic expression], it deserves the full extent of its majesty; therefore, he says: "Of which the qualities, ornaments," and so forth.
Now, one might object: "But according to the opinion of the ancients, *rasa* and the like are themselves merely ornaments such as *rasavat* and the rest.
How then can they be the objects to be ornamented? To this, he replies: "But *rasa* and the like..."
The reason for this is that ornaments serve as embellishments, whereas rasa and the like are primarily the objects to be embellished.
For when rasa and the like occupy a subordinate position, they constitute ornamentation; but when they possess primacy, they are strictly the objects of ornamentation.
Since the established principle is thus,
he concludes that the suggested meaning alone is the soul of poetry with the words "therefore, the suggested [meaning] alone," etc.
By the phrase "having become the sentence-meaning," he indicates its state of predominance.
Because that which is subordinate lacks selfhood (*anātmatva*) in its state of non-predominance;
this is the view of the author of the *Dhvani*.
To demonstrate that he himself follows this [view], he says: "This very position," and so forth.
By the word "only" (eva), the impossibility [of the term's application] in other alternative positions is excluded.
It is "inducing" (*āvarjaka*), meaning it forcibly directs [the mind] toward itself.
The reason for this is stated as: "because of the function of the phoneme," and so forth.
Whether those who maintain that the suggested meaning constitutes the very soul of poetry, or those who do not maintain this,
by all of them alike it is impossible to deny the function of suggestion (*vyañjanavyāpāra*).
If it is not denied, what follows from that? To this he says: "And in the recourse to that," and so forth.
That other alternative is established as being untenable by these aforementioned arguments.
As for the objection raised there by the author of the *Vyaktiviveka*, he sets it forth with the words: "As for what the author of the *Vyaktiviveka* [says]," and so on.
"By way of being a mark" means by way of being an indicator.
"Because of the absence of identity and origination" [means]:
when there is the relationship of mark and marked between a property (dharma) and its locus (dharmin), identity is the necessary connection.
However, in the case of cause and effect, there is indeed what is called "the arising of that [effect] in the absence of that [cause].

The meaning is that if either of these two, which possess a necessary connection, were not present, then—due to deviation—the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) would be impossible.
Since this is so, therefore that statement is one made without due consideration.
This view of the author of the *Vyaktiviveka* is, in effect, like the cawing of a crow.
Thus, whatever collection of arguments exists for the establishment of the theory of *dhvani* is exceedingly profound;
it is useful only for the critical investigation of those two types of poetry where *dhvani* and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* prevail.
With the intention that this [analysis] is not of much use in the investigation of *citrakāvya* (poetry of variegated beauty), he concludes with the words "tadetat kuśāgrīya... and so forth.
Here, in *citrakāvya*, it is not elaborated upon.
The meaning is that it is merely restated according to its utility.
Now, he restates only that much of the utility of *dhvani* which pertains to the discussion of variety, beginning with the words "There exists, indeed... (*asti tāvat*).
To the question, "If it exists, what follows from that?", he says: "In that regard, of the suggested meaning... (*tatra vyaṅgyasya...*) and so forth.
When [suggestion] is predominant, it is the highest variety of poetry called *dhvani*;
when it is subordinate, however, it is the middle variety called *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*.
He states the scope of *citra* (figurative poetry) with the words "therein, the highest is *dhvani*" and so forth.
And since that [suggestion] is known to be rooted in both denotation (*abhidhā*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he says: "by its being rooted in indication and denotation.

When it is rooted in indication, it is called "that in which the expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed" (*avivakṣitavācya*), because the aspect of the expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed when there is indication characterized by the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*).
But when it is rooted in denotation, it is called "that in which the expressed meaning is intended but has another purpose" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).
In the case of the denotative function (*abhidhā*), because there is no sublation regarding the expressed meaning, there is "intendedness" (*vivakṣitatva*);

and because it is intended as a subordinate element to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), there is "subordination to another purpose" (*anyaparatā*). Thus, that which is rooted in denotation possesses "intendedness and subordination to another purpose.
In this way, generally speaking, *dhvani* is twofold: that rooted in indication (*lakṣaṇāmūla*) and that rooted in denotation (*abhidhāmūla*).
In that context, he states the internal subdivisions of that which is based on indication (*lakṣaṇāmūla*): "The first [is] *arthāntara*.

The first, which has indication as its basis, is twofold: that in which the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*), and that in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*).

When, while not abandoning its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthatayā*), there is an implication of another for the sake of establishing itself, it is "that in which the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning."

For example: Whose speech, emerging from the lotus-mouth of the wise— beautiful to hear at its beginning, wholesome in its conclusion, easily grasped by people, washed at every syllable with the clear and sweet essences of various scriptures, and permeated by the fragrance of the buds of discernment blooming within the heart— is not for the delight of the learned?
In this case, when such words— characterized by instruction— shift toward another meaning,
because such a distinction is impossible for mere words alone;
then, when they abandon their own primary meaning and surrender themselves for the sake of another, it is called *atyantatiraskṛtavācya* (the completely set-aside literal sense).
For example: some of dull intellect sit like the mute; others, in their presence, shrink away from making even a poorly considered inquiry; yet others loathe them;
some praise them excessively for unworthy reasons. By such people, knowledge is scorched like a firebrand; by what means does it not falter when it reaches the presence of a wicked ruler?

In this case, within the *vidyā* (the science of grammar), [the literal meaning] such as "femininity" (*hlī*), "disgust" (*bhatsā*), and so forth—just as in the case of the location of a hamlet on the Gaṅgā and the like—is in every way impossible because it would abandon its own inherent meaning for that which is conjoined with it; thus, there is "complete cancellation of the literal sense" (*atyantatiraskṛtavācyatā*).

In this manner, under the category of "where the literal sense is not intended" (*avivakṣitavācya*), there are two varieties: "that where the literal sense is transmuted into another meaning" (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*) and "that where the literal sense is completely cancelled" (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*).
Now, the directions for the subdivisions based on denotation (*abhidhāmūla*) follow.
"The second as well" means that the second type is rooted in denotation (*abhidhāmūla*) and is known as "that which has a meaning other than what is intended" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).
In that case, in some instances, the sequence of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is not perceived.
In some cases, [the sequence] is perceived.

Therefore, even that which has a "non-primary intended meaning" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*) is of two kinds: that in which the sequence of the suggested meaning is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*) and that in which the sequence is perceptible (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*).

Now, in order to establish the specific domains of these two types of suggestion rooted in indication (*lakṣaṇāmūla*) and denotation (*abhidhāmūla*)—namely, their nature as matter-of-fact (*vastu*), poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), or aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—he says, beginning with "rooted in indication," and so forth.
For that which is rooted in *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function) is necessarily rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśakti*) and consists of a real entity (*vasturūpa*).
Indeed, whatever collection of objects exists—consisting of universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and so forth—all this is called a "real entity" (*vastu*).
That very same [entity], when accompanied by the artistic embellishment (*vicchitti*) conceived by the poet, becomes an "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*).

The *rasas*, however, are specific types of aesthetic experience (*pratīti*) in the minds of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*), consisting of love and other emotions manifested through the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*).

Now, that type of suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) known as "the expressed where the intended meaning is not the primary one" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*), which involves a non-perceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*), is invariably rooted either in the power of the sense (*arthaśaktimūla*) or in the power of both [word and sense] (*ubhayaśaktimūla*).
It is invariably of the nature of a fact (*vasturūpa*) or of the nature of a poetic figure (*alaṅkārarūpa*).

In that context, when the aesthetic moods (*rasa*), the transitory emotions (*bhāva*), the semblances of aesthetic mood (*rasābhāsa*), the semblances of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*), the emergence of emotion (*bhāvodaya*), the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*), the transition between emotions (*bhāvasandhi*), and the commingling of emotions (*bhāvaśabalatā*) are manifested, no sequence is perceived; this is what is meant by "the non-perception of sequence" (*asaṃlakṣyakramatva*).

Among the aesthetic moods, the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) consisting of union (*saṃbhoga*) is as follows: When she had just attained the budding of her breasts and was resting on the couch of dalliance, her lover, his lips quivering, silently requested a kiss from her with a sign of his eyebrows.
Covering her face, which was full of smiles, with the hem of her garment against her broad cheeks, the slender woman shook her head, causing her cluster-like earrings to sway gently.

In this context, there is no perceptible sequence between the expressed meaning— which consists of the narrative of the heroine and the hero— and the aesthetic experience (*rasasaṃvit*)— which is the realization by the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*), characterized by the melting away of all other objects of cognition and becoming one with the described subject. Even though such a sequence exists, it is perceived as if it did not exist, like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals.
An example of love-in-separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*) is as follows: She neither turned her face away from the rising sun nor did she utter words harsh with manifest anger;
she merely gazed at her beloved with glances from eyes possessing straight eyelashes, looking upon him as if he were no different from her own father.
In such cases as these, the lack of sequential order (*akramatva*) is to be understood as previously explained.

An example of the Comic (*hāsya*) is as follows: "Adorned with ornaments that are like the foam of death, and dressed in water-attire, she strikes her swelling breasts with playful gestures, emitting a glistening sound as she approaches these young men."

In this context, when young men have approached her who was once adorned with bright finery following her husband’s death, the way she suddenly weeps with a tender voice and strikes her breasts with graceful movements reveals a sense of humor arising from the impropriety of her secret passion manifesting in such a manner.

An example of the pathetic (karuṇa) sentiment is as follows: "O you who are skilled in the characteristics of literature, today you enter into a new widowhood now that the venerable Lord Viṣṇudeva has passed away."
O you who bring delight to the ears with your breath, it is now appropriate for you to offer this palm-leaf fan as a festival of your arrival.

As for the *raudra* (fierce) sentiment: May your fierce arrows be victorious—those which, while you, O illustrious Ballāla, were engaged in the sport of hunting, severed the trunks of wild buffaloes leaping in rage, scattering their entrails amidst the streams of blood, and left half their faces visible as they were torn apart by the tusks of those beasts. At that moment of the "consecration" with the fat of lordly tigers, may those formidable shafts prevail!

Just as in the case of Vīra: "This entire world, from the Creator down to the smallest insect, possesses sight; yet there exists a divine eye, unattainable by others, which is supreme and unbearable in both respects:

in the plowshare of the Lord of Beings (Śiva), it causes the awakening of destruction for the lowly Kāma; and in the arrow of King Ballāla, the lord of the earth, it crushes the pride of rival kings."

As an example of the *bhayānaka* (the terrifying): "Of your enemies' excellent women, who were hidden in mountain thickets and had not seen the sun for so long, only their footprints remained as signs."

An example of the loathsome (*bībhatsa*) is as follows: For those who thoroughly enjoy that certain supreme bliss of their own self, a sense of revulsion arises toward this expansion of sense objects;
for others, however, there is rather an ever-increasing desire to taste them, like flies toward food that is fouled by phlegm and smeared with vomit.

As an example of the marvelous (adbhuta): "Having finally sketched her in my mind after a long time, thinking she was consistent with the supreme qualities I had heard [of], I am not clever enough to place that form—even if it be only in servitude—into the company of this [present] girl, whose appearance is so utterly dissimilar."

In this context, the statement— that the mental image of the heroine, which had been previously sketched by the hero’s mind in accordance with her excellent qualities heard from others since he had not seen her form for a very long time,
now appears so utterly dissimilar to the actual form of the heroine before his eyes that she cannot even be regarded as a servant— reveals the ultimate pinnacle of her physical beauty.

As for one who is peaceful: "Do not fear, O noble one; do not be distressed. Let there be discipline; let there be no affliction. Strive so that your learning does not perish; indeed, do not abandon the greatness of your mind.
Considering the lords—who tear asunder the essence of your own Raurava hell—as mere straw, I shall maintain my life with a morsel of food obtained by wandering for alms."
Thus, the suggestion of rasa (rasadhvani) has been illustrated by way of a mere indication.

Now, the suggestion of emotion (bhāvadhvani): for "emotion" (bhāva) consists of love (rati) manifested toward an object other than the heroine—such as a deity, a guru, a king, or a prince—as well as the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) such as despondency (nirveda), when they are manifested as the primary sense of the sentence.
For example: "Today, having fallen asleep, I saw on the bank of the Yamunā a cowherd boy standing there, skilled in playing the flute."
Upon seeing him, my senses became fixed on no other object and I dissolved within; yet, even as that occurred, I was awakened by the long-accumulated sins of my past.
And as it is said: "Distraught by the suffering of saṃsāra, I previously searched with great effort for Brahman and indeed beheld this world in its various forms;
but now, O Guru, since you have placed [the hand of knowledge] upon my head, all this has become Brahman alone—neither this world nor I myself remain."
And so it is: O King Ballāla, this is indeed the ultimate attainment of the highest fortune and the full fruition of prosperity, that we may worship these two feet of yours!
For even he who might stand long at the threshold of your gate, barred from entry—would he not be counted as equal to the sovereigns of Cola and Pāṇḍya?
In this manner, the nature of emotion (*bhāva*) directed toward objects such as a son, which is characterized by instability, should be inferred for oneself.
An example of a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) is as follows: "Repeatedly smelling the fragrance intensified by the scent of the blooming lotus, his reddened eyes closed again and again."
The bee now kisses the mango sprout that was previously enjoyed by the beak of his beloved.
And so forth.

In this case, because its object is an animal, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is merely an appearance (*ābhāsa*), due to the absence of qualities such as being noble and self-controlled (*dhīrodātta*).
As it has been said: "The erotic sentiment belongs to a person of superior character and possesses a brilliant attire."

An example of the appearance of existence (bhāvābhāsa): Having stretched out her branch-arms, darkened by swarms of humming bees, the mango creeper embraces the southern breeze with the warbling of cuckoos and asks after its well-being.
In this case, because affection is superimposed [upon another], the emotion becomes a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*).
An example of the emergence of emotion (*bhāvodaya*) is as follows: "At dawn, the beloved, with her eyes, indicated the footprints on the couch of dalliance..."
Having raised her brow slightly in a curved arch,
she became angry with a sweet, hidden smile.

Herein occurs the emergence of both shame and joy. An example of the conjunction of emotions (*bhāvasandhi*) is as follows: For a moment his eyes are slanted, harsh, and reddened; then for a moment he closes his eyes; then for a moment his trunk moves restlessly back and forth; then for a moment it rests against his tusk; then for a moment his gait is uneven and agitated; and then for a moment he resumes his graceful play. The elephant maintains equal attention toward the three drums and the six bees alike.

In this case, regarding the elephant intoxicated with rut: that which is for a mere moment the crooked, harsh, and reddish gaze of its eyes; immediately thereafter, the closing of those very eyes; likewise, the momentary restlessness of coming and going in its trunk; immediately thereafter, its resting upon its tusks; and the uneven agitation during its movement—for all these, occurring in such rapid succession—[constitute its state].
Immediately following this, there was this sequence of playful activity;
these two distinct and diverse movements, characterized by the properties of emergence and suppression, appeared moment by moment,
bestowing upon one another neither anger toward the three-fold objects nor joy toward the song of the bees, which was signaled by the sound of those very bees.
It reveals the agitation caused by the passing of time;

and in all three sentences regarding the dual activities, because of the repeated use of the word "moment by moment" (*kṣaṇaṃ kṣaṇam*), it shows how the great impetuses of the onset of fury— arising from the successive falling of arrows upon the enemies, resembling the leaping waves of a thoroughly agitated ocean— increase more and more.

In this way, they are made to understand that their appearance occurs in the midst of those who are capable of overcoming [the world], whose expansion is caused by an attachment to the pleasure of hearing the songs of bees.

By the use of the present tense in the word "dhatta" (they bear), it is indicated that because the state has begun but is not yet completed, there is no undesirable consequence in either of the two alternatives.

Likewise, by means of the movements of his trunk and hands— which are rendered momentarily agitated through their association with qualities such as being harsh and reddened like a tongue, moving restlessly back and forth, and being unevenly tossed about— and by means of the qualities of his state characterized by writhing, resting upon the tips [of his tusks], and the commencement of a graceful playfulness;
and even that equal distribution of attention toward the three enemies and the six-footed bees, which reveals only the undesirable side in one particular case—
therefore, this is a *sandhi* (fusion) of the two emotional states of anger and joy.

The variegation of internal states (*bhāva-śabdalatā*) is as follows: In the midst of her circle of friends, she revealed through speech what had arisen from her secret conduct; toward me, she looked with glances that were playful, full of longing, bashful, and gracious, while employing the mode of giving instruction.

In this case, one should not consider envy (*asūyā*) and the other emotions to be the expressed meaning (*vācya*), because they are superimposed upon the side-long glances (*kaṭākṣa*). Therefore, it is within the heart that the variegation of emotion (*bhāvaśabalatā*) is thus manifested. An example of the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*) is as follows: "The two [lovers] moved forward face-to-face in the presence of their elders, their attentions faltering in their haste to clear the path."
Both of them, having moved their flanks in opposite directions, repeatedly retreated with shame.
In this context, there is the subsiding of both *mati* (intellect) and *vibodha* (awakening).
Regarding these suggestives of rasa and so forth, the detailed exposition should be sought elsewhere;

for the author of this work, being intent on elaborating upon *citrakāvya* (poetry of striking form), has treated this matter with extreme brevity. Therefore, we have demonstrated only a mere direction by means of examples.

Now, in the case of *saṃlakṣyakrama* (perceptible sequence), that which is rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) necessarily takes the form of either a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) or a fact (*vastu*). Among these, an example of the form of a poetic figure is as follows: "Her darting glance, upon reaching the vicinity of my elders, seems to kiss me; having become nails, it seems to scratch me with exquisite grace; and having attained the state of arms, it seems to embrace me."

Here, by means of the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), there is suggested the figure of *vibhāvanā* (the production of an effect in the absence of its cause), characterized by the arising of the pleasure of sexual union despite the absence of causes such as kissing.
An example of *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) is as follows: "When he stands before her, her gaze suddenly becomes timid;
when he speaks jestingly, no reply ascends to the tip of her tongue."
And I do not even perceive his touch, for my body has become stiff with pride; O friend, even this union has become like a separation—what am I to do? What will the Creator ordain?
In this matter, because of the delusion that a non-entity is an entity, an object characterized by naivety is communicated.

Now, the suggestive meaning (vyañjaka-artha) based on the power of the sense (artha-śakti-mūla) is of three types: that which is inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavī*), that which is produced by the bold assertion of the poet (*kavi-prauḍhokti-niṣpādita*), and that which is produced by the bold assertion of a speaker fashioned by the poet (*kavinibaddha-vaktṛ-prauḍhokti-niṣpādita*).
Each of these is twofold—being either in the form of a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra-rūpa*) or in the form of a plain fact (*vastu-rūpa*)—and thus there are six varieties in total.
And since the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) is of six kinds—consisting of both the form of a fact (*vastu*) and the form of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*)—this [suggestion] has twelve varieties.
To explain: by means of a self-possible fact (*svataḥsaṃbhavi-vastu*), there is a fact; by means of a self-possible fact, there is an ornament;
and by means of a self-possible ornament (*svataḥsaṃbhavy-alaṅkāra*), there is a fact.

Thus, there are four ways in which a figure of speech [is suggested] by that [fact]. Likewise, there are also four ways: a fact [suggested] by a fact accomplished through the bold assertion of a poet;

a fact [suggested] by a figure of speech accomplished through the bold assertion of a poet; and a figure of speech [suggested] by a figure of speech accomplished through the bold assertion of a poet. Thus, there are four [types] as well.

Even though this [poetic suggestion] is produced by the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a speaker who is bound to a specific form, the fourfold nature of its objects (*viṣaya*) should be investigated.

The detailed exposition (*prapañca*) regarding this has been presented by us at length in our commentary on the *Kāvyaprakāśa* titled *Saṃpradāyaprakāśinī*; therefore, it should be understood from that source.
However, it is not elaborated upon here for fear of increasing the bulk of the book and because it is not relevant to the present context.

A mere indication is given here: among these, an instance of one thing [being established] by another thing that exists inherently is as follows: "Even today there is no poet in the world capable of ascending to the level of the ancients;
yet, O King, if there is this reproach that 'this man is not ancient,' what can he do?"

Here, by means of a *vastu* (fact) that is inherently possible (*svataḥsaṃbhavin*), the fact characterized as the speaker’s proclamation of his own greatness—namely, "I am such a person"—is communicated.

An instance of a theme [suggested] by a poetic ornament composed by a poet is as follows: "O friend, if your gaze were like sparks from a burning *khadira* wood charcoal, harsh and fixed; if your tongue were fierce in threatening the virtuous and flickering with moving black fingers;

if your teeth were a mockery of the cruel fangs in the forest of Death’s sport; and if your two shanks were like the abode of serpents—then the world of snakes would be reduced to nothing but anthills."

Here, by means of the figure of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) produced through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, the fact (*vastu*) is suggested: that the weakness of the ignoble, ordained by fate, protects the entire world in some respect.

An example of a figure suggested by another figure produced through the bold assertion of a speaker created by the poet is as follows: "Day after day, [life] is equal to the day of a relative's death and a festival of wine—[a day] characterized by unrestrained embraces, uninterrupted conversation, and the consumption of wine."

May there be, day after day, the great festival of the death of kinsmen, where people are rendered helpless by grief, embracing shadows that cannot be avoided and engaging in unrestrained conversation with outcasts.
Thus [it is said].

Through the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) produced by the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a wanton woman composed by the poet, there is communicated the figure of *vyatireka* (contrast), which consists in the realization of the extreme excellence of this great festival for the death of his kinsman over and against [the joy of] embracing and so forth. In this manner, other [figures] are also to be inferred.
Now, a brief indication of the nature of subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*):
"Subordinated suggestion is that which is subordinate to the expressed meaning," and so forth.

Being subordinate to the expressed meaning (*vācyāṅgatva*) is [equivalent to] being non-hidden (*agūḍhatva*); not being subordinate to anything else (*aparāṅgatva*) is [equivalent to] being non-obscure (*asphuṭatva*).
The varieties [of subordination], such as "doubtful predominance," "equal predominance," "suggested by intonation" (kāku),
and "ugliness," have been demonstrated in the context of *samāsokti* and other figures; the phrase "by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* and others" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

In this regard, the status of being a subordinate element to the expressed meaning (*vācyāṅgatva*) is as follows: "O King Ballāla! In the empty palace of your enemy, a parrot repeatedly attempts to climb the hand of a beautiful woman depicted in a painting out of a desire for conversation;
alas, a young swan, moving its beak-tip over the row of anklets whose sweet tinkling it hears, cries out."

Here, although the extraordinary power of the hero—which has rendered the enemy king’s palace empty—is suggested (*pratīyamāna*), it exists as a subordinate element (*vācyāṅgatva*) because it serves to establish the narrative of the parrot and the swan.
In this way, other varieties such as "unconcealed" (*agūḍha*) and so forth should also be understood.

Having thus introduced the nature of poetry characterized by suggestion (*dhvani*) and that in which the suggested is subordinated (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) as a preliminary, and desiring now to treat the type of poetry called "figurative" (*citra*) which is intended to be explained in this section, he says: *Citraṃ*...

The word "tu" (but) indicates that there is a greater multiplicity of divisions in comparison to *dhvani* where the suggested meaning is subordinate (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*); this is the sense of the suffix "-tara.
Now, in order to introduce the initial aphorism (*sūtra*), he says: "For instance" (*tathāhi*)—and then follows the aphorism.
In this context, there are three types of tautology: tautology of meaning, tautology of sound, and tautology of both sound and meaning.

One might ask: "What is the connection between beginning with 'Now, the Citra' and then proceeding to describe the varieties of *paunaruktya* (redundancy)? To this he replies: "First, regarding *paunaruktya*," and so forth.

The mention of these varieties of *paunaruktya* at the outset is for the purpose of establishing the classification of levels (*kakṣyāvibhāga*)—since they will be defined later as resting upon word, meaning, and both—and for the sake of clarifying that very classification; thus, the term *paunaruktya* is repeated for each individual variety.
Therefore, one should understand the classification of the categories as follows: alliteration (*anuprāsa*), rhyme (*yamaka*), and so forth are verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*);
simile (*upamā*), metaphor (*rūpaka*), and so forth are semantic ornaments (*arthālaṅkāra*);
while the *lāṭānuprāsa* and others are ornaments of both.

Now, one might object that since the cognition of meaning is preceded by the cognition of the word, it is not appropriate to first point out the redundancy of the meaning; to this, he says: "With respect to the meaning," and so forth.
"Internal" means being primary;
"indication pertaining to the meaning" means the indication of redundancy concerning the object of meaning.
"By long-standing renown" means in accordance with the established tradition of former teachers such as Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, and others;

for they previously defined only the figure of speech called *punaruktavadābhāsa* (the semblance of repetition) as a figure of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*). And, intending to show that the three types of repetition [previously] mentioned are fully accepted [by them], he says: "In the verbal system," and so forth.
The word *iti* establishes its meaning as "fitness"—namely, that the word *iti* signifies "manner" (*prakāra*).
Now, one might ask: why is it not accepted that the three [words] alone serve the purpose of completion? To this, he says: "From the word *tri* itself," and so forth.
Herein lies the intention:
The number three is already understood through the very act of differentiation;

however, the completion [of that understanding] is established by the word "tri" (three), according to the maxim: "When something is already established, a new rule is formulated for the sake of restriction."
Therefore, the word *iti* is intended here in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*).

Nor should it be thought that the use of the word "manner" would entail redundancy; for the word "manner" brings about the manner of redundancy itself. When there arises the inquiry as to by what manner that threefold manner of redundancy occurs, the word *iti* expresses that specific manner.
Everything is pure.
The threefold nature, which has been analyzed and understood, is concluded by the word "three" (*tri*).
Therefore, the word is considered to be expressive of this threefold character.
Thus [it is said].
Now, in order to distinguish the portion to be abandoned among these repetitions, the sūtra states:
"Among those, repetition of meaning is a fault rooted in the words. (RuAss 2)

He reveals what is to be excluded by one who has already grasped [the object], using the phrase "by way of being firmly established or not firmly established. The phrase "for the sake of resting upon the acceptable" means for the sake of not distracting the cognizer's comprehension, which is already directed toward another counter-correlate within the acceptable [object].
For when that which is to be abandoned has been discarded through discernment, the investigation of what is to be accepted occurs spontaneously.
Regarding the phrase "in the determination of the three":

in this context, the bringing forth of the substance (dravya) should be understood as following upon the bringing forth of the state (bhāva); the meaning is that once the three types of tautology have been determined.
Now, it is said that a fault is "fully grown" (*prarūḍha*). What is this "full growth"? To this he says: "In accordance with its appearance," and so forth.

The meaning is: if that which appears correctly immediately after hearing [the teaching] should remain uncontradicted until the final state of rest, being perceived exactly as it is, that is "full growth."
Regarding the repetition according to the specific instruction, the Sūtra states:
"That which appears as if it were a repetition is the semblance of repetition. (RuAss 3)
The *āmukha* (introduction) is the commencement.
By the phrase "alteration at the conclusion," the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) from that which is to be abandoned (*heya*) is shown.

Now, one might object: since it is called a "semblance of tautology" (*punaruktavadābhāsa*) in the section on the defined objects (*lakṣyapada*), it would be more logical to define it by emphasizing its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
However, because [the definition] is dependent upon poetry (*kāvyaparatantratayā*), he says "the indication of the object to be defined" (*lakṣyanirdeśa*) and so forth.
By resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which the refinement (*saṃskāra*) does not appear as a tautology"—the dependence on the poetic figure (*alaṅkāryapāratantrya*) is implied.
Thus, unlike worldly ornaments, it is impossible for poetic figures to exist as something separate from the object to be ornamented (*alaṅkārya*).
Rather, it is necessarily dependent upon poetry itself.
Desiring to dispel the fear of futile entreaty regarding the exceedingly profound portion, he says: "But the subdivisions...
Subdivisions (*prabhedāḥ*) are intermediate distinctions.
"In *maṅkhīye* means composed by the poet named Maṅkha.
Regarding *ahīna*: *ina* means a lord; thus, *ahīna* refers to the lord (*ina*) of the *ahi*s (serpents), that is, the sovereign of the bhujaṅgas."

The appearance of tautology at the beginning—such as *valayaṃ* and *kaṅkaṇān*—is resolved by a different meaning in the conclusions: that this [being] has the body-coil (*vapurvalaya*) and the bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa*) of the great lord of serpents (*bhujaṅgādhīśa*), who is not deficient (*ahīna*).
Likewise, [the name] *Śailādi* means "one whose offspring is from Śilādi," and [the phrase] "his conduct is like that of Nandin, the son of Śailādi."

And [the name] Śailādi means "he who gladdens Śailādi" by his conduct; and [the names] Kṣatakandarpa and Kṣatadarpā mean "by whom Kandarpa and Darpā were destroyed," or "he by whom Kandarpa and Darpā were destroyed."
Likewise, "vṛṣa" means a bull and also a man, and "go" means a cow; furthermore, "vṛṣa" means excellent.
Similarly, one whose eyes are like fire (śikhin) and fire (pāvaka) is called "śikhipāvakalocana."

Likewise, in the phrase "the Lord of Pārvatī, honored by all auspiciousness" (*sarvamaṅgalāsahitaḥ pārvatīśaḥ*), there is a repetition (*paunaruktya*)—namely, that he is honored by all auspicious things—which constitutes a semblance of a flaw (*āmukhābhāsana*);
furthermore, one should consider the difference in the final meaning (*paryavasānānyathātva*).
Now, to demonstrate this through a different example by means of a separate compound formed with distinct words, [the author] says: "dāruṇa" (terrible).
In consideration of the tautology, "dāruṇā" is in the ablative case;
however, in its final sense, it is in the nominative case.
Thus, [the compounds] are *bhasma ca bhūtiśca* and *bhasmavān abhivṛddhiḥ*.
Likewise, "raktaṃ" (red), "śoṇāṃ" (the red one), and "rudhiravacchreṇam" (a streak of blood) should be understood [as examples].
Thus, two types have been illustrated with reference to nominal endings (*subanta*).
Now, with reference to verbal endings (*tiṅanta*)—[the example is] "bhujaṅga" (serpent).
*Kuṇḍalī* means a coiled serpent or a snake; thus, *bhujaṅgakuṇḍalavān* means "one who possesses a serpent as an earring.
*Śaśī* means the moon, which has white rays (*śubhrāśu*) and cool beams (*śītagu*).
"Śam" means Śiva; "śubhrair aṃśubhiḥ" refers to the faculty of sight as being cool;
and "haraḥ śivaḥ" and "ceto haraḥ" are to be construed together.
In the expression "śaśiśubhrāṃśuśītaguru," the tautology (paunaruktya) is demonstrated by the three words [śaśi, śubhra, and śīta].

However, in the case of "pāyāt" and "avyāt," since these depend on a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), they ultimately function as qualifiers of the departure [expressed by] "itaḥ"; thus, by virtue of being in the ablative case, there is a change from the forms "pāyāt" and "avyāt.
For the grammatical refinement (*saṃskriyā*) is indeed such that it appears like a tautology (*punaruktavad-ābhāsa*).
This is resorted to in order to manifest the fact that the ornament depends solely upon that which is to be adorned.

Now, for the occasion of discussing the repetition of words (*śabdapaunaruktya*), there is the aphorism: "The repetition of words consists of the repetition of mere phonemes (*vyañjana*) and the repetition of the collection of vowels and phonemes.
Here, the first term is the subject (*uddeśya*), while the latter two are the predicates (*vidheya*).
The meaning is that verbal repetition (śabdapaunaruktya) is of two kinds: based on the mere consonants and based on the combination of vowels and consonants.
Now, one might ask what happens in the case of the repetition of vowels alone; to this he says: "In the context of poetic ornaments," and so forth.

For *alaṅkāra* (ornament) is indeed strikingness (*vicchitti*); thus, the sense is that in the context of such [ornaments], the mere repetition of single vowels does not deserve to be counted as an ornament because it lacks beauty.
Regarding that, there is a sūtra concerning the consonants alone:
When there is a restriction on the number [of syllables], alliteration (*chekānuprāsa*) occurs first.
What is this restriction of number? To this he says: "The [similarity] of two consonants," and so forth.
Here, the restriction of number refers to the manifold dissimilarities between the various collections of consonants situated in pairs.
What is its name?
The *dardura* is a frog;
having compressed its body, it brings forth its form.
The *sitacchada* are swans.

In this context, in examples such as *dardura-duradhyavasāya*, there is a restriction regarding the number [of repetitions]. Now, one might ask: "What kind of ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is present in the phrase *sāyaṃ kāyam*? To this, he says: "In this case, by the word *sāyam*," and so forth.
For, with respect to the similarity consisting solely of the letter *ya*, there is the *cheṣānuprāsa* (alliteration of remaining consonants) in the form *sāyaṃ sāyam*.
In the phrase "sāyaṃ kāyam," there is *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration) based on the anusvāra and the single letter *ya*.

This being the case, there is a *saṅkara* (commixture) in the word *sāyaṃ*, characterized by two figures being expressed by a single expression; that is to say, "expression" (*abhidhāna*) means a denotative word (*vācaka-śabda*), and thus the meaning is a commixture characterized by the entry of multiple expressive elements into a single denoter. Wishing to define the term "clever" (*vidagdha*), he says: "those who are clever."
The meaning is that it is called "clever alliteration" (*śekānuprāsa*) because it is cherished by those who are clever.
Now, the aphorism for another type of alliteration:
"But otherwise, it is rhythmic alliteration" (*vṛttyanuprāsa*).
He states that non-identity (anayathātva) occurs in three ways, beginning with "mere similarity of phonemes" (kevalavyañjana):
similarity of mere phonemes constitutes non-identity because of the absence of being a collective whole;
whereas similarity of a collective whole occurs in one way [only], due to the lack of multiplicity.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the groups beginning with *trya* (triad) and so forth are different because they exceed the number two.
He provides the definition of the term *lakṣya*: "But *vṛtti*...

That function of suggestion (*vyañjanavyāpāra*) belonging to phonemes (*varṇa*) which possess specific restrictions, and which has as its object the *rasas* such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, is called *vṛtti*.

Since this operation of phonemes exists within this poetic operation consisting of the arrangement of phonemes, he says "tadvatī punaḥ" (but that [poetry] which possesses it) and so forth, using the term "varṇaracanāvṛttiḥ" (the function of phoneme-arrangement) by way of metaphor.
He demonstrates its threefold nature with "sā ca paruṣā" (and that is harsh) and so forth.
Harshness of phonemes consists in their being disagreeable to the ear.
That which is composed of harsh-sounding syllables is the Gauḍīyā style; that which is composed of soft-sounding syllables is the Vaidarbhī;
and that which is composed of middling-sounding syllables is the Pāñcālī.
These *rītis* have been established by Vāmana and others as the very soul (*ātman*) of poetry.
However, let us set aside for a moment this discourse on the soul of poetry when we examine the underlying logic.

For even among verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*), there is the ornament of phonemes (*varṇālaṅkāra*) consisting of *vṛtti* and alliteration (*anuprāsa*), which is extrinsic; since these [styles] possess that as their quality, they are merely subordinate to it. Enough, then, with this digressive display of pedantry.
"Endurable" means "emitting a flow of poison";
this refers to their being difficult to endure in relation to their rays.
In comparison to the wind, however, they were like droplets of water mixed with poison;
they were straight, falling without curvature;

possessing white and black luster due to their shimmering pupils, their color and arrangement were unstable; they were turned askance as if striving to emerge from the corners of the eyes; and they were languid, turning back as if out of lingering passion.

As it is stated in the *Bhāvaprakāśa*: “Laziness (*ālasya*) is that turning away from a desired object due to shame and the like. Let them be full of intent, as if saying, “Let us see,” being full of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). *Rasa* [is used] in the sense of passion, poison, potency, the bitter and other tastes, mercury, and liquid.

Smeared with the redness of anger across their range of vision, they are "conforming to pride" (*mānānuviddhāḥ*). Anger (*roṣa*) arises from perceived or heard offenses, while pride (*māna*) is [the opposite]; they are "merged with that" (*tena saṃmūrcchitāḥ*), meaning they are as if blazing.
Here, there is a deviation consisting of the repetition of mere consonants (*kevalavyañjanapaunaruktya*).
As for the meter, it is harsh (*paruṣā*) due to the description of anger.
Regarding the phrase "with ostentation": although the poet's speech may spread at its outset, sporting with a powerful display of words,
it nevertheless does not provide delight to the minds of the wise, for it is merely made resonant by mediocre and beautiful qualities and ornaments.

As long as there is no rasa— such as the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and others— that follows the essence of the shimmering elixir (*rasāyana*) and remains motionless, there exists in all four quarters of this verse the ornament of mere similarity of phonemes (*varṇasama*).

One should understand that in the phrase "bhphaṅkārita" and so forth, there is a similarity of the whole [sequence] in one way, whereas in "rasāyana rasā," there is a mutual similarity between the three groups beginning with "rasa."

And thus, in "āṭope" and so forth, the Gauḍīyā style is to be seen; in "amandasundara" and so forth, the Vaidarbhī; and in "guṇālaṅkāra" and so forth, the Pāñcālī—each according to its respective meaning.
For that which is an excellent arrangement of phonemes (varṇa) is indeed that which follows the aesthetic sentiments (rasa) and other such elements.
That is alliteration (anuprāsa), and it is of two kinds according to the conditions of *cheka* and *vṛtti*.
Where two groups attain various kinds of similarity through the skillful handling of sounds by experts, it is called *śreka-anuprāsa* (alliteration).
The function (*vṛtti*) is the activity of the consonants directed toward the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*);
this arrangement of letters, arising from their conjunction, is intended as *vṛtti*.
That [alliteration] was previously defined by the ancients as being threefold, according to the divisions of Vaidarbhī and so forth;
however, it is here intended as *vṛttyanuprāsa* (phonetic alliteration) because it is characterized by that [threefold division].
Thus, the ornament of phonemes has been shown to be of two kinds.

Now begins the section on verbal ornaments (*śabdālaṅkāra*). Among these, there is a rule for the definition of *yamaka* (chiasmus): "The repetition of a combination of vowels and consonants is *yamaka*. (RuAss 6)

The repetition of a collection of sounds consisting of vowels and consonants in that very same form is *yamaka* (rhyme). Its varieties, such as the repetition of a verse-quarter (*pādāvṛtti*) or the repetition of a half-verse (*ardhāvṛtti*), have been elaborated upon in many ways by the ancients. Since these have become mere excrescences in poetry, they are not detailed here.

However, with the intention that this triad of variety brings about the differentiation of all these [types], he says: "In this [context], in some cases there is a difference in meaning," and so forth.
There is a difference in meaning in both of the two groups being compared, and in some cases there is a meaningless *takā* (the particle *tu*).
