In some cases, one [of two things] possesses meaning while the other is meaningless; this triad of distinctions encompasses all specific instances.
Regarding the phrase "whosoever":
whosoever beholds her eyes—which are as beautiful and lovely as lotus petals and long—[that person is blessed].
In each case, no delight whatsoever arises in other eyes;
this [is said] regarding the two-fold nature—both meaningful and meaningless—as in: "O Rāvaṇa, by the merits of the world, you have become the ornament of Laṅkā."
By him, the essence of Sarasvatī herself was spontaneously increased within Vālmīki.
In this regard, in the phrase “rabhūrabhūri,” there is meaninglessness;
in “laṅkālaṅkāre” and so forth, there is duality of form.

Thus, when there is repetition of meaning, it is analyzed as the figure of speech "pseudo-repetition" (punaruktavad-ābhāsa); whereas when there is repetition of sound, the figures of speech are alliteration (anuprāsa) and yamaka.
To distinguish the portion to be rejected in the case of both types of tautology, the aphorism states:
"Tautology of word and meaning is an established fault. (RuAss 7)
He states the purpose of the mention of "deeply rooted" (praruḍha) with the words beginning "the mention of 'deeply rooted'" (praruḍhagrahaṇam), and so forth.
The distinction that is about to be stated is one in which the repetition has not yet taken root;
its difference from that which has taken root consists in its being free from the nature of a fault.
He confirms this very quality of being free from the nature of a fault by means of the consensus of the learned, beginning with the words "as they say," and so forth.
The meaning is that the repetition of a word or its meaning is a fault only when it falls outside the scope of restatement (*anuvāda*).
Now, with reference to the portion to be adopted (*upādeyāṃśa*), the sūtra states:
"But *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) consists in a difference of intended meaning. (RuAss 8)
Where, despite the repetition, the word and its meaning remain the same while only the intended sense (*tātparya*) is different,
this is *lāṭānuprāsa*, so called because it is a fondling (*upalālana*) of the people of Lāṭa.

Therefore, because it is not universal, some call it "vulgar alliteration," as in the verse beginning *tālā jāgranti*. The poetic qualities (*guṇas*) arise when they are perceived by connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
The lotuses become truly lotuses when favored by the rays of the sun.

In this case, there is a difference in intended meaning (*tātparya-bheda*) regarding the two qualities, "lotus" (*kamala*) and "word" (*śabda*), insofar as they serve as the basis for praise and so forth.
Now, one might object: where it is only the base (*prakṛti*) and its meaning that are repeated, and not the suffix (*pratyaya*) and its meaning—
To the question, "What figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) is there here?", he says: "In this [verse], 'the lotus-leaf,' etc.
Regarding the phrase "of the case-ending, etc.":
for the first word, *nayana* (eye), because it occurs within a *bahuvrīhi* compound, possesses the gender, number, and case-ending of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*).
The second [instance], however, possesses its own gender, number, and case-ending;
therefore, there is no tautology here regarding the case-ending and so forth,
nor is there any loss of the quality of *lāṭānuprāsa*.
Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the tautology of the meaning of many words.

This being the case, *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration) should be understood as being of two kinds: that which is based on the connection of words (*pada*) and that which is based on the nominal stem alone (*prātipadika*).
He shows its distinction from *ananvaya* (non-identity) with the example: "kāśāḥ kāśā iva," and so forth.
In the case of *ananvaya*, indeed, one and the same thing possesses both the status of the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

Although in that instance the definition involves a redundancy of meaning (*arthapaunaruktya*), nevertheless, due to the fear of fault, a redundancy of words (*śabdapaunaruktya*) is certainly accepted.

Because there would be the fault of violating the rule that "the detailed explanation must correspond exactly to the initial statement," and because in the case of *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration), even the repetition of words is a defining characteristic— this is the distinction. This is what he expresses with the words beginning "mutual dependence" (*anyonyāpekṣā*).
The repetition of both word and meaning when they are mutually dependent constitutes *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration of the Lāṭas).
In *ananvaya* (self-comparison), however, the meaning alone is repeated; this is the sense.
On this point, there is a summary verse beginning with "But in *ananvaya*," and so forth.
This is due to propriety, characterized by the maintenance of uniformity between the initial mention and the subsequent detailed explanation.
Where those same words and meanings occur, but the intended meaning (tātparya) differs,
that repetition is desired by the teachers as *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration of the Lāṭa style).
In the case of *ananvaya* (self-comparison), the identity of words would occur only out of fear of falling into a fault;
however, in this *lāṭānuprāsa*, the defining characteristic is indeed present directly.
Now, there is a rule for the restriction of those figures of speech based on repetition:
thus, there are five figures of speech regarding repetition. (RuAss 9)

Just as they remain grouped by category by resorting to such repetition, so too should it be understood that similes and the like also remain grouped by category by resorting to similarity and so forth;
with the intention that this is already understood by those who know the principles [of logic], he says: "It has been explained by the word itself" (*nigadavyākhyātam*).
The utterance of the word *nigada* is equivalent to an explanation, because its meaning is understood through that alone; such is the meaning.
Now, the aphorism is for the purpose of illustrating variety: "When letters are the cause of forms such as swords and the like, it is a *citra* (puzzle). (RuAss 10)
He states the connection [of this section] with the words "the discussion of tautology" (*paunaruktya-prastāva*) and so forth.

The meaning is that the description of the artistic figures (*citra*) such as the sword-arrangement (*khaḍgabandha*), which consist of the tautology found in the recitation of phonemes arranged in a sequence upon specific locations— that is, specific parts of the sword and so on— is appropriately connected to the discussion of tautology.

Now, one might ask: how can this be a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*), given that letters arranged as written characters lack the capacity to denote meaning? To this, he says "even though," and so forth.
For the arrangement of a sword and the like belongs only to the written syllables, not to those [sounds] inherent in the auditory ether (*śrotrākāśa*).
Expressiveness (vācakatva), however, belongs only to those [sounds] inherent in the auditory ether (śrotrākāśa) and not to those arranged as written characters (lipi).

This being the case, although it is not logically possible for the figures of speech (alaṅkāra) consisting of expressive words to apply to those found in compositions such as the *khaḍga-bandha*, nevertheless, because worldly people perceive expressiveness even in written syllables, the status of being a figure of speech consisting of expressive words is applied to them by metaphorical extension (upacāra); this is the intended meaning.

Therefore, one should not think that poets need not pay heed to this [topic], because it is intended to satisfy those of dull intellect and because it falls outside the scope of expressive words (*vācakaśabda*).
He states the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) with the words "by the inclusion of 'etcetera'," and so forth: "according to the possibility of etymological derivation."

Just as the word [“bandha”] connects with each [term] individually, it follows that the inclusion and authorization of poetic compositions such as the *padma*, *muraja*, *gomūtrika*, and so forth—according to their etymological derivation and according to their possibility—is permitted; this is the remainder [of the sense].
It “shines forth” (*bhāsate*).
O assembly, you shine with a brilliance that is the very essence;
"batā" expresses wonder;
you are adorned on all sides by the manifestation of aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others.
With delusion destroyed and ignorance eliminated,
she cultivated her self through those formative impressions; she had cultivated herself with a desire to know the truth regarding the discourse on purity.
Or rather, she is merely clever in debate out of a desire for victory;
therefore, the meaning is that she resembles a semblance of a goddess, but not the true Dharma.
Desiring here to instruct on the method of extraction, [the author says]: "This is the eight-petaled [lotus]," and so forth.
There are four petals in the cardinal directions and four in the intermediate directions; the first syllable is in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Now, regarding the syllables on the petals, there is a recitation of two by two, starting from the eastern petal and proceeding clockwise.
In the cardinal petals, there is both entry and exit.
Here is the summary: one should write one [syllable] in the pericarp, and two in each of the directions and intermediate points.
This lotus arrangement (padmabandha) occurs when there is entry and exit in all directions.
By attributing the status of expressive phonemes to the phonemes of written characters due to their similarity,
the artistic arrangement known as *khaḍgabandha* and so forth is accepted as a poetic ornament (*kāvyālaṅkāra*).
Thus [it is said].
Thus ends the section on verbal figures of speech in the *Sañjīvanī*, a commentary on the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, composed by Śrī Vidyācakravartin. Now follow the figures of sense.
In this context, there is a sūtra intended first to define simile (*upamā*), which serves as the seed for various other ornaments, through its specific varieties of similarity and difference:
"Simile exists when there is a commonality between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, characterized by an equality of both difference and non-difference. (RuAss 11)

That which is compared—that is, that which leads to similarity—is the *upamāna* (the standard of comparison); it is a non-contextual object, and it is invariably possessed of superior qualities because its qualities are superimposed [upon the subject]. That which is compared—that is, that which is led to similarity—is the *upameya* (the subject of comparison); it is the contextual object, and it is invariably possessed of inferior qualities because its qualities are subordinate [to those of the standard]. The aspect of identity-in-difference between these two is the connection with a common attribute (*samānadharmābhisambandha*).
"That is the figure of speech called *upamā* (simile); such is the meaning of the aphorism.
Desiring to explain this and for the sake of distinguishing the categories of the treatise, he says: "The figure of speech of meaning (*arthālaṅkāra*).
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that this so-called similarity (*sādharmya*) occurs only between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)?"

It is not [the case] for cause and effect and so forth. Since these two are established as being thus endless, what is the purpose of employing the word "upamāna" (standard of comparison)? To this he says: "of the upamāna and the upameya," and so on.
This undertaking is made when [the relationship] is pure.

This is for the purpose of establishing the rule that the status of being an ornament belongs only to those things that are well-known as the object of comparison (upameya) and the standard of comparison (upamāna).

Therefore, although the relationship of subject and object of comparison can be conceptually constructed through intention in cases such as Mount Meru and a mustard seed, it does not fall within the scope of an ornament;
this is because it lacks conventional recognition (*apratītatvāt*), which should be understood.

In order to demonstrate the exclusion (*vyāvartya*) of the [view of] difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*), he analyzes the modes of similarity (*sādharmya*) with the words "wherein there is similarity," and so forth. The phrase "as one individual" (*vyaktirekavat*) employs the suffix *vati* according to the rule "tatra tasyeva" (Pāṇini 5.1.116).
The meaning is "as in the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction).
The phrase "as in this [verse]" implies that it will be illustrated [later].

To reinforce with authoritative consensus the statement that "simile can only exist when there is equality between the object compared and the standard of comparison," he says "as they say," and so forth.
The phrase "the Commentator and others" is to be supplied as the subject.
"Sāmānyam" means commonality (sādharmya).
"Distinction" (viśeṣa) means "dissimilarity" (vaidharmya).
[It refers to] similarity, that is, comparison (upamā);
the meaning is that comparison occurs when there is a weighing of both similarity (sādharmya) and dissimilarity (vaidharmya).
He demonstrates the purpose for its being placed first in this enumeration with the words "And it is indeed simile" (upamaiva ca).
[This is] by way of the diversity of its types;
for instance, "The face is like the moon" is a simile.
"Face is like face"—this is *ananvaya* (non-correspondence).
"The face is like the moon; the moon is like that [face]"—this is *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison). "Having seen the face, I remember the moon"—this is *smaraṇa* (recollection).
"The face itself is the moon" is a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
"The heat is pacified by the moon-like face" is a transformation (*pariṇāma*).
"Is it the moon or rather the face? is a doubt (*sandeha*).
"The face is the moon"—this is the *bhrāntimān* (error), because the cakora birds rejoice [at it].
"It is the moon itself, not the face"—this is *apahnuti* (concealment).
"Surely it is like the moon"—this is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
"Look at the moon" is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
In this rainy season, the face and the lunar orb are both pale; this is one instance of *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing).
"In autumn [everything] is beautiful" is another.
"This and that are beautiful" is the *dīpaka* (illuminator).
"The face alone is beautiful; the moon alone is pleasing" is the *prativastūpamā* (simile by correspondence).
"On earth is the face; in heaven is the moon" is the *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration).
"Defiling the face is the darkening of the moon"—this is an *nidarśanā* (illustrative metaphor).
"The face is superior to the moon; the moon is superior to the face"—this is *vyatireka* (distinction).
"The face together with the moon" is *sahokti* (concomitance);
"the moon is not beautiful without the face" is *vinokti* (contrastive exclusion); "the face, delightful with its digits" is *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
"The two moon-faces are delightful with their digits"—this is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
"Salutations to you, O Moon; you are gracious"—this is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
"Anger on the face is not a fault, for the streak of the spot does not lead to the moon's disparagement"—this is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle).

Thus, because she serves as the source for various ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) by virtue of her own variety of modes—which consist of specific types of similarity and distinction—she is mentioned first among the ornaments of meaning (*arthālaṅkāra*). Fearing to reveal her gross divisions in detail, he says: "And of this, the *pūrṇā*... and so forth.

In the case of *pūrṇā* and *utpā*, there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) because they lack the quality of having been previously mentioned as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*). Indeed, these two—*pūrṇā* and *utpā*—are technical names for types of similes.

Among them, a simile is called *pūrṇā* (complete) when all four elements—the object of comparison (*upamāna*), the object compared (*upameya*), the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the word expressing the comparison (*upamāpratipādaka*)—are explicitly stated.
When one, two, or three [of these] are omitted, there is *luptopamā*.

The thousands of varieties and subdivisions of these two have been demonstrated by us at length in our *Kāvyaprakāśabṛhaṭṭīkā*, the *Saṃpradāyaprakāśinī*; and in the *Laghuṭīkā*, they have been shown according to their utility. Therefore, this should be understood from those works.

Furthermore, this teacher, wishing to establish the threefold variety of the entire expansion of similes (*upamā-prapañca*)—a variety not previously established by others—says: "In that case also, of the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*)," and so forth.

By way of "concomitance" (*anugāmitā*), meaning its fitness for being connected to both [the object of comparison and the standard of comparison], the common property such as "loveliness" (*hṛdyatva*) is expressed in a single form, as in "The face is lovely like the moon. This constitutes one variety.
Now, the second [type] is the separate exposition by way of the relation between the *vastu* (the subject) and the *prativastu* (the correlate).
This means that a single meaning, existing as the *vastu* within the object of comparison (*upameya*), is indicated as the *prativastu*.
When there is such a separate exposition, [it constitutes this figure].
He states that there is a further internal distinction with the words "and by separate mention," etc.
Regarding the phrase "merely a difference in the relata":
in such examples as "her neck bent, her face resembling a lotus with its stalk turned back," that with which the common attribute is connected is the *sambandhī* (the relatum).

The neck in one case and the stalk in another are distinct; yet, due to that limiting condition (upādhi) of their difference, the attribute of non-difference, though itself undifferentiated, is indicated as if it were differentiated.
This is one form of variety. Thus [ends] the "Comparison by Corresponding Objects" (prativastūpamā).
Just as in the case of *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism),

the logical principle that applies when describing a non-differentiated phenomenon through its distinctions is also applicable here; this is what is meant when it says "as in the case of *prativastūpamā*."

The point is that the same logical principle which applies when a non-differentiated property is described through its divisions is applicable here as well. However, when— such as in the example "this necklace placed upon the shoulder is like a gushing waterfall"— the commonality (*sādharmya*) is mediated by the substratum (*dharmin*),
then because the two possess a state of identity (*aikātmya*), there is no relation of *vastu-prativastu* (original and counterpart).
Rather, he says "or the state of being an original image and its reflection" because of the cultivation of the relationship between an original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).
A reflection is a likeness;
for in the case of necklaces, waterfalls, and so forth, there is an understanding of their commonality through the analogy of the original image and its reflection.
In this system, he illustrates the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (simile) by saying "like a simile" (*dṛṣṭāntavat*). The underlying intention here is as follows:
whatever similes exist—whether complete, elliptical, or with their various subdivisions—all of them expand in three ways according to the threefold variety demonstrated by us.
Regarding the phrase "great in radiance":
by stating that she is great in comparison to her radiance, it is intended to imply that she is slender in comparison to herself.
This aforementioned greatness of radiance is a common attribute of the Goddess when compared to the flame of a lamp.
For indeed, both of these are minute in comparison to themselves, yet they are great in comparison to their radiance;
likewise, the possession of formative activity (*saṃskāra*) is relative to speech. In that regard, the formative activity of speech is its articulation (*vyākṛti*).
In the case of the Goddess, however, there is the persistence of the latent impression of her naturally established divine majesty;
whereas in the phrase "by the three paths," a common attribute is being perceived.
Nor should a break in the structural continuity (*prakramabheda*) be suspected here.
Because common attributes such as "purifying the world" are so well-known in both cases that they do not require explicit verbal expression;

and this being so, one should understand that the example cited refers to the description of a common attribute—even if it is not explicitly mentioned—through its persistence (*anugāmitā*) and uniformity (*ekarūpya*).
Alternatively, the term *trimārgayā* itself may, by way of the principle of *tantra* (economy of expression), be construed as an epithet of the Goddess as well.

For instance, the Goddess’s possession of three paths is well known, whether according to the Vedic process of *trivṛtkaraṇa* (the tripartition of elements) or according to the Tantric process of the *Tripura* and other systems.
As for the Himalaya mountain, its common attribute with the lamps and the paths to heaven is purity (*pūtatva*).
The state of being adorned (*vibhūṣitatva*) is a complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*) with respect to the initial and final sentences,
but it is a simile lacking the common attribute (*luptasādhāraṇadharmā*) with respect to the middle sentence;
even in that case, it may indeed be complete.
And because it exists in the form of a garland, it is called "garland-simile" (mālopamā); such various forms are to be understood.
Now, he provides an example by way of the relation between the primary object and its counterpart (vastu-prativastu-bhāva), beginning with the words "yāntyā" (as she goes).
This is the speech of Mādhava, whose mind was agitated by love upon directly perceiving the charms of Mālatī.
As she was traveling from the grove toward the city on a female elephant, under the pretext of conversing with her companions, she turned her neck again and again;
thus, her face—resembling a lotus whose stalk has been twisted by the scratching of a *kalahaṃsa* bird against its stem—was borne by her, and her side-glance was fixed in my heart.
That side-glance is the radiance of the eye cast toward the corner of the eye.
He is as if pinned down;
in what manner?
Even though he is violently shaken, he cannot be unfastened.
"In whatever manner" means as much as is necessary.
Of what kind is the glance?
It is smeared with nectar.
For at that time it was the life-sustaining remedy,
whereas now, smeared with poison, it burns.

Here, a single attribute is presented through the relationship of distinct correlates by means of the two words *valita* and *āvṛtta* in the form of *vastu-prativastu-bhāva* (the relation between the subject and its counterpart).

This relationship of "object and its counterpart" (*vastuprativastubhāva*) depends solely on the *dharma* (the property), whereas the relationship of "original image and its reflection" (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) depends on the *dharmī* (the substratum). To establish this distinction, he says, "with reference to the *dharmī*," and so forth; [as in the example] "this is a Pāṇḍya."
Because things such as necklaces and waterfalls possess the status of subjects (*dharmin*), there exists a relationship between the original form (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).

When difference and non-difference are weighed upon a scale, that similarity is called a simile (*upamā*). By virtue of the interruption of common attributes (*dharma*), it attains a threefold variety.
He formulates the *ananvaya* (non-comparison) in a sutra:
"When one and the same thing serves as both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, it is *ananvaya*."

[Objection: But how can the state of being the object of comparison (*upameyatva*) and the state of being the standard of comparison (*upamānatva*) coexist in one and the same thing? To this he replies with the words "with reference to the expressed meaning" (*vācyābhiprāyeṇa*), etc. That is to say: the former form, which is the state of being the object of comparison, follows from the perspective of the expressed meaning; whereas the latter form, which is the state of being the standard of comparison, follows from the perspective of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). [Objection: What is the point gained by the conjunction of two contradictory properties in one and the same thing? To this he replies with the words "but for a single [thing], the contradictory," etc.

"Of equal religious practice" (*sabrahmacārī*) means "similar. The purpose of applying this single metaphorical comparison is to exclude any connection with another similar thing; that is the meaning.
Since there is thus no association with any other similar thing, he states that this designation is "significant" (anvartha) by saying, "Therefore, because of non-association," and so forth.
Yoga is the basis for the application [of the term].
By the word "api" (also/even), the exclusion of other similar things is conjoined. As in the phrase, "O Arjuna."
Utprāsanam (derisive laughter) is the full comprehension of the intended meaning.
In this context, the first two words, *arjuna* and *bhīma*, refer to their literal denotations (*vācya*), while the latter two refer to their suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*).
The conjunction of contradictory properties serves to exclude similar instances;
therefore, due to the absence of such a concomitance, this would be a case of non-concomitance (anvaya).
Now, he formulates the simile of mutual comparison (*upameyopamā*), which results in the cessation of the third [possible] co-religionist:
"When two things are compared to each other by turns, that is *upameyopamā*. (RuAss 13)
The meaning is that when there is an exchange of the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), there is the figure of speech known as *upameyopamā*.
He explains this with the words "by the word 'that' (*tacchabdena*)," and so forth.

By stating that the word "that" refers back to the status of being the standard and object of comparison, any suspicion that it might refer back to the immediately preceding non-repetition (*ananvaya*) is dispelled.
Because there is no positive concomitance (*ananvaya*), he says "paryāya," etc., in order to demonstrate another point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Here, "simultaneity" (*yaugapadya*) means the inclusion within a single sentence;
because that is absent, he says "ata eva ca" (and for this very reason), meaning that there is indeed a difference of sentences.
In this regard, the intention is as follows:
the object of comparison (upameya) is that which is to be designated (uddeśya), whereas the standard of comparison (upamāna) is that which is to be predicated (vidheya).

And this being the case, a reversal of the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is not possible without a syntactic unity of sentences (*vākyaikavākyatā*);
whereas in the case of *ananvaya*, there is indeed a syntactic unity of words (*padaikavākyatā*). Therefore, the relationship of reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) is not possible here.
Because it consists of distinct sentences, there is the perception of a variety based upon them;
another [variety] is based on similarity.
He says, "But this [variety], however, of the property," etc., to indicate that two types of variety are possible.

Commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) is a designation by way of a single uniform form; however, the relationship of "thing and counterpart" (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*) is well-known. As in the expression "like space."
Here, the quality of purity (*nairmalya*), which is suggested, possesses commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) by virtue of being pervasive (*anugāmitva*).
Regarding the term *sacchāya*:
*chāyā* means "splendor" (*śobhā*); here, the state of being well-shaded (*sacchāyatva*) is distinct due to the difference in its relata.
The reversal of the status of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison cannot occur without a change in sequence;
therefore, *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) is the exclusive domain of two distinct sentences.
Now he formulates the definition of recollection:
"Recollection is the memory of another object resulting from a similar experience. (RuAss 14)
The recollection of another similar object resulting from the experience of one similar object is the figure of speech *smaraṇa*.
He explains: "another object" (*vastvantaram*);
the sense is that, by virtue of being mentioned together with what is similar, it is indeed something similar to another object.

Since a property (*dharma*) residing in two [entities] and remaining fixed in one cannot be established without dependence upon its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), he states the definition of inference based on inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*): "Inseparable connection," and so forth.
*Avinābhāva* is pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For, upon seeing a cow or the like, there is no necessary recollection of another object similar to a *gavaya* or the like.
Because identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*utpatti*) lack probative force (*aliṅgatva*) due to the absence of either one;
"excellent" (*atiśayitā*) refers to this speech of the charioteer, who, having observed Lava desiring to fight, addresses Candraketu with curiosity.
At that very moment, the phrase "of equal form" reveals the emergence of a similar experience.
Memory caused by dissimilarity is not the figure of speech *smaraṇa*; thus he says: "But in the absence of similarity...
He provides a counter-example with: "Here, along the Godāvarī..."

For in this case, memory arises precisely from the sight of an object previously experienced, and not from the experience of something similar. By way of incidental discussion, he exposes the hidden fault of *abhavanmatayoga* (incoherence of intended connection) with the words "and here, of the qualifiers of the agent," etc. Since the qualifiers of the agent—such as the cessation of hunting—which belong to the state of the hunter, are qualifiers of Dāśarathi, the agent of the act of remembering expressed by "I remember," and since these [qualifiers] such as the cessation of hunting occurred during the state of being remembered and were thus previously experienced; [therefore, the connection is established].

It is logical that the state of being remembered (*smartavya*) occurs at the time of the hunt; however, the claim that it occurs at the time of the rememberer—expressed as "I remember the cessation of the hunt"—is incorrect, because it would mean the cessation of the hunt occurs at the time of the recollection.
Indeed, the memory is not of the cessation of the hunt qualified by the removal of fatigue and so forth;

rather, the cessation of the hunt and such are merely qualifiers of the object to be remembered (*smartavya*). Therefore, since even the intended meaning is not realized, this is the fault known as *abhavanmatayoga* (non-connection of the intended sense).
Now, if the figure of speech *preya* consists of the emotion (*bhāva*) of love (*rati*), then it is not remembrance (*smṛti*).
However, when it consists of a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*), then it can sometimes take the form of remembrance as well.
Then, as to what constitutes the distinction (*vaidharmya*) of this ornament of recollection (*smaraṇālaṅkāra*), he says: "But [in] the *preyaḥ* ornament... and so forth.
He demonstrates this by providing an example: "Oh, even in anger, her face is lovely," and so on.

Here, for the hero who is deeply attached, the recollection occurs solely through the power of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of his affection for his beloved, which—by virtue of their capacity to overwhelm other impressions—repeatedly manifest themselves.
Not from a similar experience;
he brings forth another point of dissimilarity with the words "In that case also, by the determinants (*vibhāva*), etc.
When memory is manifested by means of the determinants, the consequents (*anubhāva*), and so forth, [it is not the same as aesthetic emotion].
For at that very moment, there is the figure of speech *bhāva* (intention).

By the words "by whom you were seen," the similarity between the two eyes of the spear-striker— characterized by the flowing of blood and the flame of fire— and the two [eyes] of the God of Love, the enemy of the Hero, who burns at the time of the enemy's downfall, is intended to be expressed.

In this context, that which is indicated by the phrase "you were seen by those who experienced another similar object" is not the figure of speech *smaraṇa* (recollection), because it does not produce the recollection of the Enemy of Smara (Kāma); rather, it is the figure of speech *viśeṣa* (particularity), consisting in the effecting of another matter—the form of the setting [of the sun]—due to the curiosity regarding the sight of the Enemy of Smara, which was otherwise impossible.
This is because there is the realization: "By seeing this, that too has been accomplished."

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the definition of the figure *viśeṣālaṅkāra* (the extraordinary) is the production of another object that is impossible [to produce], yet here we do not perceive such a production"? To this he says: "Of the act of producing," and so forth.

Since the meanings of the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* follow all verbal roots, the general sense of the root *kṛ* (to do/produce)—which is the essence of action—is possible even in the context of perception (*darśana*).
As we have stated in the *Prayogadīpikā*:
"Those verbal roots whose agents are indifferent (*udāsīna*) should be understood as having the sense of 'existence' (*asti*).
Those whose agents are active (*vikurvāṇa*) or instigating (*prayuñjāna*) have the sense of the roots *bhū* and *kṛ*."
Thus it is said.
Those whose agents remain indifferent are verbs having the sense of "to exist" (asti); those whose agents undergo transformation are verbs having the sense of "to become" (bhavati);
but those whose agents exert effort are verbs having the sense of "to do" (karoti).
Therefore, it is established that this vision is indeed the meaning of the verb "to do" (*karoti*), because its agent is one who employs [the action].

Now, one might object: "Since the sight of the hero of the poem is the cause for the cessation of curiosity regarding the sight of Smara’s enemy (Śiva), why should this not be *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication)? To this, he says: "In another view," and so forth. In our own system, this is the figure of speech *viśeṣa* (distinction).
According to another opinion, there is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication),
while the sense is that *smaraṇa* (remembrance) does not occur in every case;
for in the absence of *kāvyaliṅga*, the cause of a particular aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) consists in the impossibility of the action being accomplished.
Recollection (*smṛti*) is that wherein one similar thing is remembered from another similar thing;
it is distinguished from "the Beloved" (*preyas*) by the absence of similarity and by its ineffability.

Having thus distinguished the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) in which difference and non-difference are equal, and desiring now to emphasize the predominance of non-difference, he says: "Therefore, these [beginning with] 'similarity'... Therein, he first formulates *rūpaka* (metaphor), which is the seed of those figures of speech rooted in superimposition (*āropa*): "Superimposition, when non-difference is predominant and the object of superimposition is not denied, is *rūpaka*. (RuAss 15)
In expressions such as "The face itself is the moon," the similarity consists primarily in non-difference.

The meaning of the sūtra is that the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) occurs when there is no denial of the object—such as the face—which serves as the locus for the superimposition (*āropa*) of properties like "moon-ness.
He explains this with the words beginning "of non-difference" (*abhedasya*).
The existence of difference as a reality has been shown through the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) by means of its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

Now, explaining the meaning of the word "superimposition" (*āropa*), [the author] analyzes its object by first distinguishing the objects to be excluded: "Superimposition is the [cognition] of one thing in another. For superimposition is indeed the determination (*adhyavasāna*) of another, such as the moon, in something else, such as the face.
And because it resides in two places, it is grasped by both the subject (*viṣayin*) and the object (*viṣaya*).
In this way, two types of *śabda* (verbal expression) are established.
When there is a negation of the object, such as "it is the moon itself, not the face," then it is the figure of speech called *apahnuti* (concealment).
The distinction is that it is called *rūpaka* when there is no concealment [of the object].
He provides the etymological definition of the term to be illustrated: "because the object (*viṣaya*) is made to possess form (*rūpavat*) by means of the subject (*viṣayin*).
The meaning is that *rūpaka* is so called because the subject makes the object possess its own form.
From the section on analogy (*upamā*) onwards, he recalls the chapter on similarity (*sādharmya*), beginning with "But similarity... and so forth.
Regarding that matter, for the sake of confirmation, he says "Analogy itself... and so forth.
[In this context,] "with its distinction concealed" means that the distinction is not denied.

He establishes, by way of logic, the priority of description for *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and other figures over those rooted in *adhyavasāya* (determination), which itself is rooted in *āropa* (superimposition)— beginning with the words "by non-difference from superimposition" (*āropādabhedena*).
[The word] *prakṛṣyate* means that because it conveys extreme similarity, it becomes a proximate aid to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
The word *iti* is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetau*).
Since the determination (*adhyavasāya*) is thus intensified through non-differentiation,
the remainder of the sentence is that the classification of the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) based upon that [non-differentiation] will be performed later.
In this regard, the following should be considered:
whatever group of figures of speech (alaṅkāra) is to be analyzed here, as well as those already analyzed, [should be understood in their proper context].
And all of that [is either] here a proximate assistance or, conversely, a remote assistance with respect to its flavor.
In this regard, although those who provide immediate assistance hold primacy, nevertheless, because they are more subtle, they are explained by prioritizing gross ornaments.
He states their causes: "And this is partless," and so forth.
"Successive" means handed down through tradition.
The mention of "first" serves as an introduction for the exposition of other classifications.
He demonstrates the twofold nature of that which is partless with the words "the first," and so forth.
The *mālārūpaka* (garland metaphor), which is devoid of other accompanying forms, exists in a state of association with various metaphors.
He states the twofold nature of the *sāvayava* (metaphor with parts) in the verse beginning "the second, *samasta*" and so forth.
Here, the word *vastu* denotes a "thing" or "referent."

That whose object consists of all things without exception, comprising both the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), is "having all things as its object" (*samastavastuviṣaya*). On the other hand, that which is not applied to some portion of the qualifiers, but is applied to other portions of the qualifiers and to the qualified, is "partially manifest" (*ekadeśavivartin*), because it functions by qualifying only one part.
He states that the "transferred" (*paramparita*) is of four kinds, beginning with: "The third, however, is [divided into] *śliṣṭa* (pun-based) and *aśliṣṭa* (non-pun-based)," and so forth.

The meaning is that, having attained a twofold form— namely, *śliṣṭaśabda* (with punning words) and *aśliṣṭaśabda* (without punning words)— each [type] exists individually as well as in the form of a *mālā* (garland). He concludes the discussion of the divisions with the words "Thus, there are eight," referring to the simple (*kevala*) variety which is without parts (*niravayava*).
The *mālārūpaka* (garland metaphor) is partless (*niravayava*),
while that which has all things as its object (*samastavastuviṣaya*) is with parts (*sāvayava*); likewise, that which manifests in one part (*ekadeśavivartin*) is also with parts.
The *śliṣṭaśabda* (homonymous) simple *paramparita*,
the *śliṣṭaśabdamālā-paramparita* (string of homonyms), and the *aśliṣṭaśabda-kevala-paramparita* (non-homonymous simple).
It is also "successive" (*paramparita*) when there is a succession of strings of words that are not directly joined.

However, when the metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*) of the subject (*viśeṣya*) is understood by implication through the power of the metaphorical identification of the qualifying attributes (*viśeṣaṇa*), then it is a "metaphor based on insinuation" (*samāsoktirūpaka*).
Alternatively, what was stated in brief—
that distinctions such as these are not elaborated upon due to their coarseness— is expressed by the words "others, however," and so forth.
Regarding the term "servant" (dāsa):

The word *asmi* is a particle used in the sense of "I. Here, there is a metaphorical representation (*rūpaṇa*) of the sprouts of horripilation as thorns; and because this occurs without the accompaniment of another metaphor, it is a pure (*kevala*) metaphor.
"Pīyūṣaprasṛti" means a handful of nectar.
"Dātra" and "lavitra" mean a sickle; "lūni" and "lavana" mean the act of cutting.
Distraction of mind during the night due to separation, appearing twice, and rising twice—this is the "uninterrupted garland.
Regarding the term "extensive":
a *patrapātra* is a vessel fashioned from *palāśa* leaves.
The meanings have been stated: *bhakta* is boiled rice,
and *dhana* is cooked grain.

Here, in the speech of the rustic folk, because it refers to the objects of all the constituent parts, there is a *sāvayava-rūpaka* (figurative identification with parts) whose scope encompasses the entire subject matter.
[The word] "shines" [is used];
the king is a *kṣitibhṛt*, and he alone is the *kṣitibhṛt*, the mountain.
The sword (*nistriṃśa*) is a *khaṅga* (sword), and that very thing is a streak at the edge of a *tamāla* forest;
here, by implication, the state of being a woman forcibly abducted by fame is understood—thus, it is an *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) *sāvayava* (composite) metaphor.
However, regarding the portion "of the mountain" (*kṣitibhṛtaḥ*), there is a commixture (*saṃkara*). With this intention, he says: "regarding 'of the mountain' (*kṣitibhṛtaḥ'), etc."
Regarding the passage beginning with "What [is there] for the lotus," and so forth:

here, in the phrase "Why does he not kill? and so on, the negation of killing and the like is first expressed by the particle *na*; however, this is subsequently set aside by means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*) asking "why? Consequently, the resulting meaning is "He certainly kills," and so forth.
Here, the metaphor "the moon of the face" (vaktrendu) is the cause of that nectar residing in the moon which is linked with the nectar of her lower lip;
otherwise, how could the statement "that [nectar] also exists here" be coherent?
Therefore, because it appears by means of the metaphor of the moon, it is both "transferred" (paraṃparita) and "pure" (kevala).
To demonstrate this, he says: "In this regard, by the metaphor of the moon-like face," and so forth;
and "the swan of the minds of the wise. Here, *mānasa* refers to the mind (*mānasa*) of the learned (*vidvas*), and he is the swan (*haṃsa*) therein.
The very closing of the lotuses of the enemies—which are like the goddess Lakṣmī—is itself the non-closing of the [actual] lotuses.
O you who possess a garland of rays, shining with light therein!
The seeking out, that is, the searching for, of *durgas*—abodes surrounded by rivers, mountains, and the like.

The very absence of that [world] is the search for Durgā Kātyāyanī therein; Nīlalohita is the fuel (samit) for the battles (saṃgrāma), those [battles] themselves being the fuel-sticks (edhāṃsi); Vaiśvānara is indeed the acceptance of them;
and delight in truth is itself [the fire].
While Satī was present, there was displeasure at that arrangement.
Dakṣa is Dakṣa Prajāpati; "vijaye-prāgbhāvaḥ" means the state of being foremost, that very precedence over Vijayā—that is, Arjunī—and birth before her; therein lies Bhīma.
In the phrase "for a hundred years," the accusative case is used in the sense of duration (*antasaṃyoga*).
Perform the actions!
Here, when the learned have the realization "you are a *haṃsa* [the Swan/Self]" in their minds, the inquiry arises: "How is it that he possesses the nature of a *haṃsa*?"
It brings about a double entendre (*śleṣa*) upon the word *mānasa*;

by means of that understood double entendre, the state of being a swan (*haṃsatva*) alone is established. Thus, this is a case of *śliṣṭaśabdaparaṃparita* (transferred based on a word with double meaning), and it takes the form of a garland (*mālārūpa*).
Intending this very point, he says: "In this case, you yourself," and so forth.
There is no contradiction because there is merely an appearance (*ābhāsanamātra*) of two meanings characterized by capability and the quality of being fear-inducing;
or else, let there simply be *śleṣa* (paronomasia) regarding that particular part.

In the case of the words *dakṣa* and *bhīma*, the pun (*śleṣa*) itself is where the comprehension comes to rest; that another aspect [of the figure] is illustrated here is entirely clear. Regarding the word *yāmi*:
*taraṇḍa* means a small boat.

Here, the establishment of the metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) of the body as a boat depends upon the metaphorical identification of birth, old age, and death as an ocean; thus, this is merely a non-literal (*aśliṣṭa-śabda*) compound metaphor (*paramparita-rūpaka*).
As for the term "couch" (*paryaṅka*): [it follows the same principle].
Paryaṅka means a seat or a mat;
vaṃśa means a family or a bamboo;
styāna means thick or solid.
This is a specific type of *murala-uddeśa* (an indirect indication through a wall).
A *sauvidalla* is a chamberlain (*kañcukin*).
This is clearly an instance of *śliṣṭa-śabda-mālā-paramparita* (a chain of paronomastic words).

Now, one might object that in the verse "nanu kṣmāsauvidalla," the representation of the earth as a queen and so forth is not explicitly stated by the words; to this, he says: "here, *kṣmā* etc. [is used].
One might further ask what the purpose of this example of "partial dissimilarity" (*aṃśaviṣama*) is; to this, he says: "and so forth" (*evamādayo 'pi*).
Nevertheless, the distinction between *samāsokti* (condensed expression) and other figures is indicated here without providing specific examples.
In the phrase "the mountains are lamps," there is a *saṅkara* (blending) [of metaphors].
In the phrase "the servants of the earth," there is also the variety known as *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (metaphor by succession), and so forth.
Not only does this *paraṃparita-rūpaka* occur through the method of agreement (*anvaya*), but it can also occur through the method of distinction (*vyatireka*); thus he says, "And this," and so on.
Regarding the term *saujanya*:
it should be understood that the desert wastes are utterly unsuitable for the water that is the nature of goodness (*saujanya*),
and that the wall of the sky is not a substrate for the painting that is the nature of virtuous conduct (*sucarita*).
[This occurs] through evil intent, wicked purpose, and corrupt desire.
Now, in a metaphor (*rūpaka*), since that which is superimposed possesses the status of the subject (*dharmin*), it is logical that it should possess a specific gender and number.
Among these, the possession of a specific gender is pervasive (*vyāpta*), whereas the possession of a specific number is sometimes deviant (*vyabhicarati*).
To the question, "What is the [logical] status in that case?", he says: "And here, of that which is superimposed," and so forth.
True; it is appropriate for the locus (dharmin) to possess the gender and number inherent in it, yet in that regard, there is a certain way of accounting for the alteration of the gender.

However, the alteration of number is possible because the superimposition occurs upon each individual [element]. Having cited this as an example, he makes the point clear with the words "Just as in some cases," and so forth;
for in forest fires, the superimposition occurs upon each individual [flame].
The meaning is that even though [the sage] Kapila resides in a stream, the numerical category of "plurality" is still applicable.
It will be established as a settled principle that, because there is no room for both, *śleṣa* (paronomasia) subverts all other ornaments;
therefore, he states with an example how *rūpaka* (metaphor) is subverted by that *śleṣa*: "bhramim aratim... and so forth.
Here, *bhramiḥ* means the whirling of the head, and *aratiḥ* means restlessness.
Lassitude is the cessation of what is desired; fainting is the suspension of the senses;
swooning is their blindness; darkness is the state of being as if filled with smoke within.
"Physical debility" is the lack of strength in the limbs;
"death" is well known.
By these eight causes, which are indeed the effects of poison, the object in the form of *garala* (poison) is manifested; thus, the pun on the word *viṣa* here is caused by the metaphor (*rūpaka*).
As in the example beginning with "O learned one, in the mind" (*yathā vidvanmānasa*),
however, since the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is established first, it serves as the cause for the *rūpaka* (metaphor).
In such cases, they say that there is only *śleṣa*, and not *rūpaka*.
The word "logicians" (nyāyavidaḥ) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

As for that similarity which has non-difference as its primary feature, it is considered to be of two kinds: through superimposition (āropa) and through identification (adhyavasāna). Through superimposition, there arises the metaphor (rūpaka).
In reality, because difference exists, this cannot be an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole);
and because there is no denial of the object, this cannot be an *apahnuti* (concealment).
Therefore, by means of the form of the subject, the possessor of form is considered to reside within the object.
Because it is produced by means of superimposition, this is considered a *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification).
The third variety therein is designated as "transferred" (paraṃparita);
its establishment is seen through both similarity and dissimilarity.

That by which the subject is superimposed upon its respective objects is the state of being designated by the number of the objects; this occurs even when there is a difference in the numbers of the two substrata.
If a metaphor already established previously gives rise to a paronomasia, then it remains a metaphor; otherwise, it is considered paronomasia.
Now, the aphorism for the ornament of *pariṇāma* (transformation), which possesses the characteristic of being useful to the subject at hand—unlike *rūpaka* (metaphor):
"When that which is being superimposed is useful to the subject at hand, it is *pariṇāma*. (RuAss 16)
In order to demonstrate, after analysis, its utility for the subject at hand, he says: "The superimposed is the *rūpaka*," and so forth.
"The superimposed" refers to [qualities] such as being the moon.
This is because of the absence of utility for the subject at hand.
The subject under discussion consists of the face and so forth;
in that context, there would be utility up to the point of entering into the meaning of the sentence if there were an intention to employ superimposition (āropa).
However, that is not present in a metaphor (rūpaka).
The status of *rūpaka* (metaphor) is established by the mere statement "the face itself is the moon.

Therefore, in the figure of speech *rūpaka*, the superimposed attribute—such as "moon-ness"—partakes in a connection with the subject (*prakṛtārtha*), such as the face, solely as an "enlivening factor" (*uparañjaka*) by means of producing the cognition of identity (*tādrūpyapratīti*). As for the case of *pariṇāma* (transformation): [it differs].

Furthermore, in the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation), that which is being superimposed not only serves as an embellishment for the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), but rather, by concealing the nature of the subject, it functions as its very self. Therefore, in this case, the intention to effect a superimposition extends up to the point of entering into the sentence;
and that intention is effective only when the non-subject (*aprakṛta*) assumes the form of the subject.
But it is not as in the case of a [conventional] form, where the subject undergoes the acquisition of the nature of the non-subject;
this is what he expresses by saying, "the subject being superimposed in the form of the [object]," and so forth. Herein lies the following objection:

Even though superimposition (*āropa*) resides in both [the locus and the object], there is not a single mode of operation for both the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) and the non-subject (*aprakṛta*),

because of the restriction of the intended expression by way of the relationship between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*). Indeed, the object is precisely that which possesses the quality to be superimposed (*ādheya-guṇa*).
The subject, moreover, necessarily possesses qualities derived from the object.

This being the case, if what is intended by the imposition of subjecthood upon the object is merely the cognition of its identity with that [subject], then the purpose of the imposition is fulfilled simply by this much: that it possesses the capacity to generate the cognition of such identity, which is what constitutes its "coloring" (uparañjakatva) function.

Therefore, in a *rūpaka*, the superimposition of the form of the non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) upon the contextual (*prakṛta*) occurs solely for the purpose of establishing the cognition of identity between them;
whereas in a *pariṇāma*, the intention of superimposition extends until the end of the utility of the contextual object.
It is simply the attainment of another state—characterized by the apprehension of a non-contextual form—by that which is under discussion, while remaining unswerving from its own nature.

Otherwise, according to the logic of *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), the nature of the subject would be concealed, and thus the subject itself would not be perceived; what, then, would be the utility of the subject in that case?
And in the absence of that [superimposition], what would be the distinct object-domain of *rūpaka* (metaphor)?
Here, it has been revealed as a secret that even the ancient masters have for the most part continued to follow a trace of delusion.

To summarize the distinction between the domains of *rūpaka* and *pariṇāma* (transformation), there are these two intermediate verses: "When the object [the *viṣaya*] conceals itself by assuming the form of the subject [the *viṣayin*],"...
In that case, its nature as a metaphor consists in its association with the act of coloring.
But when an object, without deviating from its own form,
assumes another form for the sake of being experienced, that is considered transformation (pariṇāma).
Thus it is said.
Now, is this transformation of characteristics (lakṣaṇapariṇāma) not also described by the Sāṅkhyas?

For indeed, they enumerate three kinds of transformation: transformation of attributes (dharmapariṇāma), transformation of characteristics (lakṣaṇapariṇāma), and transformation of states (avasthāpariṇāma).
To the question, "What is the difference between this [transformation] and their transformation of characteristics?", he says: "In accordance with scripture," and so forth.
Scripture (āgama) is the word of a reliable person (āptokti). Concomitance (anugama) is pervasion (vyāpti).
Exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is absence (vigama).
Due to the absence of that [definition], there is a distinction from it.
Indeed, this is not a transformation of the definition in poetry, nor is it proclaimed in the form of scripture or in the form of inference;
so enough with this prolixity.

In that regard, concerning the subject matter of the Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and other scriptures, we indeed made a formal declaration while still in our childhood, immediately following the grace of the venerable Guru: "For the benefit of my own self, I shall know the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Upaniṣadic, Sāṅkhya, and Pātañjala scriptures, along with the Purāṇas and all other [texts]."
For the amusement of living beings, the illustrious poet Cakravartin [composed] the *Bharata*, the *Nīti*, the *Vātsyāyana*, the *Ṣaḍbhāṣākavitā*, and the *Lakṣaṇavatī*.
Thus.

Desiring to overcome the aged oxen of wicked logicians through competition, and being intent on refuting them, I have this other verse: In every house there is Sāṅkhya, and in every courtyard of the Upanishads; at every door are the Śiva-āgamas, and on every path are the words of the ancient poets.
Whatever is recited by those who are envious, dull-witted, of feeble intellect, and by ancient logicians—all that is indeed the drum of the fame of the knowledge of the poet Cakravartin.
Thus [it is said].
O Great King, these blessings and favors from the learned men who dwell at the court of Vīraballāla spread forth through me.

What are they? [I am] the sovereign of Saṃskṛta, the lord of Prākṛta, the crest-jewel of Śaurasenī, the god of love to the Magadhi, the supreme lord of Paiśācī, the royal swan of Apabhraṃśa, the universal emperor of Alaṅkāra, and the supreme teacher of the school of Dhvani.
The supreme lord of yogins, one who was deeply proficient in the reality of all self-knowledge beginning with Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Yoga, and Sāṅkhya;
who had mastered the entire collection of sciences and arts acquired through hearing; who was a forest fire to those hostile to the science of non-duality; and who was a Skanda to the Kali age.

We, whose impetuosity has been stilled by such titles as "Abhinava-Bhaṭṭācārya," "Supreme Preceptor for the Establishment of Vedic Learning," "Lion among the Prābhākara Proponents of Kāvyamīmāṃsā," and "Coyetee of the Disciples," [have been honored] at the gate of the great King Hoṣala’s lineage by means of eulogies, stone inscriptions, and other records.
In this work, however, may the affectionate and discerning scholars subject my *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* to the touchstone;
let us now return to the subject at hand.
And he explains that this figure of speech, *pariṇāma*, is of two kinds by means of the passage beginning with "its grammatical coreferentiality" (*tasya sāmānādhikaraṇya*), etc.
Regarding the word "having crossed" (*tīrtvā*):
*dhunī* means a river.
By the phrase "with himself as the third," the dismissal of the retinue—excluding Sītā and Saumitri—is indicated.
*Ātara* means the fare for crossing;
[he gave] that to the ferryman Guha.
By the word *vyāma*, its measure is expressed; here, it indicates the two arms.
However, the fact that her breasts are graspable by them is presented as the reason for her following him with difficulty.
In this context, it is not merely intended to convey the perception of similarity between the unrelated subject (*aprakṛta*) and the friend (*maitrī*).
Moreover, there is also utility for the subject at hand, consisting in the means for crossing the river.

Therefore, since that which was not originally the subject has assumed the form of the subject and thus serves the purpose of the subject, there is no deviation from the original nature of the subject; this is what constitutes "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
To demonstrate this, he says: "In this [verse], the friendship with Saumitri," and so forth.
The mention of *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical coreferentiality) is for the purpose of manifesting the first mode [of metaphorical identification].

Since that which has assumed its original form is of use to the subject at hand, he says "Friendship toward a brother," etc., in order to reveal its utility as the seed of the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation).

Because the scope of the figure *pariṇāma* is thus established through the employment of coreferential construction, he begins with the words "In this matter, just as... in order to demonstrate that there exists a similarity with the figure *samāsokti* (condensed expression).
When the unstated subject is implied through the similarity of qualifiers, it will be called *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression). For example:

"The moon, with its passion fully aroused, seized my face with its trembling pupils in such a way that she did not even notice her entire garment of darkness slipping away before her due to her own passion."
Here, by means of reasons such as the absence of redness and the flickering of the pupils, a specific quality of the heroine and the hero is apprehended;

it is not merely "perceived" (lakṣita), but is intended as something that enters into the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) and is thus useful for the subject at hand. And that [quality] exists precisely in the form of the twilight glow, the stars, and so forth, which serve as the locus of superimposition (*āropa*).
By this, it is shown that there is no deviation from the actual nature (*svarūpa*) of the subject under discussion.

Therefore, superimposition (*āropa*) extends until the end of conventional usage; it is not merely a superimposition of form according to the logic of metaphor (*rūpaka*). Thus, one should understand that the similarity between *pariṇāma* (transformation) and *samāsokti* (speech of summary) lies in this point. For this reason, he says: "In the same way here too."

If so, what is the mutual distinction between these two? He says: "Only there," and so forth. *Prayoga* means inclusion by means of a word. Now, if both are included by the word, how then can there be the state of being a transformation (*pariṇāmatva*)? To this he says: "But because of identity" (*tādātmyāt*).
Indeed, even when identity (*tādātmya*) exists, the nature of transformation (*pariṇāmatva*) is not lost merely because of the usage "milk is curd.
He provides an example by way of contrast: "Now, as for being cooked" (*atha paktrimatām*).
*Pāka* means softening (*viklitti*).
Maturity consists in being purposeful and an abundance of defining characteristics.
"The crooked path" refers to those who resort to it and rely upon it.
"Following that" means immediately after that.
Regarding this, he states the application of the definition: "In this case, the assembly of kings," and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "proper" (*ucita*), the state of being relevant to the subject matter (*prakṛtatva*) is indicated.

When that which is being superimposed is employed for the sake of the subject at hand, it is then *pariṇāma* (transformation); thus, its distinction from *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) is established.
For that [metaphor] is a coloring agent in a *rūpaka* due to the superimposition of mere form;
here, however, there would be a connection with the subject matter (*prakṛta*) due to the superimposition of conventional usage.
From this, the reverse should be understood for *pariṇāma* and *samāsokti*;
the mutual distinction between them is made by the presence or absence of the *upādāna* (the subject of description).
When the object is being doubted, that is doubt.
He reminds [the reader] of the context for the sake of connection: “When non-difference is primary,” and so forth.
To the objection, “Once the object has been ascertained, what doubt remains? he says: “The object under discussion,” and so forth.

Having taken as a basis the intended meaning (the *prakṛta*), whose characteristics such as the suffixes *ṇu* and *kha* are already well-known, when there arises doubt regarding a non-intended object (*aprakṛta*) such as the moon—and because doubt resides in two objects—the intended meaning also mounts the swing of doubt.

Thus, the doubt that is evoked by mere creative intuition (*pratibhā*) through its application to both the intended and the non-intended is the figure of speech "Doubt" (*sandeha*); it is not, however, a doubt that flows spontaneously, as in the case of [mistaking] a post for a person.
To specify its particular nature, he says: "And that is of three kinds," and so forth.

What is meant by "youth"? It refers to *utkalikā* (longing), *utkaṇṭhā* (yearning), *samaya* (convention), and *sampradāya* (tradition)—that is, the staff of instruction, the rod for the pointing out of syllables.
The goddess is the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgārī) [and] Love (manmatha).
Here, because no certainty is expressed, the doubt is "pure" (śuddha).
He demonstrates the "doubt containing certainty" (niścayagarbha) by distinguishing it, saying: "certainty."
Since it is taught at the conclusion of the doubt, the certainty—or rather, the semblance of certainty—existing in the middle must be investigated.
"This is Mārtaṇḍa.
It has not come from here; it does not spread toward all directions because its nature is that of light which flares upward alone.
Tirastiryak:

here, by means of the horsehood and so forth of the countless [beings], there arises precisely the removal of doubt regarding [the subject's] being the Sun (Mārtaṇḍa) and so on; through that, however, there is a definitive ascertainment of the hero’s form by way of direct apprehension (*śṛṅgāhikayā*). Thus, these are "semblances of certainty" (*niścayābhāsa*).
For this very reason, there is the emergence of doubt once again; thus, there is the state of containing a certainty [within the doubt].
He analyzes the third [type] with the words "ending in certainty" and so forth:
"Is it the moon? and so on.
Because it is stated [in the text] that "it is ascertained from another," one must supply the phrase "having thus doubted" at the end of the second half-verse.

Furthermore, regarding a certain object that is to be doubted, he says "in some cases" and so forth, meaning that even when superimposing attributes, those attributes may also belong to a different locus.
"Colored" means...
"Colored" means brought to another color;
"withdrawn" means contracted.
Here, he demonstrates their state of being distinct through the passage beginning with "here, superimposition," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: since even a possibility (*sambhāvanā*) is perceived here, how can this be the figure of speech *sandeha* (doubt)? To this, he says: "Some [say] through identification (*adhyavasāya*)," and so forth.
Determination (*adhyavasāya*) is the act of poetic fancy (*utprekṣaṇa*).
Some hold that this doubt is based on poetic fancy; others maintain that it is indeed poetic fancy itself.
In both cases, the reason for the particle *nu* is precisely its function of indicating doubt or possibility;
however, in reality, there is no perception of possibility here,
because a deliberation (*vitarka*) lacks any leaning toward a single alternative.
Therefore, the sense is that this doubt itself is like a swinging scale with no fixed end.
If a doubt, by means of the subject at hand, touches upon that which is not the subject at hand,
this is considered the figure of speech "Doubt" (sandehālaṅkāra) arising from creative intuition (pratibhā).
Now, the aphorism concerning error:
"The cognition of another object due to similarity is error. (RuAss 18)
The meaning is that error is a misconception caused by similarity; he says "imperfect knowledge," etc., for the sake of providing a definition.
He provides the definition of the term *lakṣya* (the object to be defined) with the words "Error is the mind," and so forth.
Fearing that mere mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) might be considered ornaments [in themselves], he says "employed through similarity" and so forth. [The example is:
"A bimba fruit on her lip."
A *śoṇa* gem is a ruby (*māṇikya*).
Regarding what was stated—that [the bee] has emerged and settled down due to similarity—the author, wishing to offer a counter-argument, says "gāḍhamarma... and so forth.
[He then mentions] "Dāmodara."
The crushing of the vital points of the chest and thighs is the cause for the sky appearing as having a hundred moons.
He states that even an error caused by similarity is indeed extraordinary and constitutes the seed of poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*)—beginning with the words "even that caused by similarity.
*Vicchitti* is extraordinary beauty.
"Like shell-silver" means "just as in the case of shell-silver.
He explains that this principle regarding what is non-worldly (alaukika) applies equally even in cases of doubt by saying, "In this way, [it is] a post," and so forth.
"That which is an error produced by similarity is considered to be *bhrāntimān* (the locus of error)."
Now, the aphorism for the figure of speech *ullekha* (description):
"The apprehension of even a single object in multiple ways due to the influence of various causes is *ullekha*."
When a single object, through its connection with various properties, is apprehended in multiple ways due to the influence of different causes, there is the figure of speech *ullekha*.
And that multiplicity arises either from a difference in the perceivers or from a difference in the objects.
He explains this [with the verse] beginning: "Where a single object... and so forth.
In that manner of expression,
it is grasped— that is, known;
"ullekhana" means retention.
But if there were an absence of various kinds of phenomena, there would be no delineation by means of mere manifold apprehension; thus he says, "And this is not so," and so forth.
This is performed;
the meaning is that the delineation is accomplished.

Now, one might object: "We do not observe that the apprehension of various things occurs merely from the conjunction with diverse dharmas. To this, he says: "And therein, through inclination, desire for gain," and so forth.
*Ruci* means delight;
*arthitva* means the wish to obtain.
*Vyutpatti* is the knowledge of the convention (*saṃketa*) regarding the meaning of words.
"According to what is appropriate" means according to what is suitable (*yogyatā*).
The meaning is that without overstepping those [three], among the three beginning with inclination (*ruci*), one, two, or even all three act as the motivators as appropriate.
Regarding this, he says for the sake of confirmation: "As it has been said:
'According to inclination,' and so forth."

The meaning is that, according to the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) regarding the intended object (*rurci*), even when a single object has been established and determined through synthesis (*anusandhāna*), the manifestation (*ābhāsa*)—that is, the cognition (*pratīti*)—becomes differentiated; it arises as having the nature of multiple descriptions.
This is what is meant by the passage beginning with "the penance grove" (*yastapovanam*).
The single region of Śrīkaṇṭha alone is perceived by sages and others in the form of a penance grove and so forth.
Thus, the cause for this manifold perception is its connection with various attributes such as being a penance grove;
for in that region, qualities such as being a penance grove exist by its very nature.

Otherwise, there would be no delineation [of the distinction], because it would result in mere metaphor (*rūpaka*). He applies the definition [to this case] with the words: "For here, only one," and so forth.

Regarding the terms "collective" (*samasta*) and "individual" (*vyasta*): when sages and others are described as having ascetic groves and so forth, such inclinations (*ruci*) and other qualities may exist either collectively or individually.
To ensure the purity of the subject matter, he raises an objection with the words "Now, in the midst of this," and so on;
for [the qualities] such as being a "thunderbolt-cage" (*vajrapañjara*) are indeed [included within] "asceticism" (*tapas*), and so forth.
It is not the case that this [figure] lacks an object distinct from metaphor (rūpaka).
For in whichever part there is a metaphor, if a striking peculiarity (vicchitti) consisting of *ullekha* is not possible, then there is no dispute at all;
but if it is possible, [then *ullekha* exists].
In that case, confusion alone would be logical;
however, it is not possible to deny its very nature.
To demonstrate that this [cognition] has a distinct object for one who possesses the error, he raises an objection with the words "If that is so," and so forth.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
it means that which is devoid of form (*rūpa*) is the object (*viṣaya*) therein.
He reveals the seed of the suspicion that [the cognition] possesses error by saying, "because of its nature as such."
Although qualities such as being a grove of asceticism (tapovana) do indeed exist in the countryside,
in reality, the countryside is not of that nature.
Therefore, the meaning is that one possesses a deluded cognition because of perceiving what is not of that nature as being of that nature.
He refutes this with the words "not so," beginning with "in manifold ways" and so forth.

For even that which possesses variety in the form of being apprehended in manifold ways is not endowed with its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), even if it is erroneous; therefore, he says: "But the occurrence of confusion... and so on.

Therefore, he raises an objection so as to distinguish its scope even from that of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole): "If this is so, [then] there is difference where there is non-difference," and so forth.
For in reality, there is no difference between the whole (*avayavin*), namely the inhabited region (*janapada*), and its parts (*avayava*), such as the groves and hermitages.

Such being the case, let there be *atiśayokti* here in the form of "difference where there is non-difference"; what is the point of imagining a separate figure (*alaṃkāra*)? This is the essence of the objection.
He refutes this: "This fault does not apply," and so forth, beginning with "because of the difference in perceivers.
For in hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), there is no requirement for a difference in perceivers.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, there is utility here":
this is not merely a hyperbole.
Nor should it be suspected that the difference between perceivers is irrelevant; thus he says, "And of that," and so forth.
Since this is the case, its inclusion [within other categories] cannot be established in any way.
He illustrates its distinctness from *rūpaka* (metaphor) with the example: "Nārāyaṇa...
[The verse continues: "He is called Nārāyaṇa by those whose youth has passed; he is called the Beloved of Śrī by young women."
The young girls, however, saw him in this very same way out of curiosity.
At the moment of his entry into the city, he alone was seen by the elderly women as Kṛṣṇa himself, Nārāyaṇa, the direct bestower of liberation;
for such was the nature of their inclination and other factors.
Furthermore, he was looked upon by young women with the thought, "He is the beloved of Lakṣmī’s very life," and by girls out of mere curiosity;
the particle *evam eva* is intended here in the sense of "just so" or "in this manner."
And one should not suspect here that curiosity (*kautuka*) is the motivating factor, because other motivators are employed; thus, desire (*ruci*) and the like are not the motivators in this case.
For even curiosity is impossible without desire and so forth.

Having thus illustrated [the difference] through the distinction of the perceivers (*grahītṛ*), he illustrates it through the distinction of the objects (*viṣaya*) with the words "In the same way, the teacher in his speech," and so on.
In speech, he was Vācaspati, for he was an authority and thus not to be transgressed;
likewise, on his chest he was Pṛthu, being most extensive, and also the king named Pṛthu;
in fame he was Arjuna, being pure, and also Dhanañjaya.

In such passages as these, there is indeed only one protagonist to be described, who is perceived in manifold ways due to the diversity of the objects—beginning with his speech—and independently of the diversity of the perceivers, by virtue of [their] inclinations and so forth; thus, this constitutes the figure of speech *ullekha* (multiple description).
To explain the internal distinction between these two types, he says "But this much," etc. Here, he raises an objection regarding the absence of *ullekha*: "Now, this," etc.
For it will be stated that *śleṣa* (punning) subverts all other figures of speech;
therefore, the objection is that when *śleṣa* is present, another figure of speech that fulfills its own definition cannot exist, so the mention [of such a figure] here is not appropriate.
He refutes this with the words "True," and so forth.
True;
by the aforementioned principle, the poetic figure *ullekha* (multiple description) is sublated through the device of *śleṣa* (punning).
Nevertheless, since that which does not exist in its own nature cannot be sublated, the very fact of sublation serves as the mark for the actual existence of *ullekha*.
The term "ullekha" (multiple description) means that [the object] appears in manifold ways due to the power of specific variations in form and apprehension;
since this is the case, its absence is not absolute, and thus it is indeed a distinct poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
To establish this very point, he demonstrates the independence from *śleṣa* (paronomasia) within this very example with the words "yadevaṃvidha" and so forth.

In this instance, although there is no *śleṣa* (punning) in the phrases "untransgressible in speech," "vast in chest," and "spotless in fame," it does not follow that there is an absence of *ullekha* (figurative delineation).

Because it is thus, therefore, in such subjects as these, the ornament of *ullekha* (multiple description) alone constitutes a distinct excellence; the meaning is that it is superior—that is, more praiseworthy—than other ornaments.

In this way, according to the principle of being the locus of excellence for *rūpaka*, *atiśayokti*, *śleṣa*, and so forth, this [ornament] can also serve as the locus of excellence for other ornaments;
however, that should be investigated by oneself.
With the intention of stating that the logical principle has already been established, he says: "In this way, in other figures of speech," and so forth. "Nidarśanīya" means "to be illustrated.
In some places, the reading is "kārakāntareti."
If, by the power of various dharmas, that which is one is perceived as if it were manifold,
because of the appearance of diverse forms, that is known as "ullekha" (the mental delineation).
That which is one is indeed perceived as manifold due to the differentiation of forms; if, by the power of preference and so forth, this manifoldness were uncreated in the world, [it would be so].
