For this [cognition] is not accepted as an error because it perceives what lacks that form as having that form;
nor could it be a hyperbole (atiśayokti), since hyperbole consists in representing difference where there is no difference.
In the first case, there would be no multiplicity [of cognitions], nor in the last case would there be a difference among knowers;
for without a difference between the object and the knower, the manifestation of mental imagery is impossible.
Even though there is no sublation on account of the double meaning (śleṣa), nevertheless its concealment [is not possible];
for it ought to remain exactly as it is, even without relying upon that double meaning.
Now, for the purpose of concealment, there is the sūtra:
"Concealment (apahnuti) occurs when there is a denial of the object. (RuAss 20)

Now, one might object that even when there is a mere denial of the object, as in "this is not a face," it is not *apahnuti* (concealment/denial). To address this, he recalls the governing principle: "only when there is the cognition of another thing. Therefore, the meaning is that *apahnuti* consists in the establishment of something non-contextual by means of the negation of the contextual.
As the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* states: "When the contextual is denied and something else is established, that indeed is *apahnuti*."

"Now, if the cognition of another object arises here through similarity, what is the distinction between this and an erroneous cognition? To this, he says: "The non-denial of what has been introduced," and so forth.
"What has been introduced" (*prakrānta*) means that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*).
For in this case, there is no denial of that [subject].
The distinction [in the case of] "delusion" (*bhrāntimat*) is that there is no denial of the subject matter (*anapahnava*).

However, regarding "description" (*ullekha*), the distinction is not merely the non-denial of the subject matter; rather, it should be understood as also involving apprehension in multiple ways (*anekadhāgrahaṇa*).
The expression "this" (*idam*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) of the action.
As for this statement of concealment (*apahnuti*), its meaning is that it functions by way of contrast with the non-concealment of what has been introduced.
To extract its definition, he says: "Because of the context of superimposition" (*āropaprastāvāt*), and so forth.
The context of superimposition begins with metaphor (*rūpaka*).
To explain the variety of its types, he says: "Of that, there are three," and so forth.
"Threefold" means of three kinds. This refers to the variety [of the shadow of bondage] consisting of the three types.
He distinguishes the threefold nature [of negation] with the words "preceded by denial" and so forth.
"Chhalādayaḥ" refers to *chhala*, *chhadma*, *kaitava*, *nibha*, and the like;
for even by these, the very meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is established.
In that case, what is the specific distinction in the third variety? To this he says: "The former," and so forth.

"That which is this" refers to the denial of the subject at hand (*prakṛtāpahnava*) by saying "not so" to me; in the second half [of the verse], there is the proof of something not at hand (*aprakṛtasādhana*).

Although this is indeed a case of *apahnuti* (concealment), because it is permeated by a defect, it is merely a semblance of an example (*udāharaṇābhāsa*). Therefore, he says: "In this [verse], of the moon," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the hare as the counter-entity":
the superimposition (*āropa*) of the mark of a falling meteor—which serves as the actual object corresponding (*prativastu*) to the hare that is intended to be concealed—is alone what is logical.
However, because that [quality] does not exist in the moon, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not established.

Having thus explained that even an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) endowed with the defining characteristics becomes a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*) when permeated by defects, and desiring now to provide a correct illustration, he says: "That is as follows."
Regarding the phrase "pūrṇendoh" (of the full moon):
pride (*māna*) is anger born from perceived or heard offenses.
A person who is inflated by that—meaning an arrogant person, a world of amorous passion—is characterized by self-conceit, which is an intolerance for conciliation.
Hevāka is self-will.
Here, the logical connection holds that it is not even a mandala, but rather a parasol; this is a superimposition preceded by negation (apahnava).
He provides an example preceded by a superimposition (āropa), beginning with "vilasadamara... and so forth.
Restraint is the subduing of the mind;
by that [restraint], they have been cast down and overcome.
Herein he dwells among the clusters of trees.
But it does not exist in the peacock; thus, there is a state preceded by superimposition. By the phrase "running together," the simultaneous pervasion of that region by fame is indicated.
In the phrase "mistaken for pearls," there is indeed the cognition that these are not pearls,
but rather mere droplets of water.
In this very way, wishing to establish that apahnuti (concealment) functions as a subordinate element of utprekṣā (poetic fancy), he introduces [the verse] beginning with "atra śūnyam" and so forth.
For in the reading beginning with "I think I am dying," there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) due to the power of the word *manye*;
however, because of the word *chadma* (disguise), there is also a concealment (*apahnuti*), and that concealment will serve as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the poetic fancy.
Thus, the status of being a subordinate element to a poetic fancy belongs not only to the third variety [of concealment].
Since both of the previous two divisions are also possible, he says: "But I [perceive] the moon," and so forth.

The mention of "diversity of statements" (*vākyabheda*) is for the purpose of manifesting the first two types of division. In this way, even the three-fold *apahnuti* (concealment) is indicated as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). Now, one might ask: why is the aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*) based on the reversal of the sequence between concealment and superimposition (*āropa*) not mentioned even when [the particle] *chalāt* and so forth are employed? To this, he says: "In this case too... (*etasminn api*).

In this regard, the underlying intention is as follows: although two distinct varieties indeed arise from the reversal of the sequence between concealment (apahnava) and superimposition (āropa), there is no aesthetic charm (camatkāra) whatsoever.

For it is not the mere occurrence of difference that is the cause for the manifestation of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), but rather the occurrence of a difference characterized by aesthetic charm (*sacamatkāra*).
And such charmingness would exist only if there were a difference in the sentence;

however, in the case of a single sentence, even if there were a reversal of the sequence of words such as *cchala* and so forth, there would be no difference whatsoever in the cognition [of the meaning].

Since it is understood as a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) in relation to that action, there is a rule regarding its primacy; therefore, in the usage of *atha* and *śrāddha*, it is not counted as two [separate particles].
To demonstrate the very absence of variety with examples, he says: "In that case, *apahnava*," and so forth.
This refers to what was stated immediately prior here, namely, the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of *udbhrānta-ujjṛmbhita*.
"Moonlight is ash" means the scattering of powder;
"disappearance" means concealment during the night-side, that is, dissolution.
Otherwise, however, your visibility would be established.
"Mudrā" refers to the alms-bowl; for that purpose, there is a skull, which is a "mudrā-skull.
"Parimala" means rubbing; by that, the mark produced by it is perceived.

Just as falsity arises through the implication of meaning by means of the employment of *śruti* (direct statement) and so forth, it can also occur in another manner; thus he says, "In some cases, however," and so on.
[This refers to] another entity capable of subverting the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).
Regarding the phrase "in that [place]":
for when it is stated here that "the crest of smoke transforms into the form of a line of hair," what is understood is not a line of hair, but rather a crest of smoke.
By this, although it is being understood, it should be considered as having been demonstrated.
When one thing is negated and another is established, that is *apahnuti* (concealment).
It is threefold, based on the other words used: by means of the negative particle (*nañ*), by words such as "shadow" (*chāyā*), and so forth.
Metaphor (rūpaka) and the like may take the form of a striking poetic figure through the balance of difference and non-difference;
however, they primarily depend upon superimposition (āropa) in the aspect of non-difference.
Clarifying that very same connection and introducing the discussion on *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), he says: "Thus, when non-difference is predominant," and so forth.

Figures such as *rūpaka* (metaphor) up to *apahnuti* (concealment) are rooted in superimposition (*āropa*). However, figures such as *utprekṣā* have the determination of identity (*adhyavasāya*) as their core.
Therefore, the commentary says "therein" (*tatra*);
the meaning is: "among those [cognitions] which contain within them a determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*).
Now, the aphorism (*sūtra*):
When there is a determination in which the predominance lies in the operation [of the mind], it is poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
Adhyavasāya is determinate cognition. In the world, it is of two kinds: correct in nature and false in nature.
Even though it has these two forms, it is not a poetic figure (alaṅkāra).
For there is no distinction whatsoever between the correct determination "this is mother-of-pearl" and the false determination "this is silver.

However, that which is grasped here as a figure of speech (alaṅkāra) in the form of superimposition (*adhyāsa*)— namely, the thought "this is that very thing"— even by one who knows both to be distinct,
is indeed a form of extraordinary aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*), because it possesses a supramundane nature.
And for that [cognition], there are two possible courses:
sometimes the predominance belongs to its own nature as the determining subject, and sometimes to the object that has been determined.

And such being the case, when the object has become the focus of the mental determination (adhyavasāya), and that determination is predominant, then there is the figure of speech known as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy); this is the meaning of the sūtra.
He explains this by its constituent parts, beginning with "by the swallowing up of the object" (*viṣayanigaraṇena*).
"Swallowing up" (*nigaraṇa*) means "swallowing" (*nigalana*).
The meaning is that there is a denial of the [subject's] own nature.
In other words, it is intended that here there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the subject—which has swallowed the object and is perceived through identity with that object.
By this, it is shown that only a non-worldly (*alaukika*) determination serves as the seed of the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
In order to reveal that which is to be excluded by the apprehension of the predominance of the operation (*vyāpāra*), he says: "And that is of two kinds," and so forth.
Therein, he states the essential nature of the probandum (*sādhya*) with the words: "where the probandum [is]," and so forth.
Regarding the term "probandum" (*sādhya*): when there is a single sentence, its connection is with the sense of the word *tat* (that), which is implied.
Even a word beginning with *yat* occurring in a subsequent sentence enters into a relationship with its referent independently of the employment of the word *tat* in a preceding sentence.
The meaning is that where there is a cognition of the subject as unreal, that is the "probandum" (*sādhya*).
Here, this should be reflected upon:

When one, while indeed cognizing a face as a face, conceives of it as "certainly the moon," then the moon—the object—appears as unreal in its capacity as a face; thus, the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is what is to be established (*sādhya*).

[The opponent objects: "Let the identification be either something to be established or something already established; how can there be unreality in the cognition of non-difference? To this, he says: "And as for the unreality," and so forth.

When a quality such as sweetness, which resides in the *viṣayin* (the object of comparison) like the moon, is attributed to the *viṣaya* (the subject of description) such as the face— in the state expressed by "this is surely the moon"— it is perceived that this [quality] exists only in the *viṣayin* and cannot exist in the *viṣaya*.
Even when there is a manifestation of the non-difference between the object and the subject, [the cognition] does not take root because of the perception of the unreality of the attribute (*dharma*).
Therefore, the activity of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāna*) is that which is to be accomplished.
Now, what is this "attribute"?
And what is its extent?
To address the question of whether the apprehension of the reality or unreality of its substratum occurs, he says: "Dharma consists of qualities and actions," and so forth.

By stating that dharma consists of qualities and actions, he provides a complete description of dharma, thereby indicating that the possibility of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) arises from being rooted in both of those.

For the possibility and impossibility of this dharma are such that possibility exists by virtue of having the object as its locus, whereas impossibility exists by virtue of having the subject as its locus.
This being the case, the cognition of truth and untruth is not devoid of a valid basis.
Why? Because, in that state, since the cognition of ultimate reality does not arise with respect to the locus of possibility, untruth is cognized.
Since the reality of that which is other than it is indeed its ultimate truth; he draws out the meaning already discussed with the words "of which there is unreality," and so forth. And therefore:
Since such a determination (*adhyavasāya*) is what is to be established, the meaning is that in poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), the operation of determination itself is primary.
Now, he analyzes the "established" (*siddha*): "Where [it is] established," and so forth.
The term "established" (*siddha*) constitutes a single sentence as before.

"He" has been indicated; as to who that is, he says: "where, in reality, the subject... and so forth. But when there is a usage such as "the moon is like the face," then even though the subject (*viṣayin*) is not real in fact, it is perceived as being real. He states the reason for this perception of reality with the words: "And reality... and so forth.
The perception that the locus of possibility is not ultimately real is the cause of its unreality;
since this is so, the object as determined is indeed primary,
and that will be described as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).

When there is the cognition of being a probandum (*sādhyatva*), he then explains the synonyms of "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*) with the words "therein, being a probandum," etc. The extraction of the characteristics already discussed is introduced with "thus, in this way," etc. He states its twofold nature in a general sense with the words "and that [ascertainment] is expressible," etc.
There too, he shows its fourfold nature by way of generality, stating: "And that [is] genus, action," and so forth.
[This is] by way of being the object of determination (*adhyavaseyatva*) and by way of being possible (*saṃbhavyatva*).
Now, why is there the inclusion of what is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*)?
Since this is also possible in the case of the subject at hand (*prakṛta*), he says: "Of that which is under discussion," and so forth.
For the subject at hand is worldly; because it is devoid of the interruptions [found in poetry] created by a poet's imagination, it does not serve for aesthetic variety (*vaicitrya*).
He shows that even the fourfold division is twofold, beginning with "each one [consisting of] existence and non-existence," and so forth.
It is of the nature of existence (bhāvarūpā) and of the nature of non-existence (abhāvarūpā);
this is the distinction based on the difference in function (vyāpāra).
Previously, [the author] spoke of the "eightfold distinction" and so forth, referring to the distinction based on the possessor of the function and the distinction based on the cause of the function.
The sixteen-fold division is doubled by way of being with or without a cause (*nimitta*) and with or without material cause (*upādāna*), as indicated by the words "of these" and so forth.
Then, he states again their threefold nature according to the form of the possible reason (*hetu*) and so on, with the words "and among those, each one" and so forth.
He concludes the discussion [of the subject] with the words "this is the course" and so forth.
Regarding that, he states the portion to be excluded: "In that case also, of the substance," and so forth;
"to be discarded" means to be removed.
To distinguish the perceived [portion], he says: "And of the perceived," and so forth.
The meaning is that they are thus many in brief; however, once the examination of their characteristics has been performed, some are subtracted.
He introduces those which are subtracted with the words, "Nevertheless, of the cause," and so forth.
"By them" means by those [factors] which lack a causal basis (*nimittānupādānanibandhana*).
"This type" means the type of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that is being perceived; such is the meaning.

The claim that "the non-apprehension of a *nimitta* (cause/sign) is impossible" is not substantiated by the evidence [of the verse] beginning with "in the absence of *iva*, etc. For if either the non-apprehension of *iva*, etc., or the mention of the *nimitta* were absent, there would be no basis for conceiving of any poetic figure (*utprekṣā*). Indeed, in the case of a verbal *utprekṣā* where the *nimitta* is not explicitly stated, the cognition of the *utprekṣā* arises solely through the power of the employment of words such as *iva*.

Furthermore, since here [in this context] what is being perceived is barren because it lacks any basis of apprehension (*anupādāna*), the restriction regarding the basis and the material cause (*nimitta-upādāna-niyama*) arises solely by the force of the causal motive (*nimitta*).
He states "mostly" (*prāyaśca*) and so forth to show that even the imaginative attribution (*utprekṣaṇa*) of an essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not possible.

By the use of the word "mostly," it is indicated—according to the principle of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis)—that although the imaginative attribution of an essential nature may occasionally occur, it is not to be dismissed simply because the object to be imagined is expressed through a different stylistic turn of phrase (*bhaṅgyantara*).
He concludes the discussion on the suggested [suggested-poetic-fancy] with the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way).
"Yathāsambhavam" means without exceeding what is possible.
For instance, suggested poetic fancy (*pratīyamānotprekṣā*) is, first of all, based upon expressed poetic fancy (*vācyotprekṣā*).
The sixfold expressed *utprekṣā* has been thus indicated:
namely, four types of *utprekṣā* based on genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*) as the objects of the poetic fancy.
Each of these genera is further celebrated in twenty-four ways.
Just as poetic fancy based on genus (*jātyutprekṣā*) is twofold— consisting of the conceit of existence and the conceit of non-existence—
each of these two types is further twofold: that which has a quality (*guṇa*) as its cause and that which has an action (*kriyā*) as its cause.
Thus, there are four types.
Furthermore, these consist of those with grasped signs (*upātta-nimitta*) and those with ungrasped signs (*anupātta-nimitta*), making eight types.

Even these eight types are threefold—by way of being the nature of the cause (*hetu*), the nature of the essence (*svarūpa*), or the nature of the poetic fancy regarding the fruit (*phala-utprekṣā*)—and thus there are twenty-four varieties in total.
By this same method, the other three types of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) should each be understood as being twenty-fourfold.
Thus, each consists of a triad of aggregates (*skandha*); these three aggregates—by way of fancying the cause, the essential nature, and the result—are each eightfold.

To illustrate: the fancying of the cause (*hetūtprekṣā*) consists of the generic form of fancying a cause based on qualities that have been adopted, and which takes the form of conceit regarding existence (*bhāvābhimāna*).
That same [superimposition] is fourfold by way of the nature of conceit regarding existence: namely, that which has an unappropriated quality as its cause,
likewise that which has an appropriated action as its cause,
and that which has an unappropriated action as its cause.

Thus, by way of having the nature of conceit regarding non-existence, the category of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on cause) is eightfold. In this same manner, the categories of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on intrinsic nature) and *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on result) are each eightfold. Consequently, *jātyutprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on genus), through its three categories, is twenty-fourfold. Likewise, *guṇotprekṣā*, *kriyotprekṣā*, and *dravyotprekṣā* should each be understood as twenty-fourfold.

In that regard, within the metaphorical fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on substance (*dravya*), there is a reduction of sixteen types due to the occurrence of metaphors based on cause (*hetu*) and effect (*phala*).
Therefore, from a broad perspective, eighty-four varieties are to be stated.

However, in the case of the suggested (*pratīyamānā*) metaphor where the cause is not explicitly mentioned (*anupātta-nimitta*), there is a reduction of forty-eight types when all possible occurrences are considered.
Furthermore, when there is a lapse into *svarūpotprekṣā* (imagination of the essential nature) regarding the apprehended sign (*upāttanimitta*), there is a loss of sixteen varieties.
Therefore, thirty-two varieties are to be understood as being implied (*pratīyamāna*).
Regarding the variety within this [type] which possesses both forms (*ubhayarūpā*), he says "And this," and so forth.
The meaning is that it is also a figure of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*) because it relies upon the sense (*artha*).
Its object consists of qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and so forth.
A certain word with double meanings (*śliṣṭaśabda*) serves as its cause.

For *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is indeed a figure of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*), whereas *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is a figure of both word and sense (*ubhayālaṅkāra*) and a sublater of other figures. Nevertheless, when it is based on words that are paronomastic with respect to the attribute (*dharma*), this [fancy] is possible and is not sublated.
And it does not mean that both [types of] ornament are attained simultaneously;

rather, just as in this case *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), so too is *upamā* (simile) its subordinate element. To this effect, he says: "In some cases, at the stage of the syntactic connection of word-meanings," and so forth.
At the stage of the integration of the meanings of the words, the process begins with *upamā*.

Thus, although it is initially introduced as a sentence-meaning simile (*upamā*), by the power of reflecting upon the intended meaning of the sentence, the operation of the conceiving subject— the one who entertains the possibility— culminates in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
This occurs through a process of successive ascent, wherein the operation of conceiving expands higher and higher until it finds its final rest in the cognition itself.
Now begins the section on Apahnuti (Concealment).

With the intention of stating that since Apahnuti was previously mentioned as a constituent part of Utprekṣā (Poetic Fancy), this is now its proper occasion, he says: "In some cases, [it arises] from sound and so forth," and so on.

Regarding the various types that have been mentioned and those that will be mentioned hereafter, he says "and therefore, what has been said and what will be said," etc., because there is no limit to their diversity.
Now, one might ask: "If they are infinite, how can they be shown by way of examples? To this he says: "But for the present," etc.
"By way of mere indication," and so forth;
that is to say, just as even those things illustrated by way of mere indication can be understood in their entirety through reasoning (*nyāyataḥ*), so it is here.
Desiring to reveal the order of the topical outline (*uddeśakrama*), he says: "In that regard, *jātyutprekṣā* (genus-based poetic fancy) is as follows:
'May He protect you'.
Here, the quality characterized by crookedness (*kuṭilatva*) is the cause (*nimitta*).

The word "sprout" (aṅkura) denotes a genus (jāti). Therefore, this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding a genus, which takes as its cause a quality that has been metaphorically attributed and which consists in the conceit of existence (bhāvābhimāna).
In this case, although the essential nature (svarūpa) is fancied, it is not the cause or the effect.
Furthermore, that specific portion was not intended to be cited here because it would contradict the order of the enumeration.
Thus, the specific details to be illustrated among the examples should be understood by oneself;
since the sequence is not intended to be emphasized, we do not elaborate upon each one individually.
Here, he demonstrates the nature of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on genus (*jāti*) by analyzing it through the verse beginning with "atra aṅkura... and so forth.
Next is the poetic fancy based on action (*kriyā*), beginning with "limpatīva... and so forth.
He analyzes the nature of the poetic fancy based on action through the verse beginning with "atra lepana... and so forth.

Nor should it be thought that because rain has the sky as its agent, it does not belong to darkness; for even the sky can only be an agent of raining when it is presided over by darkness. By this, it is shown that even a possibility derived through a traditional succession constitutes *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
[The author] states "In the latter half, however," etc., to answer the question: "What is the reason for not citing the latter half [of the verse] as an example?"
"It is indeed simile (*upamā*) and not poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

Regarding this, here is the rebuttal: if the element of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is established through common worldly usage, then it is indeed a simile, because both [the object compared and the standard of comparison] are established; in that case, the word "as" (*iva*) indicates their similarity (*sādharmya*). But when [the object of comparison] is imagined by the poet, then it is indeed poetic fancy.
The word "iva" (as if) indicates a possibility because the object of comparison is impossible according to worldly experience;

for regarding this, there are two intermediate verses: "When this element of comparison is established through worldly experience, then it is indeed a simile (*upamā*), and the word *iva* indicates the common property (*sādharmya*)."

But when this [subject] is not established in the world and is merely imagined by a poet, then it is indeed *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), since the word "as if" (*yathā-iva*) has the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
Thus it is said.
Now, regarding the poetic fancy based on a quality (*guṇotprekṣā*): "This is that very spot...
This is Sītā’s response to Daśarathi as he is setting out.
He demonstrates its nature as a fancy based on a quality by stating: "Suffering is the quality."
Now, regarding the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) concerning a substance (*dravya*),
[the author] demonstrates its nature as a substance in the passage beginning with "of the moon" (*candrasya*).
Furthermore, he reveals the underlying common feature present even in the four examples in the passage beginning with "these are based on the conceit of existence" (*etāni bhāvābhimāna*).
Then, regarding the conceit of non-existence, [the text says] "the surfaces of the cheeks";
"with difficulty" means with great effort;
"of such a kind" refers to those [cheeks].
The excellence of its loveliness, which is to be realized solely through one's own experience, is illuminated;
the natural state of emaciation is [described],
and the absence of mutual sight is imagined as the cause.
For this very reason, there is the conceit of non-existence.
This is what [the author] demonstrates with the words "not seeing here...
and so forth, because the underlying logic is easily understood.
One should not suspect the fault of a violation of sequence, as this is merely an illustration according to the maxim of the "grain from the cooking pot" (sthālīpulāka).
However, with regard to the actual order, one should provide examples by prioritizing the poetic conceits (utprekṣā) concerning genus (jāti) and so forth.
Having this in mind, he says: "In the same way, it should be inferred for genus and the rest as well."
Thus, the tetrad beginning with birth has been illustrated as being of the nature of conceit regarding non-existence.
Now, the eightfold division based on the grounds of qualities and actions must be illustrated.
Desiring to provide an example of that which is based on qualities, he says: "navabisalatā... and so forth.
That has already been distinguished.

Thus, since the state of being caused by a quality (*guṇanimittakatva*) is extremely clear in the three types of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) concerning action and so forth, [the author], intending to provide examples independently of [further] illustrations, provides an example based on the state of being caused by an action (*kriyānimittakatvena*), beginning with "Such as this" (*idṛkṣam*). Here, emaciation (*kṣāmatā*), characterized by the action of going away, is indeed the cause for the poetic fancy of invisibility.
Up to this point, the group of sixteen has been explained as that which is to be understood.

Now, regarding the twofold nature of this group of sixteen— which was previously asserted based on the appropriation and non-appropriation of signs— the author demonstrates the examples for the appropriation of signs by showing them immediately following the preceding examples,
starting with the words "these [are] signs," and so forth.

By taking up the states of being "hollow" and "becoming emaciated," [the author] shows that even non-inclusion is demonstrated within the very examples already cited, such as "as if he were smearing," and so forth.
Here, in the imaginative conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*) of the act of smearing and so on, the cause—namely, the spreading of disease and the like—is not explicitly mentioned.
By this much, the thirty-two varieties have been illustrated.
Now, it should be illustrated in three ways by way of its nature as consisting of thirty-two causes and effects.
Therein, he illustrates it by way of its causal form with the words "from the pain of separation" and so forth.
Here, the quality of suffering is poetically conceived (utprekṣita) as the cause.

In this way, birth and action are to be understood as the causes [of the metaphorical identification]. Since these two are absent in the case of a metaphor based on substance (*dravyotprekṣā*), the eightfold set of conditions that serves as its basis must be set aside.
Now, he provides examples by way of their essential nature, beginning with "frequented by Kubera," and so forth.
"Juṣṭām" means served or frequented. The northern direction, frequented by Kubera, is conceived as the role of the *pratināyikā* (rival heroine).
*Samaya* refers to a specific occasion;
*saṃketa* is characterized by not going elsewhere at other times.
The state of being the heroine (*nāyikā*) is understood to reside in the southern direction.
*Vyalīka* means an offense;
here, the very nature of the sigh itself is to be imagined,
not its cause or its result.
In this way, it should be understood that the three types beginning with *guṇotprekṣā* consist of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the object].
Now, as for *phalotprekṣā*, there is the verse beginning with "of the Cola king" (*colasya*).
Here, the act of seeing is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as having the result of splitting open [the earth].
In this manner, the status of genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) as effects (*phala*) should also be understood.

Since the relation of cause and effect is impossible in the case of a material object (*dravya*) used as a source of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), the sixteen varieties based on that [material object] must be excluded.
Thus, all eighty types of expressed fancy (*vācyotprekṣā*) are, in their entirety, as if already illustrated by these examples.
Concluding this, he says: "Thus, regarding the expressed *utprekṣā*," and so forth.
Now, the suggested (*pratīyamānā*) variety is illustrated by the sequence beginning with "mahilāsahasra... and so on:
"O fortunate one, she does not fit within your heart, which is filled with a thousand women."
Devoting himself to no other task throughout the day, he makes even his slender body grow thin.
The accusative case in "divasam" (for a day) is used in the sense of continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
He reveals the suggested poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) by means of the words beginning with "amāntīti atra" and so forth.
Since the logic is easy to understand, [the author], fearing prolixity, says: "In the same way regarding other varieties.

He provides an example of that which was indicated as being possible even when based on meaning (*arthāśraya*), where a word connected to the object of the property (*dharma*) has its cause in a *śliṣṭa* (double-meaning) word—namely, the verse beginning with "śliṣṭaśabda... and so forth.
[The term] "ananyā" means...
"He is famous as a renouncer" is the manner of singing [the verse].
"Mārgaṇas" refers to arrows and beggars.
To explain the application of the target, he says: "In this case, regarding the subject of Dharma."

The state of being an object of search is the poetic figure *dharma*; since the rest of the sentence culminates in a sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), the *śleṣa* (punning compound) does not subvert the *utprekṣā*.
As for the word "kastūrī":
*rolambāḥ* refers to bees.
The *aṅka* is the conclusion;
the *sthāsaka* is the *carcikā*.
He establishes the nature of the *upamopakrama* with the words "In this case, although... and so forth.
The meaning of the rule is: "Some teachers hold that the suffix *kvip* is added after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*) in the sense of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
Here, by the power of the *kvip* suffix, even though the object of comparison is not explicitly expressed, the sense culminates in a possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).

Since there is no established necessity for the luster of the throat to take the form of a *tilaka* (mole) or the like, its being in the form of a *tilaka* and so forth might occasionally occur; thus, in the aspect of the standard of comparison, it possesses nothing but the life-force of possibility, and not actual reality.
Therefore, the conclusion rests upon poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
With this in mind, he says: "Nevertheless, of the object of comparison," and so forth.

This is because, in the present context, since the existence of the object of comparison—such as a *tilaka* mark—is impossible on the neck of a peacock, mere poetic probability (*saṃbhāvanāmātra*) is what is appropriate.
Because the emergence of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) arises from the act of conceiving [an object] as something else,
he says "or like" (*yathā vā*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate that even when another suffix with the sense of comparison (*upamā*) is employed, it still begins with a comparison.
For even in the expression "keyūrāyitam" (it acted like an armlet), through the power of the *kyaṅ* suffix, there is the cognition of a comparison between the armlet and [the subject].

Since there is no restrictive rule regarding its usage as there is with armlets (*keyūra*) and the like, when there is a possibility of it being such [i.e., a figure of speech], it results in nothing other than *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).

Now, considering that even in the case of a comparison (*upamā*), where the element of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is not established in reality but is produced by the poet’s imagination, the entire comparison—even if initially perceived through the power of the expressive words—results in *utprekṣā*, he says: "And this," etc.

He states the reason for the absence of conceptual proliferation with the words "iti tu" (but thus). Regarding the phrase "gone to the shore," the hurried movement is the cause for the appearance of foam.
In this case, the word *iva* suggests the possibility of a loud laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*).

As for what the author of the *Vyaktiviveka* maintains regarding such a subject—namely, that "since the unreality of the contextual meaning is already perceived by words such as *iva*, words like *chala* (deception) are redundant"—that is weak.
For indeed, even in the absence of words such as *chala* in such a context, the unreality of the contextual meaning is not understood.
Rather, it is simply the state of being a cause for a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*),
as in the reading "by successions of foam" in this very same passage.
Therefore, the variety of poetic fancy characterized by concealment (*sāpahnavatva*) has its sole refuge in the employment of words such as *chalāt* (as if).
Intending this very point, he says: "In this regard, the word *iva*, etc.

Now, for the purpose of elaborating upon that very *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), he demonstrates through the insertion and removal of various words—which serve as the seeds of those respective figures—that the variety of figures emerges; he does so with the passage beginning "as if another," and so forth.
Even when the word *apara* ("another") is not employed, Indra (*pākaśāsana*) is understood as being established [in the comparison], and thus it remains a mere *upamā* (simile).
But when that [comparison] is employed, the king under discussion alone is determined as being "as if" seated upon another throne;
and because the word *iva* indicates that this determination is something to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*), it is indeed a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
This is because, upon the removal of the word *iva*, there is the perception of the predominance of a specific variety of metaphor (*rūpaka*).

Thus, wishing to explain how, within this [figure of speech] which is filled with manifold variety, there is a rule regarding expressibility in some parts while there is freedom of choice in others, he first explains *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause) with the words beginning "In such a manner" (*tadevaṃprakāra*). "Connected with the subject at hand" (*prakṛtasaṃbandhin*) means connected with the object of comparison (*upameya*).

When a cause for a particular property (*dharma*) is postulated, that property—by virtue of being determined (*adhyavasāya*) and by virtue of being treated as non-different (*abhedopacāra*)—is relied upon as the ground for the postulation (*utprekṣā-nimitta*) as if it were non-different; thus, it necessarily becomes the expressed object (*vācya*).
Regarding this, two rules are to be kept in mind: either its reliance on non-difference with the property of the standard of comparison (*upamāna-dharma*), or its status as the expressed object.
If this were not the case, then the cause being postulated would be like a painting without a wall; thus he says, "Otherwise, with reference to what?
He causes this systematic arrangement to be understood through an example, starting with "As if not seeing," and so forth.
Here, the two cheeks are the subject (*prakṛta*); their attribute, emaciation, is the property related to them, and the act of seeing is postulated as the cause of that [emaciation].
Furthermore, in this poetic fancy (*utprekṣaṇa*), the mere paleness of the cheeks is not the sole cause;

rather, it is that paleness which, in the world, belongs to two people who have not seen one another, and which is here determined (*adhyavasita*) as non-different from that [paleness of the cheeks]. This very [paleness] thus fancied is the result of the cause characterized by [the act of] seeing.
Therefore, identifying this [result with the cause], he says: "In this case, of the two cheeks," and so forth.
The meaning is that although that [cause] is distinct, it is determined as non-different at the stage of the result.
For the very state of being emaciated is the result with respect to the act of not seeing;
in that regard, the cause is the motivating factor for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣaṇa*).
The meaning is that the arrival at a state of emaciation by two people who do not see one another is determined (adhyavasita) as being non-different from that [state of mutual absence].
This is a causal poetic fancy (hetūtprekṣā) characterized by the action of conceiving an absence.
He states that "the same logic applies" even to a causal poetic fancy characterized by the conception of existence, with the words beginning "In this way, let it be seen," and so forth.
For here too, suffering is imagined as the cause for the silence residing in the anklet.

And in that imagination, the very silence of the anklet—determined through its non-difference from the silence of worldly suffering—is both the ground (*nimitta*) and the result of the imagination of suffering.
He states, "In this way, everywhere," because this process is uniform in every case of the poetic fancy of a cause (*hetūtprekṣā*).
Now, regarding the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on essential nature (svarūpa), in some cases the subject (dharmin) is determined as being situated within another subject,
while in other cases it is the attribute (dharma) itself that is so situated.
In both instances, the causal factor (nimitta) is sometimes explicitly expressed.
But sometimes he begins to analyze [the objection] that it is not so, with the words "In the case of *svarūpotprekṣā*, where the substratum...
and so forth, and "May He protect you...
and so forth; for here, the similarity (*sādharmya*) between the digit of the moon and the sprout of a skull is unestablished.

The characteristic of crookedness is explicitly mentioned by means of the word [in the example], whereas in the case of "like the shore of the ocean of passion," it is not mentioned because its quality of causing agitation is well known.

Now, he demonstrates the mention or non-mention of the ground (nimitta) when a property (dharma) is determined as residing in a substratum (dharmī)—starting with the words "And where, indeed, the property alone... and so forth.
"Having obtained the consecration"—
this is the connection with "the earth of his enemies.
Herein lies the contemplation of the Dharma.
And it distinguishes the grasping of signs by saying, "here, being situated on the earth," and so forth;
and "as if possessing a mark" (lipmatīva).
It distinguishes the non-grasping of signs by saying, "here, being enveloped in darkness," and so forth.

Now, one might object: "In order to provide variety for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣaṇa*) regarding a quality (*dharma*), let the act of smearing (*lepana*) be fancied as pervading [the object]. To this, he says: "But in the case of pervasion and so forth... [meaning] "another cause (*nimitta*) would have to be sought.
Just as in the fancy of smearing, pervasion is understood as the cause; [so too must another cause be found here].

For no other ground for such a pervasion or conceptualization is perceived; thus, there would result the twofold fault of postulating what is not perceived and abandoning what is perceived—this is the intended meaning. He also brings forward another fault with the words, "And not of the object... and so forth.
If pervasion (*vyāpana*) alone were the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣaṇa*), it would not be logical for it to be something implied (*gamyamāna*).
The reason for this is stated: "because it [pervasion] serves as the substratum (*ādhāra*) for that which is fancied.
That which is fancied is the object of the fancy (*utprekṣin*).

Because it is appropriate to express that which is under discussion precisely by designating it as the substratum for that [action], he concludes that the act of smearing itself is what is being figuratively imagined (utprekṣya), stating: "Therefore, as has been said, like Meru."

Now, beginning with the point that the non-mention of the cause in the case of a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) constitutes an impossibility, he states: "In the case of *phalotprekṣā*, etc.
Whatever is the cause of that result according to the established order of the world (*lokasthiti*), that very thing serves as the ground for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣaṇanimitta*).
If that [cause] were not taken up,
then for what would that very thing, being merely imagined as a result, be stated to be a result?
Therefore, in the case of an imaginative attribution of a result (*phalotprekṣā*), there is indeed a necessary rule regarding the taking up of its cause.
Having cited this, he demonstrates it with the words "of those situated on the chariot.
Here, because the northern direction is the birthplace of horses, traveling toward it is the cause for the replacement of the ancient steeds;
that very fact serves as the basis for the poetic fancy (utprekṣaṇa).
If that [transformation] were to proceed without such grasping (*anupādāna*), for whom would it be the fruit when it is being conceptualized?
Having this in mind, he says: "In this regard, of the transformation," and so forth.
By this, having shown the fall of certain [beings] among the various categories seen as being moistened by the *āśīviṣa* (venomous snake), [the author] demonstrates it again.

To explain: among those sixteen varieties which have their causes apprehended (*upāttanimitta*), if each one individually consists of the imaginative conception (*utprekṣaṇa*) of cause, essence, and effect, there are forty-eight.
If the imaginative conception of cause and effect falls upon a substance (*dravya*), there is a reduction of eight types; thus, there are forty.

However, when the cause is not apprehended (*anupāttanimitta*), since the nature of cause and effect is absent in the group of sixteen, they consist solely of the single form of the imaginative conception of essence; thus, there are only sixteen.
Therefore, there are exactly fifty-six divisions.
Since this conceptualization has been elaborated with such extremely subtle analysis,
he states the reason for it with the words "tadasau" and so forth.
The differentiation of categories exists in the form of genus, quality, and so forth;
although it is extensively established and possesses abundant occurrences,

because it is difficult for those of superficial intellect to ascertain within the objects of definition (*lakṣya*), it is impossible for them to comprehend it even up to its application to those objects.
The meaning is that it has been explained at length.

Now, [the author] demonstrates—starting with the words "And of this"—that even though a word beginning with *atha* indicates probability (*saṃbhāvanā*), one should not mistake its mere usage for a figure of speech called *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
This is because, as he states, "there is an absence of the necessary conditions (*sāmagrī*) for *utprekṣā*."

The equipment for poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consists in the possibility of conceiving the subject under discussion as something else, due to its connection with qualities or actions belonging to that which is not the subject;
in the absence of such [a connection], it is merely a conjecture (*vitarka*), a simple inference using "surely" (*nūnam*).
This he recalls: "as was illustrated previously," and so forth.

Regarding this, there are summary verses: "Because of the connection with qualities or actions, there may be a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) regarding the subject matter (*prakṛta*) as having the nature of the non-subject (*aprakṛta*); it is expressed by means of *iva* and so forth, while the other [type] is otherwise."
That [poetic fancy] is fourfold, consisting of the imagining of genus, action, quality, and substance;
furthermore, it is eightfold according to the presence or absence of the conceit regarding genus and so forth.
When based on qualities and actions, it should be known as sixteenfold;
and when the cause is established otherwise through the appropriation of the causal basis, it is thirty-two-fold.
When the cause or the essential nature is the object of poetic fancy (utprekṣya), there are again sixty-four varieties;
however, because it is impossible for a substance to possess the nature of a cause or a fruit, those specific divisions are excluded.
When it is perceived in that manner, there is no apprehension of its cause, nor is its own nature [apprehended] by those particularities; therefore, this [cognition] would be deficient.
In some cases, this [metaphor] is not contradicted by the transition to a portion of the property through a pun;
it may also begin with a comparison (upamā) and even involve a negation (sāpahnavā).
Now, concluding with *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), he introduces *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) by way of its connection [to the former], stating: "In this way, of the identification (*adhyavasāya*)...
and "in the state of being established (*siddhatva*)...
When the subject (*viṣayin*), which is the object of identification, is predominant, the identification itself is "established."
Now the aphorism:
But when the predominance of what has been determined [as primary] is expressed, it is hyperbole (atiśayokti).

In order to distinguish the scope of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), he says: "In the case of *adhyavasāya* (identification), there are three [factors]," and so forth. The nature of *adhyavasāna* consists of an activity;
the object (*viṣaya*) is the contextual subject matter, while the subject (*viṣayin*) is the non-contextual element.

The nature of *adhyavasāya* (determination) has been analyzed in the section on *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). It is recalled here for the sake of clarifying the understanding—beginning with the words "for of the object" (*viṣayasya hi*) and so forth.
"Being internalized" (*antarnītatve*) means being swallowed up (*nigīrṇatve*).
Therein, he analyzes the scope of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy): "When [the object] is to be established (*sādhyatve*), there is primacy of its own nature.

He analyzes the scope of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole): "When [the object] is already established (*siddhatve*), there is primacy of the identified [object]. The "identified" (*adhyavasita*) is the object (*viṣayī*) whose identification has been made subordinate (*guṇīkṛta*).

He states that the object (*viṣaya*) does not deserve primacy with the words "primacy of the object" (*viṣayaprādhānyam*). It is simply not possible [for the object to be primary] because the very perception of the nature of the object, which has been swallowed up by the subject (*viṣayin*), is what is concealed.
The sense is: "How can there be the possibility of predominance [in this case]?
He concludes the definition of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) with the words: "And when the object of identification (*adhyavasita*) is predominant.
He enumerates its varieties with the words: "Of that," and so forth.
Examples in order: "The lotus is not in water," etc.

Here, having swallowed (nigīrya) the objects characterized by the face, eyes, and body, the subjects characterized by the lotus, the blue water-lily, and the golden creeper are determined as non-different from them.
He explains the manifestation of non-difference where there is difference: "In this case, of the face and so forth," etc.
One beauty is one thing, and there is also some indescribable grace of bearing;
a dark-complexioned woman is not merely a line among ordinary creatures of the Creator.
*Laḍahatva* is maturity (*prauḍhatva*).
It demonstrates a distinction where there is no distinction, in the passage beginning with "here, *laḍaha*," and so forth.
Here, a distinction based on attributes (*dharmaniṣṭha*) within a single object is shown despite the absence of actual difference.
In order to demonstrate [the difference] by way of their respective substrates and their distinct objects, he says: "Just as...
and "Nārāyaṇa...": "He is called 'Nārāyaṇa' by those whose age is matured; 'Śrīvallabha' (Beloved of Śrī) by young women."
But by the young girls, he was seen in this very same way out of mere curiosity.
In this regard, although there is no difference between the aged and Śrīvallabha, they perceive him as "Nārāyaṇa" because of their particular inclination; likewise,
for young women, although there is no difference between him and Nārāyaṇa, they perceive him only as "Śrīvallabha."
It is because they have that very same requirement;
for the ignorant, however, "whatever it may be" means simply that a new object is to be seen, as that is how they have been trained.

Alternatively, it was explained in the context of the discussion on "highlighting" (*ullekha*) that each and every instance of preference, desire, and proficiency [regarding the object] is the cause for the perception of difference.
Having this in mind, he says: "Even here, although [the object] is non-different...
The ellipsis to be supplied is "of the non-different substratum."
By way of the distinction of objects;
[the term] "one whose age has matured" and so forth; and regarding the connection with "beauty," there is a connection with the non-connected.
In this case, there is a lack of connection regarding the relation to the dharma because it rests upon a single creator.
Now, in order to demonstrate that it also rests upon different creators, he says: "Or, for example...
[referring to] "at the beginning of its creation."
The phrase "having erotic sentiment as its sole flavor" (śṛṅgāraikarasaḥ) is to be connected with each [element]. In the expression "a flower on a sprout" (puṣpaṃ pravāle),
although there is no direct connection between the flower and the sprout and so forth, a connection is established through the possibility implied by the word "yadi" (if).
This is because, at the time of flowering, the state of being a sprout has departed.
Nor should it be thought that this is merely a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on the predominance of the activity of imagination;
for in the syntactically connected sentence "therefore he would imitate," the predominance belongs to the object of the identification (*adhyavasita*).
Therefore, this is a hyperbole (atiśayokti) supported by a poetic fancy (utprekṣā).

Bearing this in mind, he says: "In this case, there is a connection [of identity] through a supposition. Now, even without the mention of poetic fancy, he provides an example of a connection where none exists: "The burning is water; the spreading is fire."

Here, although there is no actual relation [of cause and effect], the emission of water from bodies that are burning, steaming, and gasping, and the whiteness resulting from immersion in the flickering of the lamp-flame as it is observed to be melting due to the heat, are stated as established facts.
This is what is expressed by the words "here, of the burning and so forth," etc.
Regarding the subversion of the temporal sequence between cause and effect, he states the two-fold division with the words "cause and effect," etc.
The reversal of the effect is its occurrence at a prior time;
this is the "heart.
In this context, the heart being presided over by Dayitā is the cause for the flower-bowed god's arrow being presided over [by her].
Furthermore, a cause is that which exists at a fixed time prior [to its effect];
since it is presented here in a different manner, there is a reversal of the sequence [of cause and effect].
[The term] "uninterrupted" (avirala) [is used].
The *nīpa* is the *kadamba* tree;
the onset of the rainy season is the cause of death for the wives of travelers.
By the two past participles here—"arrived" (*āyāta*) and "dead" (*mṛtā*)—the simultaneity of these two events is expressed.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that a discussion of non-difference and so forth is incoherent when there is difference? To this he says: "In these five.
The meaning is that it takes as its objective domain that which transcends the world, characterized by its excellence over the world.
Therefore, the primary sense of identity within difference is not what is intended here. This is the point.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the definition of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) is the determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*) where there is difference?

Therefore, [the definition] is too narrow (*avyāpaka*), as it does not apply to cases such as 'difference where there is non-difference' and so forth? To this, he replies with the words "And here, that which is called *atiśaya*," etc.

Here, when there is difference, the determination of non-difference and so forth—which is the result called *atiśaya* and serves as the motivating cause (*prayojaka*) for the hyperbole—is present; therein lies the determination of non-difference.
But not [the comparison] of two things that possess the actual fruit.
He demonstrates this with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*) and so forth:
the natural beauty established by the actual nature of things (*vastuvṛtta-siddha*) in speech and the like is [compared] with the beauty of lotuses and the like provided by the poet.

The basis for speaking of non-difference where there is difference—namely, that which is determined as non-different through the absence of distinction—is the determination of non-difference between the lotus and the face, and so forth; this [determination] can be applied.

If that were the case, there would be the fault of over-extension (*avyāpti*); therefore, he says: "Difference in non-difference," and so on. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of "non-connection in connection" is intended.
Regarding the phrase "in the modes" (*prakāreṣu*):
the plural number refers to its internal subdivisions.
For when there is a description of difference despite an actual non-difference, there is certainly no determination of non-difference between the two fruits.
However, since the result (*phala*) in that case is also determined as being non-different [from the cause], he says: "In 'another loveliness' (*aṇṇaṃ laḍahattaṇaaṃ*), etc.

For in such cases as "another loveliness," there is no difference whatsoever between that established loveliness which is the actual object and that superior [loveliness] presented by the poet as something distinct.
However, there is a distinction between the two fruits [of the simile] only insofar as they are produced by the Creator (Prajāpati) and by the Poet respectively.
This same principle applies here as well to the figure of speech known as *asambandha* (non-connection), as he states: "the same elsewhere.

In that case too, in verses such as "lāvaṇyadraviṇa... and so on, there is indeed a non-connection regarding the Creator's relation to the wealth of beauty; however, this does not mean that the slender maiden lacks her own innate beauty, which is bestowed by the Poet and related to the Creator.
The connection between the two [types of] beauty is as follows;
one should understand that this is also the case in the verse beginning with "In the creation of her...
It is said, "only by intending that [result]," etc., because the defining characteristic, which has been determined to be primary, exists solely with the intention of the result.

Now, wishing to analyze once more the manner in which cause and effect are characterized, he says "the fivefold manner" (*prakārapañcaka*) and so forth, in order to dispel the suspicion of redundancy.

Because it serves as the locus of the state of being an effect, there is a connection even in that case; and since it is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*), it is not meaningless. Thus everything is clear.
For the determination of non-difference occurs with respect to the result, which is designated as excellence (*atiśaya*).
Furthermore, it is not the case that the non-difference of the two possessors of the fruit is not established there.

Now, concluding the two figures of speech based on *adhyavasāya* (poetic identification) and desiring to treat another category (*dharma*), he says: "In this way, by means of the basis of *adhyavasāya*" and so forth.
Even among those based on implied comparison (*gamyamāna-aupamya*), he treats that pair which deserves primacy by virtue of its logic—therein, too, by means of the words "padārtha" and so forth.
Among these, the first sūtra concerns *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing).

When a comparison is implied through the connection of a common attribute belonging to the meanings of words—whether those things are the subject at hand (prastuta) or not—the figure is Equal Pairing (tulyayogitā).
Regarding the intelligibility of the comparison (*aupamya*), there are two governing conditions: its being inherent in the meanings of the words (*padārthagatatvena*).
Furthermore, he explains the definition as "in the absence of the use of *iva* and so forth," and so on.
There are two domains: those that are contextual (*prākaraṇika*) and those that are non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*).
The two properties are quality (guṇa) and action (kriyā);
therefore, a fourfold classification should be understood.
Among the contextual subjects, there is a connection with qualities.
And there is a connection with an action;
likewise [it applies] to those not under discussion.
For the connection with an action of similar quality is indeed "equal conjunction" (*tulyayogitā*).
He reveals this etymology [of the word *sajjā*]: "anvitārthā" means "possessing a corresponding meaning"; it is "anvarthā. It is "sajjā."
He reveals this etymology [of the word *saṃjñā*]: "anvitārthā" means that its meaning is consistent with its derivation; it is "anvarthā. It is "saṃjñā."
The days were adorned with clusters of well-prepared sunshades,
while the lotuses possessed well-formed petals that were born in abundance; among them, some were of a pale yellow hue.
But elsewhere, it is the flower [that is meant].
He demonstrates that [the word] has as its object the subject matter at hand and is connected with the action, stating: "here, it is a description of the season," and so forth.
The season is summer.
Regarding the qualities among those subjects under discussion, he says, "In the same way, even with respect to a quality.
As for the term "yoga-band" (*yogapaṭṭa*),
since austerity (*tapas*) is the topic at hand, the yoga-band and other such items are relevant to the context.
Propriety is connected with the nature of conceit regarding qualities; for there is the challenge: "If they are appropriate, then let them be so called.
By this, the variety consisting of conceit regarding the existence or non-existence of qualities and actions is also indicated.
"Run, O white horse!"— thus [was it said]. The dust that had fallen upon the face of the King of Gūrjara, who was defeated by Aśvapṛtanā,
was wiped away by a certain slender woman out of compassion.
But fame, through your sword-blade,
demonstrates a connection with an action whose object is non-contextual— here, "with respect to the Gūrjara," and so forth.
Because of the expression "even by a mere day" in comparison to the Gūrjara, the slenderness [of the sword-blade] is non-contextual.
Regarding the description of the *asilatā* (sword-blade), however, because its subject is the hero being described:
"tvadaṅga" means that for everyone who beholds the softness of your limbs, the hardness of the *mālatī* flowers and the like appears in their minds. This is the sense.
In this instance, there is a connection with the quality of hardness (*kaṭhoratva*) in non-contextual objects such as the *mālatī* flower and others.
He concludes the discussion on *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) with the words "Thus, this... [evameṣā].
Alternatively, *tulyayogitā* is to be understood when it occurs among contextual objects or among other [non-contextual] ones.
Because it is connected with qualities and actions, and because it is common [to many], it possesses a composite meaning.
Now, by way of introducing the figure of speech *dīpaka* through its connection [with the preceding], he introduces it with the words "of the relevant and the irrelevant," and so forth.
Now the aphorism: *Dīpaka*, however, [consists] in the [simultaneous] application of the relevant and the irrelevant. (RuAss 24)

The phrase "connection with a common property" (*samānadharmābhisaṃbandha*) is supplied [from the previous context]. Recalling the governing topic (*adhikāra*), he explains it with the words beginning "of the comparison" (*aupamyasya*) and so forth.
Here, both the contextual (*prākaraṇika*) and the non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*) are taken up.
In these cases, a common attribute established in one instance benefits the other;
therefore, because it provides assistance through the nature of illumination, this is considered "lamp-like," and thus it is called *dīpaka*.
This is what was stated by the words beginning with "the contextual and the non-contextual," and so forth.
He states that the understandability of the comparison is just as before, saying "because of the use of *tatra*, *iva*, and so forth.
Furthermore, he says "and that," etc., because the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*) here is distinct from *tulyayogitā* (parallelism),
since it is real (*vāstava*) due to the presence of both contextual and non-contextual subjects.
In the preceding case of *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing),
[the distinction] is "intentional" (*vaivakṣika*), established by the speaker's intention.
The reason for this intentionality is stated as "purely contextual" (*śuddhaprākaraṇika*) and so forth.
For when [the object] is purely contextual, its status as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is real;
but when it is purely non-contextual, its status is that of the object of comparison (*upameya*).
This very point is clarified by the passage beginning with "being contextual" (*prākaraṇikatva*), and so forth.

Now, one might ask: if the connection with the action pertains to each individual [element], how can it be said to reside in the "object" (*padārtha*)? To this he says: "of many [elements] by a single action," and so forth.
The meaning is that because the property being connected is unitary, it is metaphorically designated as the "object.
Therefore, since the status of residing in the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is real, he states "in reality," and so forth, to show that the threefold classification is logically established.
It remains thus:
O Lord of Men, the sky shines by means of the sun, poetry by its aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), youth by its vigor,
the ocean by its nectar, and this world by you.
The lord of rivers is the ocean; this is the meaning.
Since this [simile] pertains to the action mentioned in the opening sentence, it is an *ādādīdīpaka* (an illuminator starting from the beginning).
He causes it to move.
"Abode" (*nilaya*) means a house and also the setting [of the sun].
"Coral-red" (*pallavarāga*) refers to a specific kind of ruby (*māṇikya*) or a deep, fixed dye (*yogāḍharāga*).
This too is an "illuminator of the beginning" (*ādidīpaka*); it is used to indicate that the status of being the first word is the governing factor for the action— (as in the phrase) "(yathā vā)"—
(meaning) "uneven" (*viṣama*).
This is the "middle-illuminator" (*etanmadhyadīpakam*),
because the verb is placed in the middle of the sentence,
as in the phrase *kivaṇāṇa* ("of the miserly").
The wealth of the miserly, the jewel on the hood of serpents, the manes of lions,
the breasts of women who protect their families— how can these things be touched by those who have attained immortality?
The meaning is that they do not touch life. He concludes the triad of illuminating actions with the words "evam eka" (thus, one).
Following this very principle, he speaks in order to illustrate the *kārakadīpaka* (the illuminator of grammatical factors), saying: "And here, 'just as' (*yathā*), etc.
[He says] "of the virtuous" (*sādhūnām*) to explain the nature of the *kārakadīpaka*, stating: "because of the instrument (*upakaraṇāt*) in this case."
He states that *mālādīpaka* (garland-like illuminator) will be discussed in another context, saying: "But by way of a different shadow [of meaning]...

*Dīpaka* (the illuminator) is a literal simile based on both the relevant (*prakṛta*) and the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*), occurring in initial, middle, or final sentences through the distinction of action (*kriyā*) and agent (*kāraka*).
Alternatively, he defines *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) as residing in the meaning of the sentence:
"When a common property residing in the meaning of a sentence is stated separately in two sentences, it is *prativastūpamā*. (RuAss 25)
He states the connection with the words "padārthārabdhe" (composed of word-meanings).

Here, in order to dispel the suspicion that there might be various [other] ornaments [involved], he analyzes the scope [of this figure] with the words "tatra sāmānyadharmasya" and so forth. Having taken as examples [the particles] "iva" and others, the simultaneous mention of a common property (*sāmānyadharma*) has been illustrated only in the case of *upamā* (simile), as in: "like a lamp with a great, blazing crest."
Even when there is a repeated description through the relation of "thing-to-thing" (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*) by employing particles such as *iva*, it is still that same [simile].

However, when there is a single description without employing *iva* and so forth— whether the subject (*prastuta*) and the correlate (*aprastuta*) are presented collectively, in which case it is *dīpaka*,
or likewise individually, in which case it is *tulyayogitā*.
Both of these have been demonstrated immediately above.
Furthermore, when there is repeated instruction, there are two possible modes: either the nature of a pure universal form, or the relationship between an original image and its reflection.

"Pure universality" (*śuddhasāmānyatva*) refers to the separate designation of a property (*dharma*) based solely on the difference between its relata. Similarly, when terms such as "as if" (*iva*) are not employed, it is a "simile by correspondence" (*prativastūpamā*).
He explains the simile by correspondence with the words beginning with "of the word *vastu*," and so forth.
In this context, the word *vastu* refers to the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*).
Simile (*upamā*), however, is similarity; it is called by its etymological name because it occurs with respect to each individual sentence-meaning.

Now, if the nature of *dharma* consists in being repeatedly described as a pure universal form, then what is the purpose of another synonym? To this he says: "Only in poetry," and so forth. When there is a repetition of that very same [term] in the absence of the relationship between a primary statement (*uddeśa*) and its subsequent specification (*pratinirdeśa*), then, in the absence of another synonym, the fault of being "unrenewed" (*anavīkṛta*) would occur.
Therefore, it is the convention of poetics that there should be a separate mention by means of a different synonym;
this is the domain of *prativastūpamā* (the simile based on a parallel fact).
Now, when there is a relationship of image and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) with respect to the substrata (*dharmi*), [it is *dṛṣṭānta*].
Then he says, "The example will be stated," beginning with "In the second manner," and so forth.
He recalls the section on similarity by saying, "Thus, in this way, through comparison," and so forth.
[He mentions] "the cakorī birds."
"Āvantya" means those originating from Avanti.

He demonstrates that *dharma* has the nature of a pure universal (*sāmānya*) and is also a synonym for another term by saying "herein lies skillfulness," and so forth. To indicate a different variety [of expression], he says "not only," and so forth.
For the sake of brevity, he first demonstrates the same example by way of contrast [with the previous one], beginning with "vināvantīḥ":

"It should be known as *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) because of the similarity between the meanings of two distinct sentences, due to the non-inclusion of words such as 'iva' and the like, even though the property (*dharma*) is stated more than once."
Now he provides a scriptural illustration for that as well: "The illustration for its explanation by way of the original image and its reflection. (RuAss 26)
He explains: "Not only for him," and so forth.
He states the twofold nature according to the principle of *prativastūpamā* (simile by correspondence): "This one also," and "the ocean has been crossed."
"Unwearied in the guru’s household" means having become solely dependent upon him through constant service.

Here, there is a relationship of original and reflection between many monkey-warriors and Mount Manthācala with respect to their shared duty (*dharma*). There is also a relationship of shared duty between the service of divine speech and the crossing of the ocean, as well as between being unwearied in service to the guru and being submerged in the netherworld (*pātāla*).

[Objection: But since "knows" (*jānāti*) and "you should know" (*jānīta*) are mentioned as distinct from "knowledge" (*jñāna*), how can this be cited as an example? To this, he says: "In this case, although... and so forth. [He states:
"This is not the basis. For it is not intended that the analogy has knowledge as its basis.
This is because knowledge is used figuratively [in that case].
However, where there is an intention to speak [of it as such], nothing is lacking; therefore, he says: "And that which is the basis," and so forth.
This refers to similarity (*sādharmya*).
And as for the word *kṛtam*:
the meaning is that when pride was directed toward your mind by you, the enemies were destroyed at that very moment.
The two *ca*s (conjunctions) indicate the identity of form and time between the two actions, because of this.
He illustrates the reflection by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) with the words "because of being placed here," and so forth.
Being cast down and being made to face pride are stated by way of agreement (anvaya),
while being situated in darkness and being the crest of the mountain of sunrise are stated by way of difference (vyatireka).

Because of the introductory statement "not as long as," there is a reflection by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) in the teaching of the property-bearer (dharmin) and its properties (dharma) according to the principle of the original object and its reflection.
The ornament of illustration (dṛṣṭāntālaṅkāra) should be known as that which rests upon the meaning of distinct sentences.
He provides a definition of *nidarśanā*: "The production of a reflection, understood through a connection with a real entity—whether possible or impossible—is *nidarśanā*. (RuAss 27)
He states the connection: "a reflection," etc.
He explains it with the words: "there, in some cases," and so forth.
"Connection with a real entity" (vastu-sambandha) means a connection with the meaning of a sentence (vākya-artha).
Thus, this [figure] is of two kinds: that involving a possible connection with a real object and that involving an impossible connection with a real object—[as described in the] *Cūḍāmaṇi*.
For example: "The mountain, making known to the virtuous that hospitality—the honoring of guests—must be performed toward the sun who has arrived as a guest, supports him."

He explains this as follows: "He causes [the mountain] to understand" (*bodhayati*) means "he places [himself] in a state of understanding. The term *ācārya* (teacher) is applied to the mountain because it is capable of causing understanding; even though the mountain is insentient, just as one says "the fire of cow-dung teaches," the mountain renders the householder capable of the act of understanding, and thus the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is employed to express the exercise of that capacity.
A connection with the actual entity is possible;
"may he protect" means that Śiva may protect.

"In which the moon touches the playfulness of the god of love's bow"—since it is impossible for the playfulness belonging to one thing to be touched by another, this is an *asaṃbhavadvastusaṃbandhā* (a connection between things that cannot possibly exist).
[Objection: In that case, would this not simply be a *asaṅgati* (inconsistency)? To this he says: "Playfulness similar to [that] playfulness," and so forth.
Because it relies on secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), it is not far removed [from its primary meaning].
To state another variety, he says "this too" and so forth.
Because it is connected with the same action as that which was just cited, it functions as a word-meaning (padārtha).
Regarding the phrase "at your feet":

since the jewels of the [toe]nails are naturally red, the application of lacquer (*alaktaka*) itself does not serve as a means of whitening; therefore, he says "some," etc., to indicate that those who entertain the notion of this being an illustrative example are dull-witted.
He states that when there is independence from the sentence-meaning, it is an example (*dṛṣṭānta*);
but when there is dependence, it is an illustration (*nidarśana*), as in the passage beginning with "where, however, in the context...

The meaning is that by means of resorting to the unity of the sentence—through the superimposition [of the qualities] in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—it is brought under the scope of the "context" (*prakṛta*) due to its connection with a single action.

The meaning is that in such a sentence, it is indeed an *nidarśanā* (illustrative metaphor), because it is rooted in the impossibility of establishing a connection between the contextual and the non-contextual sentences. Even where the state of mutual dependence is not very clear, he shows by means of an example that there should be no notion of it being a mere *dṛṣṭānta* (simile): "And thus, 'If the body of the people dwelling in the hermitage were difficult to obtain even in the inner apartments' (*śuddhāntadurlabhaṃ vapuḥ*), etc. Here, the word *yat* ("if") in the preceding sentence gives rise to the word *tat* ("then") in the subsequent sentence, as in "then [they] have been driven far away" (*tarhi dūrīkṛtāḥ*). Because of this mutual dependence between the two sentence-meanings, it is indeed an *nidarśanā*.
This [is the case]. He states this very point with the words, "by the aforementioned reasoning.
Alternatively, he speaks of its variety with the words, "and this [variety] occurs through generality alone," and so forth.
