The "introduction" (*upoddhāta*) is the presentation [of a subject] through a connection with the meaning of a sentence in a general sense, by means of another variety of poetic charm (*vaicitrya*). He distinguishes this other variety [of charm] with the words beginning "occurring in the object of comparison" (*upameya-vṛtta*) and so forth.

For in examples such as "difficult to obtain even in the inner apartments" (*śuddhānta-durlabha*), there is the presence of that which occurs in the object of comparison (*upamāna*) superimposed upon that which occurs in the object of comparison (*upameya*).
Now, there is also the reverse case—namely, *viyoga* (separation).

In the verse concerning women who have become pale due to the cause of separation, where it is said that "the paleness on the surface of their cheeks would be indistinguishable from the pollen within the heart of a date-palm cluster (*sakharjūrī-mañjarī*)," a simile is perceived;

for here, the paleness residing in the cheek (*upameya-vṛtta*), which is the subject of comparison, is impossible to distinguish from the pollen residing in the date-palm cluster (*upamāna-vṛtta*), which serves as the standard of comparison.
This is what he says here: "In this case, the surface of the cheek," and so forth.

And because of the variety within this very type, he says: "This type [is characterized] by the impossibility of the connection (*anvaya*) of that which resides in the object of comparison (*upameya*) with that which resides in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)," as in the example "the veins on a shaven head."
O fool, you hold a jujube fruit steady upon the peak of Mount Maṇḍaśiras, and a jujube upon that jujube;
your body is twice the height [of the mountain], yet you are deluded—how many people are being crushed!
The *chreka*s are those who are deceived;
they are *chralyante*, meaning they are led astray by deception.

Here, because of the cause of being *chreka* and *chralana*—characterized by a succession of foolish actions that are fruitless and poorly executed—the connection of the implied attribute residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*) with the attribute residing in the object of comparison (*upamāna*), such as "bearing jujube fruits" and so forth, is impossible.
And that [sequence] exists by way of the logic of a chain, because it stands in the state of a row through mutual dependence.
He says, "This too," because it can also exist in the form of a garland, characterized by standing in a row without mutual dependence.
The word "api" (even) is displaced [in the sentence].
The meaning is: "even by means of a garland.
"In the forest" means that it was like weeping in the wilderness, because such an excessive burden of suffering was experienced in the absence of people who could share in that suffering.

A corpse has been anointed with agallochum, sandalwood, and other unguents; yet such a preparation is useless for its own sake, for his own enjoyment, or for the enjoyment of others. It is like planting a lotus on dry land, because it is unsuited to that which is cherished by the world.
The word "for a very long time" (*suciram*) is connected with each subsequent clause. Rain fallen upon saline soil (*ūṣara*) is useless because of its overflowing fruitlessness;
a tail that has been bent down remains unbent even after a long period of conditioning, because no impression (*saṃskāra*) has been established.
The whispered recitation was performed for one who was deaf;
*jāpa* refers to a silent or secret utterance.
This was undertaken out of intense longing, even though he was known to be an unworthy recipient.
"The blind man’s face was adorned" means it was done to no purpose and resulted in being an object of ridicule for others.
The word *yat*— which is qualified by the sense of the entire sentence, namely "that an ignorant person was served"— takes up the action that constitutes the primary meaning of the sentence.

The fact that serving ignorant people is like wailing in a forest—where the occurrence of the subject (the thing compared) is superimposed upon the occurrence of the object of comparison (the thing to which it is compared)—is established as *mālā* (garland-like) because the connection [of the attributes] is impossible.
Now, he says "In some cases, however," etc., to show that the variety of *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile) arises even without explicit verbal expression, through mere implication (*arthākṣepa*).
For a negation necessarily presupposes a prior affirmation, and thus implies that affirmation.

The meaning is that even the impossibility of a connection [of the probans] with the object of negation, due to its non-occurrence, serves in some cases as the basis for an *udāharaṇa* (illustrative example).
The intention is that in such a case, it is necessarily based on the meaning (*arthī*).
Regarding the term "utkopa":
here, by the force of the prohibition of the form of abandonment—expressed as "the swan’s gait was released from the two feet"—the attainment of the swan’s gait by the two feet is implied.
Being unable to connect directly [with the primary meaning], that [implied sense] brings about a cognition of similarity.
This is what he says here with the words "In this case, [the word] 'liberated'... and so forth:
"If a reflection were to convey either a possible connection with a real object or an impossible one, then that would have to be recognized as an illustration (*nidarśanā*)."
When two sentences connected to the subject matter stand in the relation of original and reflection,
they constitute a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration) if they are independent, but a *nidarśanā* (exemplification) if they are dependent.

Thus have been analyzed the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) that fall under the category where non-difference is predominant. Now, he formulates the definition of *vyatireka* (distinction), wherein difference is predominant: "When difference is predominant, *vyatireka* occurs when the object of comparison (*upameya*) is either superior or inferior to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). (RuAss 28)
When difference (*bheda*) is predominant, the term "similarity" (*sādharmya*) is understood to follow.

By reminding us of what was stated previously regarding the predominance of difference—that is, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—the author introduces the section with the words "Now," and so forth.
He reveals that the two types of impossibility (*asambhava*) constitute the seeds of differentiation by stating, "Difference is distinctness," and so on.
Lest there be a misconception that the word *viparyaya* refers to false knowledge or delusion, he says: "Inversion (*viparyaya*) is the state of having inferior qualities.
Regarding the phrase "desiring to see":
here, the thousand eyes possess superior qualities in comparison to the blossoming of the blue lotus.
"Even though it has waned, it has waned"—
here, even though youth is subject to decay, it possesses lesser qualities when compared to the moon that increases ever further;
he joins these two points together with the words beginning "here, in full bloom," and so forth.
In a comparison where difference is predominant, a negative concomitance (vyatireka) is established,
arising either from the superiority of the object compared or from its inferiority relative to the standard of comparison.

He formulates the definition of *sahokti* (conjoined expression): "When one of the two—the object of comparison (*upamāna*) or the subject of comparison (*upameya*)—is indicated as predominant, while the other is connected with it through the sense of 'together' (*saha*), that is *sahokti*. (RuAss 29)
Recalling the context, he analyzes its causal totality (*sāmagrī*) with the words "the predominance of difference" (*bhedaprādhānya*) and so forth.

Now, one might ask: since [difference and non-difference] are co-ordinate in meaning, how can there be a predominance of difference? To this he replies: "the relation of subordinate and principal" (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), etc.
This is true.

Here, by the force of the meaning of the word "together" (*saha*), there is indeed similarity (*sādharmya*). However, the predominance of difference (*bheda*) occurs here through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka-naya*); it does not rest upon a foundation of similarity, but rather, as the sense is, it rests upon a foundation of the relationship between the subordinate and the predominant (*guṇa-pradhāna-bhāva*). Now, one might ask: if they share a common connection, what kind of relationship between the subordinate and the predominant could there be? To this, he says: "The application of the meaning of the word 'together'... [and so forth].

For the sense of "together with" (saha) necessitates that the third case-ending be employed in the quality of a subordinate attribute (*guṇa*). Now, if there is the sense of "together with," one might ask: what constitutes the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)? To this he says: "And the state of being the standard and the object of comparison," and so forth.
For that [third-case ending] is intended to signify the status of the standard of comparison because it functions as an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*) for that which ends in the third case.
But for the other [term], because it functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it possesses the status of the object of comparison (*upameya*).
Therefore, the sense is that this is merely intentional (*vaivakṣika*) and not real (*vāstava*).
He states the reason for its unreality with the words "of both," and so forth.

[Objection: But what is the determining factor for whether both [the agent and the instrument] are contextual (*prākaraṇika*) or non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*)? To this he says: "By virtue of the semantic force of the word *saha*.

[Objection: If it is indeed a matter of speaker's intention (*vaivakṣikatva*), then in which form should which [of the two] be intended? To this he says: "Of that which ends in the third case," and so forth.
[Objection: But even the principal [element] ought to be designated by the third case ending. To this he says: "And it is expressed through words" (*śābdaśca*).

For the word *saha* invariably implies that the term ending in the third case functions as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) in the verbal expression, while the other term holds the status of the primary element (*pradhāna*). If so, what is the status with respect to the actual meaning? To this he says: "But in reality... (*vastutastu*).
There is the predominance of even a subordinate factor and the subordination of even a predominant factor; this is "reversal.
By the word "also," instability is likewise implied.
Even though such is the established order of reasoning, he says "tatrāpi" and so forth, because there is another specific factor that serves as its motivator.
Furthermore, even hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is not its root in its entirety; therefore, he says "sā ca" and so forth.

Here, the reversal of the fixed rule of cause and effect consists in their simultaneity, and not in the effect existing at a prior time, because they possess the sense of being co-existent (*sahārtha*).

He states that the determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*) occurs in two ways, beginning with "And the determination of non-difference... and so forth. Thus, this threefold [classification] has been proposed.
He proposes another variety by saying "And coexistence (*sāhitya*) here... and so forth.
That is to say, it also manifests through a distinction based on the association of the agent, the object, and so forth.
Here are the examples in order:
in the phrase "by your offenses" (*bhavadaparādhair*), the offenses possess the status of a subordinate element (*guṇa*) because they are expressed by the third case ending.
Since *santāpa* (distress) ends in the nominative case, it possesses primacy;
therefore, the predominance of the distinction here is based solely on the relationship between the subordinate and the principal,
and not on the action of increasing.
And that relationship of subordinate and principal is prompted by the sense of "together" (saha).
Since both [the offenses and the limbs] are the subjects under discussion, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison is determined by intention.
Furthermore, because the offenses end in the third case-ending, it is certain that the qualifiers function as the standards of comparison, such that "the offenses increase."
However, because of the predominance of the burning (*santāpa*), it functions as the object of comparison; thus, "the burning increases.
This relationship of subordinate and predominant status is verbal (*śābda*).
But with respect to the meaning (*artha*), it is the burning itself [that is compared].

Since it is also possible that "offenses increase," this logical sequence should be applied to other examples as well. Here, he shows that the basis is the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) characterized by the simultaneity of cause and effect, in the passage beginning with "of these offenses" (*atrāparādhānām*).

"The sun has set"—this means that scattered things should be withdrawn and unified. Here, he shows that the basis is a superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) of non-difference upon a foundation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), stating: "In this case, 'setting' (*astaṅgamana*), etc.
It has a dual meaning: in one sense it is a mountain (*giri*), and in another sense it is exhaustion (*avasāda*).

Regarding "with the petals of the night-lotuses," he again shows that the basis is a superimposition of non-difference upon a foundation of non-*śleṣa*, stating: "In this case, 'separation' (*vighaṭana*), etc."

Thus, he explains that in the absence of that specific quality—characterized by being rooted in hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) and so forth—mere *sahokti* (joint description) is not a figure of speech, using the words "etadviśeṣa...
He provides a counter-example with "anena sārdham...".
He further states, "etānyeva...", indicating that even the aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*) characterized by the coexistence of agents is demonstrated in these very cases.
For in these cases, there is a co-agency with the agent regarding [actions such as] tormenting or offending—as in the phrase "dyujana" (heavenly beings). *Dyujanāḥ* means the gods (*devāḥ*).
The destruction of the Daitya army was the fulfillment of the desire of the heavenly beings along with Death.
Here, he demonstrates the coexistence of actions: "In this case, the action of *karoti*," and so forth.

Although the death of the inhabitants of heaven (*dyujana*) possesses the status of an agent with respect to its own action, because that [action] is subordinate, there is no coexistence of agents here.
As for that which is [called] the wheel (*cakra*):
The action of "doing" (karoti) is the primary element; in relation to that, because it possesses the status of an object (*karman*), this [action] is accompanied by the object—this is the meaning.
In this way, the various ways in which it is accompanied by the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth should be inferred.
Furthermore, he says "And this... to demonstrate its variety.
"Utprekṣiptam" refers to the raising of the bow, the striking together of the bowstring,
and the drawing back after the twanging.
The discharge of the arrow and so forth are the successive actions of an archer.
Among those, up to the point of drawing [the bow], only that many [actions] were described because they were already established.
In that regard, for the exceedingly affectionate Kauśika, the raising of his hair occurred simultaneously with the raising of the bow.
Because they were seized by envy, the kings were satisfied with the mere lifting [of the bow], yet at the moment the bow was bent, their faces bowed;
for while the father, who had drawn up the wager, continued to harbor doubt as to whether [the prince] would truly succeed in bending it.
Simultaneous with the twanging of the bowstring was the striking of the mind by doubt;
simultaneous with the successful wagering for Vaidehī was the drawing of the mind, which had not yet been drawn away.
The "drawing together" (*samākarṣa*) is as follows:

the illustrious Rāmacandra brought about the destruction of the sprout of Bhārgava’s ego—which remained unbroken until the breaking of his bow—at the very moment that [the bow] was broken. Because these actions are connected in this manner, they constitute a "garland" (*mālā*) here through their collective nature;
other instances should likewise be understood as forming a garland.
When there is a verbal expression of the relationship between the subordinate and the predominant,
Sahokti (Concomitance) is considered to be a type of Atiśayokti (Hyperbole) based on mutual dependence, occurring between two things of equal status.
Now, he states the connection with *vinokti* (the figure of "without"): "The rival of *sahokti*," and so forth—meaning its counterpart or opposite.
Regarding this, the aphorism is:
*Vinokti* is the absence of existence or non-existence of one thing without another. (RuAss 30)
He explains [the passage] beginning with "of the being" (*sattvasya*) and so forth;
the meanings of the words *abhāva* (non-existence) and *artha* (object) are each connected [to the preceding term] by way of transposition.
The absence of beauty is ugliness, and the absence of that [ugliness] is beauty.
Where there is no beauty without some object, that is one form of *vinokti*;
where there is no ugliness [without some object], that is the other. This is the meaning of its two forms.
[Objection: Is it not sufficient that some reality or unreality exists? Why then resort to the cumbersome reliance on two negations? To this he says: "And here," etc.
[The phrase] "occasioned by the exclusion of another" [is used].
If the exclusion of one thing does not necessitate the exclusion of existence and non-existence,
then there is no figure of speech called *vinokti*;
for in the statement "when this exists, that is non-existent," there is no particular aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*).

The meaning is this: the *vinokti* ornament consists precisely in the exclusion of existence and non-existence as necessitated by the exclusion of something else. When this [exclusion] is present, there is the affirmation of a thing—namely, its existence or non-existence—which is manifested as the primary fruit of the ornament. Thus he says: "And so, even when there is the exclusion of another," and so forth.
An example of the sequence [of types] even for that which has two forms is "vinaya" etc.

Here, by the removal of the moon-like quality (*satkatva*) of discipline (*vinaya*), there is the removal of the cleverness of the night of glory (*śrīniśāvidagdhā*); thus, this is an example of the absence of a substantive (*sattvābhāva*).
Furthermore, when *vinaya* and so forth exist, the presence of Śrī and others is manifested as the fruit.
Having this in mind, he says: "In this context, *vinaya* and so forth," etc.

To demonstrate that even in the absence of the word *vinā*, if its meaning is present, it is indeed *vinokti* (the figure of speech based on "without"), he says: "In this context, the word *vinā*," etc.
"Just as in the case of co-utterance" means that this same principle applies even in the case of co-utterance (*sahokti*).
He provides an example here: "birth is useless."
In this case, however, it is understood that the birth of the lotus is not beautiful without the sight of the moon;
therefore, this is *vinokti* (the figure of speech of "without"). The distinction is that when the word *vinā* ("without") is not employed, it is *ārthī* (implied).
Intending this very point, he says: "In such cases, it is merely *vinokti*," and so forth.

He further states that here, the manifestation of the relationship between cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) serves to impart a specific charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) to *vinokti* itself, and not to constitute a separate figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*); thus he says: "And this [relationship] is mutual," and so forth.
This refers to the subject matter already illustrated.

"This birth is useless"—this is the subject that has been stated. For in the world, without one with deer-like eyes, there is no brilliance or confidence in the discernment of diverse worldly affairs; and without a friend, there is no nobility of intention.
The meaning of the verse is that [the qualities] do not belong to this son of the king in that same way.
He demonstrates the absence of these qualities by stating, "because of the absence of unloveliness here," and so forth.
Eloquence, confidence, and a beautiful disposition are the objects characterized by loveliness (*śobhana*).

He concludes: "This [vinokti] is of two kinds. If the cessation of existence and non-existence is described by means of another's cessation, then it would be a twofold *vinokti*; in this case, affirmation (*vidhi*) would be the result.

Now he introduces the figures of speech based on the charm of epithets (*viśeṣaṇa-vicchitti*), namely *samāsokti* (brief expression) and *parikara* (circumlocution): "Now, regarding 'epithets'... The charm of epithets is of two kinds: similarity (*sāmya*) and intentionality (*sābhiprāyatā*). Regarding similarity, he introduces *samāsokti* with the words "In that regard, first," and so forth.
In this regard, the Sūtra states:
"When the unmentioned [subject] is understood through a specific similarity, it is *samāsokti* (speech by ellipsis). (RuAss 31)

Where, in the qualified element (*viśeṣya*), there is an intention directed solely toward the contextual subject, yet through the similarity of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), the non-contextual is understood as well—this is *samāsokti* (speech by ellipsis), because it is expressed in a concise manner (*samāsena*).
Desiring to explain this, [the author] says "here, the contextual... and so forth, for the sake of distinguishing its scope;
in some cases, it is the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*).
The word "of both" is to be supplied [as the object of the verb]; "the state of being cognizable in some cases" is to be supplied as referring to "one or the other."
"By means of a statement based on *śleṣa* (punning connection)" means: by not establishing a *śleṣa* between the two components, namely the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
"By means of separate mention" means: [by mentioning them] individually.
The meaning is: by the separate employment of words for the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*).
This twofold denotability (*vācyatva*) is also the domain of the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
When the state of being difficult to traverse pertains to the subject at hand due to the similarity of the qualifiers, then it is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description).
The distinction is that when the subject matter is irrelevant (aprastuta), it is *samāsokti* (speech of brevity).

One might ask: "If the irrelevant subject is to be implied (*gamya*), and there is a similarity even in the substantive (*viśeṣya*), what would then be the case? To this he says: "When there is similarity even in the substantive, because of the attainment of *śleṣa* (punning).
This means, in effect, because of the attainment of *dhvani* (suggestion) based on *śleṣa*.
Now, it may be objected that the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *dhvani* based on word-power (*śabdaśaktimūla*) both involve the employment of punning words across three distinct domains.
Among these, when it is *śleṣa*, both meanings must necessarily be expressed (*vācya*).

And this expressibility is possible only when both meanings are either contextual (*prākaraṇika*) or non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*), because in such cases, both the qualifying (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) portions are composed of punning words; thus, it constitutes the figure of speech *śleṣa*.
Since denotation (*abhidhā*) is unrestricted, both meanings may be expressed.

Now, when one meaning is contextual (*prākaraṇika*) and the other is non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*), then the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs precisely by virtue of the separate employment of words for the substantive portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*).

If, however, there is the composition of paronomastic words even for the substantive portion, then because denotation—being restricted by context—is exhausted solely by the contextual meaning, the comprehension of the non-contextual meaning belongs exclusively to suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
It would be the subject matter when there is an expression of non-compound (asamāsa). In that case,

regarding the qualifying portion (viśeṣaṇāṃśa), there is the employment of words that convey two meanings, whereas regarding the qualified portion (viśeṣyāṃśa), there is a focus solely on the contextual meaning.
In that case, because the non-contextual subject is understood through the similarity of the adjectives, it is *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression) as defined above.

However, when there is a pun (*śliṣṭatā*) not only in the adjectives but also in the substantive portions of both the contextual and non-contextual subjects, then it is no longer *samāsokti*, since its defining characteristic is the similarity of the adjectives alone. Furthermore, how could it be considered the figure of speech *śleṣa* (pun)? For in that case, the defining characteristic is simply that both meanings are directly expressed (*vācyatā*).

For here it is not possible for both [the contextual and the non-contextual] to be the expressed meaning, because denotation—which favors the context—cannot touch upon a non-contextual object; because the non-contextual is perceived immediately following the syntactic connection (*samanvaya*); and because there would be the undesirable consequence of the suggestion (*dhvani*) rooted in the power of words being swallowed up by the pun (*śleṣa*).
"This main road is secluded for those who know the secret of the illustration of sound"—enough said.

Now, he distinguishes the difference between *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression) and *rūpaka* (metaphor) by means of the passage beginning with "by the power of the similarity of adjectives" (*viśeṣaṇasāmyavaśāt*), etc.;
for the particle *hi* indicates a reason.
Since the unmentioned subject is understood through the similarity of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*),
it is therefore unable— due to the absence of contact with the substantive portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*)— to endow the substantive, which is the contextual subject, with its own form. Rather,

it superimposes as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) upon the usage of the contextual subject (which is understood through the qualifiers) the usage belonging to itself (which was understood through the qualifiers).
This is what he says: "It is perceived as being delimited by the subject at hand," and so forth, beginning with "and because of its being a delimiter.
He states that the superimposition of conventional usage does not differ from the case of a metaphor, beginning with "and because of its being a delimiter."
It is the superimposition of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), but not the superimposition of form (*rūpa*).
[Objection: But when there is the superimposition of form, what would happen? To this he says: "the superimposition of form," and so forth.
[This means] by being encompassed through the state of being concealed.
Because it is characterized by the form of the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) and because it is colored by the form of that which is not at hand (*aprakṛta*), it is indeed *rūpaka* (metaphor).
This has been analyzed as appropriate in the section on the ornament of transformation (*pariṇāmālaṅkāra*).
On this point, there are intermediate verses: "If the non-contextual [object] is perceived through a single commonality with a distinguishing part..."
Having superimposed conventional usage upon the subject at hand, it then becomes subordinate.
Because the subject at hand is thus expressed in brief by means of the superimposition of an irrelevant narrative,
this is considered *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation).

If there were equality between the qualified portion [of the subject] and that which is represented by the form under discussion, such that the non-contextual object becomes the thing to be identified, then the poetic figure would be *rūpaka* (metaphor).
Thus it is said.
In order to elaborate upon its specific characteristics, he says: "And that is the equality of qualifiers," and so forth.

"Commonality" (*sādhāraṇya*) is the possibility of the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) existing in both [the subject and the object of comparison]. "Containing a comparison" (*aupamyagarbhatva*) results from resorting to a compound (*samāsa*) that contains such a comparison.
The meaning is that the similarity of those qualifiers occurs in these three ways;
therefore, *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression) is also threefold.
The examples follow in order, beginning with "upoḍharāgeṇa" (by one whose passion has been aroused).
*Rāga* means both the crimson glow of twilight and passion;
from the word *tāraka*, there is the understanding of both a star and the corner of the eye;
and *mukha* means both a beginning and a face.
"Timiram-aṃśukam" means a garment resembling darkness.
To apply the definition, he says: "In this case, of the night and the moon," and so forth.
"Nāyakau" refers to the hero and the heroine.

The term *puṃsām striyaḥ* is a singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). Here, by the power of the closely connected qualifiers such as "having aroused passion," the night and the moon are indeed perceived as being distinguished by the behavior of a hero and a heroine.
Now, how is it determined here that there is a superimposition of behavior (*vyavahāra*) and not a superimposition of form (*rūpa*)? To this, he says: "without abandoning," and so forth.

If there were a superimposition of form (*rūpasamāropa*), then, according to the logic of metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*), each respective form would abandon its own nature by being concealed and would instead assume the identity of the concealing factor, which is the form of the object of comparison.

However, in this case, the night and the moon— both of which are known in their substantive aspect as being devoid of any counter-correlate and therefore have not abandoned their own forms— are perceived as qualified by the attribute of being "lovers" (the *nāyaka*), an attribute made known through the similarity of their qualifiers.
Therefore, this is merely a conventional designation.
"Tanvī" [refers to her state];
"puṣpa" is the menstrual flow (*ārtava-rajas*).
And [the word] *prasūna*.

Here, there is an equality of identical meaning (*ekārthatā-sāmya*) between the qualifiers such as "thinness" (*tanutva*) and so forth in both [senses], but not a state of being "punned" (*śliṣṭatā*).
This is what he states with the words "here, thinness," and so on.

One might ask: "Since there is a similarity in attributes such as thinness and so forth, how can there be the cognition of the conventional designation 'creeper'? To this he says: "And therein, the creeper is one," and so on.
For expansion belongs only to the creeper; the superimposition of that [expansion] onto the tremulous-eyed woman is the cause for the cognition of the conventional designation 'creeper.
One might further ask: "Since expansion resides exclusively in the creeper, how can it be common [to both]? To this he says: "But expansion," and so on.

Just as the commonality of qualifiers and the superimposition of properties (*dharma-samāropa*) are causes for the superimposition of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-samāropa*), so too is the superimposition of effects (*kārya-samāropa*). To demonstrate this, he says: "And thus, [regarding] the effect," and so forth.

For here, difference—which is based on the superimposition of effects—is easily understood through the aforementioned method of the superimposition of properties; furthermore, he will treat it separately as purity later on.
Therefore, it is not illustrated here.
In such cases, the non-contextual meaning cannot be understood without the superimposition of either a quality (*dharma*) or an action (*kārya*).
This is because the denotative function (*abhidhā*), being restricted by the context, is exhausted solely with respect to the contextual meaning.

Therefore, the superimposition of either a quality or an action is itself the cause for the comprehension of the non-contextual meaning, as it is brought about by the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

This *samāsokti* (synecdoche), based on the commonality of qualifiers, has its scope clearly distinguished only by those who know the logical principles (*nyāyavid*). With this in mind, [the author] says "And this," and so forth.
The meaning is that, in comparison with the former, this *samāsokti*—based on punning qualifiers—is the latter; that is to say, it follows from the former.
Regarding the verse "dantaprabhāpuṣpacitā":

in this sentence, where the intended meaning is not explicitly stated, as soon as it is heard, the well-adorned appearance of the deer-eyed woman is understood through the reason of her being covered with flowers that are the luster of her teeth.

Therefore, by virtue of the effect characterized as "well-adorned appearance," the qualifiers—namely, "the luster of the teeth are like flowers"—are intended to function as a compound of simile (*upamāsamāsa*).

Now, by means of flowers—understood through a compound involving the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopī samāsa*) as "flowers resembling the luster of teeth"—and other such elements like flower-buds, there arises the cognition of the behavior of a creeper (*latāvyavahāra*) when the similarity of attributes is present.
This very point is made clear here by the phrase beginning with "the luster of teeth.
By stating that there is a "cognition of the behavior of a creeper," the author indicates that a metaphorical compound (*rūpaka-samāsa*) is not applicable here.

Since it has been established that *samāsokti* (synecdoche) occurs when there is a superimposition of function (*vyavahāra*), whereas *rūpaka* (metaphor) occurs when there is a superimposition of form (*rūpa*), therefore, even though a metaphorical compound (*rūpaka-samāsa*) is well-known, it does not logically apply here. [Objection: "In cases such as these, if the basis for resorting to a prior compound of comparison (*upamā-samāsa*)—namely, [the quality] such as being well-dressed—is not mentioned, then what would happen? To this, he says: "In this very case, by the words beginning with *parīta*, etc."

Regarding the phrase "surrounded by a mass of hair-locks like a garland" (*parītā keśapāśālivṛndena parigatā*), there arises a doubt: is this a *upamā-samāsa* (simile compound), such as "here [are] teeth whose radiance is like flowers," or is it a *rūpaka-samāsa* (metaphor compound), such as "the radiance of the teeth itself is the flowers"? Thus stands the uncertainty.
Because there is neither a proof nor a refutation for either simile (*upamā*) or metaphor (*rūpaka*),
the previous construction was based on the assumption of a "conflict" (*saṅkara*) consisting of doubt (*sandeha*).
Nor should it be thought that a compound (*samāsa*) is incompatible with doubt.

Since doubt, which is evoked by the poet’s creative genius (*pratibhā*), constitutes a form of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*), it is first employed here by means of the figure of *saṃkara* (commixture).

Then, at the time when the doubt is resolved, in the phrase "with flowers resembling the luster of teeth" and so forth, there is—as before—the compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopa-samāsa*). Upon the perception of the behavior of a creeper (*latā-vyavahāra*), the final rest is found precisely in the figure of *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation).

This being the case, this variety of *samāsokti* (speech by compounding) should be understood as twofold: that which contains a simile within the compound (*upamā-samāsagarbha*) and that which contains a commixture [of figures] within the compound (*saṅkara-samāsagarbha*). Now, one might ask: why is this variety of *samāsokti* not also accepted as based on a simple metaphorical compound (*rūpaka-samāsa*)? To this he replies: "But by virtue of containing a metaphor... Previously, in the case of a metaphorical compound, and then in the case of relying on a similitude-compound (*upamā-samāsa*) by virtue of containing that [metaphor], although there is indeed a similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*), [the distinction remains].
Nevertheless, that is not the cause for *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
Why? Because once the behavior (*vyavahāra*) of the creeper is perceived through the very medium of its partial manifestation (*ekadeśavivartin*), *samāsokti* would be redundant.

One might object: "In the case of a compound of simile (*upamā-samāsa*) or a compound of commixture (*saṅkara-samāsa*), why would *samāsokti* not likewise be redundant? To this he replies: "And it was not previously shown," and so forth.

This is the logical principle characterized by the reversal of *samāsokti* (synecdoche). Regarding this, he states the reason: because there is no such thing as *upamā* (simile) or *saṅkara* (commixture) existing in a "partially manifest" (*ekadeśavivartin*) form.
For neither the figure of speech *upamā* nor the figure of speech *saṅkara* has been taught by any authority as being "partially manifest."

Therefore, because they are suspected of being independent figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), they are not capable of subverting other [figures]. Metaphor (*rūpaka*), however, being taught as "occurring in one part" (*ekadeśavivartin*), is indeed capable of subverting others. For this very reason, when there is a possibility of metaphor in such a context, there is a possibility of "Speech through Synecdoche" (*samāsokti*); thus, he says "And that is 'occurring in one part'... etc., in order to demonstrate this with examples.

"Having gazed [at her] with eyes of lightning"—the meaning is that the cloud, having gazed at the face of the woman going to meet her (abhisārikā) during the night with its lightning-eyes, roared most piteously as if with the thought: "Along with the falling showers, the moon has been vomited up by me.
Here, he shows that the *ekadeśavivartin* metaphor (*rūpaka*), being intertwined [with other figures], leaves no room for *samāsokti*—this is indicated by the words "here, gazing," and so forth.
For gazing is indeed a property of a person, not a property of a cloud;

therefore, when the connection is made according to the person, it is the lightning itself that constitutes the "eyes. This is thus a metaphor (*rūpaka*) alone, and not a simile (*upamā*) or a combination of figures (*saṅkara*).
Consequently, the representation of the cloud as the beholding person follows by implication; this is what is meant by "partial transformation" (*ekadeśavivartin*).

The sense is this: since "it resounds most piteously" serves as the very basis for the *pratīyamānotprekṣā* (suggested poetic fancy), there is no possibility at all for *samāsokti* (condensed metaphor).
Regarding the phrase *magaṇanā*: "leaves" (*patrāṇi*) refers to petals; these very leaves are the palm-leaf folios (*tāladalāni*).
"Ways of writing" (*lipayaḥ*) refers to the modes of script; these very ways of writing are the arrangements of syllables (*akṣarasanniveśāḥ*).
The scribe is the embodied soul (*dehin*) and the calculator (*gaṇaka*).

Among these, by virtue of their capacity for transformation (*rūpaṇa*), Madana is perceived as being represented as the Great King (*mahārāja*), and Madhu as the chief of the illustrious administration (*śrīkaraṇāgraṇī*).
He demonstrates this very point with the words "here, indeed, the written leaf," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "Why could this not be a simile (upamā), such as 'like petals' and so forth? To this he says: "The bee is ink," and so on. For the application of ink is impossible in the case of bees; thus, [the term] sets aside the compound of simile (upamā-samāsa) and, because it is possible within the function of a metaphorical expression (gaṇaka-vṛtti), it establishes the compound of metaphor (rūpaka-samāsa). This is the sense. Now, one might ask: "In the context of the discussion on *samāsokti*, why is there this demonstration of the varieties of *rūpaka* with examples? To this he says: "And its abundance," and so forth.

Regarding this *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) metaphor, there are two intermediate verses here: "The *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) occurs when there is a certainty [of the comparison] through a compound of comparison;
however, it occurs through a compound of commixture (*saṅkara*) when there is a doubt regarding the compound."
The application of the previously mentioned *rūpaka* compound does not occur here,
because the intended meaning is fully established through a *rūpaka* that functions by partial transformation (*ekadeśavivartin*).
Therefore, in order to manifest other subdivisions, he describes the types already mentioned, beginning with "tadevam" (thus, in this way).

This [metaphor], indeed, is taught as being threefold due to the variety of its qualifiers: namely, that which arises from a *śliṣṭa* (punning) qualifier, that which arises from a *sādhāraṇa* (common) qualifier, and that which arises from a qualifier containing a comparison (*aupamyagarbha*).
Among these, there is one kind arising from a *śliṣṭa* qualifier.
Furthermore, it is twofold by way of the superimposition of a common property (*dharmasamāropa*) and the superimposition of an effect (*kāryasamāropa*).
It is also twofold by way of the *upamā-samāsa* (simile-compound) and the *saṅkara-samāsa* (compound of commingling), even when containing a simile within it.
However, the two types of *rūpaka-samāsa* (metaphor-compound)—distinguished as *śliṣṭa* (pun-based) and *aśliṣṭa* (non-pun-based)—are not its domain.
Therefore, there are five types.

Thus, since the similarity of qualifiers has been established, resulting in these five types, he further describes this [classification] as consisting of three groups along with their internal subdivisions, beginning with the words "thus, pure effect" (*śuddhakārya*) and so forth.
The purity of the effect (*kārya*) consists in its being unmixed due to the aforementioned similarity of qualifiers.

The meaning is "prior to" the emergence of a distinction based on the similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*). The underlying intention here is this: *samāsokti* (synecdoche) occurs when that which is not the subject of the context (*aprastuta*) is implied through the similarity of qualifiers.
And that similarity of qualifiers is figurative (*upacarita*), existing when there is a superimposition (*samāropa*) of the mere effect (*kārya*).

Just as in the verse about to be cited beginning with "yathā vilikhati," that is the first group; when, however, this [verse] is used in its primary sense, then it is the second group as previously illustrated fivefold;
but when it consists of both, it is the third group.
The demonstration previously made of the fivefold [simile] was based on the reliance upon logic, which is grounded in the identity of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) through non-metaphorical usage.
Now, he recalls that very same previous demonstration with the words: "and the identity of the qualifiers.
But surely, in the case of a pure superimposition of the effect (*kāryasamāropa*), the identity of the qualifiers is metaphorical (*upacarita*).
Since we do not perceive any other purpose that is non-figurative, pervasive, and uniform in nature, he says: "And in all these cases," and so forth.
By the word "only" (*eva*), he intends to show that the concise statement has that single [purpose] as its very life-force.
He demonstrates its fourfold nature by saying: "And that is worldly," and so forth.
[These are] things, universals, qualities, and so forth.
And by means of this fourfold superimposition upon conventional usage, each of the three aggregates also manifests in four ways.
Therefore, he says, "Thus, it is accompanied by much elaboration," because the concise statement is possessed of manifold expansion.
Desiring to set forth the first group there, he says: "In that regard,
regarding the task of purification," and "he writes," meaning he writes it out clearly.
A firm seizing by the hair, an improper pulling of the leaf-patterned garment, and the dragging away of the cloth—these constitute the act of a forceful lover (*haṭhakāmuka*).
The word "forcefully" (*haṭhāt*) is an adverbial modifier for the action of dragging.

Here, because [the description] is figurative, the similarity of the modifiers does not carry great weight toward the comprehension of the unmentioned subject; rather, there is simply a superimposition of the pure action itself. Thus he says: "In this case, 'leaf-patterned garment' and so forth."
Because it is utterly impossible [to find] *khadira* leaves, there is the taking of leaf-patterns (*patrāvalī*).
By means of the "equality of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*), he causes one to remember the sequence of those things mentioned out of order, so that the natural order may be restored.
For when there is a "equality of the qualifiers" through wordplay (*śliṣṭatā*), then there is a double meaning (*ubhayārthatā*).
When there is commonality, the possibility for the grounds of application exists in both cases;
when there is the status of being a qualifier containing a simile, then it is a different type of compound.
It should be understood that the comprehension of the unmentioned subject occurs precisely through the force of this distinction and the lack of parity.
Then, he provides an illustration by way of both [qualities]: "lirlūnāni" (mowed).
By "sapless" (*nīrasaiḥ*) is meant dry and heartless;
by "thorny" (*kaṇṭakibhiḥ*) is meant possessing small spikes and being associated with murderous persons.
He joins [the verse] with the state of being composed of both, using the words "here by the thorny ones.

Desiring to demonstrate the distinctions arising from the manifold basis for the superimposition of conventional usage upon the three desired heaps, he says: "the superimposition of conventional usage," and so forth, ending with "he embraced the sky."
*Ambara* refers to both the sky and clothing;
*nimagracarapuṣpa* denotes the autumn season due to its burning heat;
and *taruṇa* means powerful as well as young.
Here, there is a similarity of qualifiers among the young men who are like clouds;
elsewhere, there is the superimposition of an effect.
In this case, there is the superimposition of worldly convention upon a worldly object.
And regarding the examples demonstrated therein,
he states that "the worldly object is of various kinds" by saying "and the worldly," and "by which."
It is of a single form and unchanging throughout the states such as waking; it is imperishable even in deep sleep.
It is concealed within these;
for this very reason, it proceeds as the innumerable.
In the waking state, Viśva is the first.
The Taijasa is the second in the dream state,
and the Prājña is the third in deep sleep;
the fourth is devoid of numerical designation because it is the thread that runs through all states.
For it has been stated by the venerable Gauḍapāda: “Māyā is the fourth state.
By those who perceive You in such a way, the case-ending expressing transcendence (*paratva*) has been dropped;
the distinction that "there is something higher than this" has been elided.
I consider that you have been defined by them;

for the definition of the Supreme Lord is indeed oneness in all states of existence, immutability, and incalculability—meaning there is no differentiation whatsoever from space, time, or any other factor. This alone is the defining characteristic.
This is the reality well-known from the scriptures and the treatises.

Now, in all the commentaries on the *Kārikās* and other works, it is stated that since an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is indeed devoid of numbers such as singularity and so forth, there is no "singularity as a correlate" (*pratiyogy-ekatva*), but rather only "non-dual singularity" (*abheda-ekatva*). Observing the indeclinable to be of this nature, the elision of case-endings—such as the nominative and others—is performed after the base (*prakṛti*) which possesses "posteriority," characterized by its being subsequent [to the base]. This definition of an indeclinable is established by the rule beginning with: "That which is similar in the three genders... and so forth.
This is a matter not established by grammatical analysis; here, there is simply a lack of identity between the qualifiers. [The term is] "sīmānam."
In this case, because it transcends the limits of the eyes, it is not an object of the means of valid cognition known as perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because it lacks a fixed relationship due to its non-connection with anything else, it is not an object of inference (*anumāna*).
Because there is no contact with words, it is not an object of ordinary verbal testimony (*śabda*). And because it has never been seen before, it is not an object of analogy (*upamāna*).

Because it follows from the sense (*arthāt*) that there is no non-attainment of the object, and because the object is established, even though no specific means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is mentioned by the words "nor what is not," in reality, such beauty involves the superimposition of entities like the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as established in the Mīmāṃsā and other systems.
Since that which is characterized solely by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is not in contact with other means of knowledge, the qualification here is unique.
He demonstrates the diversity of scriptural matters with the words "In this way, in reasoning," and so forth.
Regarding the term *svapakṣa*: "wing" (*pakṣa*) refers both to a feather and to the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
"Weapon" (*heti*) refers both to a weapon and to the logical reason (*hetu*), which is the mark (*liṅga*).

"Distinction" (*viśeṣa*) means excellence (*atiśaya*) and the specific nature of an entity (*padārthaviśeṣa*). "Measure" (*māna*) means proof (*pramāṇa*). "Weak fire" (*mandam agnim*) refers to a feeble digestive fire.
Here, the manifestation of sluggish digestion, swelling, and the defect of *timira* occurs due to the absence of the physician who is the "Lord of Herbs" (the Moon).
In this case, since there is similarity even in the substantive portion (*viśeṣya*), another example must be sought.
Alternatively, by supplying "of the Moon" as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the term "of the Lord of Herbs" should be intended as its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "by those whose intent is spreading":

even by those who know the intended meaning (*tātparya*) and those who delight in inference, he is unknowable—he cannot be described as having limitations, nor can he be defined; rather, he is the supreme Guru.
The multitude of qualities residing in your heart has been determined by the wise to be an operation that surpasses all other operations within the multitude of qualities of unprecedented activity.
Regarding this multitude of qualities, he states "here Bharata," etc., because the designation of *rasa*—such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth—is superimposed upon it;
for they declare that *rasa* was first conceived by Bharata.

Because of the traditional teaching that "the production of rasa results from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory states (vyabhicārin)," [the author] establishes its conventional usage with the words "for thus here," and so forth. It is not to be understood through the power of intention (tātparya-śakti).

For *tātparya* (the intended meaning), according to the theory of *abhihitānvaya*, is the power of syntactic connection (*samanvaya-śakti*) that transcends direct denotation (*abhidhā*). Since this power rests solely upon the connection, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—which is perceived immediately after that connection—is not known through it.
Nor is it the object of inference, because there is no fixed relationship with the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Furthermore, it is not the "denoted" (*vācya*), because it is not the object of a direct linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).

It is not even suggested (lakṣya) because there is no sublation of its primary meaning and so forth; rather, being immeasurable due to the melting away of other objects of knowledge, it is determined by the wise to belong exclusively to the connoisseur— having transcended the functions of denotation, indication, and intentionality,

and being apprehended by the function called suggestion (vyañjanā), which is unique to poetry, unprecedented in other sciences, and which, by excluding both the worldly object of imitation (anukārya) and the imitator (anukartṛ)— the latter being dependent on the effort of dramatic performance— is accessible solely to the sensitive reader.
This is merely a brief indication; a detailed exposition would be found in the *Rasamīmāṃsā*,
but it is not provided here as it is not useful for the present subject at hand.
It has been explained in detail in the *Saṃpradāyaprakāśinī*, a commentary on the *Kāvyaprakāśa*; therefore, one should ascertain [the details] from that very source—enough said.

He states, "In this same way, other [matters]," meaning that the superimposition of entities such as the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) and so forth is to be understood according to this method.
"They perceive," etc.
Herein is this invitation: for the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā) is indeed fourfold—consisting of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī.

Among these, *Parā* is that which, having withdrawn the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) consisting of name and form into its own self, takes the form of the light of its own nature and transcends the three states of waking and so forth. *Madhyamā*, on the other hand, presides over the initial vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in order to manifest the expansion of names and forms; residing in the abode of the *kanda*, it extends as far as the *maṇipūraka*.

The state of dream-consciousness is *madhyamā*, which possesses the power of *paśyantī*; it consists of internal discourse (*saṃjalpa*) that culminates in the apprehension of phonemes, words, and so forth; it is presided over by the fluctuations of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) agitated by the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), extending from the *maṇipūra* up to the *anāhata* [cakra]; and it has arisen from the *pārā* [state] as the activity of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-vṛtti*), becoming oriented toward the entire universe while consisting of indistinct phonemes that have attained the state of seeds (*bīja-bhāva*).
Vaikharī, which consists of external verbalization, is gross and arises from the *madhyamā*; it extends outward from the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound as far as the cavities of the mouth.
The specific distinctions regarding the etymology and other attributes of these [four levels of speech] have been elaborated upon in the commentary on the first verse.
Now, at the time of dissolution, following the absorption of the waking state, Vaikharī merges into Madhyamā.

The *madhyamā* dissolves into the *paśyantī*; the *madhyamā* dissolves into the *paśyantī* by way of the dissolution of the dream state, and that [the *paśyantī*] dissolves into the *parā* by way of the dissolution of deep sleep.
The state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is said to consist of the supreme fourth stage (*parā turīyaparvātmikā*).
This being so, the Self, as the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), resides in the supreme (*parā*) state; the wise [reside] in the fourth (*turīyā*) and the visionary (*paśyantī*) states.
In the *madhyamā* stage there is the Taijasa, and in the *vaikharī* stage there is the Viśva; such is the general direction of the meaning of the scriptures.
Now, we shall explain this according to the connection of the words.
O Lord, whose nature is to prevail through the mastery of the senses,

when such a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and aesthetic unity (*sāmarasya*) has effortlessly arisen during your firm embrace while sporting with your supreme Goddess, how could there be the restless activity of external speech— the utterance of flatteries— or the movement of the palate and lips? How indeed could such things exist?
The meaning is that there is no such thing as frivolous speech at all.
Why is it not present? To this he says: because the internal *paśyantī* conceals itself as if out of shame; being more internal than even the *madhyamā*, she does not wish to manifest her own self.

In the fourth stage (*turīyaparvan*), because the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) do not arise there, even the *madhyamā* [speech] breaks apart due to the essence of the desire to emerge as a sweet resonance.
The meaning is that it does not uproot the sweet sound which consists of internal discourse (*antaḥsañjalpa*).
In that state of supreme concentration (*parā samādhi*), there is the non-arising of both *paśyantī* and *madhyamā*.

The intended meaning here is: "How indeed could the manifest speech (*vaikharī*) proceed? In this case, regarding a reality established by scripture (*āgama*), a worldly convention consisting of erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) has been superimposed.

Just as when your firm embrace with another goddess, your chief queen, is taking place, some other woman from the inner circle—precisely because she belongs to the inner circle—seeing your embrace, [conceals] herself as if out of shame.
Wherein it conceals and protects;
neither internal nor external, yet situated in the middle;
with a sweet resonance arising from the middle movement, it breaks asunder through the essence of the desire to emerge.
Desiring to sing, she desists out of curiosity;
therein, how could an external courtesan, who is under another's protection, expand her fickleness in uttering flatteries?
Regarding this, he says "here, the scripture" (*atrāgama*) in order to apply the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
He recalls what has already been stated regarding the various ways in which worldly objects are employed in poetry, beginning with the words "laukikavastu" (worldly object).
Now, an objection is raised: "Has it not been stated that the definition of *samāsokti* (condensed expression) is the similarity of specific qualities?
In the case of the superimposition of a mere effect (*kārya*), however, that [definition] is non-pervasive. To this he replies: "In that regard, [in the case of] a mere effect," and so forth.

For when there is an imposition of a pure effect— as in the case of [the verse] "she scratches her breast" and so forth— although the scratching of the breast and such, which is the effect of *haṭha* (forceful practice) or *kāma* (desire), does not primarily possess the status of being a qualifier of the *khadira* tree and so on;

Furthermore, if there is a qualification by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then the application of the definition must be performed in some manner or other. [The opponent asks: "But why resort to metaphorical designation? To this he replies: "In accordance with the previous treatises," and so forth.

Now, where the application of *samāsokti* (synecdochical metaphor) is inconsistent, he says "But here," and so forth, in order to make it consistent through the application of logical reasoning (*nyāyasañcāra*). Regarding the phrase "the bow of Indra":
"Bearing the rainbow of Indra, which resembles fresh nail-marks upon her pale breasts, and propitiating the spotted moon, the autumn night increased the suffering of the lover even more."
*Payodhara*, *medha*, and *kuca* all mean "breast.
The description of her as being "besmirched" (*sakalaṅka*)—due to the emergence of a blemish from an excess of grace—is intended to reveal her status as a paramour's mistress.
Furthermore, the autumnal sun causes greater heat than the summer one.
Regarding this, the discussion begins with "First of all... and so forth.
Having proposed the thesis that "the perception of [the character] as a hero exists," he challenges it with "But not here.
Having proposed the thesis that "the perception of [the character] as a hero exists through the presence of sorrowful gestures," he challenges it with "And not here."
The meaning is that there is no reason for the perception of [the autumn] as a heroine (*nāyikā*) based on its being accompanied by a lover (*sākūta*).
Anticipating the objection that such a reason does exist, he refutes it with the words "making serene" (*prasādayantī*), and so forth.

First of all, because of the similarity in the qualifying attributes characterized by being both "blemished" (*sakalaṅka*) and "serene" (*prasāda*), there is indeed the perception of autumn as a heroine.
If you think that the heroism of Indra and Arjuna is perceived through their similarity to those [two], this is not tenable.
Why? Because of the lack of correspondence with the qualifier "the bow of Indra, resembling fresh nail-marks."

The rainbow is a qualification of autumn alone, not of the heroine. One might argue: "Since there is a comparison through the qualification 'resembling fresh nail-marks,' let there be an *ekadeśavivartinī* (partially manifest) simile; by the force of that [simile], let the understanding of Indra and the sky as the hero and heroine arise. To this, he replies: "Nor by a partially manifest...
If a partially manifest simile had been stated by someone, then by its force the understanding of these two as the hero and heroine would occur. However, such is not the case here.
And this has not been stated by anyone;
therefore, by what power of that [statement] is the establishment of these two as leaders [of the path]? Desiring to provide a resolution to this, he says: "It is said."
"Existing in one part," and so forth.
Although this [type of inference] is not explicitly mentioned, there is nonetheless no prohibition against it.
To the question, "If there is an absence of both explicit mention and prohibition, how can its existence be established? he says: "By the general definition."

Now, one might object: "If a simile (*upamā*) that functions through a single part is possible here, then it would follow that this is merely the figure of speech *arthopamā*, not *samāsokti*. To this, he says: "Now, here," and so forth.
The word "now" (*atha*) indicates a new topic.
If the hero is perceived as the subject (*adhikārī*) by virtue of being the object of comparison (*upamāna*), [then it is indeed *samāsokti*].
There would be the apprehension of the figure of speech *upamā* (simile).
For no hero (*nāyaka*) qualified for such a role is perceived here;
rather, there is only the perception of the sun and the moon being treated as heroes.
Because these two alone are metaphorically designated as the "protagonists" (*nāyaka*) in this autumn;
since the figure of speech here is primarily *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation),
it is proper to arrange the words accordingly— hence he says, "In this case," and so forth.
Even though the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamānatva*) resides in the ear that has been wounded by a fresh nail-mark, it must be transferred to the rainbow.
Why? Through the examination of the actual state of things (*vastuparyālocanā*).
He clarifies that very examination of the state of things with the words beginning "resembling a rainbow" (*indracāpābham*), and so forth.
Since the cognition [of the injunction] arises precisely from the co-occurrence with other word-meanings and so forth, [the opponent asks:
"Where has the transfer of a property residing in one thing to another been seen? To this, he says: "Just as by curd," and so on.

For in the case of "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), the injunction is understood as pertaining to the act of offering; however, that same [injunction], in the case of "He performs the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*)...
Thus it is established.
The meaning is that one should apply the same analysis here as when [the properties] are gathered in the case of curd;
therefore, he concludes that this is indeed *samāsokti* (synecdoche) by stating, "thus, it is enlivened by simile."
Because the rainbow, which is the object of comparison (*upameya*), is conceived as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it is sustained by a metaphorical comparison (*vaivakṣikopamā*).
Now, in order to demonstrate that case where, setting aside *samāsokti* on logical grounds, only a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartinī upamā*) prevails, he says: "But here again...
[and] "as if with eyes... and so forth.
Here, he explains the cause for the perception of the beauty of the lake as being a heroine: "the beauty of the lake.
The perception of her as a heroine does not arise through *samāsokti* (synecdoche) due to the similarity of attributes;
for this very reason, he states that there is no superimposition of behavior (*vyavahārasamāropa*), saying: "therefore, she is a heroine."

In this case, the heroine is the standard of comparison for the beauty of the lake, but not by means of a superimposition of the essence of worldly behavior as a property of the lake's beauty; therefore, in such a context, since there is no other way, one must resort to a "partially manifest" (ekadeśavartinī) simile.
To the question of how it can be so employed when it is not explicitly stated, he says: "But by those... (yaistu).
The meaning is that we have already established this through logical arguments;
however, even by those who have not stated it, it must necessarily be included because there is no other possible alternative.
Now, was it not previously refuted that [the simile] applies only partially?
To the objection that there is a contradiction because [the figure] has already been established as *samāsokti*, he says: "But where, in the case of 'the mass of hair' (*keśapāśa*) etc.

Even when a simile has been stated in a compound such as "the luster of teeth like flowers" (*dantaprabhāḥ puṣpāṇīva*), if—by the power of a further compound such as "with flowers resembling the luster of teeth" (*dantaprabhāsadṛśaiḥ puṣpairiva*)—a similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*) is established, then in that case, it is more appropriate to regard it as *samāsokti* itself, which is evoked by qualifiers containing a simile within them.

But now, since there is no other possible way [to interpret] the phrase "as if with eyes," it is established that this is indeed a *ekadeśavivartinī* (partial) simile; thus, because there is no contradiction, everything is clear.
Now, he says "And that... and so forth, to show that there is another variety within this [simile] when it is manifested by an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration).
The subject to be supported (*samarthya*) is the contextual matter (*prakṛta-artha*), while the supporter (*samarthaka*) is the non-contextual matter (*aprakṛta*).
Now, regarding the word *upagūḍha*: it means embraced (*āliṅgite*);
[the verb] *yayau* means she departed (*apagatā*).
In that case, it pertains to the capacity [of the action] and is "incomplete"; here, however,
it pertains to the agent of the capacity.
Regarding the application in both cases, he says: "In this context, by way of being embraced," and so forth.

"Being embraced" (*upagūḍhatva*) and "having a glance like a peaceful flash of lightning" constitute the similarity of the qualifiers; through the *samāsokti* (condensed metaphor) evoked by that, there is the cognition of the behavior of a hero (*nāyaka*).

This being the case, this particular essence (*viśeṣātman*), which is embraced by the *samāsokti*, is supported by the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) in its universal aspect (*sāmānyātman*).
And there arises a justification for the general form [of the expression].

Due to the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the qualifier "embraced" (*upagūḍha*)—referring to those whose breasts have fallen away—is clearly common to both meanings. Furthermore, the phrase "having calmed the waves" (*śāntataṭit*) contains an internal simile (*upamā*).

"Her side-glances are like lightning"— this is the meaning established by a *samāsokti* (poetic suggestion through compounding), which contains within it a feminine and masculine gender indication as its constituent parts, and is manifested through the effect of a metaphorical relationship (*bhajanarūpa*). By means of this *samāsokti*, the behavior of a hero (*nāyaka*) is superimposed, thereby transforming the general form into a specific one.
This is supported by the account of the sun and the twilight.

By virtue of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), he says "with the speed of its drawing" (*ākṛṣṭivega*) for the sake of aesthetic charm; it refers to that Mount Mandara which was used as the encircling rope (*veṣṭana*).
The word *pāda* means both "the foot" and "a peripheral mountain.
Here, he says "here, by the slough," etc., in order to demonstrate the simultaneity of the metaphorical expression (*samāsokti*) and the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
By describing the Mandākinī as being "encircled by a band of slough," there is a superimposition (*samāropa*) of the Mandākinī upon that [mountain], through the concealment of its [actual] nature.

Furthermore, the fact that the mountain encircling its edge is itself the encircling of the base of her foot is determined through the poetic figure of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole), characterized by the identification of two distinct things based on a pun on the word "foot" (*pāda*).
And once so determined, this gives rise to a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) in the passage beginning with "the pain of churning," and so forth.
And since that [simile] brings forth a *samāsokti* (condensed expression) based on the relationship between husband and wife regarding Amburāśi and Dākini, these two possess simultaneity.
Thus he shows the same elsewhere as well: "In this way, 'the nail-marks'...
By the phrase "entered into another poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*)," their simultaneity is indicated.

He concludes that such variety is to be understood with the words "Thus, this... and so forth: "When the unstated subject is understood through the similarity of its qualifying attributes, that by which the meaning is expressed in brief is considered *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation)."
In the superimposition of a pure effect, the similarity would be merely figurative;
the superimposition of conventional usage is what directly motivates this [superimposition].
If there were equality of qualifiers through the elimination of other compounds,
simile would not sublate this [metaphor], which exists as a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartinī*).

This [simile] is observed in the figure of arthāntaranyāsa (corroboration), in the relation between the corroborated and the corroboration, as well as in connection with utprekṣā (poetic fancy); in some cases, it may exist within a single time frame.
He defines *parikara*:
*Parikara* is the state of a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) being intended with a specific purpose (*sābhiprāyatva*).
He states the connection [between the verses] with the words "viśeṣaṇavaicitrye" (due to the variety of qualifiers).
He explains [the meaning] with the words "viśeṣaṇānām" (of the qualifiers), and so forth.

What is called "clarity and profundity" (*prasannagambhīratva*) consists precisely in the fact that the words contain within them suggested meanings (*vyaṅgyārtha*); it does not mean that the suggested meaning must surpass the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
He speaks to provide an etymological explanation, saying "And thus":
being directed toward the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is being subordinate to the expressed meaning (*vācyāṅgatā*).
"Of the king" means of a king, and not of just anyone; even there, it refers to one whose wealth is honor, and not to one who can endure humiliation.
[It was] for Duryodhana, who wields a bow and is not unarmed, but not for one who fights with difficulty;
it was before him, and not out of his sight.
"While the kinsman of the Kurus, Karṇa, and Śalya were looking on"—
this is the genitive case used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*);
thus, the meaning is "disregarding Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śalya while they were looking on."

By not saying "of Duḥśāsana" but rather stating "of him who dragged the hair and garments of the Pāṇḍava bride," the intent is to establish that he must be killed. He must be slain while still alive, and not while unconscious or dead.
His chest is [pierced] by sharp fingernails as if crushed by a razor, and not by being split open with weapons.
"Neither too hot nor having stood overnight—
this was drunk by me today," says Bhīmasena.
He demonstrates the underlying intention (*sābhiprāyatā*) with the words "here," and so forth.
He shows this even in a sentence: "In this way, O King of Aṅga," and so forth.
The *parikara* (poetic elaboration) is characterized by the incorporation of suggested meanings within the qualifiers;
it is a *parikara* because the suggested meaning constitutes its elaboration (*parikara*).
He defines *śleṣa* (paronomasia):
*Śleṣa* occurs when there is similarity even of the substantive (*viśeṣya*), or when two [words] are employed. (RuAss 33)
When two meanings are either both contextual or both non-contextual, then there is *śleṣa* (paronomasia) when there is a phonetic identity between the qualifier and the qualified.

However, when the two meanings are of a mixed nature (one contextual and one non-contextual), then there is *śleṣa* upon the separate mention of the qualified portion; such is the meaning of the aphorism.
He states the connection [between this and the previous case] with the words: "In the case of a mere qualifier," etc.
The word "this" (*idam*) is a qualifier.
He explains it with the passage beginning "there, of the two," etc.,
[stating that it applies] only when there is equality between the qualifier and the qualified.
The meaning is: "only when there is identity of words in both cases.

Even regarding the referent portion (*viśeṣya*), if there is identity of words, then by means of context, subject matter, and so forth, the primary denotation (*abhidhā*) would be restricted; it would not, however, be *śleṣa*.
For a word with multiple meanings is restricted to only the contextual meaning by means of context and other such factors.
However, since there is no restrictive cause in the first two modes, both [alternatives] should be stated.
Since this is the case, he says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) that the option (*vikalpa*) is established as being twofold in its combined form (*śliṣṭaprakāradvaya*).
The first two types are *śliṣṭa* (pun-based), because they possess the quality of punning even in the referent of the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
In the phrase "by whom [the world] was destroyed," *anaḥ* means a cart (*śākaṭa*).

By his non-existence—that is, by not being subject to saṃsāra—he conquered the body of the Daitya Bali; at the time of the distribution of the nectar in ancient times, he was made into a woman, that is, he was brought into the state of womanhood. And he is the slayer of the arrogant serpent Kāliya and others. He possesses the *aravalaya*, which is the discus (*cakra*).
Kṛṣṇa, who in his Varāha incarnation supported Mount Govardhana, the cow, and the earth;
and whose praiseworthy name the immortals call "the Moon-Head-Taker"—
for Rāhu, the moon-seizer, devours the moon.

May that Mādhava— who brought about the destruction of the Andhakas and their companions, the Vṛṣṇis, yet established them in their abode— protect you at all times. Furthermore, he by whom, having destroyed the Mind-born (Manmatha), the body of Viṣṇu— the conqueror of Bala— was turned into a weapon for the destruction of the cities in ancient times.
And he whom they call by the name "Hara," which is worthy of praise like a portion of a host [of gods]—
the destroyer of the demon Andhaka, the husband of Umā, the lord of Gaurī— may he protect you always.
Here, both Hari and Hara are equally the subjects of the context (*prākaraṇika*).
Regarding the phrase "of those led [there]":

*lubdhaiḥ* means by hunters; *madhulampaṭaiḥ* and *vyādhaiḥ* are adjectives for the former; *bhūri* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*); *ekadā* refers to bees (*śilīmukhaiḥ*) and at other times to many arrows (*bhūribāṇaiḥ*); and *vana* means water as well as a forest.
Of lotuses (*kamala*), i.e., *padma*s, and of deer;
here, the lotus and the deer are irrelevant to the context.
[The phrase] "by her own will" (*svecchayā*)...
The object consists of the country, the treasury, women, and so forth;
[the terms] "dehi," "vitara," and "dehavān" [are used];
and by hundreds of seekers, that is, by caravans of beggars.
At one time he does not go to speak; at another time, by means of hundreds of arrows through various applications numbering in the hundreds, he inflicts suffering.
*Jīvita* means livelihood (*jīvikā*), and *jīva* means the living being (*car*).
The Lord is "durvidagdha" (difficult to please).
Here, the "Lord" is the contextual subject, while the "mind-born one" (Kāma) is non-contextual; here, there is the employment of two distinct subjects as the objects of qualification.
Regarding the application [of this principle] to all three examples, he says: "In this case, *harihara*, etc.
Furthermore, regarding its threefold nature, he says: "And this [is] of word and meaning," and "the acute accent (*udātta*), etc."
Even in worldly words, the comprehension of meaning arises solely from the difference in accent.
The effort consisting of the operation of the palate, lips, and so forth, is the cause for the distinctness of words.
Regarding word-pun (*śabdaśleṣa*), he states another indicative mark: "where, generally... and so on.
But he says that the *śleṣa* of meaning (*arthaśleṣa*) is otherwise: "for this very reason.
He states the *śleṣa* of both [word and meaning] (*ubhayaśleṣa*) by means of their combination.
He provides an example of the *śleṣa* of both: "the state of having red petals," and so on.
And they are clothed in tattered rags;
they are "vikaca," meaning both blooming and devoid of hair.
Bearing a stalk joined with water, and not at all maintaining friendship with dull-witted people;
possessing a luster and beauty among flowers other than the *kusuma*—
the text shows the double entendre (*ubhayaśleṣatā*) here in the passage beginning with "raktā" and so forth, [referring both to the lotus and to a passionate woman].
He states the reason for not citing separate examples with the words "due to the bulk of the text" (*granthagaurava*).
Then, he begins the discussion regarding its scope and lack of scope with the words "And this... (*eṣa ca*), etc.

Some maintain that when other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) do not apply, this [figure]—if it were not commenced [separately]—is stronger because it leaves no room [for others], and thus, by subverting them, it produces merely the semblance (*pratibhāmātra*) of those [other figures].
Regarding the phrase "by which [the mind-born] was destroyed":
others, however, say that its scope is distinguished from other figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*); thus, because it has its own distinct occasion, it does not invalidate others.
