Therefore, they maintain that when there is an overlap with another figure, there is a mixture (*saṅkara*), or else, by logical principle, it is sublated due to its weakness.
In this regard, wishing to reveal that there is no room for his own [opponent's] position, he says: "In that context, of the former," and so forth.
The phrase "by virtue of having multiple meanings as their object" is to be connected with each [of the two categories].
The first pair of types consists of having multiple contextual meanings as their object and having multiple non-contextual meanings as their object.
For both of these are indeed the domain of *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing),
whose definition is the connection of the subjects at hand with a common attribute.
However, where there is a scope consisting of multiple objects of two forms, the third variety prevails, and there *dīpaka* (illumination) is effective.

Its defining characteristic is the connection of both the relevant (prastuta) and the irrelevant (aprastuta) through a common attribute; therefore, this pair of ornaments pervades the domain of *śleṣa* (paronomasia). To show that it is also pervaded by other ornaments, he says: "following upon that" (*tatpṛṣṭhe ca*).

Since its subject matter is not thus distinct [from that of other figures], other poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) are sublated by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), leaving nothing but a mere flash of intuition (*pratibhā*).

This being the case, even that subject matter which was suspected to be distinct is in fact not distinct; thus he says, "By whom [the world] was destroyed," and so forth. He states that even that subject matter which was suspected to be distinct is in fact not distinct by saying, "By whom [the world] was destroyed," and so forth.

Having thus established that there is no contradiction with other [theories] because there is no room for objection, he states "alaṅkārya... and so forth in order to demonstrate that this [figure] pertains to both word and meaning.

For in the world, the relationship between the adorned and the ornament is established through the relationship of locus and occupant (āśrayāśrayibhāva), as in the expression "an ear-ornament resting on the ear.
Therefore, in examples such as *raktacchada* ("red-winged"), because it rests upon the meaning, this is an ornament of meaning (*arthālaṅkāra*).
In cases such as "nālam," however, since the difference in words is manifest, it is a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāra*).

Now, one might object: "If the difference in meaning entails a difference in the words themselves, then even in examples like *raktacchadam*, there would be no identity of words. To this he says, "Even though... and so forth.
[The reason is] "because it is logically established" (*aupapattikatvāt*).
For the demonstration of the difference between words is indeed established through the reasoning that "there is a difference of words for each distinct object.
However, in actual cognition, oneness alone is determined.

Therefore, because the essence of cognition lies in its unity despite the process of sequential association, and by relying on the philosophical view that establishes the oneness of the word, there is no difference between the words.
In cases such as *nāla*, however, the difference in words conforms to the cognition [of the meaning].
Therefore, in cases such as *raktacchada*, because the words are identical, there is a semantic fusion (*śliṣṭatā*) of the two meanings according to the maxim of "two fruits on a single stalk";
but in cases such as *nāla*, it is a fusion of the two words themselves, according to the maxim of "lac and wood."

Regarding the verse beginning with "raktacchadam" and so forth, he raises the objection that there is a figure of speech because of the word "punaḥ," stating: "In the previous case, it is a connection... He refutes this, saying: "No; because of the substratum... and so on.
For the status of being an ornament is suspected in the world [to apply] here as well, based on the previous connection; he refutes this with "No," beginning with "the substratum," and so forth.
For the status of being an ornament (alaṅkāratva) is established in the world through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka),
and indeed only by way of the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva); the meaning here is that it is the same in this case as well.

Having thus established the status of both as figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), he begins the analysis of their relationship as the sublated (*bādhy*) and the sublator (*bādhaka*) with the words "And thus, *sakala*... and so forth.

Since the status of both as figures of speech has been proven in this way through their lack of scope for coexistence, in examples such as "*sakalakalam*," there is only *śleṣa* (punning compounding), not *upamā* (simile).
The reason for this is that verbal similarity, unlike the similarity of qualities or actions, does not serve as a basis for *upamā*.
"The orb of the moon is endowed with digits, but it is accompanied by a clamor"—here there is merely a similarity of sound.
Therefore, it is concluded that this is indeed *śleṣa* (paronomasia), which serves as the cause for the emergence of the suggestion of a simile (*upamā-pratibhotpatti-hetu*).
Now, one might object: if *śleṣa* is the sublater because it leaves no room [for another figure], then...

If that is so, one might ask: why is there a sublation (*bādha*) between metaphor (*rūpaka*) and poetic identification (*samāsokti*)? To this, he says: "But when [the figure] contains a pun (*śleṣa*)," and so forth. For metaphor, having brought forth a completed pun, comes to rest in its own essential form; thus, it is the sublater of the pun. In that case as well, if the pun, being previously established, brings forth the metaphor and then rests in its own form, [it remains].
In that case, the metaphor (*rūpaka*) is indeed sublated,
as in examples such as *bhramimarati* and so forth;
this has been discussed in the section on metaphor (*rūpaka*).
Even if a metaphor (rūpaka) that is already established brings about a pun (śleṣa), it shall still be considered a metaphor; otherwise, it is regarded as a pun.
Thus it is said.
Regarding *śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇā* (metaphor based on double-entendre adjectives):

however, in the case of *samāsokti* (condensed expression), which is based on double-entendre adjectives, because the substantive element (*viśeṣya*) is merely implied (*gamya*), *samāsokti* itself is the sublater.
For in *śleṣa* (double entendre), the defining characteristic is precisely that [the meaning] is directly expressed (*vācyatva*).
Therefore, because it is devoid of the defining characteristics [of a valid simile], the appearance of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also certainly sublated.
To demonstrate that even another qualifier acts as a sublator of the *śleṣa*, he says: "But here," and so forth.
"Even though Vivasvat is renowned throughout the worlds as being composed of the three Vedas (*trayīmaya*), that he went toward Vāruṇī..."
The western direction belongs to Varuṇa, as does wine (surā).
For this very reason, he has fallen from the mountain of setting (astaśaila).

Falling (pātitya) means contact with a lower region; and because of that very state of having fallen, there is also defilement (upahati). The meaning is that he entered the midst of the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni) for the sake of purification.
He explains [the verse] with the words "of Vivasvat, according to the nature of things," and so forth:
although the Lord of the Three Worlds exists as one whose essence is the Veda (trayīmaya), his two actions— namely, his contact with Vāruṇī and his entry into the foremost reality—
are both superimposed upon the activities of Vivasvat through an *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) rooted in *śleṣa* (punning wordplay).
This is that excellence called the "connection with that action" (or "the single action").

Although there is indeed only one action, it is determined as non-different even while being differentiated by the difference among the agents; yet, that [action] is that very action (or the single action).
This is a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) caused by that [yoga].
Here, in this *utprekṣā*, the meaning—

which is adorned by the figure of speech "contradiction" (*virodhālaṅkāra*), which is referred to by the pronoun "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) as having the form of an appearance of contradictory conduct— is imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the cause for the state of falling.
And [the phrase] "for the sake of purification" functions as the result;
therefore, there is both a *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the cause) and a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result).
Furthermore, he states that the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction) is also present because its defining characteristic is fulfilled, saying: "and of the *virodhālaṅkāra*..."

Therefore, the simultaneous occurrence of the figures of speech *virodha* (contradiction) and *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) falls within a single instance; however, the sequence of cognition is such that contradiction is resolved at a subsequent time.

This being the case, *śleṣa* (punning paronomasia), acting as a sublater of all [other figures], sublates the figure of contradiction and establishes itself through mere creative intuition (*pratibhā*).
The intention is that when there is contradiction and sublation, the sublation of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) caused by it is already established;
therefore, this is indeed *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

However, regarding cases in dramas and the like where there is a suggestiveness (*sūcakatva*) characterized by the introduction of a seed (*bīja*)—which consists in the hinting of a future event—the author states "But where... and so forth, for the purpose of critical investigation (*mīmāṃsā*).
Even though it is devoted to the subject matter at hand and even though it is grounded in the present tense,
it is called "upakṣepa" (the introductory statement);
"upakṣepa" is its technical designation.
As it is said: “The ‘planting of the seed’ is the introduction.
Regarding the phrase “of two meanings,” it is not intended there to state that the two meanings are connected by being within the scope of non-differentiation.
What then? Only one subject is introduced as the topic; however, that which is yet to be spoken is merely indicated. Therefore, there is no *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Nor is it *dhvani* (suggestion), because in the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is a rule that both [meanings] must be expressed.
Why? Because there is no intended comparison (*aupamya*) due to the lack of connection with the future matter (*bhāvyartha*) that is to be introduced.
Furthermore, there is no other possible category apart from *śleṣa* and *dhvani*.
In this regard, the objection is raised: "What is to be done? He provides the answer with the words "It is said," and so forth.

However, since there is no possibility of expressing both [the literal and the suggested meanings] simultaneously through punning (*śleṣa*), such a case does not apply at all; therefore, this is exclusively the domain of *dhvani* (suggestion).
He establishes this with the words "tathāhi" (for instance):

since there is no relationship between the expressed and the suggested meanings when sound is based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*), a comparison is constructed to establish that relationship.
If that relationship can be easily established through another means without depending on comparison, then what is the point of insisting on *upamādhvani* (suggestion of simile)?

It is not exclusively a matter of what is to be accomplished (kārya), because even *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) is established in that domain through another appropriate relationship. For this very reason, the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* has logically stated that *dhvani* based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) is twofold: in the form of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) and in the form of a fact (*vastu*). "Wherein either an ornament or a fact itself appears from the word, etc. [Dhvanyāloka 2.19]
That [suggestion] arising from the power of words (śabdaśaktyudbhava) should be known as twofold, according to whether it is predominant.
Thus it is said.
This being the case, even in the present instance, a suggestion based on the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla-vastudhvani*) is to be understood through the relationship of indication.
An example here is "O Kauśika, immediately...
from the drama *Hariścandracarita*.
The direction of Kauśika and so forth is the direction of the owl, which is joyful in nature, for they chirp with joy at dawn;
or else, Kauśika is Indra,
and his direction is the East, due to his expansion [therein].
For at dawn, the eastern quarter extends itself;
the sky, like a kingdom, having been abandoned at will, and the moon, bearing a dusty luster like that of bark garments, has gone to the mountain of setting.
Then the night, his beloved, as if consoling her son—the bed of white water-lilies—now wailing with swarms of bees emerging from their slumber, departed quickly along with him.

However, regarding the matter to be indicated, [the poet] says "here, at dawn," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that this is indeed *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact): [namely,] that Viśvāmitra, under the influence of anger, voluntarily abandoned his kingdom and set out for Vārāṇasī;
and his beloved wife Auśīnarī, consoling her weeping son Rohitāśva, set out along with him.
Thus, it is shown that here there is only the suggestion of a factual matter.

Now, one might object: "Since there exists a connection of comparison in the phrases 'having the luster of grey bark' and 'as if it were a thread,' how can this be considered *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact)? To this, he replies: "But by means of the bark and the thread.

For similarity is indeed possible independently of the meaning intended to be suggested (*sūcanīya-artha*). One should rest with that much alone—namely, the fact that they pertain to the subject at hand—because [the similarity] would otherwise be useless for the meaning intended to be suggested.

Therefore, because there is a connection between the suggested meaning and the suggestor through the context, this is indeed a case of *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) based on the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*).
This should be understood in the same way everywhere in dramas and other such works.

Now, to show that even where there is neither *tulyayogitā* nor *dīpaka*, there is no scope for this [type of suggestion] that is distinct from other figures of speech, he says: "In this [case]," etc.
In this instance, there is first the perception of the qualifiers—such as "pulling the hair," "making the face contort," and so forth—as referring to the lover (*vallabha*).
Then, following the friend’s remark, "As she speaks thus, her shame has vanished," the lover performs a denial with "No, no! while using the pretext of [removing] the bodice (*kūrpāsaka*).
For here, there is neither *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) nor *dīpaka* (illumination); therefore, one should not suspect that this is a distinct domain of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
The reason for this is: "because negation exists. He raises an objection: "In reality.
For negation proceeds in reality for the sake of similarity, whereas here similarity proceeds for the sake of negation; thus, the objection is that this is not a negation.
He refutes [the objection] by stating "not in either case.
This refers to the actual meaning, which is the subject at hand;
for the definition of *apahnuti* (concealment) is indeed the denial of the subject at hand.
And since that [denial] is possible in both ways, it is *apahnuti* (concealment).
Regarding this, he states the summary verse: "In the manifestation of similarity.
This refers to the form of denial (*apahnava*) which culminates in the initial similarity.

In the section on *svaprastāva*, specifically within the discussion of *apahnuti* (concealment), [the author] concludes that it consists of a similarity which results ultimately in a second concealment: "Therefore, it is a different ornament... and so forth.
Paronomasia (śleṣa) occurs when there is a similarity of words between the qualifier and the qualified;
however, if one [of them] has an unintended meaning, and there is a difference in the words denoting the object to be distinguished, it is not paronomasia.
This [defect], which resides in both the word and the meaning, subverts all poetic ornaments;
furthermore, if it pertains to a previously established element, it is subverted by logical necessity.
Thus, although this figure of speech, *śleṣa*, was elaborated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* with a passion for logic, it has been refuted at every step by him.
The arguments for the refutation are not written here because they would be inappropriate;
however, they have been demonstrated in detail in the *Saṃpradāyaprakāśinī*, a commentary on the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, and should therefore be understood from that very source.

Desiring to define *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), [the author] shows another connection following the conclusion of the connection based on the charm of adjectives: "From the relevant to the irrelevant," and so forth.

In this regard, the aphorism is: *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* occurs when there is a cognition of the relevant from the irrelevant, whether through the relation of general and particular, cause and effect, or similarity. (RuAss 34)

*Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description) occurs when there is an understanding of the relevant subject (*prastuta*) by means of relying on a relationship such as the universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) relation with something irrelevant (*aprastuta*).
He explains this [with the words]: "In this case, of the irrelevant...
For the irrelevant cannot be described unless it has the purpose of conveying the relevant.

Because it is not the subject under discussion; and connection (*saṃbandha*) is that which makes the subject known, and it is of only three kinds: the relation of general and particular, the relation of cause and effect, and similarity (*sārūpya*).

In this regard, there is the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) based on either the universal (*sāmānya*) [indicating] the particular (*viśeṣa*), or the particular [indicating] the universal; as well as the relationship of cause and effect (*kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*) and similarity (*sārūpya*).
Among these, the cognition of the particular from the universal, or the cognition of the universal from the particular, constitutes a twofold distinction.
The same applies to the relationship of cause and effect.
Although this is not the case when there is similarity (*sārūpya*),
and thus [the inference] is of five kinds,
nevertheless, even in the case of similarity, there is a twofold division based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), just as with the other types of distinctions.
Now, this [suggestion] is threefold according to the possibility of the expressed meaning: as both [the expressed and the suggested], and so forth.
However, when there is the employment of punning words (*śliṣṭa-śabda*), it is not sublated by the pun (*śleṣa*), because that which is intended for the context is not the expressed meaning.
Thus, "taṇṇātthī" and so on.
There is nothing whatsoever provided by the wife for her husband that is not governed by destiny;
it is the provision for the traveler of Time who never ceases his journey.
This has been explained previously.
He demonstrates the cognition of the particular from the general with the words "here, Prahasta," and so forth;
[the phrase] "this belongs to him" [is as follows].
"From his mouth, how much of this?"—
the meaning is that compared to the dullness of what is about to be described, his dullness is slight;
thus it is said, "this."
What is that? It is that one who mistook a drop of water on a lotus leaf for a pearl;
such a person is not excessively dull-witted.

He alone is truly dull-witted who, while taking up that drop of water—which dissolves upon contact with the tip of his finger—thinking it to be a pearl, does not sleep due to inner grief, lamenting: "My pearl has flown away!"
Here, he demonstrates the cognition of the general through the particular with the words "here, of the dull-witted.

"We see"—this is a statement by the hero (nāyaka) in the form of describing the heroine's (nāyikā) situation to a friend. With the thought, "Let us see what she does," I maintained a steady composure consisting of silence, avoidance of conversation, and so forth.
But she, thinking, "This rogue indeed does not say a word to me," fell into a state of anger.
Thus, while he was in that altered state, so skillful in the art of glancing with mutual shyness, I laughed under a pretext,
and she too shed tears that robbed her of her composure.
The meaning is that when she was filled with tears, her fortitude itself was abandoned.
Here, he demonstrates the perception of the effect from the cause by stating, "here, likewise, having mounted the stream [of tears].
While the cessation of pride—the actual effect—is the subject at hand, the mention of tears—which is not the primary subject—is intended to be expressed as something incidental.
By the phrase "the moon as if smeared with collyrium," the beauty of her face is [described];
by "the glances of the does as if rendered dull," the flickering movement of her eyes; and by "the coral leaf as if its redness has faded," the luster of her lower lip.

The quality of having a melodious voice (*snigdhakaṇṭhatā*) is understood from the phrase "the duty [of singing] has indeed begun in the throats of the female cuckoos," while the abundance of the mass of hair is perceived from the phrase "the peacock feathers seem as if they were being censured.
He demonstrates the perception of a cause from an effect with the words "here, by those that are being imagined," and so forth.
"Being conceived" means being imagined.
Here, one anticipates the objection of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with the words "But [from] the effect," and so forth.

For instance, in the verse beginning with "with his long locks hanging down" (*lambālaka*), there is a cognition of the cause—the slaying of the demon Gajāsura—by means of the effect, namely, the state of having long hanging locks, and so on.

Regarding the phrase "by the blow of the discus": here, because the effect—consisting of the absence of the embrace of Rati and the reduction of the act to mere kissing—is distinct, the cutting off of Rāhu’s head serves as the cause.
He demonstrates the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in this case with the words "for here," etc., and he refutes it with "this is not a fault."

Since both [the cause and the effect] are under discussion, when the description of the effect is striking by virtue of its dependence on the cause, the communication of that cause through such a medium is the province of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
However, when the effect is not under discussion, it is the province of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise); such is the distinction.
He concludes by defining their distinct scopes with the words "Thus, where... and so forth.
"Such as that" means just as it is under discussion;
"he brings" means he causes it to come by virtue of his power.

And this being the case, since the very subject at hand is being introduced as an embellishment for itself, he speaks again—starting with "Therefore, by this," and so forth—in order to proclaim *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
"O King!
[refers to] the hunchback woman who was appointed to feed the parrot.
"Kumāra" is a form of address; "his ministers" refers to those in charge of the communal meals;
"rājaśuka" means an excellent parrot.
In this context, since even the conduct of the royal parrot is relevant as a subordinate element to the hero's majesty, it should be understood as *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) alone.
He states the opinion of others: "But others [say]...
regarding that which has the form of a cause, characterized by the flight of the enemies.

In such a case, there is no contradiction whatsoever even if others consider this to be *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), for when both [the cause and effect] are relevant to the context, it is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis);
however, when the effect is irrelevant, it is *aprastutapraśaṃsā*. With the intention of showing that this distinction is not arbitrary, he says: "in every respect" (*sarvathā*).
Now, he states that these are to be understood as examples of similarity (*sādharmya*) by saying, "These are [examples of] similarity.
However, those based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) are to be inferred.
Since the distinction caused by similarity is easily understood through this method of similarity, he illustrates it through dissimilarity with the verse beginning, "Blessed are... (*dhanyā*).
He demonstrates the dissimilarity (vaidharmya) with the words "atra vātā iti" (here, winds).
He says "vācyeti" (regarding the expressible), meaning that they need not be cited separately when the expressible [meaning] is possible.
[The example is] "kastvaṃ bho" (who are you, sir?).

When asked, "Who are you?", the Śākoṭaka tree says, "O sir, listen, I shall tell you," and so forth. Thereupon, another question is asked: "Do you speak as if out of dispassion? To that, the reply is: "It is well understood."

Now, as to the question "Why this?", the remaining answer shows the impossibility [of the opponent's position] with the words: "here, by the insentient. But if it is argued that in this way impossibility is established, he says: "with reference to what is under discussion."

Since it is understood that the *śākoṭaka* tree is indeed planted at the very front, its impossibility [as the intended meaning] is entirely appropriate; for, being based on *jahatsvārthā* indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the literal sense is completely set aside.
"Hollows within" (*antaśchidrāṇi*)—the hollows are apertures and gateways to misfortune.
"Thorns" (*kaṇṭakāḥ*)—these are bristles and obstacles.
In this case, the flaws in the expressed meaning (vācya-artha) serve as the cause for the state of being fragile in its qualities; thus, there is a dual nature.
Since the cognition occurs through the intended sense (tātparya) of what is presented, it is indeed consistent because of the superimposition (adhyāropa) upon that.
This is what he says: "In this case, in the expressed," and so forth.

And this very point should be understood in the case of being "pregnant with *śleṣa*," because the qualities of the "holes" (*chidra*) and "thorns" (*kaṇṭaka*) are intertwined; thus he says, "and this very [point].
He demonstrates the distinction of its scope through the figures of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) and *dṛṣṭānta* (example): "In that case, here...
For in *arthāntaranyāsa*, there is the expressibility of the universal and the particular, or of cause and effect; whereas in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), however—
In both cases, there is express denotation (*vācyatva*).
Since the subject at hand is always understood [through implication], this is simply *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) because of the expression of the non-subject.
Indeed, *aprastutapraśaṃsā* is the comprehension of the subject from something else.
That [consciousness] is considered to be fivefold through its differentiation into universals, particulars, and so forth.
Furthermore, that [inference] is of two kinds by virtue of its connection with similarity or dissimilarity;
moreover, it is threefold according to the possibility or impossibility of the subject matter.
Because that which is intended is understood [indirectly], it is distinguished from *paryāyokta* (periphrasis);
it is also distinguished from the figures of speech *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) and *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration).
He states the connection for the purpose of providing an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroborative illustration) with the words "by the aforementioned method.
The "method" (*naya*) refers to that which has been explained through its connection with generalities, particulars, and so forth. In this regard, the aphorism is as follows:
Arthāntaranyāsa (corroboration by a general principle) is the support of the subject under discussion, as indicated, by means of both a general rule and a specific instance, or by cause and effect.

The meaning is that *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle) is the corroboration of the subject under discussion, which has been indicated as being capable [of proof] through these two types of relations.
He explains this with the words "of that which has been indicated," and so forth;
[it refers to] that which is worthy of corroboration, but not that which is independent of corroboration.
It has been stated that regarding the temporal sequence—whether [the capacity] precedes or follows—the choice is optional;
however, it is not by way of being "new" (apūrva). For comprehension occurs precisely through the fact of being indicated, and not through the quality of being new.
To the question, "What is the fault in [its] being unprecedented (*apūrva*)? he says: "of the nature of inference" (*anumānarūpa*).
The meaning is that if it were perceived in such a way, it would necessarily follow that it is simply of the nature of inference.
He enumerates the distinctions with the words: "In that regard, the universal," and so forth.
He excludes the distinctions [of objects] that lack variety even in terms of their possible existence, beginning with the word "hi" (for).
"Uṭṭaṅkita" means firmly established.
"Anantara-ratna" refers to a collection (*sannipāta*), which is an assemblage of many things.

In this context, within the convergence of qualities, the general characteristic consisting in the submergence of faults serves as a support for the particular through similarity. "Transcendent" means that it is precisely the transcendent conduct of men that bestows stability; the sense is that it establishes magnanimity.
But lineage is not the cause here;
Agastya was one who drank the wind and fire.
The jar stands in the place of his lineage—what authority does it have regarding the drinking of the ocean?

*Līlāyitam* (sportiveness) stands for conduct. Here, the specific instance characterized by the life-story of Agastya supports the general proposition through similarity (*sādharmya*). "Suddenly" (*sahasā*) refers to the act of determination; for lack of discrimination, which consists in acting impulsively, is the very ground of calamities. By this, the effect—being the ground of calamities—is shown through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with the cause, which is the absence of impulsive action.

It is an illustration by way of similarity (*sādharmyeṇa*): "The prosperity of those who act with deliberation chooses [them]," because the cause— acting with deliberation, which consists in the absence of acting impulsively— is the means of attainment, and the choice of prosperity is its effect.

Since similarity (*sādharmya*) is primary here, he connects [the verse] by prioritizing the meaning of the second half: "In this case, because of acting impulsively," and so forth. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "of the cause consisting in acting after reflection";
that is to say, of that very same cause.
The pair "pṛthvī" refers to the Earth and the serpent; that triad consists of the King of Tortoises and the aforementioned pair.
"Didhīrṣā" means the desire to support.
Here, the act of stretching the bowstring is the cause, which—by virtue of its common property—is capable of effecting the result, such as stabilization.
He applies this [verse] here: "In this matter, 'the bow of Hara'...
"Alas! Indeed!"—for surely a great offense has been committed against life, since, upon seeing such a defeat of the Suhmas, such an unpleasant thing has fallen to be spoken.
Therefore, they alone are truly fortunate.

"Those who have gone to destruction without witnessing the defeat of their friends"—here, the general statement is supported by a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*). He connects this by stating: "In this case, life is the agent..."

For misfortune (*adhanyatva*) is brought about by a fault committed during one's lifespan (*āyuḥ*). In contrast to that misfortune—which is caused by reaching exhaustion through factors incompatible with life—a general principle (*sāmānya*) has been stated as a supporting argument based on its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
This serves to remind us of the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatā*).
He reveals indifference toward those [examples] that have been set aside with the words "for" (hi) and so forth:

"When that which was under discussion is supported by its capacity, and is not explicitly stated [as such], this is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration); it is eightfold, beginning with the general (*sāmānya*) and so on."

He clarifies the connection with the meaning of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) as follows: "In this way, though the subject is not the one under discussion," and "the subject is that which is to be understood";
for it is indeed the introduction of the implied meaning that is occurring.
In this regard, the Sūtra states:
*Paryāyokta* (Indirect Expression) is the description of that which is to be understood by means of another mode of expression. (RuAss 36)
Paryāyokta (periphrasis) is the expression, by means of another mode such as the effect and so forth, of that which is already being understood.
He explains this with the words "yadeva" and so on.
He establishes the expression of that which is already implied by the phrase "of that very thing which is implied."
He explains "by way of another turn of phrase" with the words beginning "for not," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "If there is a mention of the effect (*kārya*) and so on, how can there be a mention of that which is to be understood? To this he replies: "even of the effect, etc.
He recalls what was previously established regarding the distinction from *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) with the words: "and this," and so forth.
"They have been touched"—
this was explained previously.
He applies it here [to the phrase] "of Hayagrīva."
The effect [in this case] is the touch of the flower-cluster (*mañjarī*).
However, *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is the description of that which is to be understood by means of its effect and so forth;
it differs from *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) because the expressed subject here is distinct from the contextual subject.
He states the connection with *vyājastuti* (ironical praise) as follows: "In the case of being understood," etc. The aphorism:
*Vyājastuti* occurs when censure and praise are understood through praise and censure, respectively. (RuAss 37)
When praise is understood through censure, there is one [type of *vyājastuti*], and when censure is understood through praise, there is another.
Therefore, the analysis [of the compound] is "praise in the form of a pretext" (*vyājarūpā stutiḥ*) and "praise by means of a pretext" (*vyājena stutiḥ*).
He explains this with the words beginning "where praise," and so forth.

"From another means of valid cognition" means from one capable of making [the object] appear clearly. "By way of concomitance" means by way of the connection with the meaning. As for the second type, it says "even where," because it is praise under the guise of censure (*nindā-vyāja-stuti*).
Thus, due to this division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*), there are two types of *vyājastuti*.

Now, one might ask: since the element to be understood through praise and censure is already under discussion, what is the distinction from *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise)? To this, he says: "Praise and censure," etc. "O, O!
refers to the Bodhisattva Jīmūtavāhana.

For he [the Bodhisattva] bestowed benefit upon another only at certain times; you, however, act as a companion to the desert in carrying the burdens of infamy acquired through hostility toward all and every one who desires [your favor].
Therefore, since you have surpassed the Bodhisattvas with such ease, there is no need for an elaborate expansion of words in praise of you.
The meaning is that it encompasses [the whole].
He shows that praise implies censure by saying, "here, the opposite," namely,
"the spot of the moon."

The praise is understood as follows: "While there exist dark objects such as the moon, the spot on the moon, and so forth—the tilaka of the circle of the earth—nothing at all has been whitened by your glories.
This is what is expressed here by the words "dhavalatva" (whiteness) and so on. "Anavakḷptiḥ" means insufficiency or inadequacy.
However, to show that this [figure] lacks propriety where the element to be conveyed (gamyāṃśa) is subordinate, he says: "What with these accounts?
Here, by the statement "Alas, my beloved wanders about," the fact that the censure results in praise is not made manifest; thus, due to impropriety, there is a state of obscurity (kliṣṭatā).
This is what he says here: "Even though it has been introduced in this context...
*Vyājastuti* (disguised praise) consists of two types: praise in the form of a pretext, or praise that is itself a pretext.
Its distinction from *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description) lies in its nature as being either praise or censure.
He states the connection for the purpose of raising an objection: "gamyatvam eva" (only the state of being cognizable).
"Viśeṣa" means excellence (*atiśaya*). The meaning is: "having as its object that which is to be understood through the apprehension of excellence."

Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "Paralipsis (ākṣepa) is a semblance of negation intended to bring about the comprehension of a specific distinction between two contextual matters—one already mentioned and one yet to be mentioned. (RuAss 38)
*Ākṣepa* (objection) is the apparent negation of a contextual subject—whether already mentioned or yet to be mentioned—for the sake of conveying its specific distinction.
This twofold *ākṣepa* should be understood as being of a different nature [from other figures].
He explains this with the words: "In this context, the contextual," and so forth.
Of that which is intended to be predicated in such a manner;
for this very reason, that [reason] has been applied to what is not its proper domain—this is the meaning.
For this very reason, having its essential nature sublated, it becomes a fallacy (ābhāsa).
To the objection, "What is the use of this effort?", he replies: "Because it belongs to that" (*tasyaitattayā*).
"Otherwise" (*anyathā*):
if there were no purpose for the comprehension of a specific [meaning], then, because the injunction would terminate [merely in its own enjoining], it would be like the bathing of an elephant.
For an elephant, even while already bathed, immediately becomes grey with dust;
with reference to its possession of these two forms, he says "sa ca" (and that).
The meaning is: because it has been introduced as a subject of description, it is undertaken to be explained.
Regarding this, [the author] asks: "What is the specific type for what? and answers with the words beginning "by way of the aforementioned object. "Futility" (kaimarthakya) means pointlessness.
"Indication" (āgūraṇa) means proof by implication.
Therefore, [anticipating the objection] that there is a difference in kind (*vijātīyatva*), he says: "And thus" (*evam ca*).
He states that the portion to be negated is distinct in both cases with the words: "In that case, as stated" (*tatrokta*).
Consequently, he says "therefore, a distinction" (*ato vailakṣya*) with the words: "by that, here" (*tenātra*).
"Because it is not conveyed by the words":
this means that the state of not being conveyed by the words results from dependence on the force of a fallacious negation.
"In the case of the stated object": [this refers to the aforementioned context].
There is a twofold [negation] because of the negation of both the entity and the statement regarding the entity.
As for the phrase "to be stated later":
since the entity has not been mentioned, there is a negation of the statement alone.
In that regard, he states another way of classifying them into two types with the words "therein, the general... and so forth.
Thus, there is a fourfold division.

Here, the reason for the relationship between the general and the particular—the relationship between the mode and the possessor of the mode—is independent of external objects; thus he says: "...due to the identity of the word."
"And you are a child!
"I am a boy. "Messenger, it is not our concern whether you are her favorite or not. She is dying; this is your infamy, so we speak these harsh words."
"Be gracious":
if one were to say "be gracious" when there is no anger, this statement would not be appropriate.
If one were to say, "I shall not do so again," that would be an admission of something currently existing.
If you should say, "I have no fault," you will nevertheless come to know that this statement of mine regarding the absence of fault is false.
Therefore, I do not know what it is possible to say;
thus, [the Buddha] said, "and he is a friend."
O fortunate one, wait a moment while I steady this heart, which is distressed by separation;
or rather,
depart— what can we say?
By the words "Having steadied my heart, which is distressed by separation from you, I shall speak," the calamity that is the cause of doubt regarding his life has been introduced.
Alternatively, the phrase "Pass on; what shall I say? indicates his unworthiness to speak because he is so very close [to death].
"Moonlight" [is used here].

Here, because of the intensity of the pain of separation, the moonlight, the cuckoo’s song, and so forth assume the nature of darkness, saws, and the like; since they thus lead to a miserable end, she is "deficient.
By this half-utterance, the state of her life being in peril is indicated.
Furthermore, by the words "Ah, what is the use of life?", the abandonment of life prior to that final catastrophe is expressed.
To apply these [terms] in their proper order, he says: "The first," and so forth.
"I am not a messenger" is the negation of the actual entity consisting of the nature of being a messenger;
"what is fit to be said in this regard? is the negation of speech.
Both of these refer to the subject matter already mentioned.
In the phrase "tatra ca" (and therein), he reveals the specific distinction indicated by the semblance of negation in both cases:
namely, that "denoting a real entity" means denoting an object according to its actual state.
The word "remainder" (*śeṣaḥ*) is to be understood as "a distinction is perceived. Regarding the phrase "of that which is being stated" (*bhaṇyamānasya*), it refers to that which is being expressed;
[the understanding occurs] solely by way of negation, such that "this is not possible."
Regarding the phrase "in the latter":

the meaning is that there is an *āgūraṇa* (implication) by virtue of the sense, wherein there is a prohibition of the verbal expression of the very nature of what is intended to be spoken through a general door—such as the doubt regarding life—and so forth.

In the statement "she will surely [die]," there is an *āgūraṇa* because of the prohibition of the verbal expression of another part of the matter, namely, "I am unable to live," by way of its own specific form.

In order to reveal the specific qualifier illuminated in both cases, he says: "And therein" (*tatra ca*). The quality of generating excessive anger arises from the determination regarding the departure. Here, he extracts the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) with the words: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).
Therefore, he states that the nature of the objection (*ākṣepa*) is as follows: "by that" (*tena*).
Now, one might ask: why could it not be a prohibition-objection (*niṣedhākṣepa*)? To this he says: "but by the affirmative" (*vidhinā tu*).
This means: by what appears to be an affirmation (*vidhyābhāsa*).
The phrase "it will be stated by another sūtra" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Since the affirmation is implied here through negation, and because there is no other poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) in such a case, he says "and therefore" (*tataśca*).
Because there is self-conceit (*ātmasambhāvanā*), a statement of conformity (*ānurūpyokti*) is not appropriate; thus, there is a negation of the statement.
Thus, even in the case of the statement "it is not like affection," there is a prohibition regarding vehicles.
Therefore, this is a censure directed at the aforementioned subject.
He shows that it is not the [proper] subject by saying "merely," and so forth.
For in this case, the fact that childhood and so forth are not to be abandoned does not negate [the practice], but rather establishes it; thus, one should not entertain a sense of contradiction.
Rather, he demonstrates this by means of an inquiry regarding a specific inconsistency, beginning with "Of whom then... and so on.
Here, for the sake of a summary, there is a verse: "Therefore, of that which is desired... and so forth.

Therefore, for the sake of easily establishing a distinction, the semblance of a negation (*niṣedhābhāsa*) is the cause of the statement of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), but it is not a case of actual identity with negation. Consequently, where the negation is real, there is no *ākṣepa*; he demonstrates this with an example, beginning with "But here... (*iha tu*).
In the preceding verse, since those who steal the meaning of poetry— like Daityas— prepare themselves for plunder, it was prescribed that the nectar of poetry (*kāvyāmṛta*) be protected;
however, in the subsequent verse, it is said that everyone may take it as they wish, for there is no harm in this even in the world.
The protection of poetry previously prescribed is directly prohibited.
Similarly, the provision of stone door-panels for the mountain caves to serve as a prison for the wind was prescribed;

however, in the following verse, such wretchedness in the form of anxiety is dismissed as false, and it is said that "the Kirātas do not desire enmity toward the wind through confinement," whereby the provision of the door-panels is directly negated. Thus, this pair of verses is not an example of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis).
He states another argument for the absence of [the function of] suggestion (*ākṣepa*): "Even the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*)...
He demonstrates its possibility as something suggested (*vyaṅgyatvena*) with the words "And this," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "among courtesans":

"Prostitutes are devoted only to wealth; therefore, they perform everything that is improper. Since this was said by a prostitute herself, her prohibition of trust appears to be a mere semblance (ābhāsa), for it is understood from her very words that she is a vessel of pure affection, having turned away from wealth.
Therefore, this objection concerns the aforementioned subject matter and is [itself] suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
He demonstrates this with the words "for here, of the courtesan," and so forth.
Furthermore, he shows that even in the case of being suggested, there is no [such] subject matter with the words "but it cannot be stated."

That which is a semblance of prohibition consisting of the delimitation of the ocean, serving as an *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) for the sake of establishing the intended subject at hand, is a *vastu-ākṣepa* (paralipsis of a fact) when the object is explicitly stated; it is of the nature of a statement.
Furthermore, another [type] to be described hereafter should be known as consisting of an incitement (*āgūraṇa*);
and this is twofold: general and specific.
The negation of a desired object, its sublation, or the suggestion of excellence—
these four should be known as the causes of implication when they occur together.
He introduces another objection with the words "In this way, it is accepted," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "because of the equality of the logical principle" (*samānanyāyatvāt*): the meaning is that even though a thing exists in a state of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is logically equal [to others] by virtue of existing in such a state of positive and negative concomitance.
Regarding this, the Sūtra says:
"And there is the appearance of undesirable injunctions. (RuAss 39)

The phrase "for the sake of the cognition of a specific [quality] of the contextual [subject]" is understood to follow [from the previous rule], but not "of the two contextual [subjects]," because they will be shown to have a single common object.
Previously, *ākṣepa* was defined as the semblance of a prohibition (*niṣedhābhāsa*) regarding that which is desired.
Likewise, for the sake of conveying a specific distinction, there is also *ākṣepa* as the semblance of an injunction (*vidhyābhāsa*) regarding that which is undesired.
He explains this with the words "of that which is desired," and so forth.
The word "yathā" (as) recalls the previously established objection for the sake of demonstrating an identical logical principle through the verse;
however, the passage beginning with "evam" (thus) refers to the subject at hand.
Its "nature of faltering" consists in its engagement with what is not its proper object.
"By means of an injunction" (vidhināyam) means this:

since this injunction, while appearing [positively], is manifested as a negation and thus serves as an instrument, the meaning is that this negation is determined by the manifesting appearance of the injunction.
And that [negation], culminating in a specific undesirable [consequence], constitutes the poetic figure *ākṣepa* (paralipsis); such is the construction.

Now, it has been shown that there are two kinds of *ākṣepa* (implication): one where the subject matter has already been stated, appearing as a question regarding its purpose (*kaimarthakya*), and the other where it appears as a suggestion (*āgūraṇa*). But which one is it here? To this he says: "Because of the suggestion of a prohibition (*niṣedhāgūraṇāt*)."
For here, a prohibition that has not been explicitly stated is implied by what appears to be a positive injunction (*vidhyābhāsa*).
Therefore, it should be understood that this refers exclusively to the subject matter about to be discussed.
For it has been said: "An *ākṣepa* (suggestion) is an implication (*āgūraṇa*) in the form of bringing [something forward], by virtue of having as its object that which is yet to be stated."
By the words "Go!
If you go," it is understood that if there is a desire to go, "I do not refuse."

In the phrase "Go," however, the injunction is presented by him [the lover] with the thought, "May my own course also be to that very place. Thus, through the manifestation of despair regarding life, a prohibition is conveyed.
He connects this with the words "by a certain woman," and so forth.
By the expression "by way of non-rejection," the underlying sense of "if you go" is demonstrated.
The nature of "stumbling" here is the failure to enter into the sentence directly;
and he demonstrates the result, which consists in the comprehension of a specific meaning, by stating: "and the result here is..."
The result is the absolute avoidance of what is to be avoided.
To the question "What is the cause for that?", he says: "Because of non-cognition" (*asaṃvijñāna*).
That by which an object is not correctly cognized is "non-cognition."
The word *pada*, being of the nature of a particle (*nipāta*), is used in the sense of "if" (*cet*).

For when it is said, "If you go," one understands such things as, "What is the use of my going there? or "I have no need for that. The meaning is that this very word *pada*, by conveying the intended sense, is the basis for the absolute necessity of avoidance.
Now, one might ask: by whom has this absolute necessity of avoidance been established? To this he says:
"And this. He says "or as" in order to demonstrate the removal of the prohibition by another method:
"nothing at all."
"Experienced" means they are cognizant of the matter to be told even without it being spoken.
Regarding "slack":
for a swan, indeed, becomes especially beautiful when its shoulders are slack.
The internal whiteness arises from its manifestation;
the waves possess a luster similar to that [whiteness], which is the pinnacle of purity.
He connects this with the words "what is not intended here," and so forth.
The primary admission is clearly perceived that there is nothing whatsoever to be said regarding a departure that is simply undesirable.
This being the case, this injunction—which appears as something unwanted—is a constituent part of the *ākṣepa* (implication), whose nature is to suggest a prohibition.

By the words "they should be remembered," a prohibition is even more strongly reinforced, because when such [specific] recollections are brought to mind, even the mention of going is rendered impossible.
He concludes with the words "therefore":
because it is novel and has not been refuted by others,
the negation that was not explicitly stated is indicated by means of a semblance of an injunction.
This censure, however, is accepted as having only that which is yet to be stated as its object.
Now, wishing to discuss the distinctness of *virodha* (contradiction), he says: "In *ākṣepa*, the desired... and so forth.
For in the figure of speech *ākṣepa*, contradiction (*viruddhatva*) is indeed included;

the meaning is that since this [figure] operates through two types of aphorisms—namely, by resorting to the negation of the desired or by resorting to the affirmation of the undesired—there exists a state of non-occurrence [of contradiction].
He says, "By way of this introduction," [referring to] "we shall now deal with this present contradiction.
Among those [figures], he first takes up the figure of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*), which serves as their foundation, because of its preeminence; thus he says, "Even there.
Regarding that, the aphorism is:
Contradiction is the state of having mutually opposed appearances.
The figure of speech called *virodhālaṅkāra* (the ornament of contradiction) is merely an apparent one because there exists a resolution of the contradiction.

He explains this with the words: "In this case, among the universals (*jāti*) and so forth. Of these, a universal has another universal as its similar (*sajātīya*), while anything else is its dissimilar (*vijātīya*).

"Thus, 'the quality of a quality' and so forth"— in this way he describes the various divisions, including "and therein," which refers to the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction) based on genus (*jāti*), that is, contradiction consisting in the opposition between genera.
"Is delimited" means it is undelimitable, being beyond the scope of all words.
Furthermore, in this birth, the state of having experienced [it] in such a manner is not "prior" in relation to a prior limit; this is the meaning.

Due to the specific destruction of discernment (*viveka*), a certain transformation of separation—difficult to overcome because of the accumulated darkness of delusion—numbs and torments her from within.
He explains this here as "causing numbness.
Separation is non-attainment; the meaning is that this is a descent of contradictory actions caused by that [separation].
"This is the time"—
this refers to craving, thirst, and the desire to obtain objects of value. Who knows this?
The meaning is that this is not conceivable for anyone.
He provides the application [of the term] here with the words "the ocean.
He states "in this way" because the other varieties [of this figure] are easily understood.
To the question, "What occurs here when there is the presence of *śleṣa* (paronomasia)?
he says: "Because [it] is seen in the examples cited as having distinct objects by virtue of *śleṣa*.
Therefore, when there is the presence of *śleṣa*, for those who follow the doctrine of Udbhaṭa, *śleṣa* is the sublater (*bādhaka*); for others, however, it is a commingling (*saṅkara*).
The example is "sannihita" (proximate) and so forth. "Bālāndhakāra" (the darkness of childhood) refers to the blackness of hair and fresh gloom;
"bhāsvanmūrti" (the radiant form) refers to the form of the sun, the radiant one.
This [is an example] when both contradictory meanings are based on wordplay (*śliṣṭa*);
"kupatim" [is an example] when it belongs to only one [of the two],
namely, "lord of the earth" (*pṛthvīpati*) and "wretched husband" (*kutsitapati*).
Regarding this, he states the distinction: "having a single object.
When contradiction pertains to a single object, it is the figure of speech *virodhālaṅkāra* (contradiction);
however, when there is a difference of objects, figures such as *asaṅgati* (inconsistency) will be discussed.
Contradiction, however, is that which appears as such and rests upon objects such as universals (jāti) and the like;
it is established as tenfold due to their variety, even when the object remains the same.
Now, those based on contradiction (*virodha*).
Among these, *vibhāvanā* is stated as a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) consisting of the contradiction between cause and effect.
Regarding this, the aphorism (*sūtra*) is as follows:
The non-perception [of arising] is the production of an effect in the absence of a cause.
*Vibhāvanā* is the production of an effect in a distinctive manner due to the presence of a subtle cause when the well-known causes are absent, because of the contemplation of that effect.
He explains this with the words "here, the cause":

for an effect is not possible without a cause; since it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that cause, if the effect were to occur even in its absence— [that is *vibhāvanā*].
Because that [cause] is unreal, the contradiction is difficult to avoid.

If, by some variety of expression, the occurrence of an effect even in the absence of a cause is set forth, then the contemplation of the effect as being distinguished [from its cause] is "dual contemplation" (*dvibhāvanā*). This is what was meant by the phrase "by something."
To explain what that is, he says: "And that.
It is the non-connection of a well-known cause; however, it is contradictory because of the possibility of an unknown cause.
To show its distinction from contradiction, he says: "by the absence of the cause."
Because it possesses authority, it is the effect itself that is sublated by the stronger absence of the cause,
and not the absence of the cause;
therefore, there is a distinction [between this case and others] based on a contradiction animated by the opposition of both.

He states that, by the same logic of non-difference [from the previously mentioned], there is also a distinction between this [figure] and the *viśeṣokti* ornament which is about to be described, on account of their opposition: "In this way, as for *viśeṣokti*, etc.
For in that case (*viśeṣokti*), the absence of the effect is the sublater of the existence of the cause;
therefore, that too is distinct from the [previous] opposition.
Having raised a point of doubt regarding a portion of the definition, he refutes it with the words "here, [regarding] the definition.
The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) was made;

yet, although the production of an effect in the absence of action is what constitutes *vibhāvanā*, it was nevertheless included because it is worthy of being designated by the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*).
The reason for this is as follows: "Indeed, not by all.
It is not the consensus of everyone that the effect (*kārya*) is merely the fruit of an action (*kriyāphala*); rather, it is the position held only by the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).
Therefore, since a cause can exist even apart from its specific action, the apprehension of the cause is made only in a general sense.
Here, the term "second" refers to the connection of the causes of youth with the intoxicant of pride, based on the identification of the intoxicant of youth with pride itself.
And since that hyperbole (atiśayokti) does not deviate from the figure of Vibhāvanā, it is not sublated;
rather, it remains as a supporting element.
He states its twofold nature with the words "And this... and so forth.
By this, the twofold nature of the statement of distinction (*viśeṣokti*) is also indicated.
Among these, "unaccumulated" (*asaṃbhṛta*) refers to this very [type] where the stated cause is the cause of age.
Regarding the phrase "aṅgalekhām":
the application of saffron paste from Kaśmīr indicates that the specific sign is not explicitly stated here; it refers to its innate nature (*sahajatva*).
He states another variety: "and this."
Regarding the term "sleepless":
"falling" refers to a leap taken with the resolve for death;
a "night" is a time of fear accompanied by darkness, but this [state] consists in the absence of that.
*Āghāta* means a place of execution;
*dhṛti* means sustaining; *anvaya* means following.
Regarding the first noble example, there is a disagreement concerning the second and third quarters; thus he says: "unaccumulated."

Some maintain that even in the absence of the causes of adornment and flowers, because the effects—adornment and arrows—are produced, this is indeed *vibhāvanā* (the description of an effect without its cause).

Others, however, argue that since adornment and arrows are not the direct causes of flowers and the act of adorning [respectively], but are rather proximate to them according to the logic of "another's way" (*anyāya*), the designation of this as *vibhāvanā* is merely verbal.

Furthermore, when one quality is conceived as being diminished while another remains equal, this is the figure of speech called *viśeṣokti*, whose definition was stated previously. Thus, this is *viśeṣokti*.

They say that [this is] due to the similarity and firmness with age, starting from the lack of adornment and so forth, through the gradual loss of a single quality such as the act of preparing [the body], and ending with [the state of] decoration and so on.

Others, however, say that because the state of being adorned and so forth is superimposed upon age, this is simply a *rūpaka* (metaphor), and that the distinction consisting of the lack of preparation and so forth is merely superimposed upon this very [age].
Now, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "of that which is being superimposed... [and so forth].
This is *pariṇāma* (transformation) because the act of adorning and so forth, which is being superimposed, is employed for the sake of perceiving the actual youth and beauty;
for the adornment and such are employed as a means of apprehending the youth and beauty.
For if it were merely *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), it would follow that the adornment of youth would simply be "this is the adornment of beauty," and so on.
Therefore, it is indeed transformation (*pariṇāma*).
By saying "those of today," the Master refers to himself and others as the primary examples.
The manifestation of an effect in the absence of a well-known cause is *vibhāvanā*.
And this [causality] is twofold by way of its efficient cause, due to the distinction in the production of the effect.

He states the connection with the *viśeṣokti* [figure] by saying "vibhāvanām" (the description of the extraordinary). Regarding that, the aphorism is: *Viśeṣokti* is the non-arising of an effect despite the presence of the complete collection of causes. (RuAss 42)
*Viśeṣokti* (the figure of specific mention) is employed to manifest a particularity by means of the inversion of *vibhāvanā* (poetic causation).
He explains this with the words "here, when all [causes]...
and so forth, and the term "otherwise."
For a causal complex (sāmagrī) culminates in the completion of its effect; if that very [complex] does not produce the noble [result], then what is their state of being a complex?
Therefore, it is established that if the causes are complete, the production of the effect necessarily follows;
by this, pervasion (vyāpti) has been demonstrated.
Here, one raises an objection based on appearance with the words "But as for... (yattu).
Regarding the term "something" (*kaścit*):
if the non-production of an effect occurs due to the incompleteness of its causes, then there must be some particularity (*viśeṣa*) that is to be manifested.
This being the case, a statement made to manifest such a particularity is called "particularity-statement" (*viśeṣokti*).
To explain its divisions, he says: "And that [is]...
Inconceivability means being beyond logical reasoning; it is that which has no stated cause because no such cause was mentioned. Thus, it is precisely that which has an unstated cause.
Regarding the phrase "as with camphor":
here, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is deficient in its power to burn due to the absence of a portion of ash;
nevertheless, because [the fire] possesses power toward every individual object, there is no non-production of the effect.
"Even when summoned":
the response to being summoned, the desire to go, and the collection of causes for the relaxation of inhibition constitute [the conditions].
"But 'not at all' refers to the non-arising of the effect.
In that regard, the cause is such that it can be conceived as being like a beloved in a dream and so forth;
that [cause] is singular."
The removal of the body is the collection of conditions for the removal of strength;
however, the non-arising of the effect is due to [the strength] not being taken away.
In that regard, the cause—though unstated—is impossible to conceive, and it applies to all three cases: "even though there is burning here."

To show that this [figure], namely *vibhāvanā*, is sometimes commingled with *viruddha* (contradiction) through the word "self" (*sva*)—meaning "possessing power by its own nature"—the author says: "The non-arising of the effect," and so forth.
"He who, though in his youth... refers to a certain heroine (*nāyikā*), who is an *uddīpana-vibhāva* (an excitant determinant).

Bhīrati says: "He who, by his first enjoyment, stole away my youth—he alone remains my chosen one. The spring nights are still those same ones; the *kadamba* winds, fragrant like blossoming *mālatī*, are still those same ones."
The *kadamba* here is a specific variety known as the *dhūlikadamba*, which blossoms in the spring;
"I too am that very same one" means that my ancient wife of love has not grown dull.
Nevertheless, my heart yearns for the sport of amorous dalliance there on the bank of the Revā river, beneath the shade of the cane trees (*vetasī*).
He explains this with the words "here, [the figure] Vibhāvanā," and so forth:
the presence of the one who took away her childhood and others constitutes the totality of causes for the absence of longing (*anutkaṇṭhā*).
Furthermore, by the composition of a contradiction in the phrase "the longing of the mind," the non-arising of longing is expressed;
therefore, this is *viśeṣokti* (peculiar cause).

Likewise, in the case of the two [verses] beginning with "The destroyer of childhood" (*kaumārahara*), since the causes for those [effects] are absent, the arising of the effect of longing is described by way of its opposite—the existence of that [cause]; thus, this is *vibhāvanā* (poetic fancy).
And because there is an absence of either proof or disproof regarding these two, there is a confusion of doubt.
Furthermore, because the relationship between cause and effect depends upon the presence of opposing factors, it is indistinct.
Moreover, this confusion does not occur at all times.
This is because it is pure when either the production or the non-production of the effect is intended to be expressed.
However, in the present example, the intention lies beyond both: namely, the production of longing and the non-production of the absence of longing.
Regarding this, there is a verse: "When both the existence and the non-existence of the portion consisting of the effect are required to be stated..."
In that case, there is a commixture of doubt (*sandeha*) with both *vibhāvanā* and *viśeṣokti*.
He states that another definition is too narrow: "But that which [is defined as] 'the loss of one quality' and so forth...
[This is incorrect because] the *viśeṣokti* (poetic figure of specific mention) would then have to be considered a case where the effect does not arise despite the presence of the cause;
however, in this context, the loss of one quality actually serves to strengthen the similarity, which is not the defining characteristic [of *viśeṣokti*].
The connection [to the present topic] is for the purpose of explaining another type of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) that has been promised; thus it says, "in *atiśayokti*.
Regarding this, the aphorism is: *Atiśayokti* occurs when there is simultaneity of cause and effect, or when there is a reversal of their temporal sequence. (RuAss 43)
Because it is rooted in the contradiction between cause and effect, this is stated here;
he explains it for the sake of elaboration, saying: "In this context, 'restricted'...
The departure from this nature is the destruction of the restriction regarding priority and posteriority.
He states the twofold nature [of the sword] with the words "of this form" and "as they looked on, it rose up.
While the kings were looking on with great astonishment, you simultaneously performed a feat of sorcery by the exit of fame and the entrance of glory from your sword.
In this context, regarding the entry of glory and the departure of fame, there is a simultaneous connection; "on every path" means on each and every road.
*Ābhā* means radiance.
*Lāsakī* means a dancer.
*Nari nari* means in every woman; *puṃsi puṃsi* means in every man.
Here, the cessation of pride—which is the effect produced by the rays of the arrow—is stated as having been previously established.
He applies [the principle] to both cases with the words "In the former case," and so forth.
The suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), consisting of a magical illusion (indrajāla), is produced through bold assertion (prauḍhokti).
He states the distinction with the words "And of the effect," and so forth.

However, those two cases where there is either identity or reversal of time between cause and effect are another type of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), because they subsist upon the semblance of contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*).
The aphorism for the lack of connection:
"If those two are in different locations, there is no connection. (RuAss 44)
He explains [the phrase] "of those two" as follows:
"appropriate" means that their connection is appropriate because they occupy the same location.
He states the lack of connection with the words "contradictory" (*virodhī*). Regarding the phrase "generally known" (*prāyaḥ pathya*):
for the most part, kings are by their very nature averse to their own welfare and become overwhelmed by sense objects.
Public censure falls upon faultless ministers;
sages dwell contentedly in the forest;
or rather, it is the external servants employed in counsel who are praiseworthy, while woe unto the ministers!
"He applies [the term] here" means that the cause for public censure being averse to wholesome conduct is its being divided [into various types].
He shows this even within other varieties of diversity by saying "in this way."
"She is a child" is joined [to the argument] with "and here," etc.;
he concludes with "thus."
Otherwise, in the case of a different spatial arrangement,
there would be a lack of connection (*asaṅgati*) between cause and effect if they were in different locations;
yet that [connection] is observed through a particular arrangement (*vicchitti*) by means of the determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*).
The Sūtra on the Meaning of the Poisonous:
The arising of discordant effects and purposes, as well as discordant conjunctions, constitutes the object [of this teaching].

The production of an effect dissimilar to its cause is one [type]; the production of something that is not a purposeful result is another; and the conjunction of two things that are not mutually suited is the third—thus it is threefold.
This is the connection regarding the subject matter: namely, contradiction.
He explains [the term] with "therein, by the cause";
he provides the etymological definition with "incongruous."
Regarding the word "sadyas" (immediately):
the touching of the hand is the grasping of the hand.
The form of Nīlā should be made pale-white.
Regarding the word "tīrtha":
at other sacred fords (tīrthas), those whose bodies are defiled by sin cast off their physical forms and obtain divine bodies.
But in you, O Vārāṇasī—let alone the attainment of a divine body for those who have abandoned their bodies here—even their original, prior body goes so that it shall never be regained again.
In this context, there arises the undesirable consequence characterized by the destruction of the root.
"Araṇyānī" refers to the heart's intention.
"Nibhṛtam" means secretly; "gūḍham" means hidden; "pallavayati" means reveals.
Here, there is a conjunction of disparate elements—such as the forest regions and so forth—which would otherwise not be joined.
He applies this to all three cases, beginning with the word "kṛṣṇa" and so on.
[Objection: But does not the inclusion of the "middling" and "exalted" result in the figure *vyājastuti* (feigned praise)? To this, he says: "merely" (*kevalam*).

Because [the intention] has not abandoned the shadow of either praise or censure, it can be inferred as pure (*śuddha*) due to its being easily understood. The production of causes for the dissimilar and the undesirable is considered *viṣama* (the incongruous).
Likewise, through the combination of the discordant forms, this [system] is divided into three types.
The sutra on unevenness: its opposite is evenness.
With reference to the third variety, "the reverse of the uneven" (viṣamaviparyaya) is the "even" (sama).
He explains it by prioritizing its connection [to the definition], starting with "the uneven," etc.
[He states] "because it lacks the status of an ornament" (analankāratvāt).
In the production of an object possessing its own form, there is indeed no interruption;
he states the twofold nature with the words "and that which is with...
(sasa ca), and this refers to the final division.
"You are thus":
you alone possess such incomparable beauty, and he is well-acquainted with loveliness; both of you are skilled in the arts.
The remainder is the taking of hands in marriage.

Then the state of being a quality would be superior to the universe. [The author] explains this with the word "atra" (here): "nāyaka" is a *ekaśeṣa* compound meaning both "the hero" (*nāyaka*) and "the heroine" (*nāyikā*).
"Citra" means "variegated.
"Sphāti" means "expansion" or "fullness.
"Kovida" means "one devoid of qualities."
He joins them here. The lack of conformity between two things is *ānurūpya* (inappropriateness). The union of two similar things is intended as the *samālaṅkāra* (the ornament of similarity).
Two divisions of this [category] are logically consistent due to their connection with the state of being praiseworthy.
The conjunction with the diverse is "contradiction. The Sūtra states: "The effort for the production of a result contrary to itself is the 'diverse' (vicitra). (RuAss 47)
He explains [the verse] "of whom... as follows: "an effort for a contrary result is 'vicitra' (extraordinary).
That is, contrary to that [expected result].
The meaning is "of that which has an opposite result.
He explains it with the word "extraordinary" (āścarya).
To show its distinction from the various types of inequality, he says: "And this is not..."
For here, the negation of its own [nature] implies the opposite;
however, in the case of a dissimilar instance (*viṣama*), there is a reversal.
He confirms this by means of an example: "tāmālā" and so forth.
But here it is otherwise:
it is said that [the lower lip] is to be grasped, yet the lower lip turns away from the other; the gaze is to be looked upon, yet the eyes turn aside;
the arms are to be joined, yet they fall apart; and there is weariness even during sexual delights.
He connects [the text] with "here," and so forth.
"By means of elevation" means by means of the desire for enjoyment, that is, in order to enjoy.
He says that it is "clearly pervasive" in this context:
"But effort may be manifold on the path toward a contrary result;
because of the reversal resulting from prohibition, there is a distinction from the figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous)."
The sūtra concerning the additional meaning:
"The disparity between the support and the supported is the additional [meaning]. (RuAss 48)
The author explains the additional [category] of the "unfoundedness" (*ayathātva*) regarding the substratum (*āśraya*) and the dependent (*āśrayin*),
along with its accompaniments (*sasaṅgatika*), starting with the words "contradiction" (*virodha*).
He states the twofold nature [of this unfoundedness] due to the excessiveness of the substratum and the excessiveness of the dependent, starting with the words "therein" (*tatra*).
"Here is heaven":
heaven is the celestial realm (svarga), and earth is the terrestrial world (pṛthvī).
The oceans are the reservoirs of water; "having them as its limit" is a statement regarding its being without remainder. "Oh, how much!
means that there is no such thing as a measure at all.
"Let alone filling it"—the meaning is: what possibility is there of its being filled?
To the extent that there is no movement whatsoever even for the name "empty";
"dordaṇḍa" means extended and stretched out.
The reading is *natv-añcitam*.
Because it is of no use for either going or worshiping,
the verbal root *añj* has the sense of "to move slowly";
moreover, its fierce intensity is concentrated and whirling.
He connects it with the preceding [verse]:
"A lack of conformity between the support and the supported is considered excessive;
it is of two types by virtue of the magnitude of the support and the supported."
The sūtra on mutual benefit: "Mutually" refers to the production of activity among one another.
In the case of the reciprocal exchange of actions (*kriyāvyatīhāra*), there is the ornament of mutual relation (*anyonyālaṅkāra*). He explains this with the words "here too" and so forth.

It is not on account of their intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) that there is a reciprocal production, because such production is impossible; rather, they are truly contradictory. Therefore, in this context, reciprocal production occurs solely by means of action.
Regarding the phrase "of the neck":

because the Goddess’s neck possesses thinness and loveliness, and because the pearl necklace possesses excellence of its own nature and roundness, both possess the quality of being well-proportioned and worthy of admiration.
Thus, since both possess such complete sets of qualities, the relationship between the ornament and the adorned is common to both.

He connects it here with the word "beauty" (*śobhā*). "By way of action" (*kriyāmukhaka*) means through the medium of action. The mutual production of actions is considered to be "mutual ornamentation" (*anyonyālaṅkṛti*).

The sūtra for the sake of clarification: A particularity (*viśeṣa*) is that which is without a substratum, is the supported, is both one and has multiple domains, and is incapable of producing other entities. (RuAss 50)
"Even to heaven":
even for those who have ascended to heaven, their words delight the worlds; this indicates the absence of a relationship between container and contained.
"Palace": here, a single entity is the object of many.
Regarding the phrase "even for a moment":
