here, the impossibility of performing another task consists in the fact that one's entire being is occupied with accomplishing [the primary object].
He applies this to all three cases, as indicated by the words "here, of poets."
Regarding the phrase "of whom" (*yeṣām*), although it is indicated by the genitive case, there is not merely a general connection with "speeches" (*gīrbhiḥ*),
but rather a specific relationship; thus he says, "elsewhere," meaning "in the future supramundane [state]."
The meaning of the word "what" (kiṃ) and the negative particle (nañ) is implied.
Furthermore, the distinction based on the absence of a substratum and so forth is also considered to be threefold. The aphorism is for the purpose of resolving contradictions:
Contradiction (*vyāghāta*) is the making otherwise by another of that which has been established in exactly the same way [by the first].
*Vyāghāta* (contradiction) is the making otherwise of that very thing which has been established by someone in a certain way.
He explains this with the words "someone" (*kaścit*) and "is seen" (*dṛśyate*).
The beautiful-eyed women, who are the mothers of Virūpākṣa, bring to life with their very glance one who has been burnt by that same glance;
here,
she employs the word "glances" [to signify] the state of being made alive.
"Prāṇitavya" means living. And he states "so 'pi" (that too) because this is a reason based on dissimilarity (*vyatireka-hetu*).
For the words "Virūpākṣa" and "charu-locanā" (beautiful-eyed one) contain within them the sense of dissimilarity.
And by the word "victory" (jaya), the exclusion (*vyatireka*) has been stated.
He states the connection [of this section] with the words "as before" (*pūrvavat*);
here, the lack of conformity refers to the definition of the subject matter (*prakaraṇa*).
Just as proof is established by one means, so too is sublation by another;
likewise, there is contradiction when the opposite is easily accomplished.
In this regard, there is another sutra:
"And [there is] the performance of an action contrary to the effect with ease. (RuAss 52)
The performance of what is easy [to do] in opposition to what is required by the task at hand is a cause for the obstruction of the task; this is another form of contradiction (*vyāghāta*).
He explains this with the words "contradiction" (*vyāghāta*) and so forth. This is to be construed with the term "the object of definition" (*lakṣya*).

*Vyāghāta* (contradiction) is the production of an effect contrary to that which was expected from a specific cause for the sake of a particular purpose; moreover, such a contrary production is easily accomplished due to the cause’s specific suitability. Since this is the case, he says "but not here," indicating that this differs from the calamity (*viṣama*) characterized by the arising of an undesirable result.
For here, it is not that the task is impossible to perform; rather, the task is contrary [to one's nature] yet easily accomplished.
Thus, there is a distinction from the second type of *viṣama* (incongruity), because in that case the task is impossible to perform, whereas here the contrary is an undesirable consequence.
"In this case, both are to be done.
Regarding the phrase "if [he is] a child":
here, childhood and the need for protection, which might otherwise be considered reasons for not setting out, instead establish that setting out is easy to accomplish.
To state another connection, he says: "In this way.
Regarding that, the definition of the "garland of causes" (*kāraṇamālā*) is as follows:
when each preceding member serves as the cause for each succeeding one, it is a "garland of causes. (RuAss 53)
"Regarding the passage beginning with 'When previously' and so forth:
'mastery over the senses' means that discipline arises from mastery over the senses."
From discipline comes the excellence of virtues, and from that, the affection of the people.
Although other internal distinctions such as "the essence" (*sāra*) and so forth are possible here, he states "kāryakāraṇa... [to show] that this is not a different ornament.
In the *kāraṇamālā*, each preceding cause leads to each succeeding effect.
The definition of the *ekāvalī* (single-string) ornament:
The *ekāvalī* consists in the establishment or the exclusion of a subsequent [element] by means of its being a qualifier of the preceding one. (RuAss 54)
If each preceding element is established as a qualifier for each succeeding one,
that is one *ekāvalī*; whereas that in which [the elements] are excluded (*apohyate*) is another,
namely the *purāṇī*.

In this instance, the excellence of those supreme women, their beauty, and his amorous playfulness are established as qualifiers for that [lake] which possesses the flower-weaponed god [Kāma]. He connects them with the words: "here, 'supreme women'";
"not that water."
In this [type of *ekāvalī*], for water and the other elements, each preceding one stands as the object to be excluded (*apohya*) by each succeeding one, such as the lotus and so forth.
As stated in the *Ekāvalī*: "In the *ekāvalī*, each succeeding element is established as the differentiator of each preceding one;
it is both affirmed and excluded, and for that reason, this [figure] is considered to be of two kinds."
The sūtra concerning the meaning of the "lamp-in-a-garland" (mālādīpaka):
When each preceding element conveys a quality to each subsequent one, it is a lamp-in-a-garland.
In the *Ekāvalī*, there is the quality of each subsequent member bearing the excellence of each preceding one; here, however, it is the reverse.
He explains this with the words "of each subsequent.
He states the reason for departing from the conventional order with the phrase "by virtue of being a garland (*mālātvena*)."
Regarding the term *saṃgrāma* (battle):
here, the successive acquisition of arrows and so forth by the preceding bows and so forth, through the act of illumination (*dīpana*), serves to enhance the poetic quality (*guṇa*).
He explains this with the words: "here, by means of the bow and so forth."

The Garland-Lamp (mālādīpaka) consists in the illumination of each subsequent term by the preceding one. The aphorism concerning its essential meaning is: "The progressive excellence [of successive terms] is the 'essence' (sāra). (RuAss 56)
He explains [the term] as "each preceding...
/ *Nibandhana* means binding together (*grathana*).
/ Regarding the word "kingdom" (*rājye*)...
In the word "sāram" (the essence), the word "vastu" (the thing) must be supplied;
otherwise, there would be an inconsistency with the gender.
He connects [the passage] with the words "atra rājyena" (here, by means of the kingdom).
*Sāra* (the essence) is held to be that which brings about a progressive excellence.
To state another connection [between topics], he says: "In this way, it is like a chain.
Regarding that, the aphorism for *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of the causal mark) is as follows:
When the reason constitutes the meaning of a sentence or a word, it is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of the causal mark).
The figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) is twofold, consisting of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) and the meaning of a word (*padārtha*).
He explains this with the words "where the reason... (*yatra hetuḥ*).
He demonstrates its distinction from logic (*tarka*) with the words "for not here... (*na hy atra*).
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is a relation that is free from limiting conditions (*anupādhika*). The presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
The conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) is the final application (*nigamana*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the application (upanaya) and so forth are included.
Regarding the fact that it constitutes the meaning of the sentence, he states the distinction: "pertaining to the meaning of the sentence.
By this, the rule that the nature of being a logical reason (hetutva) is necessarily verbal is stated.
He states the distinction regarding its being based on meaning with the words "pertaining to the sentence-meaning.
By this, the rule that the status of being a cause is necessarily verbal is stated.
He says "otherwise" because, if it were based on meaning, there would be the occurrence of *arthāntaranyāsa*.
For the distinction is this: in *arthāntaranyāsa*, the support of the subject matter occurs through the sense (*artha*), whereas here it occurs through the word (*śabda*).
As for the phrase "your eye": [it refers to the following].

The three propositions—the submergence of the blue lotus, which possesses a luster equal to the beauty of her eyes, into the water; the obscuring by clouds of the moon, which imitates the splendor of her face; and the flight of the swans, whose gait resembles her own movement—constitute a single unified sentence that serves as the cause for her intolerance of diversion through comparison.
Regarding the word "mṛgya" (to be sought):
the reason for the application of the eyes, regardless of the *darbha* grass, is the awakening to the object.
He applies this to both cases, beginning with "in the former," and so forth.
Desiring here to cite both the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) and the word-meaning (*padārtha*) as individual causes, he says: "In this way, one...
and "desired.
In this context, regarding the prevention of asceticism, the presence of the deity desired in the home is the sentence-meaning that serves as the cause.
Regarding the phrase "yadvismaya": here, in the context of Ānanda’s dullness, the state of being stunned by wonder (*vismayastimitatva*) is the meaning of the word and serves as the reason.
He connects this with the words "pūrvatra" and so forth.
Poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause), however, consists in the statement of a reason through either a sentence or a word-meaning.
This is not *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different matter), because the reason is based on verbal expression (*śābdatva*).
The aphorism for inference: Inference is the statement of the means of proof regarding that which is to be proven.
Inference is the presentation of a means for the sake of establishing what is to be proven (*sādhya*).
He explains this with the words beginning "wherein [there is] sound," etc.;
it is by way of the function of the word, and not that of the object.
In reality, the three-fold nature [of the reason]—namely, being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—has been stated by way of its actual existence.
He says "interruption" (*vicchitti*) to distinguish it from inferential reasoning based on logic (*tarka*);
that is to say, by virtue of the artistic variety (*vaicitrya*) imagined by the poet.
As for the phrase "as if a rift":
the smoke from the ocean-clouds covered the sky, the fireflies appeared like sparks, and the quarters of the horizon were turned tawny by the flames of lightning.
In this passage beginning with "atra dhūma," he joins the linga [penis] that has caught fire from the forest-fire of passion within a grove of travelers' trees.
This very fact— that it is rooted in a metaphor (rūpaka)— constitutes the internalization of another poetic figure.
He says "kvacittu" (but in some places) in order to show that [the simile] is distinct from other figures of speech;
"yatraitāḥ" means those women whose glances are as flickering as waves.
In that regard, the movement of the eyebrows and the falling of the glance right there are the signs of the purity of Smara’s leading the way. This is what he expresses with the words "here."

"Unadorned" (analankṛtam) means precisely that which is not mixed with figures of speech such as metaphor (rūpaka) and the like. He says "by bold assertion" (prauḍhoktyā) in order to distinguish it from reasoning and inference. By the inclusion of the word "only" (mātra), there is the exclusion of other figures of speech.
There is beauty here, but not that state of wonder characteristic of inference through logic (*tarka*).

Now, he distinguishes the scope of inference (*anumāna*), the poetic figure of causal indication (*kāvyaliṅga*), and corroboration by another matter (*arthāntaranyāsa*)—beginning with "This here," and so forth.
The "pith-meaning" (*piṇḍārtha*) is the extracted meaning, independent of intermediate particulars.

If that which is not already known is being made known, then there exists a relationship between the object to be understood and the means of understanding, and this constitutes inference (*anumāna*).

If, however, that which is already known is being corroborated, then there exists a relationship between the corroborated and the corroboration; yet, when a word-meaning is employed as a reason by being suffixed with abstract suffixes such as *tva* or *tal*, no poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) arises, as in the example beginning with "the trunks of the lord of serpents" (*nāgendrahastāḥ*).
Because of its roughness, the thighs are beyond comparison; this is because the relationship of being the reason (*hetumat*) is worldly/commonplace.

However, when a thing expressed without contact with suffixes such as *tva* or *tal* functions as the reason, then—as in the example "And the deer [is like] a blade of darbha grass"—there is a single instance of *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) based on word-meaning (*padārtha*).

On the other hand, when a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is presented as the reason without the employment of words such as *yat*, which express the state of being a reason, [it constitutes a different type].
In that case, there is another figure, *kāvyaliṅga*, based on the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).
When the causality [of a fact] is established through the consideration of the meaning of a sentence presented as something neutral, then it is *arthāntaranyāsa*.
This being so, *kāvyaliṅga* based on the meaning of a sentence occurs only when there is a relation of cause and effect.
For the meaning of the sentence is rendered dependent by this action, and thus lacks neutrality;
whereas *arthāntaranyāsa* occurs only when there is a relationship between the general and the particular,
since neutrality is possible only in that case.
Furthermore, that support of another matter by means of its presence within cause and effect does not even depend upon the previously stated definition of *kāvyaliṅga*,
because the Teachers have formulated a different definition [for that].
And this being the case, if one were to rely on the aforementioned definition, [it would lead to an over-extension].
In passages such as "yattvannetre," there is indeed *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason), distinct from *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a corroborative instance).

Furthermore, the capacity of cause and effect to serve as mutual supports has already been demonstrated in the discussion of *arthāntaranyāsa*; therefore, one must adopt this much of a distinction between their respective domains.
*Anumāna* (inference), however, consists in the description of a probans for the sake of a probandum.
Because it is distinguished from others by its mixture with that [other element], its purity, and its structural arrangement (vicchitti).
The establishment of inference would occur upon the cognition of what was previously unapprehended,
either from the meaning of a word or from the meaning of a sentence, provided there is an indication based on a logical reason.

The justification of what is already perceived is considered the two-fold *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication); when there is a state of neutrality, it becomes *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth) through the nature of being a cause.
But regarding the relationship of cause and effect, another definition of it has been stated. To introduce another connection, he says: "In this way, by means of reasoning (*tarka*)," etc.
In that regard, there is a sūtra for the purpose of establishing the respective order:
The sequential detailed explanation of the topics already indicated is "according to order" (yathāsaṃkhyam).
The figure of speech known as *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence) consists in the sequential connection of items previously mentioned with those mentioned later.
He explains this with the words "above," and so forth; "above" means "previously."
"And that" (sa ca) refers to a subsequent explanation (*anunirdeśa*) that pertains to a different meaning, rather than to the meaning already mentioned;
this is because of the implicit relationship of mutual dependence between the subject mentioned and the subject to be subsequently explained.
He draws out the cognition of the relationship [between the words] with the phrase "of those ending upwards.
The meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) is the meaning of the sentence consisting of the aphorisms (*sūtra*).
Therefore, there is a specific sequence.
Others, however, have designated this very thing as "sequence" (krama).
He states its twofold nature with the words "And that...
He states the definition of the first [type] with the words "That in which there is verbal... (śābdam yatra).

When there is a connection between individual [words] with individual [meanings], the connection—relying on the verbal sequence—is considered "verbal" (*śābda*) because its cognition does not obscure that sequence. He defines the second type: "But the 'meaning-based' (*ārtha*)," etc.

When there is a connection between a collective whole and a collective whole within a verbal context, the connection between the parts occurs through subsequent reflection; thus, it is "meaning-based."
Regarding the term *lāvaṇya*:

while you, who possess the splendor of beauty (*lāvaṇya*), the radiance [of the moon], and the quality of protecting the earth through renunciation, exist, the moon, the sun, the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), and the mountain kings [such as Meru] are rendered useless.
He connects this by saying "here, because you are the abode of beauty," and so forth.
In the phrase "kajjale" (in the collyrium), he applies the sense of "artha" (meaning/purpose): "atra kajjalādīnām" (here, of the collyrium and so forth).
By "śruti," that is, by the word itself, there is a connection pertaining to the whole.
"When there is a threefold connection between those previously mentioned and those not yet mentioned... [as stated before].
"Likewise, it is considered to be twofold: verbal and implied."
The Sūtra on the meaning of succession: Succession (paryāya) is when one [entity] occurs in many [locations], or many [entities] occur in one [location], sequentially.
When one [entity] has multiple bases, that is the first permutation;
when multiple [entities] have a single base, that is the second.
He explains it as being accompanied by a connection, beginning with the words "due to the introduction of sequence," and so forth.
He states "nanvekam" and so forth for the purpose of explaining the inclusion of the term "successive" (krama).
The meaning is that the term "successive" is used to exclude the figure of speech called *viśeṣālaṅkāra*, which is characterized by a single [subject] having multiple objects.
If this is so, then why was the term "simultaneity" (*yaugapadya*) not employed in the definition of *viśeṣālaṅkāra*? To this he replies: "And here... (*iha ca*).
The meaning is that since non-simultaneity (*amapratipādana*) is not established here, simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is established by implication as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) there.
Therefore, he states the second [type] because its object is distinct: "likewise, in one...
Therein, he says "but surely here... to show the exclusion of the figure of speech *samuccaya* (accumulation) due to the inclusion of the word "not" (*apa*).

He says "ata eva guṇa" (for this very reason, [the word] *guṇa*) because simultaneity will be taken as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) in the conjunction (*samuccaya*) to be described hereafter.
He explains the term to be defined (*lakṣyapada*) with "ata eva krama" (for this very reason, [the word] *krama*).
Because a sequence (*paryāya*) does not consist of this [simultaneity], he states "vinimaya" (exchange) to show its distinction from the figure of speech *parivṛtti* (exchange).

He demonstrates its fourfold nature with the words "therein, manifold" (*tatrāneka*). Here, that which has a manifold object is either individually functioning (*pṛthavṛtti*) or a composite whole (*saṅghātātmā*);
and each of these two types is further divided into the locus (*ādhāra*) and the located (*ādheya*). Thus, there are four distinctions.
"Is it not so, O Kālakūṭa?
By whom was this placement of your steps—each subsequent one more distinguished than the last—taught upon your supports? For previously [you resided] in the heart."
Previously, in comparison to that [earlier state], you resided in the throat;
but now you dwell in speech, which is even higher than the throat.
In this case, the substrata such as the ocean and so forth are manifold and function separately.
Regarding the phrase "from which passion has been cast off":
here, the two lower [kandukas], supported by the hands, are combined as the *apādāna* (point of departure) with respect to the action of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
This is because the multiplicity of cessations is not intended to be expressed—as in the case of the expression "in the nights."
Movement is the locus of movement.
Here, the form of the *abhisārikā* and the jackal is manifold as the substratum, having distinct functions.
"In that very place" refers to this.
In this case, multiple qualities such as "infancy" and so forth, as well as "being a wife" and so forth, are the superstrates (*ādheya*).
He applies this to all four types of collective function (*saṅghātavṛtti*) by stating, "here [is] the Kālakūṭa," and so on.
Furthermore, there is the single [term] in many, and the many in one; these are the synonyms (*paryāya*).
Because these two are due to the absence of a cause, they are neither particulars nor accumulations.

This is not *parivṛtti* (exchange), because there is no mutual substitution; rather, there are four types of *bhidā* (division) here, due to the separate formation of aggregates from that which possesses multiple forms.

Because it functions as a collection of distinct parts, its object is manifold; and that [manifold object] is twofold, existing in the relation of container and contained. Consequently, there are four divisions of this [object].
A sūtra concerning exchange: "Exchange" (parivṛtti) is the bartering of equals, of less, or of more, with those that are equal, greater, or lesser. // RuAss_61 //
The exchange of an equal thing with an equal thing is the first type of *parivṛtti*;
that of an inferior thing with a superior thing is the second;
and that of a superior thing with an inferior thing is the third.
He explains: "There is an exchange here.
He states the connection: "Because of the appearance of sequence.
Regarding the phrase "having offered his chest": in battles such as the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa, he took away the glory of the Daityas by offering his own chest.
He connects [the word] "chest" here;
the meaning of "why? is that it is considered by Aruṇāyani. He connects [the word] "excellent" here.
Regarding the phrase "tasya hi":
because he has reached old age and has departed for heaven, there is nothing whatsoever to be grieved for.
[The author] connects this with the words "here, by means of the body."
He provides an illustration by way of two forms: "In that case," etc.
There is equality between seeing and the vital breath;
there is inferiority of the non-contentious relative to the contentious with respect to the mind.
He connects it here with the word "today":
"This exchange (parivṛtti), which is a barter, is threefold, beginning with the *sama* [equal] type."
The sūtra is for the purpose of exclusion (parisaṅkhyā): exclusion is the restriction to one when several [possibilities] apply to a single [case]. (RuAss 62)

Exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) is the restriction of one thing to one place when it might otherwise apply to many, because by the rejection of one alternative, the other is specifically enumerated. He explains this along with its logical connection, beginning with "one or many" and so forth. "Impossible" means that which cannot be conceived as possible by one who perceives only the gross.
He explains the prefix *pari*: "The prefix *pari* has the sense of 'avoiding' (*varjana*).
He states its divisions: "And this [is] that... (sā caiṣā).
It is fourfold: verbal preceded by courtesy and likewise verbal not preceded by courtesy, as well as the two corresponding types of physical [conduct].
What is its ornament? It is that which is practiced by the Noble Ones.
This refers to the verbal type preceded by courtesy, excluding those instances where [the words] are explicitly uttered.
"What is to be cultivated?
refers to that which is practiced through attachment, such as association with celestial rivers and the like;
this [practice] is preceded by humility and is free from the pursuit of worldly gain.
"Devotion is the state of being.
It is the weapon of desire in the form of a young woman;
this is the unassailable one, devoid of verbal expression.

Regarding "crookedness" (*kauṭilyam*): this is unwholesome, with the exception of [the case of] wealth. Since the application [of the term] is easily understood, he says "here it is non-worldly" (*alaukikam*) in order to indicate its movement according to logical principle (*nyāya*).
For a non-worldly apprehension necessarily excludes the worldly due to their contradiction;
thus, there arises a twofold distinction based on whether that which is excluded is verbal or objective.
Since the non-worldly is sometimes well-known [to the interlocutor] and sometimes not, there is a fourfold classification.
By way of a double entendre (*śleṣabhittikatayā*),
he shows [this] with the words "they overstep":
"the path of hearing" refers both to the vicinity of the ears and the path of the Vedas.
Deformity, crookedness, and immorality;
variegated work, the colors white and so forth, and the twice-born;
a staff, a stick, and punishment.
Since the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is already established here, he states that "being conjoined with *śleṣa*" is not a subverting factor but rather one that brings about beauty.
To demonstrate its extraordinary nature, he says, "And here...

For the definition well-known among grammarians is that *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) occurs when there is a restriction of an optionality that would otherwise apply simultaneously to multiple possibilities.

Since there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "restriction" (*niyama*) in order to distinguish it from that [exclusion], it is therefore accepted here that the definition of restriction (*niyama*) consists in the form of a partial possibility; thus, the definition of exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*), which consists in a simultaneous apprehension of multiple possibilities, is the predominant one in this context. Exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*), however, is the restriction to one instance of something that would otherwise apply to many.
This is considered to be fourfold, consisting of the presence or absence of speech that excludes inquiry.
Not only is simultaneous attainment not accepted, but even attainment in an alternative manner is not desired;
therefore, in this case, the status of both exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) and restriction (*niyama*) is non-worldly.
The sūtra is for the purpose of explaining presumptive testimony (arthāpatti): "Presumptive testimony is the implication of another matter by way of the 'stick-and-cake' principle. (RuAss 63)

Just as the eating of the cake follows by way of *kaimutya* (the logic of "how much more so") from the eating of the stick, so too the occurrence of another matter is *arthāpatti* (presumption). He explains this with the words "of the stick and the cake.

Some hold that the form *daṇḍāpūpikā* is established by the suffix *-vuñ* according to the rule "dvandvamanojñe," and that the absence of *vṛddhi* occurs due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, following the analogy of *ahamahamikā* and similar forms.
Others, however, desire the formation of the word-form by means of a suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*).

He states his own view with the words "apare tv iti" (but others...). Others, moreover, explain it as having the sense of comparison (*upamārtha*) by means of the suffix *kan* [added] according to the rule "ive pratikṛtau."
He states "here" for the sake of drawing out the essential meaning.
He refutes the suspicion of inference with "nor is this.
He states "here" as a *daṇḍāpūpa* (stick-and-cake) argument for the sake of the same underlying principle.
He dispels the suspicion that this might be an inference by saying "And this is not...";
he states the apprehension based on the application of the same logic—namely, the maxim of the staff and the cake—by saying "And presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)";
and he speaks of the distinction [of this from those] because it is related to that through its belonging to the same class, by saying "And this..."
"Paśupati" refers to one who is intensely eager and whose mind has transcended the ordinary state (*unmanā*). "They might disturb" means they might cause harm or transformation;
"these states" refers to women and the like.
He shows the introduction of an irrelevant topic: "here [it is said], 'when the bow is held'";
even those who are firm become humble.
What need is there to speak of the fickle?
Here, the contextual meaning is introduced. To express a different kind of charm, he says: "But in some cases..."
"Alaṅkāra" means that which causes doubt—namely, the doubt as to whether this person should be served or not. "Vidhu" refers to the moon; "vidhi" refers to fate or destiny.
By way of punning, he states the appearance of the contextual meaning [in the phrase] "here, in the injunction.

Arthāpatti (presumption), however, is intended as the implication of another meaning by way of *kaimutya* (a fortiori). This is considered to be of two kinds: that which involves the appearance of both the contextual and the non-contextual.
The sūtra for the purpose of defining doubt:
Doubt is a conflict between [two views] of equal strength. (RuAss 64)
When two contradictory [options] of equal strength are simultaneously applicable, there is an option (*vikalpa*).
He explains: "of two contradictory [options]";
being characterized by equal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the reason for their having equal strength.
He demonstrates the distinction [between the two] by saying "because it contains a comparison," since worldly conceptualization is not like that.
Regarding the word "namantu" (let them bow): in its *saṃdhi* form, it refers to the bowing of heads; in its *vigraha* analysis, it refers to bows.

Likewise, the act of making [the earth] an ear-ornament for both the Command and the Iron Bar is explained here by the phrase "toward each rival king" (*pratirāja*); for in this context, bowing down is the duty toward the rival kings.

In that case, the heads and the necks, being equal in strength due to their status as the standard for peace and war, reach [the state of being the primary object] simultaneously despite the impossibility of such simultaneous attainment due to their mutual contradiction;
therefore, since there is no other way to account for them, there is an option (*vikalpa*) consisting of the establishment of one and the sublation of the other.
He applies the point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) by stating: "caused by bending."
The same applies to the case of "karṇapūrīkaraṇe" as well. To state another variety, he says: "aupamya" and so forth.
In such instances as "bhaktiprahve," "praṇāyinīspardhinī," and others, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) involving both the dual and singular numbers, as well as the neuter and feminine genders.
The word-breaks are "nīte hitā" and "nīta ihitā";
and "nidhī" and "nidhiḥ".
He applies them here as "netre tanuḥ" (the body [is] in the eyes).
He says "and not" (na ca) so that there may be no confusion regarding a collective [meaning].
Even though a transition [of meaning] is possible through instruction, there is no collective sense because of the absence of usage by poets;
thus, fearing a deficiency in the definition due to the fault of using what is not employed, he raises an objection with "nanu."
He refutes this, saying "not so.
Then,
with the words "or rather," he reveals the underlying connection manifested by the nature of the alternative (vikalpa), saying "and that [is] here."
He concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He says "by his predecessors" (*pūrvaiḥ*) to indicate that this is his own work.
Regarding the conflict between two rules of equal strength, there is an option (*vikalpa*) when they meet.
This is described as being twofold because it is based upon both connection and disconnection.
The sūtra is for the purpose of expressing conjunction;
conjunction is the simultaneity of qualities and actions.
The simultaneity of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*) is "conjunction" (*samuccaya*).
He explains this with the words "of qualities.
The term "option" (*vikalpa*) is stated for the sake of providing a point of connection.
"Shattered" means that the openings of the [mouths] are filled with many wild [beings].
Here, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both stainlessness and soiling.
"This" (*ayam*) means that it must exist simultaneously in a single moment; that is to say, it has come into being.
Here, [the relationship is] between the action of comparison and the action of becoming.
To explain the obstacle of variety, it says: "diverse from this" and "bearing. Bearing the thorn is the cause for activities such as lying down and so forth.
In this context, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the bed and so forth by virtue of their sharing a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatayā*).
Since the conjunction of qualities (*guṇa-samuccaya*) is also easily understood, he says "in this way" (*evam*).
He shows that [this conjunction] is possible even when quality and action are combined, saying "some" (*kecit*).
The phrase "the downward-looking eye" refers here to a modification of the eye;
each individual eye exists with a distinct function and a separate activity.
This is due to the influence of the [taste] flavor.

The aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*) here is the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), because these six modifications of the eyes are centered solely upon it; thus, the meaning is: "how is it that [the eye] is cast down in a different action? That which is cast down at the corner of the eye (*apāṅga*).
For it has been stated by me in the *Bharatasaṃgraha*: "There may be the state of the corner of the eye being cast down (*nyañcita*)."
“The upward-turned [glance] (udañcita) is that which is contracted and curved at the outer corner, with the face turned upwards”— such is the definition of the upward-turned.
The upward-turned smile is one directed upward toward the outer corner of the eye, devoid of blinking, playful,
full of significant intent, containing the emotion desired, and characterized by a sidelong, arched pupil.
*Vyāvṛttaṃ* means turned away.
As it is said: "Having looked with love far off at one who has turned aside and moved away.
*Prasādi* means clear or serene.

“They say that a face which smiles with the play of the eyebrows, yet is bright and closing like a bud, is ‘with love’ (saprema)—that is, pregnant with love. For it is said: ‘That which is pregnant with love leads to melting (drava).’”
Tremulous means having pupils with trembling eyelashes;
steady means fixed upon an object situated at a great distance;
and "with raised eyebrows" means with eyebrows tossed upward.
It would be wandering and sluggish due to intoxication.
That which functions at the outer corner of the eye is "casting a sidelong glance" (*vikṣepi*); that which functions at the side is "casting a sidelong glance.
"Vikaca" means "blooming" (*vikāsi*).

When the eyes are wide open upon what is visible, it is characterized by specific distinctions; when submerged here, it is called "contracted" (añcita); and when fixed at the tip of the nose, it is called "well-contracted" (nihañcita).
"Taraṅkottaraṃ" means "waved. "Taraṅgitaṃ" refers to a radiance resembling waves; "sāśru" means "full of longing."
“Longing, with tears bound by passion.
He connects this with the words beginning with *akekara* and so forth.

Now, one might object: although [the qualities of] intention, clarity, and love are expressed through adjectives (*guṇavacana*), they are nevertheless obscured by the meanings of compounds, secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and the like; therefore, he says: "clear, full of love," and so forth.
For compounds and the like denote a relationship (*sambandha*),
and a relationship is established in form as a quality (*guṇa*).
It does not alter the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of those words that express qualities.
The compound is *sākūta-sat-prema* (affection for the virtuous with intent). The term *prasādī* is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
He concludes: "Thus, this..."
The two [qualities] separately and the one [quality] combined—thus it is threefold.
"In the case of the simultaneity of qualities and actions, there would be a threefold conjunction (samuccaya). He states another type of conjunction with the word "one" (ekam).
The Sūtra:
"The establishment of one thing, and the performance of that [function] by another. (RuAss 66)
When one person performs a certain means for achieving a goal, another person also performs that same act out of rivalry; this is "conjunction" (*samuccaya*).
He explains this with the words "conjunction," etc.
The phrase "only thus" (*ity eva*) is to be supplied as a connective statement.
To show the dissimilarity from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he says: "And this is not so.
One [type of person] is a successful practitioner;
the other, if they possess concentration, does so by way of a mere coincidence, like the "crow and the palm fruit" (*kākatālīya*).

Just as pigeons in a threshing-floor descend each for itself, competing with one another in a "I-first, I-first" manner, so too is there a combination [of causes] regarding an entity (*bhāva*); thus, there is a great difference [between the two].
Because this policy (*nīti*) contains [the principle of] "pigeons in a threshing-floor," it is called *khalekapotikā*.
The suffix *ṣṭhan* has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
Now, how is it that the expression *kākatālīyam* is used?
It refers to the accidental arrival of a crow and the falling of a palm fruit.
By that falling [bird], the killing of the crow occurred;
likewise, there was the arrival of Devadatta and the sudden descent of the robbers, and by them his killing.
In that regard, the meeting of Devadatta and the thief is like the meeting of the crow and the palm fruit—this is one meaning of the simile.
The second [interpretation] is that "the killing of that" is like the killing of the crow;
the first is the meaning of the compound, *kākatāla*,
while the second is the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), *kākatālīya*.
And this is a compound.
From this very indicator [it is known] that "after a compound referring to that [object], the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of 'as if accidental'.
"Referring to that" means "having that object as its referent."
In this way, compounds and secondary derivatives (taddhita) such as *ardhajaratīya*, *ajākṛpāṇīya*, and *ghuṇākṣarīya* are to be understood.
He states the distinctions [of these] with the words "this" (*eṣa*) and "family" (*kula*).
Those very things by which people fall into pride are, for you, goads that ward off the wrong path;
he joins [this] with the verse beginning "amālinya."
Freedom from impurity is the cause of beauty.
He shows that each one of these acts as such for consciousness with the words "difficult to resist" (*durvārā*).
The friend of the god of love, such as springtime and so forth, is "crafty," meaning deceptive.
He connects [the passage] here with the word "smara" (love).
To the question, "How can youth beginning from nine years be inauspicious?", he says, "youth beginning from nine," and so forth.

Regarding the word "śaśī" (moon): the substantive, such as the moon, is auspicious, yet it becomes inauspicious through the power of its qualifiers, such as its greyish hue; thus, there is a dual nature of the qualified object.
In that context, [the moon] is conjoined with such things as beloved women;
he joins them here, as in the passage beginning "of the moon" (śaśinaḥ). However, it should not be construed otherwise; therefore, he says: "but not here."
It should not be explained in that way;
the ellipsis is "because of the intended expression of the conjunction of the existent and the non-existent.
Here, he raises an objection: "But, O King..."
Since both the king’s courtyard and the rogue are unseemly, how can it be said that others are seemly?
It is not a case of "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) in that sense.
He refutes this, saying: "This is not so."

When the treatment of a specific subject involves two forms, the lack of harmony between the two constitutes the syntactical fault known as *prakramabheda* (break in the established course). Since others have pointed out other faults based on this break in the course, he says: "For this very reason."
The meaning is that the other qualified object is "excellent" while the nature of the rogue is "unexcellent," thus the objects differ from their companions.
Therefore, he says "in the present case, however" to indicate how it ought to be intended.
Nevertheless, he says "even so" because the fault has not been removed.
In the previous example, he raises the objection regarding the conjunction of the auspicious and the inauspicious, saying: "But [the arrows of Smara] are difficult to ward off.
This is because there is a perception that the arrows of Smara and so forth possess auspiciousness, while qualities such as being difficult to ward off possess inauspiciousness.
He refutes this, saying: "This is not so."
He states the indicator for the difference in intended meaning with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
Although the moon and other objects have entered within [the heart] due to their beauty, their status as causes of futility is concluded by means of their greyishness and so forth.

However, in the case of the word *durvārā* ("irresistible"), it is concluded that there is simply a state of extreme hardship, in the sense of: "How can that rogue be endured? (*śaṭhaḥ kathaṃ soḍhavyaḥ*).
He concludes with the words "therefore":
"The conjunction of another action with a single action is indeed another type of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Through its association with the two alternatives of existence and non-existence, it is established as being threefold."
Thus it is said.
The Sūtra for the purpose of concentration:
Concentration is the ease with which an effect is accomplished through the application of other causal factors.
*Samādhi* is the perfect application [of the mind] to a task already begun through the conjunction of other causes. He explains this with the words "by something" (*kenacit*).
The term "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) is stated as a logical connection (*saṅgati*).
He recalls the dissimilarity from the collection [of causes] by saying, "its distinctness.
Regarding the word "measure" (*māna*): when falling at the feet is the cause, thundering is another cause.
He applies [the term] "removal of pride.
"Assistance" (*upakāra*) indicates ease.
"Concentration" (*samādhi*) is correct placement (*samyag-ādhāna*) through the application of other causes.
Regarding the objection concerning the statement, he says: "In this way, [it is] a sentence.

A sūtra has the sense of being an opponent (*pratyanīka*). When the power of the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) is rendered manifest, the disparagement of that [opposing position] is the "opponent" (*pratyanīka*). (RuAss 68)
When one is unable to insult a powerful person, insulting someone associated with that person is the counter-measure (*pratyanīka*).
He explains this with the words beginning "where [there is] a powerful person," etc.;
"associated with him" means associated with the powerful person.
"To overcome that powerful one" means to overcome him who is strong.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration, beginning with "just as in battle," and so forth.
He states the purpose, beginning with "as an antidote," and so forth.
"Of whomsoever something":
of whomsoever, namely Kṛṣṇa;
"vigraha" means strife or quarrel.
"Having a form similar to that of her beloved's face"—
here, the phrase "of Rāhu" is employed;
the statement of purpose is "because of the concealment of that [Rāhu]."
The disparagement of that [object of comparison] due to inability is the *pratyanīka* (counter-allegory).

The sūtra concerning this contrary meaning is: "The *pratīpa* consists either in the rejection of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the conceptualization of it as the object of comparison (*upameya*). (RuAss 69)

One type of *pratīpa* (the inverse) arises from the intention to express that the object of comparison (*upameya*) alone possesses abundant qualities, thereby rendering the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) purposeless due to its opposition; this is the first.

The second occurs when, out of disregard, one designates the well-known standard of comparison as the object of comparison for the sake of introducing another standard of comparison; thus it is "as if with a second.
He explains this with the words beginning "of the object of comparison alone," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "and where":
since the state of being a garland of tonsured heads belongs to the eyes alone, the wreath of blue lotuses (*kuvalayadāman*) is rendered purposeless.
He provides another example, unmixed with other figures of speech, by means of the word "lāvaṇya" (loveliness).
Since qualities such as being the abode of loveliness are present in their fullness only in the object of comparison (the face), what purpose would comparisons with the moon and other things serve?
He recalls the [concept of] *saṃbheda* (conflation): "In this case, there is also *yathāsaṅkhya* (correspondence in order)," as in the phrase "Come here, come! (*ehi ehi*).
And "e" is used as a form of address:
"O beautiful one, come here for a moment; lend me your ear and hear what must be said.
Therefore, O slender-waisted one, the moon is compared by people to your face."
By stating that "the moon's status as a standard of comparison (upamāna) must be mentioned," it implies the conceptualization of the moon as the object of comparison (upameya) due to its inferiority;
the purpose, however, is to establish the face as the standard of comparison.
He connects this by saying: "here, as the standard of comparison."

In some cases, the very status of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), by means of its disparagement, gives rise to a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*); thus he says: "But in some cases... The phrase "the measure of pride" refers to the manifestation of a standard of comparison, such as: "There exist blue lotuses like these."
Thus, there is a disparagement of the pair of eyes, which possess no commonality. He explains this with the words "herein the excellence" (*atrotkarṣe*):
just as here the object of comparison cannot endure the standard of comparison.
In the same way, due to extreme excellence, it even transcends the stage of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
He states that even the designation of "being a standard of comparison" is *pratīpa* (the inverse) by means of the words "by this [it is surpassed]" and "I alone [am such]."
The designation of the speech of the wicked as a comparison to *hālāhala* poison— which has reached the most dreadful limit— is intended for the purpose of contempt.

This is applied here in the phrase "the nature of *hālāhala*," because the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is conceived as the object of comparison (*upameya*) for the sake of its functional purpose.
In some cases, this [simile] is also inverted in two ways by virtue of its being the standard of comparison.
The "concealed meaning" (nimīlitārtha) sūtra: the concealment of one thing by another thing is "concealment" (nimīlita).
When one thing conceals another thing by means of either an innate or an adventitious characteristic, it is "closed" (nimīlita) because of that concealment.
He explains this with the words beginning "by an innate," etc.,
and states the distinction in general terms with "nor is this," etc.
For in that [figure], there is no perception of distinction because the qualities are common;
in this one, however, there is the concealment of the inferior by means of a superior quality.
This is what is meant by "apāṅga" (the side-glance).
"Aṅgalīlayā" (by the play of the limbs) means that she expanded [her beauty] through such playful grace (*līlā*).
By means of natural characteristics such as the tremulousness of her gaze (*dṛktāralya*), she conceals the tremulousness of the gaze and other traits caused by the onset of passion (*madodaya*).
He connects this with the words "here, the tremulousness of the gaze."
Regarding the verse beginning with "ye kandarāsu": those whose minds are apprehensive of your feet— that is, those who are terrified by the fear of being struck by you—
here [the poet] conceals the trembling and horripilation caused by fear through the trembling and horripilation characterized by the arrival of the cold.

He connects [the verse] here with the words "Himādrī" (O Himavat): "The concealment of another by means of one's own or even an adventitious characteristic is the figure of speech called *nimīlita* (the closed eye); it is shown to be of two kinds."
The aphorism concerning the general meaning is as follows: "The identity of the subject at hand with another due to equality of qualities is the general. (RuAss 71)

The figure of speech called *sāmānya* occurs when the subject at hand (*prastuta*) attains a state of identity with that which is not the subject (*aprastuta*) due to a similarity of qualities or through a common connection.
He explains this with the words "where the subject at hand," etc.
To distinguish it from the figure *apahnuti* (concealment), he says: "And this is not..."
For in *apahnuti* (concealment), there is the establishment of something non-contextual by means of the negation of the contextual; but here it is not so.
What then? It is identity (*aikātmya*). [This is shown in] the phrase "by the essence of sandalwood."
An ivory leaf is an earring made from an elephant's tusk;
its imperceptible movement is a sign of its identity [with the wind].
He joins [the words] here with "malayaja" (sandalwood).
The identification of the subject at hand with another due to a similarity of qualities is *sāmānya*. To that effect, the aphorism states:
"The assumption of the qualities of another while not relinquishing one's own qualities is *tadguṇa*. (RuAss 72)

The *tadguṇa* [figure] consists in the attribution of extremely superior qualities to an object that possesses only limited qualities. He explains this with the words "wherein" (*yatra*), and he defines it with the words "of that" (*tasya*).
He states that it is different from *nimīlita* (the "closed" type): "But not [that]," for in that case there is the concealment of another object;
here, however, there is the coloring of that which is unconcealed by its quality.
[The word] "distinct" (*vibhinna*) [is used].
In this [verse], the chariot-steeds were brought by Aruṇa to a non-distinction of color; yet, by means of emerald jewels dark as bamboo sprouts, they again restored their own luster through radiance.
Here, the horses' redness possesses the quality of being subordinate to that [darkness], and the redness's [subordination] is due to its being surpassed by the green.
He applies [the term] here as "ravīti" (it resounds).
*Atadguṇa* (non-possession of its qualities) is the grasping of the qualities of a superior object through the relinquishing of one's own qualities;
when the cause for such a transfer exists, the failure to assume that form is *atadguṇa*. (RuAss 73)
"Non-possessing those qualities" (*atadguṇa*) means the opposite of possessing those qualities.
He explains "association" (*saṅgati*) with the words "possessing those qualities" (*tadguṇa*).
For when there is proximity to an object of superior quality, it is logically justified that an inferior quality should acquire the qualities of that [superior] object.

The figure of speech *atadguṇa* (non-attribution of quality) consists in not imitating [another's] qualities, even when there is proximity (*pratyāsatti*). He explains this with the words "of that superior one" (*tasyotkṛṣṭasya*) and "or rather" (*yadi vā*).
Atadguṇa (Non-attribution of Quality) occurs because there is no attribution [of a quality] even when the cause for such attribution exists; this is another definition.
Here, the author analyzes the compound as "of that which is not the subject" (*aprakṛtasya*).
Thus, this [figure] is twofold.
"You are white"— O handsome one, although you are white,
nevertheless my heart has been colored by you;
O fortunate one, even though my heart is already filled with passion!
You are not placed, nor are you stained.
He is white, young, and bright;
yet, even though he is the repository of a heart filled with passion, he possesses no attachment—these are his qualities.
"Gāṅga" (the son of Gaṅgā) refers to this.
"O friend" (*aṅga*) is a form of address.
It is "accumulated" (*cīyate*), meaning it is built up;
here there is no imitation of the original form.
He applies [the analysis] to both cases with the words "in the former," and so forth.

To the question "What is the ornament in the first half-verse?", he says: "You are white. Even in the case of coloring that which is already white, the absence of its own quality (*atadguṇatva*) is quite evident.
Since it is said "because of cause and effect," the dissimilarity is evident.
There is no imitation of its qualities; rather, there are two ways [of similarity]: through the quality itself and through conformity to that quality.
The subsequent sūtra is for the sake of the answer: "From the answer, the extraction of the question occurs repeatedly; the answer is inconceivable, and the answer is further [the answer]. (RuAss 74)

Even when the question is not explicitly stated, there is one type of "misleading reply" (*durnayana*) which consists of a single reply; and when the question has been stated, that which is an impossible reply given repeatedly is the second type.
He explains this with the words beginning "where [the reason] is not being set forth," and so on.
He avoids the charge of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by saying "and this is not [the case]," and so forth.

For the definition of inference consists in the exposition of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*). He states the essential nature of the second [characteristic] with the words "and where," and he states the restriction regarding that [subject] with the words "and that."
Here, he avoids the fault of over-extension by stating, "And this is not [the case].
In an exhaustive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*), the relationship between that which is to be excluded and that which excludes is intended;
here, however, it is his own specific intention.
"Alone"—what do you ask for? The meaning is: "What is the use of this request? "What is adverse? means: what adverse course of fate has been obtained?
What is happiness? A virtuous spouse. What is suffering? A wicked world, in which the workings of fate and such are inconceivable due to their hidden nature.
He provides the subsequent connection with the words "pūrvatra" and so forth.
The term "asakṛt" refers to the repeated disclosure of the restriction regarding diversity (*nānātva*).
“An answer that is superior, an answer that is malicious, and an answer that is improbable—these are of two kinds.
Regarding the obstacle to association, he says: “from this point onward,” referring to the sutra on subtle meaning.
The subtle [teaching] is that which reveals the subtle meanings that have been discerned.
The subtle [method] (*sūkṣma*) is the disclosure of a subtle meaning, perceived through gestures and the like, to one who is clever.
He explains this with the words "here, the subtle," and so forth.
Like the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, it is sharp; thus it is "keen as a blade of *kuśa* grass" (*kuśāgrīyā*).
Therefore, this [intention] is twofold, by way of gesture (*iṅgita*) and physical appearance (*ākāra*).
Gestures are movements manifested by internal disposition (*ākūta*), produced through intelligence;
whereas physical appearances are taught as being those very same [movements], but produced without intelligence.

Just as the wise understand the changes of the pupils, the knitting of the brows, the gaze, and so forth, to be *iṅgita* (gestures), whereas *ākāra* (expressions) are states born of internal disposition (*sattva*); the former are primary, while others are considered different by the intellect.
"Intent on the time of the signal" means having the intention to know the [appropriate] time;
"one whose inner meaning is conveyed by the eyes" means one whose state of mind is manifested through the eyes.
The knowledge of the time of the signal consists of [signs such as] the knitting of eyebrows, sidelong glances, and so forth.
Having understood this subtle meaning along with its characteristics through his gestures—
that the closing of the lotus is indeed illumination—
he applies it.
Regarding the phrase "here, by the sign":

the facial expression [is indicated] by perspiration; through that, due to the smearing of saffron, there is the knowledge of the woman’s role in sexual union (*puruṣāyita*), which is the perception of a subtle meaning. The "sword-stroke" (*khaḍgalekha*), however, is the manifestation of that.
He connects this with the words "here, by perspiration."

The subtle [type of wit] is twofold: that which consists in perceiving the subtle among the learned and making it manifest, and that which consists in perceiving the subtle through gestures and facial expressions.
The sūtra for the purpose of defining *vyājokti* (concealment by pretext) is:
"Concealing a revealed matter is *vyājokti*. (RuAss 76)
*Vyājokti* (the figure of speech of "disguised statement") is the concealment, by means of a pretext, of a hidden matter that has been revealed due to some cause.
He explains it with the words "where [something] hidden," and so forth.
The etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is "the insertion of another object" (*arthāntaraprakṣepa*).
"Śailendra" means being established or being given; from the word "ādi" (and so forth), trembling and shaking are included.
The attachment to ritual duty is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
He was seen by the mountain’s inner apartments, the circle of Mothers (*mātṛ-maṇḍala*), and the Gaṇas.
[The author] connects this with the phrase "here, [his body] bristling with horripilation."
In order to pacify this inconsistency, he says "yadyapi" and so forth.
The sense is that because he spoke with a smile, saying "consider it a mere denial," its manifestation should not be considered a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
"Ullekha" means delineation (*uṭṭaṅkana*).
He raises the doubt regarding its lack of pervasiveness with the words, "But [in] *apahnuti*... The latter type consists of similarity for the purpose of concealment.
He resolves this with the word, "True."
The mention of that [concealment] there is based on the *udbhaṭa* school’s doctrine;

for in their view, since "disguise" (*vyājokti*) is not described as a separate figure, such a possibility of concealment exists. Here, however, because "disguise" is indeed described, that particular variety of concealment does not exist at all, and thus concealment is only one type.
Therefore, this is indeed *vyājokti* (the figure of concealed speech).
*Vyājokti* is the concealment of that which has been revealed by means of a prevaricating statement;
it is not intended as a denial (*apahnava*), since [in *apahnava*] there is a similarity for the purpose of negation.

The sūtra for the purpose of defining vakrokti (indirect speech) is as follows: Vakrokti is the interpretation of a statement spoken in one way as being otherwise, by means of intonation (kāku) or paronomasia (śleṣa).
*Vakrokti* (crooked speech) is the application of a statement spoken with one intention to another intention through the use of intonation (*kāku*) or punning (*śleṣa*).
He explains it [in a] coherent manner [with the words]: "the designation of speech" (*uktivyapadeśa*), and "dependent on the teacher" (*guruparatatra*).
"This [statement], 'He is preparing to go even further,' is the speech of the heroine (nāyikā).

'Because he is dependent on his elders, due to that subordination to his elders, he will not come at this time—nor will he take her'—this is the speech of the female friend (sakhī) containing a double meaning (kākugarbha).
[The commentator] connects it, saying: 'This sentence...'"
[Objection: But surely the injunction and prohibition regarding going are verbal;
therefore, an injunction prohibiting movement has been applied [here].
To this, he says: "By the force of intonation" (kākuvaśāt).
In such a context, because the particle *kāku* indicates negation, there is a transfer of meaning to the opposite sense.
[The phrase] "aho keneti" means "by what [means]—by something cruel and terrible, and by wood.
[The verb] "yojayati" means "connects"—that is, "in this [context]."
"You are Hālāhala! "O Goddess, I am so called because I possess *hālāhala* [poison] which causes fainting.
But the God replied, "I do not carry *hālā*, which is wine, nor do I have a *hala*, which is a plough."
"Are you a plowman because you possess *kiṃhala*?"—thus the queen asked again.
"It is true that I am a plowman (*hālika*) because I am capable of driving oxen (*go-vāhana*).
In this instance, there is a *sabhaṅgaśleṣa* (a pun with a break in the word).
"Vijaya" is a statement consisting of a family name (kulaka). "O Vijaye" is an address directed toward the goddess Vijayā.
"I am capable of the victory mentioned by Your Majesty,
but I am not three-eyed because of the presence of only two eyes. Here,
the word *akṣa* signifies "die" (in the sense of a gambling stake).
"What do you mean? the Goddess asked.
"If there is no purpose served by a gambling match with Lambodara, then let there be service to Gaṇapati.
The Goddess said: "Who hates Vināyaka?"
The deity said:
"In this world, the leader is Garuḍa;
[he is] 'Candra'."
The queen said, "I do not rejoice without the moon being seized as a stake.
But the king said, "If there must be an expectation of a lunar eclipse, then let Rāhu be summoned!
"Alas, Rāhu! [she cried].
"Alas!
Whose blood is this? asked the goddess.
The god replied, "Let the one who wears a garland of skulls be removed."
Regarding the phrase "devoid of wealth": *vasu* refers to riches and treasures, and the *vasus* are the eight [deities].
Regarding the phrase "you cause to ascend": [it means you cause them to enter].
*Aṅka* means marking, moving, shaking, and the lap;
thus [it is] made by Paśupati.
*Pāśaka* refers to dice.

Now, one might object: since it consists of a striking deviation from the literal sense (*vicchitti*), is not every poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) simply "crooked speech" (*vakrokti*)? To this, he says: "Crooked speech...
"Otherwise expressed application of meaning within a sentence is called *vakrokti*.
It should be understood as being of two kinds, based on intonation (*kāku*) and punning (*śleṣa*)."
The sūtra for the purpose of describing essential nature (svabhāvokti) states:
"Svabhāvokti is the description, exactly as it is, of the essential nature of subtle things. (RuAss 78)
*Swabhāvokti* (Natural Description) is the accurate depiction of the inherent nature that falls within the range of a poet’s creative intuition.
He explains this by saying, "here, the thing," and "for this very reason."
Because it is accessible only to a poet,
it is created by the poet alone;
the word *ukti* refers to the act of speaking.
He says "bhāvikā" because he will describe the dissimilarity (vaidharmya) of association by means of this.
Regarding "huṅkāra": when a slender woman removes the itch on her hair-tresses with a *huṅkāra* sound, that sound becomes an ear-ornament for the skillful man.

Of what kind is it? It is one that is carved out (*uṭṭaṅkita*) by the friction produced by the tip of her fingernail which has the shape of a beak (*cañcupuṭa*), and it is further graced by the sound *sītkāra*.
Of what sort [of woman]?
Of one with squinting eyes, who finds pleasure in the embrace of the curve of her breasts pressed against his back.
This is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state), which is the description of the inherent nature of an object that must be inferred by a wise person.
Now, through the discernment of degrees based on the variety of experience,
that which is real— which is otherwise difficult to perceive from afar— is most clearly elucidated.
Regarding this, the Sūtra states:
"The state of appearing as if directly perceived with respect to the past and the future is real. (RuAss 79)

*Bhāvika* is that which makes past and future objects appear as if they were present, because those objects are exceedingly wonderful and because they are presented by words whose syntactical connection is not confused.
He explains this with the words "past," etc.,
and "residing in the poet," and so forth.
The meaning is that *bhāvika* is the attainment of the reflection of the poet’s emotion (*bhāva*) within the listener.
Or, it is called *bhāva*:
because the future (*bhāvin*) [state] is the very life-breath of *bhāvika*, consisting solely of imaginative contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
Another etymological explanation is that "it exists here"; the term "real" (bhāvika) is to be supplied as the remainder of the phrase.
[Objection: "In the case of the example to be cited, 'The sage triumphs,' why is the perception of the past and the future not considered an error? To this, he says: "Nor is this [an error].
The sense is: if the past and the future appear precisely as past and future, what error could there be?

[Objection: "If the past and the future are manifested as past and future, that is merely the actual state of things (vastuvṛttamātra). To this, he says: "Nor is it the case that Rāma existed," and so forth.
For in the mere statement of a factual event, such as "Rāma existed," there is no quality of appearing as if it were being perceived directly;
however, in this case, there is the apprehension of a vivid direct perception.
It is not because of a determination [of the object] as being directly perceived that this is a hyperbole (atiśayokti); therefore, he says: "Nor is this... and so forth.
In this regard, the reason is:
"by way of one thing being another.
For in hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), one thing is indeed determined as being another; however, it is not so here.
When the past and the future are directly perceived, there is no determination of their being something else;
this he demonstrates with the words "for [what is] past or future.
A past thing is not determined as non-past, nor is a future thing determined as non-future.
He states that its opposite also does not exist with the words "as something that was non-existent and will come to be.
He states that even the direct perception (pratyakṣatva) found here is determined otherwise with the words "nor yet.
And he states that its opposite also does not exist with the words "or as something imperceptible."

[Objection: But surely, the appearance as if perceptible of the past and the future—which are not actually perceptible—is a case of erroneous determination (*anyathādhyavasāya*). To this he says: "For [the property of] being perceptible... If being perceptible were a property belonging solely to the power of the senses, then the non-perceptibility of the past and the future would follow, while the present alone would possess perceptibility; such would be the established rule.

For perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) is not a property of the object alone; what then? It is a property of the object only in relation to a cognizer (*pratipattṛ*). Indeed, there is no such thing as "perceptibility" in an object independent of a cognizer.

Regarding this, he states "as they say," and so forth, in order to provide corroboration from authoritative sources: for that object which, to its own perceiving subject, imitates the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the manifestation of cognition—such that if it exists itself, the appearance of cognition exists; [if it does not, the appearance does not].
If it does not exist, he establishes that "it does not exist";
this means that it is a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, he says "merely" (*kevalam*) to indicate that perceptibility is not solely a property of the object, but rather that the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) on the part of the cognizer is also required therein.
It can be said that for a cognizer who lacks the causal totality (*sāmagrī*), the object does not become perceptually manifest;
however, the intended meaning is not that it is independent of the cognizer. He analyzes that causal totality with the words "And that... (*sā ca*).

In the course of worldly life, for the purpose of perceiving mundane objects, the causal complex for direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa-sāmagrī*)— consisting of the yogis' cultivation (*bhāvanā*) characterized by one-pointedness of mind—
applies itself to extremely wonderful matters found within the subject matter of poetry (referring to "that" in the phrase *sā ca*).
For indeed, extremely wonderful things, when held in the heart with a sense of reverence, bring about such a cultivation.

And thus, while the causal complex for the direct perception of a present object exists in the case of a pilgrimage with one's mother, for yogins there is the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for the direct perception of past and future objects, as is the case for those who know the essence of poetry (*kāvyatattvavid*).

Therefore, just like yogins, the direct perception of past objects by those who know the essence of poetry is not a mere conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*); hence, one should not suspect this to be hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). Now, one might ask: "Since past and future things are perceived precisely as if they were present, why should this not be considered a *pratīyamānotprekṣā* (suggested poetic fancy)? To this, he says: "Nor [is it so] in the case of past and future things."
The reason for this is stated as "his conceit" (*tasyābhimāna*).
Conceit is the imagining (*saṃbhāvanā*), and the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that form is the definition of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
For in this case, what is not perceptible is not imagined as being perceptible.

What then? It is perceived directly; therefore, it is not a mere mental construction (*utprekṣā*). To state another reason for its not being a mental construction, he says: "Nor is it a thing (*vastu*)."

For the sense of "as if" (ivārtha) residing in a word is the cause of a simile, not of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). He states another reason why it is not [a case of] poetic fancy: "Nor is it a thing," etc.
For the sense of "as if" residing in a word is the cause of a simile, not of a poetic fancy.
The reason for this is: "because of its being based on conceit" (abhimāna).
For *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is a form of conceit (*abhimāna*), which is a property of the cognizer.
Therefore, the meaning of "as if" (*iva*)—which is the very object of that conceit—is what motivates *utprekṣā*; this is the intended sense.
To provide corroboration for this, he says: "As they say," and so forth.
The meaning is that, just as with pleasure and so forth, the term "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*) is used for the mental state of knowledge (*jñāna-dharma*) when there is conceit (*abhimāna*).
Now, one might object: "If ascertainment is then a property of the cognizer, it would not belong to the poet who composes [the work]. To this he says: "And regarding the subject matter of poetry.
For even a poet is indeed a *sahṛdaya* (a sensitive connoisseur) in relation to his own poetry.
Therefore, this is not a poetic fancy (utprekṣā).

Now, one might argue that because of the perception of something wonderful, there is "directness" (pratyakṣatva) here, and thus it is a figure of speech called *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason); to this he says: "Nor even [is it] 'extremely wonderful' (*nāpyatyadbhuta*).
For the direct perception of an extremely wonderful object is indeed the cause for its appearing as if it were directly perceived.
He states the reason for its not being a *kāvyaliṅga* with the words "liṅgaliṅgī" (the sign and the bearer of the sign).
Even though there is a state of being a cause (*hetu*), there is no cognition here by way of the relationship between the sign and the bearer of the sign;
the sense is that if it were so, the consequence would be mediacy (*pārokṣya*).
To the question, "How then is there comprehension?", he says: "Like [the experience] of a yogi.

Now, one might object: "Surely here a comprehension accompanied by aesthetic wonder (camatkāra) appears as if shimmering before us, caused by extreme wonder; therefore, this must be the figure of speech *rasavat* (possessing rasa). To this he replies: "Nor is this... and so forth.
The reason for this is "love and so forth" (*ratyādi*).
Even in the case of a sequential [recitation], there is a common manifestation of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) as it flashes forth before one through a perception accompanied by wonder;
nevertheless, there is no identity between that which possesses the aesthetic flavor and that which is its actualized state (*bhāvika*).

Why is this so? Because when there arises a cognition that resonates with the heart through the process of universalization—by setting aside specific distinctions such as "mine" or "my enemy's"—regarding the mental states of love, laughter, and so forth, which are colored by those [emotions], as well as regarding the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*); and this occurs just as it does for one who possesses the knowledge of supreme non-duality (*paramādvaitajñānin*)—at that very moment, there is the manifestation of rasa.

We shall analyze the excitants (*vibhāva*) and other factors in the context of that which possesses rasa; at that time, the state of possessing rasa consists in a realization that resonates with the heart.
We shall analyze the excitants and other factors in the context of that which possesses rasa.
Here, however, the realization of past and future [states] is not through universalization, but rather through the spectator’s sense of detachment (*tāṭasthyena*).
For distinctness (*tāṭasthya*) is indeed difference;
as, for example, among those established in the Sāṅkhya and other systems, there is no cognition of difference for those who know everything.
[Objection: But surely, when there is cognition through distinctness, the cause is the clarity (*sphuṭatva*) of the past and so forth.

At the outset there is a clear cognition, but at the point of completion there is only a cognition of commonality. Therefore, how can it be called "real" (bhāvika)? To this he says: "on account of clear comprehension.
The meaning is: it has as its cause that which is real, as brought forth by a clear cognition caused by the sign of clear comprehension.

For in cases such as "The Sage Triumphs," the life-story of Agastya (Kumbhasambhava) and others is first perceived in a detached manner as something belonging to the past; at that very moment, the establishment of *bhāvika* occurs.

Then, at a subsequent time, through the perception of the audience, by virtue of the aesthetic factors (*vibhāva*, etc. attaining a state of universality (*sādhāraṇya*) through identification with that [past state], one becomes possessed of rasa, which is caused by *bhāvika*.
And it cannot be argued that *bhāvika* is thereby negated. This is the sense.

Now, if the nature of a beautiful object were not described here, then it would not appear as something perceptible; therefore, this is called "Description of Nature" (svabhāvokti). To this, he says: "Nor is this [the case]," and provides the reason for that: "In that regard, it is worldly... and so forth.

For in the case of the description of the subtle nature of worldly objects—which is accessible only through the intuition (*pratibhā*) of discerning people—there is a common resonance with the heart (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*).

Here, however, there is a cognition of extraordinary, non-worldly objects as something utterly marvelous, characterized by a state of detached observation (*taṭasthatayā*). Therefore, these [elements] differ from those [poetic figures] that lack such resonance with the heart.

Now, is it not the case that the distinction is established such that *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) occurs when there is a commonality with the perception of worldly objects, whereas *bhāvika* (the vividly real) occurs when there is a clarity in the perception of supramundane objects?
If, then, there were clarity in the perception of a worldly object, what would happen? To this, he says: "But in some cases... (*kvacittu*).
The description of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvokti*) arises from the power of worldly objects;
the *bhāvika* style arises from the power of the perception of vividness; therefore, there is a commingling [of the two].

Because they share the commonality of resonance with the heart (*hṛdayasaṃvāda*), there is a consequence that no distinction exists between *svabhāvokti* and *rasavat*. To distinguish them in that regard, he says: "And not by resonance with the heart... and so forth.

Although there is a general resonance with the hearts of sensitive readers in both *svabhāvokti* (description of intrinsic nature) and *rasavat* (the presence of rasa), nevertheless, there is no identity between these two.
The reason for this is stated: "because of the intrinsic nature of the thing," and so forth.

Even though there is a commonality [of subject matter], the correspondence (*saṃvāda*) in *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) pertains to the intrinsic nature of the object (*vastu-svabhāva*), whereas in [the *bhāvikālaṃkāra*] which possesses aesthetic flavor (*rasavat*), it pertains to the state of mind (*citta-vṛtti*).

Since these two consist respectively in the form of the object’s nature and the state of the mind, when they coincide, there is a commixture (*saṃkara*); thus he says, "due to the correspondence of both.
This "commingling" (*samāveśa*) is what constitutes the commixture (*saṃkara*).
He states the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the accomplishment of immersion (*samāveśa*): "wherein the nature of the object...
This means that in a subject matter characterized by correspondence with the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*), there should be a description of the subtle properties inherent in the object.
"But elsewhere," however... [the rest of the sentence].

In a subject matter that lacks a description of the qualities of subtle objects and consists merely of a resonance with the movements of the mind, it is indeed *rasavat* (possessing aesthetic flavor).
