Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the defining characteristic here is being presented through a composition devoid of disjointed connections, and if so, this is simply the quality (*guṇa*) called *prasāda* (transparency)? To this he says: "Nor is this [the quality of] *śabda*... and so forth.
Although in this context the immediate presentation of meaning is caused by the lack of confusion in the words, nevertheless, this is not *prasāda*.
The reason for this is: "For that [clarity] is manifest or unmanifest," and so forth.
Whether the meaning of the sentence is manifest or unmanifest, its immediate presentation by virtue of being present in both is the very nature of serenity (*prasāda*).
As it has been said: "That which suddenly pervades another, like fire in dry fuel or like clear water, is *prasāda* (serenity/clarity), whose presence is established everywhere."
Thus [it is said].

In this context, while the meaning of the sentence "like fire upon dry fuel" is obscure, the statement of the comparison "like clear water" is explicit. Therefore, the nature of *prasāda* (clarity) consists in the immediate presentation [of the meaning] by virtue of being established in every respect. When this [meaning], having been immediately presented within the *prasāda*, is perceived with clarity, there follows immediately the recovery of its own essential form (*svarūpa*).
For its essential nature consists either in the reflection of the poet’s state of being within the listener, or in the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) characterized by repeated implantation in the mind;
however, such a reflection occurs only after the time of clear comprehension (*sphuṭapratīti*).
Therefore, *prasāda* (clarity) is established as its prerequisite constituent.
But this [moment], having been assisted by that [preceding moment], achieves its own existence immediately thereafter;
therefore, it is indeed something other than that.
He concludes that this [nature] is not included anywhere by saying, "Therefore, this...

The meaning is that it transcends all; it cannot be subsumed under even one of the categories such as error (*bhrānti*) and so forth, which might be suspected of possessing qualities like clarity (*prasāda*).
Thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever regarding its definition.
He states that there is abundance even from the perspective of the indicated meaning (lakṣya) with the words "And this [is so] in the indicated meaning.
"The Sage (muni) triumphs":
he is a sage because of his contemplation (manana).
The Great-Souled One is such because he is the Lord of Yogins;
he himself, however, was born from a water-jar (Agastya).
By him, of such a nature, in a single hollow of the palm of his hand—wherein the waters of the ocean had been entirely extracted to quench his thirst—the ocean was reduced to mere dust.
The two divine forms of Viṣṇu, the Fish and the Tortoise, renowned for their superhuman majesty and celebrated exploits among his ten incarnations,
were seen rolling about in agitation within the hollow of his palm by chance.
Here, although the sage had passed away, he was held fast in the heart through the conviction of reverence, being truly marvelous due to his supernatural nature.

Because it is presented through a composition that is free from confusion, it appears as if directly perceived; thus, it reflects such a poetic state (*kavibhāva*) within the minds of the recipients and repeatedly instills a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in their hearts—this is its quality of being an "evoker" (*bhāvaka*).
To provide further examples for the sake of abundance, [the author] says: "Or, for instance, in the *Harṣacarita*," and so forth.
At the beginning of the *Harṣacarita*, while praising Goddess Sarasvatī, Bāṇa describes the nature of the Vedas when they were enraged at the sage Krodha.

As it is said: “With their seats of reed-mats cast aside in fury, their mouths resonant with the syllable *oṃ*, filling the quarters of the sky with the weight of their matted locks swaying as they shook them, and darkening the day with the shadow of the black antelope skins whirled about by the binding of their girdles—[the Vedas], out of indignation...”

"With the cords of Brahmā swinging on the cradle of their breath, appearing as if distilling the essence of the moon under the guise of perspiration; with the sacrificial grass-strands and bark-garments of their foreheads—bright with the ashes of the *agnihotra*—serving as their raiment;
and having made circles of staffs and water-pots into their weapons: these were the four Vedas incarnate.
Regarding this, he provides the construction [of the sentence], saying: "For here, it is as if [the Vedas] were directly perceived."

Now, one might ask: does the appearance as if being perceived (*pratyakṣāyamāṇatva*) due to the power of the description refer to an actual, real object, or is it a description of something that appears as if perceived because of a particular intensity of experience? To this he says: "But here... and so forth.

"A trace" (*leśa*) means the state of having only a small remainder. He says "due to the power of the description" (*varṇānāvaśāt*). He reveals the greatness of the expression by saying "of that which is appearing as if perceived" (*pratyakṣāyamāṇasyaiva*).
He perceives that [the Lord] appears as if manifest through his own extraordinary power alone, independent of the greatness of his speech.

Regarding the phrase "even though without a parasol," here, even though he is without a parasol, he is as if surrounded by white parasols; and even though he is without a fly-whisk, he is characterized as if by a yak-tail whisk.

It is described as being "as if directly perceived" solely due to a particular intensity of power (*anubhāvaviśeṣa*), and not because of the act of description itself that it becomes as if directly perceived.
Thus, since these two types of objects have been established, he states that *bhāvika* exists in only one of them: "In this case, it is of the first kind.
As for what was said—that it does not fall within the scope of the other kind—the reason is given: "of those [objects] presented by the poet."

For those properties such as "moon-ness" or "lotus-ness" which are presented by the poet's imaginative intuition (*pratibhā*) in relation to the face and so forth, it is precisely these that constitute the state of being a limb (*aṅgatva*).
It is not, however, the case that the actual moon, its beauty, and so on—which exist in their ultimate reality—are so constituted.

Therefore, in the second type [of *bhāvika*], since the quality of appearing as if directly perceived pertains to the arrangement of real objects, it does not constitute the figure of speech *bhāvika*.
He says "Moreover, the non-obscurity of words," and so forth, in order to further strengthen [the argument] by another reasoning.

By the word "and" (ca), [he implies] such factors as the state of not having been previously produced and so on; these, along with the non-obscurity of words, are the causes mentioned in Bhāmaha’s treatise and in Udbhaṭa’s definition.

That which is described as the state of non-obscurity consists in the fact that the meaning is conveyed by words whose syntactic relations are clearly articulated, thereby producing an effect that is as if directly perceived.
How, then, could that [convention] be instrumental?
Even if it were possible for it to exist as a property residing in real entities (*vastu*), it would be entirely purposeless.
Therefore, he concludes that there is no such thing as "real" (*bhāvika*) in the second sense, stating: "Therefore, it is only real," and so forth.

Regarding this latter type, one might object: "Even if there is actual beauty, let it not be considered *vicchitti* (a striking charm) because of its mundane nature; yet, due to the power of the poet's composition or the speaker's composition, there exists an undeniable *avicchitti* (non-mundane charm) that becomes accessible to all users of language. Why, then, is it not *bhāvika* (the poetic figure of the 'realized')? To this he replies with the words beginning, "But if, even though it is real," and so forth.

If the ancient masters were to describe even the depiction of a real object as an *alaṅkāra*— possessing aesthetic charm (*savicchitti*) by virtue of its being based on beauty— just like *svabhāvokti*, then this variety of *bhāvika*, which is suspected of having as its object real-world beauty, would not be at all ill-fitting when the necessary conditions are present.

This is the intended meaning here: just as *svabhāvokti* (description of inherent nature) is described as possessing aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) by relying on actual beauty, due to the subtlety of the object's nature and because it generally accords with the experience of sensitive readers, so too this particular form of charm arising from a composition that relies on actual beauty must certainly be described as an *alaṅkāra* (poetic figure).

And this being so, since the reality of past and future existence and so forth follows from the presence of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*), and because the postulation of anything else would involve the fault of unnecessary complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*), this too is a mode of actual existence; thus, its manifestation is quite easily possible by virtue of its inherent capacity (*yogyatā*).

Furthermore, if [these] manifestations—such as the emergence of the state of conceptualization (*ullekha-bhāva*) and the variegation of the junctures (*sandhi*)—were to be spread abroad with absolute independence, there would be a transgression of the long-standing tradition.
Wishing to reveal this very intention, he says "Therefore, indeed," etc., in order to provide corroboration from authoritative experts (*abhiyukta-saṃvāda*).

Those who have formulated the definition of *bhāvika* merely as "that in which past and future events are made as if they were present" have indeed described it as being free from verbal confusion and the like;
nor have they described it as consisting of the actual arrangement of things.
Rather, it is the artistic arrangement (*vicchitti*) arising from the composition of beauty, characterized by a method similar to *svabhāvokti*, that has been celebrated as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).

Therefore, just as with the past and the future, a variety of the *bhāvika* (the "realistic" or "vivid" mode) is also admitted by relying on the reality of the present characteristics (*bhāvikalakṣaṇa*)—that is, the actuality of sounds and the foundation of real beauty.

Since the investigation must thus proceed by way of its contrast with *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), he now states the connection [between them] with the words: "By *svabhāvokti*, something..."
Actual beauty is similarity (*sādṛśya*).

And because that [similarity] is deficient due to an abundance of contrary qualities—such as being worldly, subtle, manifest, common, indifferent, perceived, and so forth—it is stated [in the verse] as "some" (*kiñcit*).
Even though there is some slight degree of similarity, nevertheless, for the sake of establishing the logical framework, we have formulated its definition here.
This appearance of past and future objects as if they were present is not real,
because it is merely the reflection of their existence projected into the mind.

There is no delusion here because it is not a misconception; it is not a *itivṛttaka* (a narrative of past events) because of its directness; nor is there hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) here because there is no determination of anything else [as being that].
Dharma is not held to be perceptible merely with respect to a present object;
for if one disregards the person who practices it, its status as perception is lost.
And if it were perceptible, its causal complex would have to arise from a marvelous object;
since perceptibility is not possible here, there can therefore be no imaginative construction (*utprekṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, because there is no relationship between the non-indicative and the indicative, *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic indication) is not accepted [as a separate figure].
Due to its neutrality (*tāṭasthya*) and the clear perception [of the relationship], the delusion that it is *rasavat* (the sentiment-possessing figure) does not arise at that time.
Subsequently, when there is a state of commonality, that which possesses rasa is caused by it;
because of its clarity, this is *svabhāvokti* (description of inherent nature) regarding a supramundane reality.
The distinction between *svabhāvokti* (naturalistic description) and *rasavat* (the sentiment-endowed) arises from their difference in correspondence;
nor is this [latter] the quality of clarity (*prasāda*), since it occurs at a subsequent stage.
For even if beauty were real, its occurrence would be possible here due to suitability; however, out of deference to ancient tradition, it has not been explicitly stated as such.
If there should be agreement with my intellect regarding the reality [of things] by someone at all,
that wise person will serve as the touchstone for my skill in exposition.
The definition of the *udātta* (elevated) style:
the *udātta* consists in the description of prosperity and the excellence of one's own hand.
The *udātta* ornament is the description of the majesty of a prosperous object as brought forth by the poet’s imagination.
He explains it along with its logical connection, beginning with the words "in *svabhāvokti*," etc.
"Existing as it is" means being worldly (or natural).
"Being superimposed" means being conceptually constructed by the mind.
"Attainment" means reaching [the goal]. "Characterized by sovereignty" is the etymological definition of the term *lakṣya* (the object to be characterized).
The pearls have been freed from their play-strings; that is, they have had their strings cut. The meaning of the sentence is that they have been drawn along by brooms to the edge of the courtyard.
This very act of drawing them forth is what is meant by "the playful sport of abandonment."
The *udātta* (the exalted), however, is the poet’s description of a prosperous subject.
Regarding the *udāttāntara* (the intermediate exalted), the rule states:
"And [it includes] the deeds of great men who serve as subordinate elements. (RuAss 81)

Previously, the connection was with the excellence of sovereignty; here, however, it is with the excellence of conduct. Therefore, the connection [between the two sections] is established through the similarity of the term "excellence" (udātta).
This is what he says with the words beginning "udāttaśabda" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "tadidam": here, the forest is the *aṅga* (subsidiary element) because it falls within its narrative; and the life-story of Rāma is the *aṅga* because it falls within the narrative of that [forest].
This is what he says here: "In this [context], 'in the forest' (*araṇye*).
And its mention here is according to another philosophical system (*darśanāntara*).
However, in the theory of *dhvani*, in the case of the second type of *udātta* (elevated style), there are only the *rasavat* and other such figures.
And this will be analyzed later:
that which constitutes a subordinate element within another subordinate element, characterized by a grand narrative style,
and which falls within the scope of the second type of *udātta* (the exalted), is pervaded by the *rasavat* (sentimental) and other such figures.
The sūtra for the purpose of [defining] *rasavat* and the others is as follows:
"When there is a composition of rasa, bhāva, their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and their pacification (*tatpraśama*), there are the figures *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita*. (RuAss 82)

Rasa is the emotion such as love (rati) manifested by the determinants (vibhāvas) and so forth; likewise, the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas) indicated by the determinants and consequents (anubhāvas), as well as love directed toward a deity, are [also] bhāvas. These same two, when occurring without a [proper] object, are termed semblances (ābhāsas).
The state of departure, however, is tranquility (*praśama*).
The meaning of the sūtra is that when these four are composed in their proper sequence, they constitute the figures of speech known as *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita*.
He explains them with their logical connections, beginning with "In the *udātta* [figure], [there is] a great man," and so forth.
The meaning is: "of those ornaments" refers to the ornaments whose nature consists in the refinement of mental states (*cittavṛtti*).
"For this very reason" means:
since all four have the nature of mental states, they are defined simultaneously by being encompassed within a single sūtra due to their having an identical status (*samānayogakṣematā*).
He analyzes the essential nature of rasa with the words "tatra vibhāvā... and so forth.

Those things which in the world are the effects, causes, and auxiliary factors of the stable emotions (*sthāyibhāva*)—such as love, laughter, sorrow, and the like—which exist in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), when they are composed in poetry and enacted in drama through the power of poetic qualities (*guṇa*), ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), and the fourfold modes of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), [become the excitants, ensuants, and transitory states].

Because it is distinguished by its manifestation (*vibhāvanā*), its subsequent relishing (*anubhāvanā*), and its direct realization (*abhimukhyacaraṇa*), it is called *vibhāva*, *anubhāva*, and *vyabhicārin*.

The specific state of the mental activity of the audience (*sāmājika-cittavṛtti-viśeṣa*)—such as love (*rati*) and so forth—which is revealed and manifested by these, is *rasa*, such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others; this is the general direction [of the theory].
The specific details should be understood from the *Sampradāyaprakāśinī* and other works.
It is not elaborated upon here because it is not applicable in this context.
He states the essential nature of *bhāva* with the words "the *bhāva* is the *vibhāva*" and so forth.
[He explains it] by means of the *vibhāva* and the *anubhāva*.

In the manifestation of a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*), the absence of any other transitory emotion is manifested. A transitory emotion manifested by the determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*) is called a "state" (*bhāva*) at the stage when it becomes the primary sense of the sentence.
That too consists of thirty-three varieties.
In the form of world-weariness, exhaustion, and so forth,
as well as when manifested toward objects such as deities other than a beloved woman, even emotions like love (*rati*) and the rest are *bhāvas*.
Therefore, it should be understood that a *bhāva* is of two types, consisting of both the transitory (*vyabhicārin*) and the stable (*sthāyin*).

As it has been said: "Attachment directed toward objects such as gods and so forth, as well as a transitory emotion (vyabhicārin) when manifested [in that way], is declared to be a state of being (bhāva)."
He states the nature of the two manifestations with the words "the manifestation of that" (*tadābhāsa*), beginning with *rasa*.
By the word "that" (*tat*), there is a reference back to *rasa* and *bhāva*.
However, their becoming a manifestation [occurs] because it is inappropriate for them to function as objects [of ordinary perception].
He states the nature of the pacification of the emotions (*bhāvapraśamasvarūpa*) with the words "the pacification of those [emotions] has been described," and so forth.
When there is the cessation of the aforementioned types of emotions, that state of transition is called the pacification of the emotions (*bhāvapraśama*).
Now, one might ask: why is pacification not also mentioned in the case of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)? To this he replies with the words "even there," and so forth.

For since rasa—which is to be relished through an uninterrupted and unimpeded perception—is of the nature of supreme repose, any intermediate state of effort is difficult to discern; therefore, this "tranquility" (praśama) should be understood as referring to the remaining categories distinct from rasa.
Furthermore, when these elements—rasa, bhāva, and so forth—are composed according to their proper sequence, they constitute the poetic figures (alaṅkāra) such as *rasavat* and the rest.

He explains all four defining terms starting with "where rasa exists" (*raso vidyate*) and so forth: that literary composition (*nibandha*), which consists of the operations of *abhidhā* (denotation) and the rest as embellished by suggestion (*vyañjanā*), wherein rasa exists, is called *rasavat*.
That very composition which is more dear [to the reader] is to be known as *preyas*.

*Ūrjasvi* (the forceful) means that which possesses strength (*ūrja*), which is precisely the power inherent in its connection [to the sentiment]. Now, one might ask: what is this so-called "strength" in the context of such a connection? To this, he says: *anaucitya* (inappropriateness).
Because the sentiment (*rasa*) proceeds through inappropriateness, there is weakness.
In the *Nibandhana*, however, it is stated that when aided by that [concentration], there is the application of power (*balayoga*).
This is the concentrated resolution.
Of what? Of the aforementioned distinction of states (*bhāvabheda*), which is also synonymous with "quiescence" (*praśama*).
Now, one might ask: what is the distinction between the *rasavat* and other such figures and the second type of *udātta*? To this he says: "In that [case] where... and so forth.

For in the systems of Bhāmaha and others, since they function as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the *rasas* and so on are themselves the primary elements and thus constitute the *rasavat* and other figures; in that context, it is appropriate to have the figure *udātta* as a secondary element (*aṅga*) whose objects are the *rasas* and so on.
This is the second possibility regarding the figure *udātta*.

In that case, however, where figures such as *rasavat* and the like have as their object only the subordinate (*aṅga*) rasa and so forth— since the principal (*aṅgin*) rasa and so forth, having attained the status of the figure to be embellished (*alaṅkārya*), are by nature the essence of *rasadhvani* and *bhāvadhvani* and thus pervade the whole— there remains no scope for the second figure, *udātta*, which is characterized by the conduct of great men (*mahāpuruṣa*). Thus, in the example cited, there is no room for the *udātta* figure.
Why is this so? To this he says: "of that object.
This is the method here:
where the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
In the view of Bhāmaha and others, who delight solely in figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), the *bhāva*s therein are considered ornaments such as *rasavat* and the like.
However, when rasa and so forth become subordinate because they do not constitute the primary meaning of the sentence,
then the second type, called *udātta*, which is characterized by the deeds of great men (*mahāpuruṣa*) acting as subordinate elements, becomes possible.

In the theory of *dhvani*, however, when rasa and the like constitute the soul of poetry (*kāvyātman*) and occupy the state of primacy, they cannot logically function as ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) because they are themselves the objects to be ornamented (*alaṅkārya*). Consequently, when rasa and the like serve as subordinate elements (*aṅga*), they become ornaments such as *rasavat* and so forth. This being the case, even the manifestation of the deeds of great men (*mahāpuruṣa*) who are heroes (*nāyaka*) characterized by rasa, bhāva, and so on, does not exceed the status of being subordinate to that rasa, bhāva, and so on; for this is due to the relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Indeed, it is the deed of the great man that acts as the manifestor.
The suggested element (*vyaṅgya*) consists of rasa, bhāva, and so forth.
Since it possesses the status of a subordinate factor that is inseparable from the state of being suggested, it is the exclusive domain of the *rasavat* ornament.
For those of shallow intellect whose minds rest merely upon the suggestor (*vyañjaka*), there arises the delusion that this is a second type of *udātta*.

"What is the use of this laughter?"—this describes the speech of the enemy's women, who, thinking that the hero seen in their dream was engaged in a jest to conceal his true appearance, said: "What is the use of this laughter?

Having arrived after a long time, will you not grant me your sight again? This heartlessness of yours is such that, at the very moment of arrival, you have a desire to depart. Even as he was saying this, she did not see him; thinking, "By whom have you been taken away?", she cried out while her neck was held fast in an embrace, her arms flailing empty.
Regarding the phrase "he weeps":
here, both the subordinate and the principal [elements] are *rasa*,
while according to another school of thought, it is the possessor of *rasa* (*rasavat*) that constitutes the *rasa*.
In his own system, however, that which possesses rasa (rasavat) is a subordinate element (aṅga).
Therefore, this example is suitable for both of these two views.
With this in mind, he says: "In both of these two views..."
To demonstrate this by analyzing it, he says: "In this case, having become the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthībhūta*).
Because it has become the meaning of the sentence, it possesses rasa in the form of *karuṇa* (pathos); the words "in another view" (*matāntare*) are to be understood as the ellipsis.
The *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment of separation) is "possessed of rasa" because it serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*);
the phrase "in our opinion" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
For in such a case, since it constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), others have maintained that the principal rasa (*aṅgin*) is the one "possessed of rasa."
However, [the view that] the primary element possesses two high-pitched accents (dvitīyodātta) has been established by those who understand the theory of sound.

They have concluded that the primary element is the object of ornamentation, that its form consists of the *rasavad* and other such figures, and that the occurrence of a second high-pitched accent is impossible for it.
He states, "In this way, regarding other *rasas*," indicating that this same analytical process should be understood to apply to other aesthetic sentiments as well.
*Udāhāryaṃ* means worthy of being cited, or capable of being cited;
it refers to the fitness of the example for citation.
The *kṛtya* suffixes are used in the senses of worthiness (*arhe*), capability (*śakye*), and the time for action having arrived (*prāptakālatāyām*).
Thus, two views regarding the figure of speech *rasavat* have been illustrated through a division of sections.

Regarding the figure of speech *preyas* and others, however, since their specific characteristics are already known, the author says "regarding the figure of speech *preyas* and others" with the intention of illustrating them in a general manner. [The example begins:
"With a firm embrace... and so forth.
By the half-utterance "O giver of honor, O destroyer of honor, me," the joy culminating in the emotional state (*bhāva*) is communicated.
To identify the indicated (*lakṣya*) emotion, he says: "here, of the heroine.

The transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) named joy, being subordinate to the erotic sentiment of union (*sambhogaśṛṅgāra*), constitutes the *preya* ornament; this is the remainder [of the definition].

The transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) is the *preya* ornament because it serves as a subordinate element (*guṇatva*) to the erotic sentiment of union (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*). He provides an example of another transitory emotion with the verse beginning "tadvaktra... (Her face...). Here, the transitory emotion characterized by anxiety (*cintā*) is *preya* because it functions as a constituent part of the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*).
He says this very thing: "here, called 'Cintā' (Reflection).
To prevent the confusion that it might be some other figure of speech, he states its synonym: "and this very same [is] *preyas*. Thus, *bhāva* and *alaṅkāra* are synonyms for *preyas*.
He states the distinction of this [sentiment] from the subsidence, emergence, and so forth of the emotion (bhāva) with the words "and here of the emotion" (bhāvasya cātra).
The meaning is that when it exists in a state of stability, it is the ornament of emotion (bhāvālaṅkāra);
however, the states of subsidence, emergence, and so forth are separate ornaments.
To the question "What are these two, tranquility (śānti) and emergence (udaya)?", he says: "Tranquility and emergence...
The state of tranquility is the "powerful" (ūrjasvī), which will be described immediately following as being characterized by composure (samāhitatva).

The state of emergence, however, is distinct from those [other states] along with "junction" (sandhi) and "intermixture" (śabalatā), in that it constitutes a separate poetic figure (alaṅkāra); this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "dūrākarṣaṇa" (drawing from afar):
it does not allow for even a moment's duration.
Here, the erotic sentiment of separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*) proceeds through impropriety, because Queen Sītā is not the proper object for such a sentiment.
Therefore, since the composition itself is forcibly made subordinate to the rasa, it is the *ūrjasvin* (the forceful) figure.
Furthermore, because of the impropriety even of the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) of longing (*autsukya*), there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) with the *preyas* (the pleasing) figure.
Intending this, he says: "In this [verse], of Rāvaṇa," and so forth.

Wishing to cite the proof for the proposition that "the state of tranquility is observed," he says: "Just as when [he was] composed. By the words "of the eyes" and so forth—meaning that the redness of the eyes, which had been turbid with agitated tears, has departed—he indicates the departure of anger.

Because the tremulousness of the pupils, the playfulness of the side-glances, and so forth have not yet manifested, there is no outward expansion [of the emotion]. Therefore, he says "of anger" (*kopasya*) to indicate that this is the state of anger subsiding.
He further states "likewise elsewhere" (*evamanyatrāpi*) to show that in this same manner, subsidence (*praśama*) should be understood in other transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) as well.
The fourfold set consisting of *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita* arises from the subordination of rasa, bhāva, and guṇa, and from the occurrence of what is improper.
A composition attains the designation of "rasavat" (possessing rasa) and so forth through its possession of flavor and attractiveness, and through the application of vigor and tranquility.
The aphorism for the sake of [explaining] the emergence of emotion (*bhāva*) and so forth is:
"The emergence of emotion (*bhāvodaya*), its transition (*sandhi*), and its mixture (*śabalatā*) are distinct ornaments (*alaṅkāra*). (RuAss 83)
This triad is mentioned because it is distinct from all the previously mentioned ornaments and serves as the remainder of all ornaments;
that is to say, its scope is distinct from [the figures] such as *rasavat* and the like.
He explains this with the words: "of the emotion (*bhāva*), having the form of a sprout," and so forth.
The emergence of the form of a sprout is *udaya*.
*Sandhi* is the placement of two contradictory elements on an equal footing.
*Śabalatā* is the connection of many successive elements through the successive sublation of each preceding one.
He states the reason for treating these separately with the words "and this exposition.
Because it consists of figures alone, it differs from *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction) and *saṃkara* (intermixture).
He explains that their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the state of being conjoined by saying, "for in the case of *saṃsṛṣṭi* and *saṃkara*..."
In the phrase "in one [instance]," the mention of the name of the adversary serves to indicate being dispirited;
being dispirited indicates agitation;
and agitation indicates contempt.
In the silence of the beloved, there is disregard;
yet that very silence is the cause for looking again.
Here, longing (*autsukya*) is the emergence of an emotion (*bhāva*), and its subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) is what is intended to be expressed in this context.
"With the left [hand]" means:

while wiping away with his left hand the stream of tears from the eyes of his beloved and with his right hand the stream from the blade of the sword, he became bewildered; this is the meaning. Herein lies the junction (*saṃdhi*) of the aesthetic sentiments (*bhāva*) of love (*rati*) and longing (*autsukya*).
This is what he says here: "In this context, it is called *sneha* (affection).

By the use of the term *sneha*, he indicates that [this emotion] has *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic) as its underlying permanent state (*sthāyibhāva*); however, when it exists merely as a transitory feeling (*bhāva*), it is simply *rati* (love), which is mere attachment.
"What improper act could there be?"—here, "where is an improper act, and where is the lineage of the hare-marked moon? constitutes deliberation (*vitarka*).
"She might be seen once more" constitutes longing (*autsukya*).
The thought is: "I have heard that this leads to the pacification of faults.
The recollection is: "Oh, even in anger, his face is lovely.
The apprehension is: "What will those who are free from sin say?"
"Even in a dream it is difficult to find"—this is dejection. "Attain composure of mind"—this is fortitude. "Who is fortunate enough to drink her lower lip?"—this is anxiety.
In this context, there is a variegated state (*śabalatā*) because each subsequent [state] exists through the suppression of each preceding one.
This is what is stated in the passage beginning with "here, *vitarka*," etc.
He concludes this very point with the passage beginning with "that [is]," etc.
The emergence, the transition, and the coexistence of a state characterized by stability and tranquility,
as well as their predominance or subordination, each constitute a distinct poetic figure.
Desiring to praise the mixture (*saṅkara*) and the combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*), he says: "Now, of these...
*Saṃśleṣa* means connection (*sambandha*). He states its twofold nature with the words: "In that regard, connection," and so forth.
When the degree of distinction is prominent, the principle of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) applies; however, when it is not prominent, the principle of inherence (*samavāya*) applies.
He establishes these distinct principles by means of examples: "the principle of sesame and rice" and "the similarity of milk and water.
He says "in sequence" in order to set forth both of these in their proper order.
When these are mixed together according to the analogy of sesame seeds and rice grains, it is *saṃsṛṣṭi*.
He explains: "Of the aforementioned figures," and so forth.

Regarding these figures, beginning with alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and ending with the commixture of emotions (*bhāvaśabalatā*), which have been described separately—if they coexist in some particular instance according to their possibility, are they then each distinct figures, or is this variety of coexistence itself a separate figure?
In order to establish the conclusion regarding this doubt, he says: "In that regard, just as... and so forth.

Just as gold and jewels, though each is a cause of beauty in its own right, produce a different kind of beauty through their combination, so too do alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and the other figures constitute distinct figures of speech [when combined].

He speaks of two types of aesthetic distinction (*vicchitti*) based on whether the distinct parts remain clear or unclear even within that combination: "And if they are distinct figures of speech... and so forth.
Therein, he establishes the distinction between *saṅkara* (confusion) and *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) with the words "In the former case," and so forth.
Since difference (*bheda*) is both intense and non-intense, he says "For this very reason," and so forth, to show that the two examples are appropriate;
for when difference is intense or non-intense, there is accordance with reality (*yathārthatā*).
He states that "commixture (saṃsṛṣṭi) is threefold," beginning with "there, sesame and rice," and so forth.

Although "confusion" (saṅkara), along with its subdivisions, has been sought after inquiry, he says "but confusion... because it will be discussed immediately after commixture. [The example begins with] "the fragrance of the flower," and so on.

"With disheveled curls and trembling eyes"—here, in the first half-verse there is *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration) with respect to the letter *bha*, and in the second half-verse with respect to the letter *la*.
In the sequence "lakalolakalo" and so forth, there is *yamaka* (chime). Thus, there is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commingling) of two distinct types of figures.
Likewise, there are examples of *sajātīya-yamaka* (homogeneous rhyme) such as *lakalolakalo* and *kalolakalola*.
This is what he expresses with the words "atrānuprāsa... and so forth, and the verse beginning with "devi kṣapeti."
Here, two similes—“like a lotus” and “as if with luster”—are conjoined. This is what [the author] expresses by saying, "here, of those belonging to the same class" (*sajātīya*).
However, in the case of "limpatīva," the conjunction of dissimilar elements (*vijātīya-saṃsṛṣṭhi*) is clear.
"Slow with joy": "manthara" means slow in action;
"haṭhena" means by force.
Here, there is a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of both figures of speech: simile (*upamā*) and alliteration (*vṛttyanuprāsa*).
To the question, "But how is the establishment of the simile determined here?", he says: "The lotus-feet" (*pādāmbujam*).
In the simile "like the lotus-feet," the connection with the tinkling of anklets (*mañjīra-śiñjita*) is the determining factor.
In the case of the metaphor (*rūpaka*) "the foot itself is a lotus," this [word *ambuja*] would be contradictory, as it is not appropriate for a lotus to possess a *śiñjita* (jingling sound).
Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), this connection with *śiñjita* establishes a simile (*upamā*). He concludes: "Thus, in this way... and so forth.
The union [of word and meaning] is held to be a "blending" (saṃsṛṣṭi), according to the analogy of sesame seeds and rice grains;
it is considered to be of three kinds, based on whether the figures of speech reside in the word, the meaning, or both.
He introduces the charge of confusion with the words "now," and so forth.
Confusion occurs according to the analogy of milk and water.
He recalls the relevant topic: "it is indeed a state of mixture. He restates the nature of the confusion already discussed: "not intense," and so forth.
Regarding that, he states its threefold nature: "and that," and so forth.

The emergence of *saṅkara* (commixture) occurs in three ways: through the relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgībhāva*), through doubt (*saṃśaya*), and through the entry into a single expressive word (*ekavācakānupraveśa*).
Regarding the example "as if with fingers":
here, the simile "as if with fingers" establishes the simile "the lotus is like the eye."
The excellence in the proof lies in the exclusion of the literal form (*rūpa*).
There is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) because the word "mouth" (*mukha*) denotes both a beginning and a face.
Due to the identification of the two mouths as non-different, there is an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) based on *śleṣa*.
Therefore, there is a relationship of primary and subordinate between these two.

This being the case, the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)— expressed by the sentence "as if with fingers" and by the compound "lotus-eyed"— is supported by those two similes as well as by the pun (*śleṣa*), and it serves as the supporter of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) "it kisses."

Because they arise from the power of those [other factors], they are both the "arisen" and the cause of the wonder-inducing quality of the "wonder-inducers"; thus, there is a relationship of subordinate and principal (aṅgāṅgitā).
Therefore, to demonstrate mutual assistance even within this relationship of subordinate and principal, another example is given: "Though consisting of the three Vedas...
Here, *vāruṇī* refers both to the western direction and to wine.
"Falling," "descending," and "affliction" [are the meanings].
He explains this with the words "here, first," and so forth.

Here, the word *vāruṇī* is a pun (*śleṣa*); the phrase "even though he consists of the three Vedas (*trayīmaya*) yet he went [there]" gives rise to the perception of a contradiction (*virodha*), and that [pun] sublates it.
In the view of those who do not accept *śleṣa* (paronomasia) as having no scope here, both [figures] are present:
the *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding cause) "I think he has fallen" with respect to purification,
and the *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding effect) "he entered for the sake of purification."
He establishes this specifically with the words "tathā hi" and so forth.
The going to Vāruṇī is imagined as the cause for falling and so on.

In that context, *virodha* (contradiction) and *śleṣa* (punning connection) have entered in; and as for the effect—falling and so on—which is the basis for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the cause, there [is] the actual falling and entering into fire, which are non-different from the falling and entering into fire caused by an injury.
The two [figures] are determined.
By that *śleṣa*, there is a relationship of mutual subservience (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) between the *hetūtprekṣā* and the *phalotprekṣā*.
One might ask: "Why is there no relationship of mutual subservience between *virodha* and *śleṣa*, or between *atiśayokti* and *utprekṣā*? To this he says: "And not *virodha*... and so forth.

Although *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is the cause for the arising of diverse flashes of intuition (*pratibhā*), and although *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) is the ground for *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), nevertheless, there is no relationship of primary and subordinate between these two [figures] and the two [others].
The reason for this is expressed by the phrase "without those two":
because without *virodha* (contradiction) and *atiśayokti*, *śleṣa* and *utprekṣā* do not arise.
Therefore, since they have no other scope, *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) must necessarily sublate [the *atiśayokti*].
Now, one might object: "Since poetic fancy cannot arise without the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) [of the object and the attribute], let there be no *utprekṣā* at all;
rather, let *atiśayokti* occupy a distinct domain."
However, since there certainly exists a *śleṣa* (paranomasia) that is distinct [from other figures], he says: "And it should not be thought," and so forth.
It has been explained at length in the analysis of *śleṣa* that there is no *śleṣa* devoid of other poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*).
Therefore, because *śleṣa* subordinates others, even the *virodha* (contradiction) that enters into it must itself be subordinated.
He concludes the section on the commingling of figures of sense with the words "Thus, regarding sense...
and "Regarding figures of sound..."; the phrase "by some" expresses a degree of disregard.
It shines: where this slope of Mount Aṣṭa shines,
it resounds with the *rāsa*— the shouting— of the Dānavas who have transgressed,
and thus it is full of resonance (*sārāva*).
"Gajatā" means a herd of elephants;
and that [herd] protects its leader exceedingly.
Of what sort is it? By means of incessant *dāna*, that is, by means of rut.
Varā means "excellent" or "most distinguished"; sā means "well-known"; sārā means "powerful";
and vanadā means "the destroyer of the forest."
Regarding the structural analysis (*yojanā*), he says: "In this context, *yamaka*," and so forth.
*Yamaka* is characterized by the repetition of a verse-quarter (*pāda*).
Furthermore, whether it occurs at the beginning or elsewhere in the recitation, because the composition remains identical, there is both direct and inverse order.
Since both of these are mutually dependent, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of verbal figures of speech (*śabdālaṅkāra*).
He refutes this with the words "But this...
and provides the reason for its lack of attractiveness with the words "of the two verbal figures of speech..."

Just as there is no mutual assistance between two words, so too there is none between two verbal figures of speech (*śabdālaṅkāra*). If one asks, "What then is the principle in such a case? he says: "Verbal figures of speech... Because they do not assist each other, there is independence (*nairapekṣya*).
Therefore, *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) is superior. He says "or else" (*yadvā*) because there might otherwise be an entry into a single expressive word due to the state of *saṅkara* (blending).
Thus, he determines that there is a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) by excluding verbal figures of speech, stating: "In this way, this... (*evameṣa*).
He analyzes the confusion of doubt with the words "the second," and demonstrates the doubt with the passage beginning "where both," etc., [and] "he who is a youth," etc.
This has been explained previously.
He applies [the analysis] here with the words "vibhāvanā" and so forth;
"elsewhere" refers to the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and other such works.
Thus, in order to demonstrate the doubt between simile (*upamā*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*), he says:
"And as in the case of 'the moon of the face' (*vaktrendu*)," and "by the beard, which is like fresh youth, the mantra is as if engraved and shines forth."
He connects [the verse] here with the words "in this face" (*vaktre*) and so forth.
He states the reason for the doubt with the words "of the compound, in both ways as well" (*samāsasyobhayathāpi*).
This is because, since [the term] *vyāghrādi* (tiger, etc. is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class), it includes the moon and other objects that possess specific qualities.

The compound *mukhaṃ candra iva* (“the face like the moon”) is an *upamā-samāsa* (simile compound). This is according to the principle that “a *tatpuruṣa* compound for which no specific rule has been prescribed should be understood as belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group,” since the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class).
In the case of the metaphorical compound "the face is indeed the moon," there is doubt between these two [possibilities] because of the absence of any evidence that either proves or disproves one;
however, when there exists a definitive presence of either a proving or a disproving factor, there is a certain determination. Thus he says, "But where...
He analyzes the nature of the proving and disproving factors with the words, "In that case, that which is favorable..."
Regarding the phrase "prasaradvindu":

*bindu* is Mahāmāyā, the material cause of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*); *nāda* is the unstruck sound (*anāhata*). To Him who, desiring to create, causes these two to expand—[to that Lord]—[belongs] the pure nectar (*amṛta*).
To Him who is the extracted consciousness for the self consisting of that [consciousness],
and who is the infinite light unconditioned by space, time, and so forth;
but at other times, [the drops] are mere droplets.
*Nāda* is the sound of the waves;
*amṛta* is the nectar;
*ananta* is Śeṣa, who remained as the residue after the churning and other such acts.
By that, the illumination is established.
Here, the metaphor "Śaṅkara himself is the ocean of milk" is supported by the following:
he shows this with the words "here, Śaṅkara himself," and so forth.

For the word *amṛta* is widely established in the sense of nectar (*sudhā*), and it is even more appropriate in the context of the Ocean of Milk; thus, this is indeed a metaphorical compound (*rūpaka-samāsa*).
Furthermore, the state of being composed of nectar does not contradict the presence of a simile (*upamā*); as he says, "But of the simile...
The meaning is that it is not a contradiction, but rather something neutral (*taṭastha*).
The reason for this is stated as: "even when [the object] is metaphorically designated as Śaṅkara.
For when something is metaphorically designated as being Śaṅkara, the establishment of its nature as a *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) is proven.
Therefore, the meaning is that the final rest (*viśrānti*) occurs in a *rūpaka* brought forth by a simile (*upamā*).
He says "yathā vā" (or, for example) in order to further strengthen this principle by means of another illustration:
"etāny avantīti.
Behold! These flowers, which are of the nature of fame produced from the Pārijāta tree in the form of a wandering [wind], I am using as ear-ornaments for the brides who are the quarters of the sky.
Here too, he demonstrates the proof of *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) by way of the absence of any sublation of the simile, stating: "In this case, [it is] an ornament.
He provides an example for the purpose of showing sublation: "As in autumn...
Here, *hari* refers to both the lion and Viṣṇu.
He demonstrates the sublation of the simile with the words "here, the Vindhya," and so forth.
For the quality of being "green with wide-open yawning" is a common property that sublates the *upamā-samāsa* (simile compound), because of the rule stating:
"That which is compared [is compounded] with *vyāghra* and so forth, when the common property is not expressed."

[Objection: But how can there be the establishment of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the absence of a means of proof? To this he says: "And therefore, by the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*). [Objection: But how is it that this simile (*upamā*), being expressed in close proximity as "just like autumn," does not establish itself as a simile? To this he says: "But not 'just like autumn'.
For a simile existing in a single part (*ekadeśavartinī*) is not intended to subvert the metaphor which, by logical necessity, has become the meaning of the sentence as a whole.
The sense is that it appears as itself as well.
Regarding this, he says for the sake of mockery: "For not by a blue jay...
[In the established usage where *cāṣa* is a collection of blue jays, the word *pañca* is used.]
Even by resorting to the non-distinction between the sounds *śa* and *ṣa*, this perception of a blue jay (*cāṣa*) is not produced;
indeed, the establishment of the form "fifty" as a collection does not depend upon that.
One might object: "In that case, there would be a breach of the established method of poetic figures (*alaṅkāra-prakrama-bheda*). To this he says: "For it is not by one alone...
It is no royal decree that "that which has been commenced must be concluded by that very same [means]," such that a contradiction with observed experience (*dṛṣṭabādha*) could be suspected.
For if one were to transgress this, there would be a subversion of both the seen and the unseen; since this is a matter of logical principle (*nyāya*), he says: "Nor is this..."
The rule that "one must conclude by means of what has been introduced" is not universally applicable;
rather, it applies only when a specific distinction is intended to be expressed.
However, in this case, since there is an intention to express an ever-increasing excellence, there is a greater degree of similarity in the metaphor (rūpaka) compared to the simile (upamā).

Therefore, by abandoning the simile residing in the individual parts, it is more appropriate to adopt the metaphor (rūpaka) which constitutes the meaning of the entire sentence. Conversely, the opposite case is indeed faulty due to the proximity of the comparison.
He confirms this very point through a counter-example with the verse beginning "yenenduḥ."
In this case, by describing the moon and sandalwood as objects of burning, a heightening of their similarity was introduced;
however, by the metaphor "the necklace acts like an axe," that heightening is brought to its ultimate degree.
He concludes the discussion with the words: "Therefore, in the primary [subject]..."
The point is that, according to the logical principle that "in the case of a general application, a simile is sublated," one must proceed solely with the metaphor (*rūpaka*).
He states "by the oceans of the Bhāṣya" to indicate that this same logic should be understood here as well:
because of the commonality of profundity, when a simile is sublated, a metaphor alone is to be seen.
He recalls what was stated—that doubt arises when there is an absence of both a proof and a refutation—by saying "sādhakabādhaka...".

Having thus distinguished the two types of doubt regarding the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), he distinguishes the third type by saying "the third, however" (*tṛtīyas tu*).
He clarifies that [third type] by saying "wherein, in one... (*yatraikasmin*).
Regarding the phrase "Murāri has emerged":
*naraka* refers to the asura and the hell (*niraya*).
The phrase "like the Gaṅgā" indicates that this [teaching] is the cause for attaining a happy rebirth (*sadgati*).
He explains this with the words "Murāri.
The simile "like the Gaṅgā" is evoked by the common epithet (*sādhāraṇaviśeṣaṇa*), because there is no difference in meaning between [the literal sense] and the sense "emerged from Murāri.
The meaning arising from the punned epithet (*śliṣṭaviśeṣaṇa*) beginning with "Naraka," as well as the pun (*śleṣa*) itself, is the cause for the comprehension of the simile.

Since both meanings enter into the single word *naraka* through a pun (*śliṣṭa-śabda*), benefiting both simultaneously, he states "here, just as... and so forth in order to show the commixture (*saṅkara*) of simile with verbal punning (*śabda-śleṣa*).
Regarding the term *satpuṣkara*: *puṣkāra* refers to the mouth of a musical instrument and also to a lotus (*padma*).
The waves are illuminated and the stage (*raṅga*) is illuminated;

it is called a "stage" because the minds of the audience take delight (*rajyante*) therein, referring to the activity of commencing the drama. The sound of the water striking [the shore] is like a drum, as is the playing of the *mṛdaṅga* drum.
He connects [the two meanings] here with the words "as if in milk," and so forth.
"They delight" is the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*).

Therefore, due to the conjunction of these factors, the phrase "perfectly endowed, shining with waves" is mixed with verbal *śleṣa* (paronomasia) because it consists of words that break into two meanings within a single word.
He recalls what has already been illustrated regarding the coalescence (*ekavācakānupraveśa*) of two verbal ornaments— the phrase beginning with "Furthermore, of the two verbal ornaments," and so on.

He states that the claim made by others— that the rule for coalescence applies only to two ornaments of different kinds— is irrelevant, using the phrase beginning with "coalescence in a single expressive word," and so on.
In this context, in examples such as "This bank shines" (*rājati taṭīyam*),
the word *eva* (alone/only) excludes both the blending (*saṅkara*) and the confusion (*sandeha*) of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal;
its status as a verbal ornament (*śabdālaṅkāratva*) consists in its belonging to the same class [of ornaments].

However, Udbhaṭa maintains that the commingling (*saṃkara*) of verbal and semantic figures of speech—which pertains to a different category from *saṃsṛṣṭi*—is included within *saṃsṛṣṭi*; thus, he states that its nature as *saṃkara* exists only in the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*). He says: "Verbal and semantic figures... and so forth:

"But *saṃkara* is threefold: through the relation of subordinate and principal, through doubt, and through coalescence in a single expressive word; however, the commingling of two verbal figures occurs in a single expressive word."
Desiring to conclude the section, he says: "Now," etc.
Regarding this, the sūtra states:
"Thus, these ornaments of word, meaning, and both have been briefly set forth in aphoristic form. (RuAss 86)
He explains [the verse] with the words "evamiti" (thus).
Among those, in the case of *paunaruktya* (repetition), there is the *punaruktavad-ābhāsa* (appearance of repetition);
in the case of *vyañjana-mātra* (mere consonants), there are *cheka* and *vṛtti-anuprāsa* (alliteration).
The *yamaka* consists of the repetition of a collection of vowels and consonants;

the *lāṭānuprāsa* consists of the repetition of both word and meaning. Thus, there are five types of repetition. *Citra* (pictorial poetry) consists of the non-repetition of syllables arranged in specific positions and joined together.

Now, when there is a strikingness (*vicchitti*) in similarity, where there is an equality between difference and non-difference, we have the similes of analogy (*upamāna*), sequence (*anvaya*), reciprocal simile (*upameyopamā*), and recollection (*smaraṇa*).

When non-difference is predominant, by virtue of being based on superimposition (*āropa*), we have metaphor (*rūpaka*), transformation (*pariṇāma*), doubt (*sandeha*), the bewildered (*bhrāntimad*), delineation (*ullekha*), and concealment (*apahnuti*).
Based on the support of identification (*adhyavasāya*), we have poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) and hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).

Based on the comparison inherent in the process of being understood (*gamyamānaupamya*), there are *tulyayogitā*, *dīpaka*, *prativastūpamā*, *dṛṣṭānta*, *nidarśanā*, *vyatireka*, *sahokti*, and *vinokti*.
Through the strikingness of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-vicchitti*), there are *samāsokti* and *parikara*.
Through the strikingness of both the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-vicchitti*), there is *śleṣa*.

*Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Praise) occurs when there is an understanding of the subject at hand (*prastuta*) from that which is not the subject (*aprastuta*). *Arthāntaranyāsa* (Corroboration by another matter) occurs when the stated subject is supported through the relationship of general and particular, and so forth. *Paryāyokta* (Periphrasis) occurs when that which is to be understood is expressed by means of a different turn of phrase.
*Vyājastuti* (disguised praise) occurs when praise is understood through censure, or censure through praise.
*Ākṣepa* (paralipsis) occurs when there is an apparent negation of a specific intended meaning regarding two contextual subjects, or an apparent injunction of something undesirable.

Furthermore, *ākṣepa* occurs when there is an apparent negation of a specific intended meaning or an apparent injunction of something undesirable, characterized by the presence of a latent contradiction (*virodhagarbhatayā*).

*Ākṣepa* (Paralipsis) occurs when there is a semblance of a prohibition for the sake of a specific meaning through the manifestation of contradiction (*virodhavibhāvanā*), or a semblance of an injunction for the undesired, due to the presence of contradiction within.

Through the presence of contradiction, *virodhavibhāvanā*, *viśeṣokti*, and *atiśayokti* arise; in between these, there are *saṅgati*, *viṣama*, *samavicitra*, *adhika*, *anyonya*, *viśeṣa*, and the two types of *vyāghāta*.
Due to the variety of chains (*śṛṅkhalāvaicitrya*), there are *kāraṇamālā*, *ekāvalī*, *mālādīpaka*, and *sāra*.
By the logic of reasoning (*tarka*), there are the figures of poetic cause (*kāvyaliṅga*) and inference (*anumāna*).

By the logic of sentence structure (*vākya*), there are: enumeration (*yathāsaṅkhya*), sequence (*paryāya*), exchange (*parivṛtti*), exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), option (*vikalpa*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), doubt (*dūya*), and resolution (*samādhi*).

By the logic of worldly convention (*loka*), there are: the adversary (*pratyanīka*), the counter-argument (*pratīpa*), the closed (*nimīlita*), the general (*sāmānya*), "of that quality" (*tadguṇa*), "not of that quality" (*atadguṇa*), and the superior (*uttara*).
When the meaning is hidden, there are *sūkṣma*, *vyājokti*, *vakrokti*, and *svabhāvokti*;
when the meaning is clear, there is *bhāvika*;
and through magnificence, there are the two types of *udātta*.

Based on the objective support of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*), there are the pure [styles]: *rasavat*, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, *samāhita*, as well as the emergence of emotion (*bhāvodaya*), conjunction (*sandhi*), and commingling (*śabalatva*).
However, through their mixture, there are *saṅkara* (blending) and *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction).
Having this in mind, he says "thus" (*evam*).

The phrase "these" (*eta*) refers back to the manner previously described; it is a designation of the nature of what has been introduced. He distinguishes the ornaments of both word and meaning according to their respective classes, beginning with the words "therein, the ornaments of sound," and so forth.
"Such as *lāṭānuprāsa* and so forth.
He reveals the remainder with the words "conjunction (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) and commixture (*saṅkara*).
Now, [it may be asked: "Is this not already stated through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)?"
Because there would otherwise be a destruction of the established order, he says: "Based on worldly convention, [the relationship is] that of the locus and the located.
Regarding the phrase "that which is to be adorned":
the word "that" refers to both the word and its meaning.
This has already been discussed in the section on *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
If one asks, "In that case, what is the basis for positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? he says: "Because of the positive and negative concomitance.
When figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*) are the effects of words and so forth, the positive and negative concomitance of words and non-words, etc., is the basis therein.

Now, one might ask: "What is the fault in [considering] sound and so forth as ornaments? To this he says: "In the case of being the cause for the status of that as an ornament. Because [ornaments] such as the *śrautopamā* (verbal simile) follow the presence and absence of words, the consequence would follow that they are ornaments of sound.
He concludes: "Therefore, [the relationship is] between the locus and the located."
The disclosure of corroboration regarding the meaning stated as "the ancient intention" (cirantaramata);

the placement of words; the arrangement of difficult points concerning the objects of inquiry; and a profound discussion on the application of logical reasoning (nyāsa) intended to reveal what is pervasive and what is not.
Thus, this extensive and harsh elaboration of Bhaṭṭa Rucaka’s words has been composed by us; let it be brought to life by this commentary, the *Sañjīvanī*.
May the learned scholars of poetry and treatises here rely upon this subtle, unconfused investigation, which is augmented by both scriptural authority and logical reasoning.
Because there is great respect for both the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* among the wise in this world, both have therefore been commented upon.

Thus ends the section on figures of sense in the *Saṃjīvanī*, a commentary on the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, composed by the great poet Śrī Vidyācakravartin— the Sahajasarvajña, a sun to the investigation of poetry (*Kāvyamīmāṃsā*), the supreme teacher of the school of Suggestion (*dhvani*), and the sovereign of the masters of poetics (*alaṅkārika*).
